--- SOURCE 5: TEACCH Method For Autism ---
URL: https://www.skillbuildersaba.com/blog/teacch-method-for-autism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from SkillBuilders ABA provides a comprehensive overview of the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children) Method for autism support and education.

**Origins and History:** The TEACCH® Autism Program was developed at the University of North Carolina—Chapel Hill in the 1960s by Dr. Eric Schopler and Dr. Robert Reichler. Initially conceived as a research project in 1964, it was formally established as the TEACCH® program in 1972. It has since expanded from clinical services into training, consultation, and research initiatives.

**Core Principles and Philosophy:** TEACCH views autism as a lifelong condition combining strengths with challenges. Key strategies include:
- Organizing physical environments to minimize distractions
- Using visual supports (schedules, cues, social stories, instructional aids)
- Establishing predictable yet flexible routines
- Creating visual work systems that break tasks into manageable steps
- Building independence through clear expectations and consistent routines

**Applications:** TEACCH is used in classroom settings, home environments, and therapeutic settings. It can be combined with other therapeutic approaches such as behavioral therapies and serves individuals across age groups from young children to adults. Professionals trained in TEACCH include teachers, psychologists, and speech therapists.

**Effectiveness and Evidence:** Research shows moderate improvements in cognition, social skills, and adaptive behaviors, especially in school-age individuals and adults with milder intellectual disabilities. Notably, 11 out of 14 studies reviewed showed statistically significant reductions in maladaptive behaviors such as stereotyped and repetitive patterns. Parents and teachers report decreased stress levels when using TEACCH strategies. An experimental study with young adults with ASD and mild to moderate intellectual disabilities involved a 20-session TEACCH-based training program, showing notable improvements in functional skills and Goal Attainment Scaling scores. A 2011 review emphasized TEACCH's educational benefits including gains in cognition and motor skills.

**Training and Certification:** Certification levels include the TEACCH® Certified Practitioner, requiring five-day training, participation in seminars, and passing an exam supported by portfolio review. Certification lasts three years and can be renewed through continuous professional development. The Autism Speaks Directory helps locate trained professionals regionally.

The article concludes that TEACCH's emphasis on structure, visual supports, and individualized planning has established it as a cornerstone of autism support worldwide, with continued research and training expected to enhance its impact.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published March 3, 2022, by ALSO孤独症 on alsolife.com) explains structured teaching (structured education) for autism spectrum disorder and how it is applied in intervention settings.

Structured teaching is based on the TEACCH program (Treatment and Education for Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children), developed by Professor Eric Schopler at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. It combines diagnosis, assessment, early education, school education, family education, and vocational training with the goal of promoting independent living for autistic children.

The method leverages the visual strengths of autistic children by organizing the educational environment and training procedures to improve comprehension, communication, perception, and motor skills. It uses visual clarity, visual restructuring, regular work routines, and visual instructions to enable effective learning.

The article outlines four steps of structured teaching:
1. Arrange training spaces according to different training content, with emphasis on visual cues and special placement of toys and items.
2. Establish training schedules/programs emphasizing procedural consistency.
3. Define training content including imitation, gross and fine motor skills, perception, cognition, hand-eye coordination, language comprehension and expression, self-care, social skills, and emotional regulation.
4. Use language, body posture, cues, labels, charts, and text to enhance understanding; apply behavioral reinforcement and behavior modification to reduce abnormal behaviors.

Structured teaching can be used in hospitals, rehabilitation centers, and home interventions. Two assessment tools are noted: the Psychoeducational Profile (PEP-3) and the TEACCH Transition Assessment Profile (T-TAP, for adolescents and adults). Before receiving an individualized education plan (IEP), children undergo PEP assessment, and programs are designed based on results given the developmental delays and imbalances typical of autism.

The ultimate purpose of structured teaching is to help autistic children complete work according to event sequence and logical structure, using visual reminders of progress. Parents are encouraged to integrate diversified teaching methods and other rehabilitation strategies for comprehensive training.

--- SOURCE 10: 星之光盐 ---
URL: https://www.autismlightsalt.com/ebps

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a Chinese-language educational resource about Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs) for autism intervention, based on the Autism Focused Intervention Resources & Modules (AFIRM) program. The site addresses why EBPs matter, what they are, how to learn them, and how to select them.

**Why EBPs:** No single intervention method (ABA, TEACCH, ESDM, PRT, etc.) can meet the diverse developmental needs of autistic children at different ages and domains. High-quality intervention requires integrating multiple EBPs based on individual needs (Hyman et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2020). Currently, no medical intervention effectively improves core ASD symptoms (CDC, 2019), and many complementary/alternative treatments lack scientific support (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2020). This site focuses on non-medical educational interventions.

**What EBPs are:** Two categories exist:
- Comprehensive Treatment Models (CTMs): Combinations of interventions built on a theoretical framework with standardized procedures (e.g., UCLA Young Autism Program, TEACCH, LEAP, Denver Model). They have high frequency, long duration (1+ years), and broad goals.
- Focused Intervention Practices (FIPs): Specific methods targeting one skill (e.g., Discrete Trial Training, visual supports, prompting). EBPs are FIPs that meet evidence standards.

The NPDC's 2014 second edition report reviewed 29,105 studies (1990-2011), selected 427, and approved 27 EBPs. The 2020 third edition added 31,779 studies (2012-2015), selected 545, and cumulatively analyzed 972 studies (1990-2017), approving 28 EBPs.

**How to learn:** The site offers online learning materials (overview, evidence base, step guides, tables, professional prompts, parent guides, additional resources, references) for each EBP, an EBPs comprehensive modular training course, and content based on the 2020 third edition report (updated as research advances).

**Who should learn:** Professionals (teachers, special educators, therapists, counselors) and parents/family members.

**The 28 EBPs** are listed with brief descriptions: AAC (Augmentative and Alternative Communication), ASI (Ayres Sensory Integration), BMI (Behavioral Momentum Intervention), DI (Direct Instruction), MMI (Music-Mediated Intervention), ABI (Antecedent-based Intervention), CBI (Cognitive Behavioral Intervention), DR (Differential Reinforcement), DTT (Discrete Trial Training), ECE (Exercise), EXT (Extinction), FBA (Functional Behavior Assessment), FCT (Functional Communication Training), MD (Modeling), NI (Naturalistic Intervention), PII (Parent Implemented Intervention), PMII (Peer-mediated Instruction and Intervention), PP (Prompting), R+ (Reinforcement), RIR (Response Interruption and Redirection), SM (Self-management), SN (Social Narratives), SST (Social Skills Training), TA (Task Analysis), TAII (Technology-aided Instruction and Intervention), TD (Time Delay), VM (Video Modeling), and VS (Visual Supports). Four methods (PECS → AAC, PRT → NI, Structured Play Groups → PMII, Scripting → VS) were folded into broader categories in the third edition.

**Choosing methods:** An EBPs matrix shows which of the 28 methods are evidence-supported across 3 age groups (0-5, 6-14, 15-22) and 12 target domains.

**Copyright:** The EBPs Guide originates from AFIRM (UNC), with Chinese translation rights held by 星之光盐 (Starlight Salt) Fan Yuebo team. The Chinese version was translated by multiple individuals and reviewed by 于洛迪 and 何昕劼.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is Page 2 of the IRIS Center module "Autism Spectrum Disorder (Part 2): Evidence-Based Practices" from Vanderbilt University, focused on what educators need to know about Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs) for children with autism.

Two federal laws—the Every Student Succeeds Act (ESSA) and the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA '04)—mandate that educators use evidence-based academic and behavioral practices to the greatest extent possible. The National Professional Development Center (NPDC) on Autism Spectrum Disorder has identified 27 evidence-based practices for improving outcomes for students with ASD.

The 27 EBPs are defined in a comprehensive table, including: antecedent-based intervention, cognitive behavioral intervention, differential reinforcement, discrete trial teaching, exercise, extinction, functional behavior assessment (FBA), functional communication training, modeling, naturalistic intervention, parent-implemented intervention, peer-mediated instruction and intervention, Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS), pivotal response training, prompting, reinforcement, response interruption/redirection, scripting, self-management, social narratives, social skills training, structured play group, task analysis, technology-aided instruction and intervention (TAII), time delay, video modeling, and visual support. (Adapted from Wong, Odom, Hume, Cox, Fettig, Kucharczyk, Brock, Plavnick, Fleury & Schultz, 2014.)

The page outlines four steps for selecting an EBP for a specific child:
1. **Identify and define the target behavior** — must be observable, measurable, and clearly defined
2. **Collect baseline data** — data gathered for at least four days or until a pattern of behavior is evident
3. **Establish a goal or outcome** — indicated in the child's IEP or IFSP, including when/where the behavior will be performed, what behavior should be displayed, and specific measurable mastery criteria
4. **Select an EBP** — considering child/family characteristics, student goals, teacher expertise, and available resources

Key considerations when selecting EBPs include collaborating with parents, recognizing that evidence-based status doesn't guarantee effectiveness for every student, and relying on trustworthy sources rather than unproven (sometimes harmful) internet treatments.

The module includes audio interviews with experts:
- **Kara Hume, PhD** (Research Scientist, Frank Porter Graham Child Development Institute, UNC-Chapel Hill) discusses selecting EBPs based on target skills, student characteristics, staff expertise, and available resources. She emphasizes implementing interventions with fidelity (as designed) using fidelity checklists, allowing time for impact, and considering more consistent implementation across settings, people, and items (rather than simply more intensive) before abandoning a practice.
- **Ilene Schwartz, PhD** (Professor Emeritus, Special Education; Director, Haring Center, University of Washington) emphasizes taking data on every instructional practice and changing instruction when child-performance data show a lack of learning.

The page also addresses the overlap between EBPs and High-Leverage Practices (HLPs), noting HLPs like functional behavior assessments, peer-mediated strategies, and building supportive learning environments overlap with EBPs for ASD.

Related resources include IRIS modules on Evidence-Based Practices Parts 1, 2, and 3 (identifying/selecting practices, implementing with fidelity, and evaluating outcomes), plus case studies on defining and measuring behavior.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Desired Results Access Project (DRAccess.org) provides comprehensive guidance for teachers and service providers on using the Desired Results Developmental Profile (DRDP) 2015 authentic assessment with young children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). The DRDP (2015) is an authentic assessment based on ongoing observations of children in their daily routines. The guide supplements the DRDP (2015) Assessment Manual and addresses how ASD may influence a child's social communication skills, patterns of behaviors and interests, and how to optimize learning environments for accurate assessment.

--- SOURCE 14: Visual Activity Schedules ---
URL: https://asatonline.org/for-parents/learn-more-about-specific-treatments/activity-schedules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Association for Science in Autism Treatment (ASAT) provides a comprehensive treatment summary of Visual Activity Schedules for individuals with autism, authored by Lisa Tereshko, PhD, BCBA-D of Endicott College (published in Science in Autism Treatment, Vol. 20, Issue 6, 2023).

**Description:** Visual activity schedules are arrangements of pictures or words that display a sequence of upcoming events (e.g., getting dressed, packing lunch, cooking dinner). They encompass three evidence-based strategies: antecedent interventions (presented before task initiation to cue expectations and reduce challenging behaviors), prompting (support to increase success completing tasks), and visual supports (reducing reliance on others for assistance). Visual schedules are particularly beneficial for autistic individuals who may display prompt dependency and have difficulty processing auditory information (Koyama & Wang, 2011; Knight et al., 2015).

**Formats:** Schedules can be displayed linearly (vertical or horizontal), in small books with icons moved to a "done" column, or using actual objects for individuals who struggle with pictures. They can also use narrative/word formats for readers. Technological options include videos, tablets, smartphones, and smart watches (e.g., iPad-based schedules for community shopping skills per Burckley et al., 2015; smart watch schedules for play skills per Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2021).

**Research Summary:** The National Standards Project: Phase 2 (2015) identifies schedule use as an established intervention for increasing independence and event planning. Hume et al. (2021) identified visual supports as an evidence-based practice. Two systematic reviews support this: Koyama and Wang (2011) reviewed 23 peer-reviewed studies (69 total participants across preschool [24.6%], school-aged [30.4%], and adults [23.2%], with 59.4% having an autism diagnosis), and Knight et al. (2014) reviewed 31 articles confirming effectiveness for teaching diverse skills across the lifespan. Visual schedules have successfully taught toothbrushing (Moran et al., 2022), medical exam cooperation (Chebuhar et al., 2013), bedtime routines (Hart Barnett et al., 2022), leisure/play skills, physical activity compliance (Becerra et al., 2021), appropriate feeding (Kirkpatrick et al., 2019), academic task engagement, choice-making (Deel et al., 2021), vocational tasks (Lora et al., 2020; Sances et al., 2019), transitions (Pierce et al., 2013), and social skills (Osos et al., 2021).

**Cautions/Limitations:** Knight et al. (2014) found that nearly all studies combined visual schedules with other systematic instruction (graduated guidance, reinforcement, prompting), which may have enhanced effects. Maintenance and generalization research is limited but promising (e.g., MacDuff et al., 1993 demonstrated generalization to novel pictures and activities).

**Recommendations:** Teams should decide interventions based on the individual's skills (symbolic representation, receptive language, reading/comprehension) and personal preference for modality. Giles et al. (2017) found similar acquisition rates between static pictures and tablet-based formats, with idiosyncratic preferences. Learner assent should be regularly assessed, and component skills (choice-making, stamina, social engagement, self-monitoring) can be built incidentally. Continued research should explore long-term effects, generalization, and technology's role in reducing social stigma.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Visual activity schedules are an arrangement of pictures or words used to display a sequence of upcoming events."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 15: Visual Schedules in the School Setting | Reading Rockets ---
URL: https://www.readingrockets.org/topics/autism-spectrum-disorder/articles/visual-schedules-school-setting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Reading Rockets explains the use of visual schedules in school settings for students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). A visual schedule communicates the sequence of upcoming activities or events through objects, photographs, icons, words, or a combination of tangible supports, telling a student WHERE they should be and WHEN they should be there.

**Background**: The strategies are based on Structured Teaching, developed by Division TEACCH (Training and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children), a statewide program in North Carolina. Structured Teaching capitalizes on the strengths of students with ASD by providing predictable routines, visual/structural supports, and clearly organized classroom spaces. There are five elements of Structured Teaching that emphasize predictability and flexible routines.

**Why use visual schedules:**
- They enhance receptive language and provide meaning to students
- Students with autism have strengths in visuospatial skills and sustained attention (Quill, 1997), and attend to visual information more successfully (Garretson, Fein, & Waterhouse, 1990)
- They help students become independent of adult prompts and cues (Mesibov, Shea, & Schopler, 2005); research confirms shifting from verbal to visual prompts increases independence and engagement while decreasing need for adult supports (Green, 2001)
- They reduce anxiety by providing clear external structure, which may be physiologically calming

**Five areas to consider when designing visual schedules** (Cox & Boswell, 1999):
1. **Form of representation** – choose objects, photos, icons, or words based on what the student understands; select a form understood on the student's "worst day" (with a substitute teacher, late bus, cancelled recess)
2. **Length of schedule and presentation format** – determine how much information to present (one piece, short sequence, or full day); consider sequencing ability, anxiety level, and ability to handle changes; present left-to-right or top-to-bottom
3. **Way of manipulating the schedule** – students may carry schedule items and match them to identical items at their destination, or mark off activities when finished
4. **Location of the schedule** – initially brought to the student, then posted in a central location (table, shelf, wall, desk) as a "transition area," or carried portably (e.g., in a binder or on a clipboard)
5. **Initiation of use of the schedule** – determine how students know when to check their schedule; visual cues (such as a card with the student's name) are often most effective for signaling transitions

**Implementation next steps**: After designing and making materials, staff must explicitly teach students how to use the schedule, minimize adult-delivered prompts (Green, 2001), prompt from behind so schedule materials are in the student's visual field, and fade prompts quickly. Use only relevant language (e.g., "Play area" instead of lengthy explanations). Once independent, staff may change the form (pictures to words if student is a fluent reader) or increase schedule length, but a more complex schedule is not necessarily "better" — the goal is independent usage.

The article was published with permission from the Indiana Resource Center for Autism (IRCA).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A visual schedule communicates the sequence of upcoming activities or events through the use of objects, photographs, icons, words, or a combination of tangible supports. A visual schedule tells a student WHERE he/she should be and WHEN he/she should be there."
</key_excerpts>

# 自闭症儿童的感觉统合障碍怎么干预？

*作者：*ALSO孤独症 *：*2022-03-08

> 儿童[自闭症康复](https://www.alsolife.com/autism/cure)有哪些注意事项？在自闭症儿童中间，共患[感觉统合](https://www.alsolife.com/column/art/1461203454686855169/)障碍是一种常见情况。感觉统合障碍又称感觉处理障碍，即人们常说的[感统失调](https://www.alsolife.com/column/art/1461203454686855169/)。孩子接受[感统训练](https://www.alsolife.com/column/art/1471682034843713537/)的前提是确实存在感统失调，关于自闭症儿童要不要做感统训练，需由专业人士的评估，每一项干预手段的运用都要从孩子的特点出发。

感统，即感觉统合，指个体对通过视、听、触、味、嗅、前庭觉和本体觉等不同的感觉通路得来的感觉信息在大脑内进行解释、联系和统一。感统失调就指一个人不能对信息进行正常的整合，无法做出恰当的反应。

 

**儿童感统失调的具体表现为：**

**✦****前庭功能失调：**多动，注意力不集中，上课不专心，爱做小动作，很难与其他同学相处，还有可能表现为语言发展迟缓，说话晚，语言表达困难等。

**✦****视觉统合失调：**能长时间看动画片、玩玩具，却无法流利地阅读，学习困难等。

 

**✦****听觉统合失调：**对别人的话听而不闻，丢三落四，经常忘记别人说的话或重要的事情。

**✦****本体统合失调：**缺乏自信心，消极退缩，平衡能力差，走路东倒西歪，不能像普通孩子一样做出翻滚、系鞋带等动作，手脚笨拙等。

**✦****触觉统合失调：**触觉异常，对冷热，疼痛反应迟钝，表现为容易紧张、不合群、偏食、脾气暴躁，害怕陌生环境、经常吃手、咬指甲等。

 

感统失调更多是作为一种伴随病症出现，如果孩子出现相关的感官障碍，医生必须考虑其它类型的儿童发育与行为障碍，尤其是自闭症谱系障碍(ASD)、注意力缺陷多动症(ADHD)、发展性协调障碍(DCD)等。

 

在自闭症儿童中，感觉统合障碍存在较高的比例，主要表现为感觉系统异常，比如感觉的高敏或低敏。**判断一个自闭症孩子是否要接受感统训练，应该先由医生对孩子进行全面的专业评估，如果存在感统失调，就需要进行感觉统合训练，改善症状。**感统训练作为一种必要的辅助，虽然有助于调整孩子的感觉输入和情绪状态，但并不是主要的康复手段。

 

**感统训练通常以游戏的形式展开，在日常生活中，家长可以借助一些玩具和设施，通过亲子游戏的方式对孩子进行训练，比如：**

✦投球、抛接球：锻炼孩子手眼协调能力和手臂动作的灵活性，学习观察和探索目标。

✦爬楼梯：学习扶栏杆上楼梯，锻炼孩子的胆量和腿部力量。

 

✦推物、拉物走：有助于孩子发展大运动，锻炼手臂推的能力，以及手、眼和腿的动作协调。

✦倒着走：培养孩子空间概念，协调身体能力。

✦踢球：发展大运动，包括腿的伸展能力，发展眼、腿的协调能力。

args.summary:
This webpage from alsolife.com is an educational article (published March 8, 2022, by ALSO孤独症) about how to intervene in sensory integration disorders (感觉统合障碍) in children with autism. 

Key points include:
- Sensory integration disorder (also called sensory processing disorder or 感统失调) is common among children with autism.
- Sensory integration (感统) refers to the brain's process of interpreting and unifying sensory information from visual, auditory, tactile, taste, olfactory, vestibular, and proprioceptive channels. Sensory integration disorder means a person cannot properly integrate information or respond appropriately.
- Specific manifestations of sensory integration disorder include:
  - **Vestibular dysfunction**: hyperactivity, inattention, restlessness in class, difficulty getting along with others, delayed language development, late talking, difficulty expressing.
  - **Visual integration disorder**: can watch cartoons/play toys for long periods but cannot read fluently, learning difficulties.
  - **Auditory integration disorder**: appears not to hear others, forgetful, loses things, forgets what others say.
  - **Proprioceptive integration disorder**: lacks confidence, passive/withdrawn, poor balance, clumsy, cannot roll, tie shoelaces, etc.
  - **Tactile integration disorder**: abnormal touch sensitivity, sluggish response to hot/cold/pain, easily nervous, unsociable, picky eating, irritable, fears unfamiliar environments, frequently sucks fingers or bites nails.
- Sensory integration disorder usually appears as a comorbid condition; doctors must consider other childhood developmental and behavioral disorders, especially autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, and developmental coordination disorder (DCD).
- A professional evaluation by a doctor is required before deciding whether a child with autism should undergo sensory integration training. If sensory integration disorder exists, sensory integration training (感统训练) is needed to improve symptoms.
- Sensory integration training is a necessary aid that helps adjust sensory input and emotional state, but it is NOT the primary rehabilitation method.
- Sensory integration training is typically conducted in game form. Parents can use toys and facilities for parent-child games, including:
  - Ball throwing/catching: exercises hand-eye coordination and arm flexibility.
  - Climbing stairs: builds courage and leg strength.
  - Pushing/pulling objects while walking: develops gross motor skills and hand-eye-leg coordination.
  - Walking backward: develops spatial concepts and body coordination.
  - Kicking a ball: develops gross motor skills including leg extension and eye-leg coordination.

# 为在中国传播自闭症的信息助力 (Help Spread the Word About Autism in China)

This article was originally written in English and has been translated into Chinese. 您的孩子是否患有自闭症？我们为您提供了一系列的教育课程和配套教材，其中包含您教学所需的全部内容。欲了解更多信息，请访问 《ARIS自闭症课程 - 语言发展入门与教学资源》 ...

SY 

[Sihan Yang](/connect/articles/author/sihan-yang)

Graduate Student · Dec 10, 2016 · 1 min read

![为在中国传播自闭症的信息助力 (Help Spread the Word About Autism in China)](https://utvrugmbdldmdpyixxjv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/connect-assets/connect/hubfs/blog-images/blog-title-chinese)

*This article was [originally written in English](http://blog.stageslearning.com/blog/autism-in-china) and has been translated into Chinese.*

您的孩子是否患有自闭症？我们为您提供了一系列的教育课程和配套教材，其中包含您教学所需的全部内容。欲了解更多信息，请访问[**《ARIS自闭症课程 - 语言发展入门与教学资源》**](https://store.stageslearning.com/products/aris)

来美国之前，虽然有听说过“自闭症”（也称“孤独症”）这个词，但毕竟生活中很少在具体的语境或情境中遇到，更别说去关注或者关心受自闭症影响的儿童及他们的家庭。

第一次在波士顿乘坐公交车，就看到车上关于为自闭症儿童提供疗育的广告，当时只是勾起了准备出国考试时记一系列医疗类单词的回忆。后来在一门课上遇到一个女孩儿，对特殊教育这个领域很感兴趣，原因是她以前偶尔会教一位朋友的弟弟数学，尽管小男孩儿患有自闭症，但却对数学有极强的天赋，这让她相信患有自闭症的儿童并不是有缺陷，只是与自己不同。因为我在教育学院学习，在很多的课堂讨论和研讨会中，都会有学生提及他们与患有自闭症儿童接触的经历以及他们的认识和启发。哪怕是我上周不经意报名参加的面向普通大众的TED公开演讲，演讲的嘉宾也提到了新科技在诊断自闭症方面的潜力。

这样高的频率显然不是巧合，这让我不禁好奇自闭症以及患有自闭症的群体在我自己国家的现状。

![blog_title_chinese.jpg](https://utvrugmbdldmdpyixxjv.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/connect-assets/connect/hubfs/blog-images/blog-title-chinese "blog_title_chinese.jpg")

**大多数患有自闭症的中国儿童未接受诊断**

上世纪80年代初，南京脑科医院确诊了中国第一例自闭症1。然而，30多年过去了，国内大部分人仍然对自闭症了解甚少，认为它是一种极少数人患上的罕见病症。这一方面是由于大多患有自闭症的儿童长期呆在家里，很少接受学校教育或与外界接触1。另一方面，中国75%到80%的人口居住在农村地区，缺少接受专业诊断的途径，因此据估计，确诊的患有自闭症的中国儿童仅占实际数量的20%左右2。尽管对于全国患有自闭症的人口数量，国内没有确切的研究数据，但国际上已有数据表明，全世界1%的人口患有自闭症3。又因为自闭症的发病率不因国籍、种族、社会背景等而异，1％这一比例也同样适用于中国。

**早期的诊断和干预十分重要**

研究表明，即便是既有诊断意识又有诊断途径的家庭，在从发现到诊断再到干预的整个过程中，也大多经历了不少的延误。一项2013的调查访问了来自全国的69位已确诊患有自闭症儿童的家长，结果显示从最早发现症状到接受诊断，中间间隔的平均时长为7.1个月，从确诊到接受干预，中间间隔的平均时长为6.5个月4。此外，很多家长因为想让孩子进入知名的疗愈中心接受干预，一般需要等待大约8个月才有新的名额。同一项调查还显示，尽管申办残疾证能够让患有自闭症儿童的家庭每月从地方政府领取一定的补助，88%的家庭不打算为自己的孩子申请，因为不希望这样的记录跟随孩子一辈子。

目前，对于自闭症还没有治愈方式，但干预手段已经被证明能够有效地提升患有自闭症儿童的独立生活能力，从而能够提高他们成年后的生活质量。然而，很多患有自闭症的中国儿童在他们第一次接受诊断前就已经错过了接受早期集中干预的最佳时期（3岁前）1。这样的延误是由多方面的原因造成的，比如对于患有自闭症的人群的服务保障体系不完善，社会给智力或精神方面的病症贴上的标签，中国父母对子女学习能力和竞争优势的期望（尤其是在独生子女政策的影响下），家长对于儿童发育的知识匮乏，老旧思想将幼儿期语言技能的延迟发展与未来的高智商划等号， 经济压力，等等1,4,5,6。

**北京星星雨：患有自闭症的儿童及其家庭的希望**

北京星星雨教育研究所的一位老师指出，更加健全的服务保障体系或许是患有自闭症的儿童及其家庭最迫切需要的，而建立这样的体系则需要培训足够数量的从业人员，提供全国范围内接受诊断和干预的机会和途径，保障患有自闭症的儿童获得教育的平等权利，开展传播关于自闭症知识和信息的活动，给患有自闭症的青少年及成年人提供更多的支持，以及出台相关政策以减轻患有自闭症儿童的家庭的经济负担。

目前患有自闭症的中国儿童及其家庭面临的挑战是棘手的，也是令人担忧的，但好在改变在一点点发生。我很高兴有类似“星星雨”这样的非政府组织，他们的网站上有很多文章以及知识问答，能让大家更多的了解自闭症；也有帮助家长及早发现自闭症症状的儿童发育对照表；有全国可以提供诊断的医院信息；同时，网站还提供了患有自闭症儿童的家长可以交流和相互支持的平台。此外，“星星雨”也为家长提供培训课程，帮助他们学习如何辅助孩子通过在家里与家长的互动活动发展和提升自己的技能。值得欣慰的是，现在国内外很多企业和个人都在关注患有自闭症的群体，也为像“星星雨”这样的组织给予了很多捐赠和支持。

**世界提高自闭症意识日**

2016年4月2日是第八个世界提高自闭症意识日。美国自闭症科学与宣传组织“自闭症之声”（Autism Speaks）将在这一天呼吁全球的地标建筑、摩天大楼、学校、企业以及家庭都点上蓝灯，也呼吁每个人穿上蓝色衣服，以此对全世界自闭症患者及其家庭表示问候和关心。

而我，则参与进了自闭症疗育学习材料和应用软件出版商Stages Learning发起的全球提高自闭症意识项目，与两名来自巴基斯坦的同学一起通过写文章和制作视频来提高像中国和巴基斯坦这样的发展中国家的大众对于自闭症的意识。

我们相信，你也可以改变自闭症患者的世界。

args.summary:
This is a Chinese-language article (originally written in English and translated) about autism awareness in China, written by Sihan Yang, a graduate student, for Stages Learning on December 10, 2016. The article discusses the state of autism diagnosis and intervention in China, highlighting that most autistic Chinese children remain undiagnosed. Key points include: The first autism case in China was diagnosed at Nanjing Brain Hospital in the early 1980s, but 30+ years later, most people still view it as a rare condition. An estimated only 20% of actual autism cases in China are diagnosed, partly because 75-80% of the population lives in rural areas without access to professional diagnosis. International data shows ~1% of the world population has autism, a rate that applies equally to China.

The article emphasizes that early diagnosis and intervention are critical. A 2013 survey of 69 parents of diagnosed autistic children found an average 7.1-month delay between first noticing symptoms and diagnosis, and a further 6.5-month delay from diagnosis to intervention. Parents often wait ~8 months for openings at known treatment centers. 88% of families declined to apply for disability certification (which would provide monthly subsidies) because they didn't want the record to follow their children for life. Many Chinese autistic children miss the optimal early intervention window (before age 3) due to factors including inadequate service systems, societal stigma, parental expectations under the one-child policy, lack of knowledge about child development, old beliefs linking delayed speech to future intelligence, and economic pressures.

The article highlights Beijing Starry Rain (北京星星雨) Education Institute, an NGO offering resources, diagnostic information, parent training courses, and support platforms. The author participated in Stages Learning's global autism awareness project with students from Pakistan. The article mentions World Autism Awareness Day (April 2, 2016 was the 8th) and Autism Speaks' Light It Up Blue campaign. It concludes with links to Stages Learning, the Language Builder app, and Autism Speaks, along with academic references.

args.summary:
This is a Chinese-language systematic review on Sensory Integration Training (SIT) for treating autism spectrum disorders (ASD), based on the work of Lang et al. (2012) published in Research in Autism Spectrum Disorders, translated by Hao Yan of East China Normal University's Special Education Department.

**Purpose**: The review aimed to systematically identify, analyze, and summarize 25 studies to explore the significance of SIT in the education and training of children with autism.

**Methodology**: Studies were screened from four databases (Medline, ERIC, Psychology and Behavioral Sciences Collection, and PsycINFO) using combined keywords (e.g., "sensory," "sensorimotor," "swinging," "vestibular stimulation" with "autism," "Asperger's," "developmental disorders"). Inclusion criteria required at least one child with autism as a subject and the use of SIT techniques aimed at reducing symptoms, improving quality of life, returning to typical environments, or improving academic performance. Studies were analyzed across six dimensions: subject characteristics, sensory deficit and behavioral function assessment, dependent variables, intervention process, intervention results, and certainty of evidence. Intervention results were classified as effective, ineffective, or mixed results. Evidence certainty was classified into three levels: suggestive, advantageous, and decisive.

**Participants**: The 25 selected studies included 217 children with ASD (195 with classic autism, 21 with PDD-NOS, 1 with Asperger's syndrome). Comorbidities included 3 with hearing impairment, 1 with visual impairment, 1 with epilepsy, and 1 with bipolar disorder. There were 176 males, 31 females, and 10 of unknown gender. Ages ranged from 2 to 12 years (mean 5.9 years).

**Results**:
- 14 studies (56%) reported SIT had no benefit, with 4 of these reporting SIT may have increased stereotyped and problem behaviors. Of the no-benefit studies: 8 were classified as suggestive evidence, 1 as advantageous evidence, and 5 as decisive evidence (all 5 decisive-evidence studies used weighted vests).
- 8 studies reported mixed results (6 suggestive, 2 decisive evidence).
- 3 studies reported SIT was effective, but ALL 3 were classified at the suggestive (lowest) evidence level.

**Methodological problems in the 3 effective studies**: 
- Fazlioglu (2008): Difficult tasks were broken into small steps with uncertain reinforcement, multiple prompting types, and SIT was combined with ABA—the reported effectiveness likely reflects ABA rather than SIT.
- Linderman (1999): Subjects received language therapy after baseline, which could affect the dependent variable of social initiative behavior; the SIT intervention process was not reproducible.
- Thompson (2011): Used repeated-measures ANOVA but did not report specific ANOVA results, only aggregate data charts and author descriptions without sufficient information.

**Discussion/Conclusion**: The review found insufficient evidence to support the use of SIT for children with autism. Due to IDEA and NCLB requirements that schools use evidence-supported interventions, the review recommends avoiding large-scale implementation of SIT in public schools funded by federal money. Some researchers suggest SIT may increase problem behaviors because it provides leisure activities, occupational therapist attention, and activity interruptions caused by problem behaviors—even if short-term reductions in problem behavior are observed, SIT may reinforce problem behaviors long-term. The ultimate conclusion is that there is insufficient evidence supporting SIT for autistic children, and practitioners should avoid SIT outside strict controls if using research-based/scientific intervention methods.

# 自闭症儿童是否需要做感觉统合训练？

*作者：*ALSO孤独症 *：*2022-03-01

> 在[自闭症康复](https://www.alsolife.com/autism/cure)领域，实证有效的干预方法有不少，随着研究的不断深入，包括感统训练在内的其它方法也加入了实证有效的范畴，但这并不代表感统训练可以无差别地适用于每一位[自闭症](https://www.alsolife.com/autism)孩子。

在美国国家自闭症中心和国家自闭症证据与实践交流中心（NCAEP）的最新的报告中，公布了28种实践被列为针对于0-22岁自闭症儿童和青少年的实证支持的干预方法（Evidence-Based Practices，EBP），其中就有感统训练。

 

**[感觉统合](https://www.alsolife.com/column/art/1457879915601903618)（***Sensory Integration**，SI）*由职能治疗师A. Jean Ayres在20世纪60年代提出。现在把Ayres提出的感统理论以及基于该理论的治疗方法，称之为Ayres Sensory Integration（ASI）。ASI是基于感统理论发展的一套完整的干预方法，包括感觉统合理论、感觉统合评估方法以及一套核心的适用于有感觉加工缺陷人士的干预设计。

 

感觉统合是人们登记、调节和辨别通过感觉系统接收到的各种感觉，产生有目的的、适应环境的行为的过程。**人们所依赖的感觉系统包括视觉、听觉、味觉、嗅觉、触觉、本体感觉和前庭觉。对这些感觉的有效整合能够帮我们发展出各种职业角色所需的技能，比如关心自己和他人，与人和物交往以及参与社会工作。**

 

**感觉统合会影响一个人懂得职业表现。**随着儿童的成长，他们通常会发展出适当的登记、调节和辨别感觉信息的精细能力，以支持有效的情绪调节、社交技能、游戏技能以及精细运动和大肌肉运动技能的发展。**感觉统合功能障碍会限制孩子的能力，使他们不能很好地做出协调的动作、计划新的任务、发展社会关系、照顾自己、参与家庭活动等。**

所有的EBP方法都有一套完整的治疗体系，包括评估、教学计划、干预、数据追踪。如果一个孩子可能有感觉加工问题，治疗师会使用特定的ASI评估方法，包括自然环境中的观察、家长访谈、标准测验和结构化的临床观察，来确定孩子的感觉使用障碍和具体的感觉统合缺陷领域，及其影响功能表现的具体方式。

 

**对于ASI感觉统合干预方案的形成和执行，一般包括以下核心元素：**

◆在职能治疗师、物理治疗师或言语病理学家的直接监督下，由有资格的专业职能治疗师或职能治疗助理进行干预；

◆干预计划以家庭为中心，纳入被干预者生活中的重要他人的相关建议，对感觉整合功能障碍有完整评估，并遵循职业道德和伦理标准；

◆治疗在一个安全的环境中进行，该环境中包括锻炼前庭觉、本体感觉、及触觉的相关设备；

◆孩子在环境本身、有挑战的活动和独特的感觉经验都能表现出适应性的反应；

◆所有的活动都以孩子为中心，由治疗师辅助进行；

◆活动具有丰富的感觉刺激，尤其是前庭觉、触觉和本体感觉，并提供了将这些信息与其他感觉，如视觉和听觉整合的机会；

◆许多活动会给孩子带来挑战，孩子需要规划如何完成当下的任务，并成功地执行；

◆许多活动会包括特殊的设备，如悬挂装置、滑板车、球，来促进孩子的姿势控制和平衡能力。

◆活动本身就是孩子的强化，治疗师需要保证孩子在进行任何活动的时候，都能调整活动能力要求以适应孩子的水平，来确保孩子有成功的体验。

**以下三要素可以帮助家长判断一家机构提供的感统训练是否靠谱：**

①老师们是否有相关资质或接受过系统培训；

②是否有完整的评估、干预计划、数据记录的体系；

③干预是否体现出感统训练的核心要素。

 

感觉统合训练一直存在争议，能被纳入EBP的实践方法一定都有它存在的价值，实证支持的研究数量越多，代表这个方法越具有“普遍适用性”，越“保险”，**但并不意味着这个方法最好。**

不是任意一种有实证支持的方法都可以直接拿来用，因为每一种能称为EBP的策略都会比想象中复杂，有其强调的重点，针对的目标也不同。某种实践方法是否适合孩子，需要对孩子的整体情况有非常清晰的认识和准确的把握，再进行针对性地选择。

 

对于自闭症孩子而言，最有效果的才是最好的方法。**如果孩子存在感统失调，感统训练是很好的辅助干预方法，但不能代替核心的ABA，而没有感统失调的孩子，就不需要感觉统合训练。**

自闭症有社交沟通障碍和兴趣或活动范围狭窄以及重复刻板行为，两大核心障碍都不是因为感统失调造成的。**感统训练只针对于有感统失调的孩子，而不针对自闭症。**

args.summary:
This article from ALSOLIFE (a Chinese autism support platform) discusses whether children with autism need sensory integration training (感觉统合训练). Published on 2022-03-01, the article clarifies that while sensory integration training has been included among 28 Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs) for children and youth with autism aged 0-22 per the latest reports from the US National Autism Center and the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence & Practice (NCAEP), it is not universally applicable to every child with autism.

Key points include:
- Sensory Integration (SI) was proposed by occupational therapist A. Jean Ayres in the 1960s; the full framework is now called Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI), encompassing theory, assessment methods, and intervention designs for people with sensory processing deficits.
- Sensory integration involves registering, modulating, and discriminating sensory input from visual, auditory, gustatory, olfactory, tactile, proprioceptive, and vestibular systems to produce purposeful, adaptive behaviors. Dysfunction can limit a child's ability to make coordinated movements, plan new tasks, develop social relationships, and care for themselves.
- ASI intervention plans include nine core elements: delivery under direct supervision of qualified therapists (occupational, physical, or speech-language); family-centered planning with input from significant others; safe environments with equipment for vestibular, proprioceptive, and tactile stimulation; adaptive responses to challenges; child-centered activities; rich sensory stimulation especially vestibular, tactile, and proprioceptive input integrated with other senses; tasks requiring planning and successful execution; special equipment (hanging devices, scooters, balls) for posture control and balance; and activities that adjust difficulty to ensure success.
- Three criteria help parents judge whether an institution's sensory integration training is reliable: ① practitioners' qualifications or systematic training; ② complete evaluation, intervention planning, and data recording systems; ③ whether the intervention embodies core sensory integration elements.

Critical conclusion: Sensory integration training is controversial despite being EBP-supported. Being evidence-based does not mean a method is "best." For children with sensory integration dysfunction, sensory training is a good supplementary intervention but cannot replace core ABA (Applied Behavior Analysis) therapy. Children without sensory integration disorder do not need this training. Autism's two core deficits—social communication impairments and restricted/repetitive behaviors—are not caused by sensory integration dysfunction, so sensory integration training targets children with sensory integration disorder specifically, not autism generally.

## 2. 结构化课堂的物理环境

#### 环境的基本调整

* 在安静且刺激少的地方固定位置
* 减少墙面和黑板的视觉杂乱
* 创建一个安静的角落以调节情绪
* 使用合适的照明（避免闪烁的霓虹灯）
* 明确划定活动区域和空间
* 展示可访问的视觉时间表

* 将学生的材料组织在标记的箱子中

## 3. 调整沟通和指令

## 4. 管理过渡和变化

过渡通常是自闭症学生面临的困难时刻，因为他们需要可预见性，并且在处理变化时存在困难。这些从一种活动过渡到另一种活动的时刻，如果没有提前预见和准备，可能会产生压力和不当行为。

预见是成功过渡的关键。提前几分钟通知学生即将发生的变化，使用具体的时间标记：“在 5 分钟内，我们将收拾书本去休息。”使用视觉或听觉计时器来具体化剩余时间，这有助于学生在心理上为变化做好准备。

建立清晰且一致的过渡例程。例如，从个人工作转到小组活动时，定义一个明确的顺序：收拾材料、合上书本、起身、推开椅子、走向小组活动区域。这种仪式化使学生感到安心，并逐步自动化预期的行为。

实用技巧

在过渡期间为自闭症学生分配一个特定角色（分发材料、擦黑板、关窗户）。这个责任给了他们一个具体的目标，并促进他们参与活动的变化。

## 5. 个性化学习策略

每个自闭症学生都有独特的认知特征，具有特定的优势和困难。识别这些特性对于调整教学策略和优化学习至关重要。这种个性化并不意味着降低要求，而是提供不同的途径以达到相同的目标。

许多自闭症学生在视觉学习方面表现出色，并且非常受益于图形支持、图表、思维导图或表格。他们在某些类型的信息上可能还表现出优秀的工作记忆，特别是那些与他们的兴趣中心相关的信息。利用这些优势来巩固新的学习。

将复杂任务分解为简单的、顺序的步骤可以促进理解和执行。提供视觉检查清单，使学生能够跟踪自己的进展并发展独立性。这种逐步的方法减少了认知负担，促进了成功感。

#### 特定兴趣的利用

利用学生的特定兴趣作为教学杠杆。如果他对恐龙充满热情，将这一主题融入数学、阅读或科学的练习中。这种个性化显著提高了学生的动机和参与度。

## 6. 调整评估

对自闭症学生的评估需要特定的调整，以便让他们能够展示真实的能力，而不因困难而受到惩罚。目标是评估所学的知识和技能，而不是与自闭症相关的困难。

时间通常是自闭症学生的限制因素，他们可能需要更多时间来处理信息、理解指令或组织回答。始终给予额外的三分之一时间，并在必要时建议将评估分为多个短时间的会议，而不是一次长时间的会议。

评估环境必须适应，以限制压力和干扰的来源。提供一个安静的空间，可能与班级分开，配有适当的照明和有利于集中注意力的家具布局。熟悉的成年人（教师或AESH）的存在也可以让学生感到安心。

#### 推荐的评估调整

* 系统性的额外三分之一时间
* 口头重述书面指令
* 简化版面和展示
* 避免双重否定或模糊的问题
* 提供选择题而不是开放性问题
* 允许使用补偿工具（电脑、计算器）
* 评估知识而不是形式
* 提供多样化的评估格式（口头、实践、作品集）

## 7. 预防和管理困难行为

在某些自闭症学生中观察到的挑战行为（危机、对抗、退缩）通常是压力、误解或感官过载的表现。采取预防性和理解性的方式而非惩罚性方式来有效支持学生是至关重要的。

行为的功能分析可以帮助识别这些行为的触发因素和功能。观察前因（刚发生了什么？）、行为本身及其后果。这种分析将帮助您制定预防策略和适当的响应。

在课堂上设置一个撤退或调节空间，为学生提供一个安全的地方，以便在情绪或感官过载时能够冷静下来。这个空间配备调节材料（加重垫、减压球、书籍），应被视为一个积极的工具，而不是惩罚。

行为方法

预防和干预策略

预防仍然是避免困难行为的最佳策略。提前预测风险情况，教授替代沟通策略，并重视适当的行为。

与 COCO 运动 的调节技巧

COCO 运动 的体育活动是情感和感官调节的优秀工具。这些积极的休息时间，定期融入日常生活，帮助学生引导他们的能量，并保持最佳的觉醒水平以进行学习。

## 8. 促进社会包容和合作

自闭症学生的社会包容并不是自动发生的，需要教师的积极支持。社交沟通和理解隐性规则的困难如果不被考虑，可能导致孤立。目标是为所有学生创造一个友好和包容的环境。

班级对差异的意识是一个重要的前提，前提是以得体的方式进行，并与学生及其家庭达成一致。简单地解释我们每个人都有不同的优点和困难，而多样性丰富了班级。避免污名化或创建简化标签。

组织结构化的合作学习情境，让每位学生，包括自闭症学生，都能贡献自己的力量。同行辅导、合作项目或合作游戏促进积极互动，让其他学生发现他们的自闭症同学的能力。

#### 预防欺凌

自闭症学生不幸地更容易面临校园欺凌的风险。对嘲笑、排斥或操控的迹象保持警惕。建立一个友好的课堂氛围，尊重差异，让每个人都能安全地成长。

## 9. 与教育团队和合作伙伴合作

成功包容自闭症学生依赖于所有相关人员之间的紧密合作：教师、家庭、健康专业人员、AESH、指导教师、教育团队。这种合作方法确保干预的一致性，并优化学生的成功机会。

与家庭的定期交流对于理解孩子的特性、习惯、有效策略和困难至关重要。父母对他们的孩子有独特的专业知识，可以提供关于孩子的运作和需求的宝贵见解。建立基于相互信任的建设性对话。

与健康专业人员（言语治疗师、心理运动治疗师、心理学家）的协调可以统一方法并获得专业建议。请随时联系您所在地区的指导教师，他们可以帮助您实施适应措施并与不同的合作伙伴建立联系。

#### 包容性的重要合作伙伴

* 家庭：对孩子的专业知识和教育连续性
* AESH：日常陪伴和细致观察
* 负责教师：协调和教学建议
* 护理团队：互补的治疗方法
* 教育团队：实践的一致性
* 学校医生：必要时的医疗调整
* 学校心理学家：评估和指导
* 管理层：机构和组织支持

## 10. 使用适当的数字工具

数字工具提供了许多可能性，以个性化学习并补偿自闭症学生的某些困难。这些技术可以作为视觉支持、组织帮助或替代沟通工具。它们的使用必须经过深思熟虑，并适应每个学生的特定需求。

平板电脑和计算机可以提供吸引人和互动的多媒体支持。教育应用程序可以提供即时反馈、个性化进展和多样化的活动格式。对于有精细运动困难的学生，键盘可以有效替代手写。

数字视觉时间表、视觉计时器或替代沟通应用程序（图标、语音合成）是促进组织和沟通的宝贵工具。这些支持可以在学校和家庭之间共享，以确保学习的连续性。

## 11. 培养专业视角和发展技能

在普通班级接纳自闭症学生质疑传统教学实践，并邀请教师发展新技能。这一持续培训的过程不仅有利于自闭症学生，还丰富了专业实践，惠及所有学生。

关于自闭症的培训使人们更好地理解这种发展障碍的特性，并获得基于科学数据的干预策略。行为、认知和感官的方法提供了互补的分析框架，以分析情况并调整实践。

通过阅读、自学、与经验丰富的同事交流逐步丰富技能。参加由机构或私人组织提供的专业培训，有助于深入了解支持的某些特定方面。

## 12. 创建有效的个性化教育项目（PPS）

个性化教育项目是正式化自闭症学生所需的调整和适应的参考文件。其撰写和实施需要协作的方法和对学生需求的准确了解。

PPS的制定依赖于MDPH团队进行的多学科评估、教育团队的观察和家庭的请求。它定义了教学目标、教育方式、所需的调整和动员的专业人员。

PPS的实施需要整个教育团队的认同和定期评估其有效性。预定的调整必须具体应用，并根据学生的进展和需求进行调整。

#### 优化PPS

积极参与教育跟踪会议（ESS），提供您的观察和调整建议。您的教学专业知识和对学生的日常了解对推动教育项目的发展至关重要。

## 课堂上关于自闭症的常见问题

保持冷静，采取善意的态度。避免额外的刺激（强光、噪音）。如果学生能够接受，提供撤退空间。不要强迫身体接触。等待危机过去，然后分析触发因素，以防止类似情况的发生。让家庭和专业人士参与，以调整预防策略。

这个决定应与自闭症学生的家庭协商后做出。如果组织了意识提升活动，优先采用以差异和互补为中心的积极方法，而不是关注残疾。强调每个人都有特定的优势和困难。使用适合学生年龄的材料，并随时准备回答问题。

识别他的特定兴趣，并将其作为教学杠杆。调整学习材料和方式（视觉、可操作、数字化）。将任务分解为短小的步骤，设定可实现的目标。尽可能提供选择。系统性地表扬他的成功和努力。COCO 思考 和 COCO 运动项目可以通过其有趣和渐进的活动成为一个很好的激励支持。

由于噪音、喧闹和缺乏结构，课间休息对自闭症学生来说可能很困难。提供安静的空间（图书馆、阅读角）。组织结构化的活动，让学生可以参与。让监护人了解学生的特殊情况。可能的话，允许进入替代活动（学校生活帮助、计算机）。重要的是尊重他的需求，同时保持社交联系。

在年初建立明确的合作框架。共同定义每个人的角色和责任。分享你的观察和策略。共同准备教学调整。确保AESH促进学生的自主性，而不是造成依赖。组织定期交流时间以调整支持。关于自闭症的联合培训增强了干预的一致性。

### Fidget spinners and other sensory toys are ubiquitous in Australian classrooms, but do they really support learning or do they undermine it?

*NOTE: This post is written from the perspective of mainstream classroom teaching. There are undeniably situations where sensory tools are used in support of regulation or harm reduction, and in clinical or at-home contexts, these might be both effective and appropriate. Our focus here is on how sensory toys impact learning and attention in whole-class environments, where teachers must consider the needs of 20–30 students at once.*

##### **What we observe in classrooms**

If you spend any time in primary school classrooms, you would’ve noticed the fidget spinners, spiky balls, pop-its, squishies, mystery bags, infinity cubes, tangles and a myriad of other toys intended to support student engagement and performance.   
  
Good intentions aside, in our experience as classroom teachers, sensory toys almost always become a source of distraction — both for the student using the toy and for those nearby. Much like the epicentre of an earthquake, the impact is strongest at the centre and fades slightly with distance. When there are multiple toys in the same classroom, the effect is amplified.

For most teachers, the distraction is obvious, but as Professor Lorraine Hammond always told us *—* *Seek evidence over anecdote*.

In cognitive science terms, there are several issues with how sensory toys affect learning. Sensory memory is the initial gateway for processing incoming information, and it’s dominated by visual and auditory input — together accounting for over 90% of what we take in. Toys that move, make noise, or are brightly coloured draw on those same sensory channels. They compete directly with instructional input — whether that’s a teacher explaining, modelling, or students working independently. This competition for attention matters, because only what we attend to enters working memory, and only then can it be encoded into long-term memory (learned).

![Information Processing Model - Shaping Minds](https://i0.wp.com/shapingminds.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/image-3.png?resize=1024%2C537&ssl=1)

Shaping Minds’ Interpretation of the Information Processing Model

##### **What the research says**

Fidget spinners burst into classrooms with bold claims: calm anxiety, boost focus, improve engagement. But surprisingly, the research is murky, especially in the context of classroom teaching. Most studies in favour of sensory interventions like fidget spinners were based on weaker measures, like students’ self-reported feedback of the toy’s efficacy. In other words, they asked students if it helped rather than measured if it did. Many of the studies also focus on clinical conditions like 1-on-1 and small group settings, not classrooms.

Before they enter our classrooms, we really need to know if the toys actually support learning or undermine it. The following studies seek to answer that:  
  
*[Tools or Toys? The Effect of Fidget Spinners and Bouncy Bands on the Academic Performance in Children With Varying ADHD‑Symptomatology (Driesen et al., 2023)](https://shapingminds.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/The-Effect-of-Fidget-Spinners-and-Bouncy-Bands-on-children-with-ADHD-2023.pdf).* This study tested over 200 primary students using both fidget spinners and bouncy bands. Fidget spinners had a consistently negative impact on academic performance across tasks. Bouncy bands were slightly better but still showed a net negative effect. The researchers concluded that neither tool should be adopted for general classroom use. Importantly, the study highlighted that the novelty and tactile engagement of these tools may actually compete with cognitive resources required for learning.

[*A Multisite Study of the Effect of Fidget Spinners on Academic Performance* (Trout et al., 2020):](https://shapingminds.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Multisite-Study-of-the-Effect-of-Fidget-Spinners-on-Academic-Performance.pdf)Conducted across several schools, this study assessed the effects of fidget spinners on short-form maths assessments. The results showed a clear decrease in performance among students using the spinners compared to those who weren’t. The authors warned that although the tools may be perceived as helpful, they likely act as competing stimuli, drawing attention away from instructional goals.

[*To Fidget or Not to Fidget* (Graziano et al., 2020](https://shapingminds.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Fidget-Article-Graziano-et-al-2020.pdf)[)](https://self-regulationlab.fiu.edu/fidgetarticlegraziano.pdf): This study focused specifically on students diagnosed with ADHD. It found that while there was a small behavioural benefit (such as reduced outbursts or increased initial compliance), the use of fidget spinners nearly doubled attention disruptions — both for the student using the toy and those nearby. The conclusion was clear: the cost to sustained attention outweighed the benefits, and teachers should be cautious in their use.

[*A Systematic Review of Sensory-Based Treatments for Children with Disabilities* (Reichow et al., 2015](https://shapingminds.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Systematic-review-of-sensory-based-treatments-for-children-with-disabilities.pdf)[)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rasd.2014.10.002): This comprehensive review examined a range of sensory interventions, including weighted vests, textured seats, and hand-held fidget toys. The reviewers found no reliable evidence that these tools improved academic outcomes. In fact, in some cases, the interventions had negative effects — either by disrupting routine, drawing attention away from tasks, or by reinforcing off-task behaviour. The authors cautioned against adopting these tools without a clear evidence base and individualised rationale.

##### **What we recommend instead**

We believe first and foremost in the power of effective cues and routines that are steeped in research and real-world success. Combined with the *safety* that teachers embed through their structured and supportive learning environments, this is the foundation of an effective classroom.

**Embed consistent participation routines**  
Tools like the *[Engagement Norms](https://shapingminds.com/posters)* and the [*TAPPLE*](https://shapingminds.com.au/posters) teaching protocol, developed by Hollingsworth and Ybarra, are great examples of tried and tested instructional routines. The key is that the routines need to become automatic for students, so time and effort must be taken to train and embed them. We have used these successfully for years with all kinds of learners.

**Reinforce hands-on learning, not hands-on distractions**  
Encourage students to use their hands for learning by guiding them to engage in gesturing, movement, physical demonstrations, whiteboard responses, pointing, tracking and tracing, and handwritten notetaking. There is significant research supporting each of these including exciting new research from Cognitive Science around handwriting and the brain.

**Maximise thinking and responding to support both engagement and encoding**  
Anita Archer says it best: *“I say something, they say something. I do something, they do something. I write something, they write something… It can never be: I say something… I say something… I say something…”* The more students think and respond, the more they learn. This constant back-and-forth isn’t just about behaviour — it’s about cognition. The more students engage with the content, the deeper it goes. In a similar vein, **Dylan Wiliam** urges teachers to avoid hand-raising and instead use *non-volunteer questioning* and *mini-whiteboards* to keep every student actively involved in the thinking process, not just the eager few.

##### **Final thoughts**

Whole-class instruction is innately complex. Teachers spend their waking lives trying to meet the needs of a diverse group of learners, and to do it every minute of every day is an absolute roller coaster. Teachers strive to maximise the learning for their students, and this often includes minimising the extraneous cognitive load that comes with disruptions. Sensory toys, especially those that use the hands and involve movement and noise, can be a major source of this disruption for both the student using it and the rest of the class.   
  
When it comes to sensory tools in a mainstream classroom, we recommend avoiding them wherever possible. If a sensory toy intervention is insisted upon, try to seek one that creates the least distraction.   
  
— Shaping Minds

# 3 studies argue against fidget spinners in the classroom

Researchers also question the use of other fidget and stress-relieving objects

![Avatar photo](https://hechingerreport.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/cropped-Barshay-headshot-2025-80x80.png)  by [Jill Barshay](https://hechingerreport.org/author/jill-barshay/)

![fidget spinners](https://i2.wp.com/hechingerreport.org/wp-content/uploads/2017/08/Schenker_HopeAcademy-037.jpg?resize=960%2C640&ssl=1)

A student plays with a fidget spinner at school. Three research studies find that the objects detract from learning. Credit: Meryl Schenker for The Hechinger Report

The fidget spinner craze may have come and gone. So 2017, right? But the research process is slow and methodical, and finally in 2019, there is more conclusive evidence that the whirring lobes of plastic are harmful to learning. Results from at least three scientific studies argue against allowing students to use fidget spinners in the classroom — even among children with attention disorders — despite marketing claims that the objects can be helpful.

To be sure, many teachers and school administrators figured out on their own that fidget spinners were a mesmerizing distraction. Some schools [banned them](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/answer-sheet/wp/2017/06/01/schools-are-banning-fidget-spinners-calling-them-nuisances-and-even-dangerous/) from classrooms well before researchers had the proof. Seeking [alternatives](https://blog.schoolspecialty.com/5-alternatives-fidget-spinner/), teachers and students introduced more fidget objects, from squeeze balls to squishy putty, into classrooms. And now top researchers are questioning whether these objects, for which there are many [teacher examples](http://www.weareteachers.com/stress-balls/) online and sometimes [official recommendations](https://www.molineschools.org/apps/pages/index.jsp?uREC_ID=723257&type=d&pREC_ID=1197296) for teachers to use them, are also counterproductive.

“They might not be called a fidget spinner but it’s the same thing,” said Paulo Graziano, director of the S.E.L.F.-Regulation Laboratory at Florida International University. “Kids with ADHD get distracted. And having something that occupies their attention is likely going to take away from them listening to the teacher and doing their work.”

“Just like with the fidget spinner, you would think they could just spin it in their hands while looking up at the teacher,” Graziano explained to me in an interview. “What we found is no, kids like to see it happening in their hands. So they’re looking down at whatever their hands are holding. If there’s a fun squeezy ball — I haven’t seen a study on it — but my impression is that they’re also looking down at it to see what’s going on….I would strongly recommend against any of these devices.”

First, the evidence. The newest study, “[Putting a negative spin on it](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/acp.3610?af=R),” published online Oct. 26, 2019 in the Journal of Applied Cognitive Psychology, looked at what happened when researchers randomly gave fidget spinners to college students and had them watch educational videos in a laboratory setting at the University of California, Santa Cruz. One video was about the Hawaiian ruler Kamehameha the Great. Another was about baking bread. Those who had fidget spinners in their hands scored worse on a memory test about the videos afterward. Even students who said they liked fidget spinners and found them helpful suffered from memory impairment.

**Related: [Teachers often ask youngsters to learn in ways that exceed even adult-sized attention spans](https://hechingerreport.org/teachers-often-ask-youngsters-learn-ways-exceed-even-adult-sized-attention-spans/)**

A [German study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41465-019-00124-9) published in January 2019 found that both fidget spinners and doodling impaired memory. But stress balls didn’t negatively affect memory. Still, they didn’t help.

Graziano, the skeptic I quoted above, was one of the first researchers to come out with a scientific study of fidget spinners, titled “[To Fidget or Not to Fidget, That is the Question,](https://self-regulationlab.fiu.edu/fidgetarticlegraziano.pdf)” and published in the Journal of Attention Disorders in 2018. He decided to study fidget spinners in 2016 after his then five-year-old daughter asked for them for Christmas. He was surprised by the marketing claims that the toys can help kids with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism and anxiety.  He was an expert in research into early interventions for children with behavior disorders, especially ADHD, and had never heard that. When he went to look for the research, “there wasn’t any,” Graziano recalled to me in an interview. “It was false marketing.”

Unlike the 2019 studies that didn’t test the devices on students with disabilities, Graziano specifically wanted to know if fidget spinners helped younger children with ADHD. He randomly gave fidget spinners to preschoolers who were attending a summer treatment program. All the children were videotaped  and researchers watched, coded and counted all the kids’ behaviors. The kids who received fidget spinners had many more moments of inattentiveness. “Attention was definitely impacted by the spinner in a bad way,” said Graziano. “It was harmful. They were more inattentive.”

But those who got the fidget spinners were less hyperactive —  *initially*. They didn’t run around as much as the other campers who didn’t get the spinners. That behavioral advantage disappeared four weeks later, however, when Graziano handed the spinners out a second time to the same randomly selected group of kids. At the end of the summer program. the two groups — spinners and non-spinners — were equally hyperactive.  (However, the behavior of both the spinners and and the non-spinners improved during the treatment program.)

In sum, Graziano found that while there may be a small behavioral benefit to handing a restless kid a fidget spinner, it is short lived, and outweighed by the harm to the child’s attentiveness.

So what is the source of the marketing claims that fidget spinners can improve focus? Graziano dug into the research history more and found [studies](https://psy.fsu.edu/clc/Publications/CLC_Rapport2009.pdf) showing that the fidgety movements that kids with ADHD sometimes do with their whole bodies can help their cognitive performance in laboratory experiments. Graziano said that the theory is that these excess body movements arouse the prefrontal cortex of their brains, jolting their brains to stay attentive. Why someone thought that a spinning object in the hands might have the same salutary effect on the brain as the whole body fidgeting is anyone’s guess. It’s a leap.

**Related: [A cheaper, quicker approach to social-emotional learning?](https://hechingerreport.org/a-cheaper-quicker-approach-to-social-emotional-learning/)**

How to handle restless, fidgety kids who have trouble paying attention is an important question for educators. Graziano says the evidence-based literature advises teachers to sit these children in front of the class and give them a lot of positive reinforcement and praise for staying on task. Assigning them active classroom jobs, such as being the door opener, can help too.

In other words, good classroom management skills work. What educators need is more research evidence for how to help kids pay attention. I wish that more education researchers would focus on this and perhaps with the current mania for “social-emotional learning,” more researchers will. Handing kids a fidget toy is easy. Teaching them to build their attention spans and focus is much harder.

## Abstract

This study addresses the research gap concerning whether the use of fidget toys or fidget spinners specifically are perceived to support children and positively influence their behavioural and emotional wellbeing as well as investigating how these perceptions relate to children’s sensory-seeking profiles. 129 parents/carers of autistic children (_n_ = 53) and neurotypical (NT) children (_n_ = 76) completed an online survey. The survey consisted of questions relating to the benefits and risks of fidget toys as well as statements about their own child’s fidget toy use. The Sensory Profile 2 was used to obtain parents perspectives on their child’s sensory behaviours. The main findings demonstrated that parents of autistic children perceived fidget toys and fidget spinners to be overall more beneficial than NT parents, especially in relation to reducing anxiety. Higher sensory-seeking scores for both autistic children and NT children were associated with greater parental agreement for fidget toys and fidget spinners being beneficial. Parents of autistic children with higher sensory seeking scores found fidget toys to reduce anxiety and spinners to be less distracting. Whereas, parents of NT children with higher sensory seeking scores perceived both fidget toys and spinners to help their child concentrate. Implications include that educators should consider parental views when forming policies about the use of fidget toys. Findings also imply that the sensory profiles of autistic and NT students should be considered in relation to the use of fidget toys.
