# TEACCH Method for Autism

August 26, 2024

Discover the TEACCH method, a game-changer in autism treatment. From structured teaching to parental involvement, unlock potential!

![TEACCH Method for Autism](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/66829f0f56d3ae52ec83c2d7/66b6c277b9d9de0992cf2ff0_teachh.jpg)

## Understanding the TEACCH Method

The TEACCH method, which stands for the Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children, is a structured form of visual learning specifically designed for children with autism spectrum disorder. Developed over 50 years ago by Doctors Robert Reichler and Eric Schopler at the University of North Carolina, the TEACCH method focuses on the individual needs, interests, and skills of children with autism to promote autonomy and independence.

### Origin and Development

The TEACCH method was developed in the 1960s at the University of North Carolina by Dr. Eric Schopler and Dr. Robert Reichler. It was created as a structured approach to visual learning, often referred to as Structured Teaching. The method aims to provide individuals with autism the necessary tools and strategies to navigate their environment and promote their overall development [[1]](#).

### Effectiveness Across Autism Severity Levels

One of the significant advantages of the TEACCH method is its effectiveness across different levels of autism severity. The structured and individualized approach can be tailored to meet the unique needs of individuals with autism at any level of severity. Whether a child is high-functioning or has more significant challenges, the TEACCH method can be adapted to their specific requirements [[1]](#).

The TEACCH method also complements other therapeutic approaches commonly used for individuals with autism, such as speech therapy. By focusing on individualized skill development, the TEACCH method can enhance language development alongside other forms of intervention.

By employing the TEACCH method, children with autism can benefit from a structured and visual learning environment that caters to their unique needs and promotes their autonomy and independence. In the following sections, we will explore the implementation and benefits of the TEACCH method, as well as the research supporting its effectiveness in improving social skills and adaptive behaviors.

## Implementing TEACCH Programs

When it comes to implementing the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children) method, there are two key aspects to consider: its applicability across ages and skill levels, and the importance of multidisciplinary team involvement.

### Applicability Across Ages and Skill Levels

One of the strengths of the TEACCH method is its wide applicability across individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) of varying ages and skill levels. Whether a child is diagnosed with ASD at a young age or later in life, the TEACCH approach can be tailored to meet their specific needs and developmental stage. This flexibility allows for individualized instruction and support, promoting the child's autonomy and independence.

The TEACCH method recognizes that individuals with ASD have unique learning styles and preferences. It emphasizes structured teaching that takes into account the child's strengths, interests, and abilities. By creating a structured environment and using visual supports, the method helps individuals with ASD navigate daily tasks, develop skills, and enhance their communication and social interactions.

### Multidisciplinary Team Involvement

Implementing the TEACCH method effectively requires the involvement of a multidisciplinary team. This team typically includes professionals such as psychologists, special education teachers, speech therapists, social workers, and residential care providers [[1]](#). Each member of the team brings unique expertise and perspectives, contributing to a comprehensive and holistic approach to supporting individuals with ASD.

Collaboration among team members is crucial in developing and implementing TEACCH programs. By working together, they can create individualized intervention plans that address the specific needs and goals of the individual with ASD. Regular communication and coordination ensure that the strategies used in various settings, such as home and school, are consistent and reinforce learning.

To ensure the highest quality of TEACCH implementation, professionals can undergo certification programs offered by the TEACCH Autism Program in North Carolina. These programs offer two certification levels: Practitioner and Advanced Consultant. Certification provides professionals with the necessary knowledge and skills to effectively apply the TEACCH method in their practice, further enhancing the outcomes for individuals with ASD.

By embracing the applicability of the TEACCH method across ages and skill levels, and involving a multidisciplinary team, individuals with ASD can receive effective support tailored to their unique needs. The collaborative efforts of professionals from different disciplines ensure a comprehensive and well-rounded approach to promoting the development and independence of individuals with ASD.

## Training and Certification

To effectively implement the TEACCH method and provide quality services to individuals with autism, professionals undergo specific training and certification programs. These programs equip them with the necessary knowledge and skills to implement the TEACCH method successfully.

### Providers of TEACCH Services

TEACCH services are provided by a multidisciplinary team of professionals who specialize in autism treatment. These professionals may include psychologists, special education teachers, social workers, speech therapists, and residential care providers. Working together, they create a comprehensive approach to support individuals with autism in various settings.

### Certification Requirements and Options

Professionals who wish to implement the TEACCH method can undergo certification programs offered by the TEACCH Autism Program in North Carolina. These programs provide in-depth training and ensure that professionals are equipped with the necessary skills to effectively apply the TEACCH method.

The TEACCH certification program offers two levels of certification: Practitioner and Advanced Consultant. The Practitioner level certification equips professionals with the foundational knowledge and skills required to implement the TEACCH method. The Advanced Consultant level certification is designed for professionals who have extensive experience and advanced knowledge in working with individuals with autism using the TEACCH approach [[3]](#).

By completing the certification programs, professionals demonstrate their commitment to providing evidence-based interventions and ensuring the highest quality of care for individuals with autism. The certification process may involve both online and in-person components, allowing professionals to gain theoretical knowledge and practical experience in implementing the TEACCH method.

These certified professionals play a vital role in the successful implementation of the TEACCH method, working collaboratively with families, schools, and other professionals to create structured environments that support individuals with autism in their daily lives.

The training and certification of professionals ensure that the TEACCH method is implemented effectively and consistently, promoting positive outcomes for individuals with autism.

## Research on TEACCH Method

The TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication-handicapped Children) method has been the subject of extensive research, exploring its impact on various aspects of autism treatment. This section highlights two key areas of research: the impact of the TEACCH method on social skills and perception, as well as studies supporting the development of adaptive behaviors.

### Impact on Social Skills and Perception

The TEACCH method utilizes visual cues and structured teaching to make learning more accessible for individuals on the autism spectrum, including non-verbal children. By incorporating visual supports and individualized approaches, the TEACCH method aims to help children acquire social skills and positively change their perception of social settings.

Research has shown that the TEACCH method can have a significant impact on the development of social skills in individuals with autism. By using visual aids and structured environments, the TEACCH method provides individuals with a clearer understanding of social cues, rules, and expectations. This enhanced understanding contributes to improved social interactions, communication, and engagement.

### Studies Supporting Adaptive Behaviors

Numerous studies have supported the effectiveness of the TEACCH method in promoting adaptive behaviors among individuals with autism. Adaptive behaviors refer to the skills necessary for daily life functioning, including self-care, communication, social interactions, and problem-solving.

Research has demonstrated that the structured teaching approach employed in the TEACCH method can lead to significant improvements in adaptive behaviors. By providing a predictable sequence of activities, visual schedules, and work/activity systems, the TEACCH method enhances individuals' abilities to organize tasks, follow routines, and transition between activities. These skills contribute to increased independence and improved overall functioning.

The use of visual supports, such as schedules, charts, and visual cues, plays a crucial role in the TEACCH method. Visual aids enhance understanding, aid in transitioning between activities, and facilitate comprehension of tasks for individuals with autism. The visual structure provided by these supports helps individuals navigate their environment and engage in activities more effectively.

By incorporating evidence-based practices and principles, the TEACCH method continues to be a valuable tool in autism treatment, supporting the development of social skills, adaptive behaviors, and overall independence.

## Parental Role in TEACCH

Parents play a crucial role in the implementation of the TEACCH method, as they are trained to apply this approach at home. The TEACCH method, which stands for the Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children method, was specifically developed for children with autism spectrum disorder [[4]](#). Implementing TEACCH strategies at home provides numerous benefits for both parents and children.

### Home Implementation of TEACCH

When parents are trained and equipped to apply the TEACCH method at home, they become active participants in their child's treatment and education. By incorporating TEACCH strategies into daily routines, parents create a structured environment that supports the child's learning and development. This involves implementing visual supports, organizing tasks and activities, and promoting independence.

The use of visual cues is a fundamental aspect of the TEACCH method. Visual aids, such as visual schedules, visual task lists, and visual supports for communication, make learning more accessible, especially for non-verbal children with autism. These visual tools serve as a universal language, providing clear and consistent information to the child about expectations and routines. By incorporating visual supports at home, parents can enhance the child's understanding, independence, and engagement in daily activities.

Parents are encouraged to collaborate with professionals involved in the child's TEACCH program to ensure consistency and continuity across different settings. Communication and coordination with teachers, therapists, and other members of the multidisciplinary team are essential to create a cohesive approach that supports the child's progress.

### Benefits for Parents and Children

Implementing the TEACCH method at home brings several benefits for both parents and children. When parents are trained and able to apply the TEACCH strategies effectively, the child's behaviors become more adaptive in their everyday routines. This leads to a decrease in parental stress as parents gain confidence in supporting their child's needs.

Furthermore, the TEACCH method promotes the child's independence and improved social integration. By creating a structured and supportive environment, parents provide opportunities for their child to develop essential skills, enhance their communication abilities, and foster independence in daily activities. This, in turn, contributes to the child's overall well-being and quality of life.

In summary, the TEACCH method recognizes the vital role parents play in the treatment and education of children with autism spectrum disorder. By implementing TEACCH strategies at home, parents create a structured environment that supports their child's learning and development. This involvement not only benefits the child by promoting adaptive behaviors and independence but also provides parents with the tools and confidence to support their child's unique needs.

## Structured Teaching in TEACCH

Structured teaching is a fundamental component of the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children) method, which aims to support individuals with autism in learning and development. By incorporating principles such as the organization of the physical environment, predictable sequence of activities, and visually structured activities, the TEACCH method provides a structured framework for individuals with autism to thrive.

### Principles of Structured Environment

In the TEACCH method, the physical organization of the classroom or learning environment plays a crucial role in supporting autistic students. The layout of the space, including furniture arrangement and visual cues, can significantly impact a student's independent functioning, recognition of rules, and compliance with limits. By structuring the environment with visual supports, such as visual schedules, task boards, and choice boards, individuals with autism can better understand and anticipate daily activities, tasks, and expectations.

A structured environment helps create a sense of predictability and reduces distractions, allowing individuals with autism to focus on tasks and learning. Visual cues, such as visual schedules and visual boundaries, provide clear and consistent information, assisting students in understanding their surroundings and navigating their daily routines [[6]](#).

### Importance of Visual Supports

Visual supports are essential components of the TEACCH method, aiding individuals with autism in comprehending and participating in activities. Visual supports can take various forms, including visual schedules, task boards, choice boards, and visual cues. These visual tools help individuals with autism better understand and anticipate daily activities, tasks, and expectations, reducing anxiety and promoting independence.

Visual schedules, in particular, are crucial for individuals with autism. They provide a visual representation of the sequence of activities, allowing individuals to comprehend and prepare for upcoming events. By following a visual schedule, individuals with autism can transition between activities smoothly and gain a sense of control and predictability in their daily routines.

Task boards and choice boards are additional visual supports that provide individuals with autism with clear instructions and options. Task boards break down activities into steps, helping individuals understand the expectations and complete tasks more independently. Choice boards offer a visual array of options, empowering individuals to make choices and express their preferences.

By utilizing visual supports, teachers and parents can enhance communication, comprehension, and independence for individuals with autism. These visual tools provide a visual structure that supports understanding, reduces anxiety, and promotes engagement in various learning activities.

Structured teaching, encompassing the principles of a structured environment and the use of visual supports, is an integral part of the TEACCH method. By implementing these strategies, teachers and parents can create an environment that supports the learning and development of individuals with autism, promoting their independence, engagement, and overall well-being.

args.summary:
This webpage provides a comprehensive overview of the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children) method for autism. Published August 26, 2024, the article describes TEACCH as a structured visual learning approach for children with autism spectrum disorder, developed in the 1960s at the University of North Carolina by Drs. Robert Reichler and Eric Schopler. 

Key points covered include:
- TEACCH is effective across all autism severity levels and can be tailored to individual needs, complementing other therapies like speech therapy.
- The method applies to individuals of varying ages and skill levels, emphasizing individualized instruction.
- Implementation involves a multidisciplinary team including psychologists, special education teachers, speech therapists, social workers, and residential care providers.
- Certification is available through the TEACCH Autism Program in North Carolina, offering two levels: Practitioner and Advanced Consultant.
- Research supports TEACCH's impact on social skills, perception, and adaptive behaviors; visual supports like schedules, charts, and visual cues are central to the approach.
- Parents are trained to implement TEACCH at home, creating structured environments that decrease parental stress and promote child independence and social integration.
- Structured teaching principles include physical environment organization, predictable activity sequences, and visually structured activities; visual supports (schedules, task boards, choice boards) reduce anxiety and promote comprehension and independence.

The article was published by a New Jersey-based site (the blog also features many related articles on DIR Floortime therapy and autism resources in NJ and Illinois).

[![mastermind behavior service logo](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe12d/66acc623619ab98795f4c99a_Mastermind.avif)](/)

# How Structured Teaching Methods Benefit Children with ASD

Transforming Autism Education Through Structured Strategies

![](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a2e76823f9feeabc203e479_mastermind.avif)

Mastermind Behavior Clinical Team

April 29, 2025

![How Structured Teaching Methods Benefit Children with ASD  ](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6627fd62e242d50407cfe155/6a551aa7af3d385f91919911_6a551aa5bb55a3fb0add1809_6a3a8e5794115a24a1be77db_6a3a8c981d0d37d846636c9f_structured-teaching-methods-be-1400.webp)

Your seven-year-old won't put on his shoes. The bus comes in twelve minutes. Yesterday this took three reminders; today he's curled up next to the front door and won't move. You're not failing — the routine just shifted slightly, and that small change is enough to derail the morning. Structured teaching is what behavior analysts and educators use to make moments like this predictable instead of explosive. The most well-known approach is TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children), and the principles behind it — visual schedules, organized spaces, clear sequences — show up across most quality classrooms and [in-home ABA therapy](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/in-home-aba-therapy) programs serving children with autism.

## Understanding Structured Teaching for Children with ASD

Structured teaching for children with ASD, such as the TEACCH method, is a well-researched approach that creates an organized, predictable environment to support learning and behavior. It emphasizes using visual aids, routines, visual schedules, and physical organization to help children understand expectations, manage transitions, and develop independence. The method involves individualized plans, visual supports, and work systems that clarify tasks, reduce anxiety, and promote participation in academic and daily activities.

Key elements include adapting the classroom environment, establishing consistent routines, and collaborating with parents to reinforce strategies at home. Overall, structured teaching aims to enhance social skills, reduce disruptive behaviors, and foster inclusion in mainstream settings by addressing the unique strengths and needs of each child.

### Why do students with ASD require a comprehensible and structured learning environment?

Children with ASD often experience difficulties with transitions, unpredictable routines, and sensory overload, which can lead to increased anxiety and challenging behaviors. A well-structured environment provides predictability, helping students feel secure and enabling them to focus on learning.

Incorporating sensory-friendly spaces and tools, such as fidget toys and quiet areas for breaks, also supports sensory regulation. [Visual aids, like picture schedules and cue cards](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/post/the-importance-of-visual-learning-tools-in-autism-education), are essential because they supplement verbal instructions and offer lasting visual references, reducing confusion and helping children understand daily routines and expectations.

### Why is structure important for children with ASD?

Structure offers stability and consistency, which are crucial for children with ASD to navigate their daily activities with confidence. Routines help them anticipate upcoming events, decreasing anxiety related to uncertainty. The physical organization of learning spaces minimizes distractions, allowing children to concentrate and participate more fully.

Furthermore, structured routines assist in developing independence and self-regulation skills by providing clear sequences of activities. A predictable environment fosters a sense of safety, promotes engagement, and supports better social and behavioral outcomes.

### What principles underpin structured teaching methods for children with ASD, such as TEACCH?

The foundation of structured teaching methods like TEACCH rests on creating environments that are organized and predictable, tailored to the neuropsychological profile of children with ASD. These strategies leverage the strength many autistic children have in visual processing, making visual supports central to instruction.

Principles include establishing consistent routines, using visual schedules, and designing physical environments that are clear and uncluttered. Visual cues—such as pictures, icons, and written instructions—help children recognize what comes next and understand expectations. Individualized work systems are incorporated to clarify tasks and enable children to complete activities independently.

This approach also emphasizes collaboration with families and caregivers to reinforce routines and strategies outside of the classroom, making the environment more comprehensible and manageable across settings. Overall, structured teaching aims to reduce anxiety, promote independence, and improve learning and social interactions by respecting each child's unique needs and strengths.

## Implementation Components of Structured Teaching

Effective teaching strategies for children with autism focus on creating structured, visually-supported, and predictable learning environments. Visual supports such as schedules, diagrams, and social stories are used to enhance understanding, foster independence, and reduce anxiety. Using concrete, simple language alongside clear instructions helps facilitate better communication and comprehension.

Creating sensory-friendly environments is also essential. This includes appropriate lighting, calming spaces, and minimizing sensory overload, which can otherwise hinder learning. Positive reinforcement techniques, such as praise or token economies, encourage desired behaviors and engagement.

Furthermore, establishing consistent routines and proactive behavior management techniques contribute significantly to social-emotional development and behavior regulation. Collaboration with families and applying evidence-based practices, like those from programs such as the Incredible Years, provide comprehensive support. Overall, these strategies collectively help children with autism reach their full potential in educational settings.

### What are evidence-based practices for teaching children with autism?

Evidence-based practices in autism education are grounded in research and include the use of visual supports, structured routines, and positive reinforcement strategies. Tailoring interventions to each child's unique needs while promoting dignity and independence is fundamental. These practices avoid punitive methods and controversial biomedical treatments.

Play-based learning and social skills training are highly recommended, with guidelines from organizations like NICE endorsing their effectiveness. Sensory accommodations, including tools and strategies to manage sensitivities, are also crucial components.

Interventions should be implemented by trained professionals such as speech, occupational, and behavioral therapists to ensure appropriateness and safety. Employing scientifically supported methods ensures educational practices are effective and respectful for children with autism.

### What principles underpin structured teaching methods for children with ASD, such as TEACCH?

Structured teaching methods like TEACCH are guided by principles that emphasize the importance of creating organized, predictable environments tailored to each child's needs. One core principle is leveraging the visual strengths of many children with autism by incorporating visual supports such as schedules, cues, and written instructions.

Establishing consistent routines and clear activity sequencing helps reduce anxiety and confusion, promoting greater independence. The physical setup of the environment—arranged to minimize distractions and clarify expectations—is a fundamental aspect.

Additionally, individualized work systems are implemented to guide children effectively through tasks, supporting their ability to plan and complete activities independently. The overarching aim is to optimize learning and daily functioning by accommodating the cognitive and behavioral characteristics of children with ASD, fostering skills that promote community participation and self-efficacy.

## Research Evidence Supporting Structured Teaching Effectiveness

Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often face challenges with unpredictability, sensory sensitivities, and difficulties in understanding social cues. A structured learning environment provides predictability and clear expectations, helping reduce anxiety and promoting a sense of safety. Effective strategies include incorporating sensory-friendly spaces, such as quiet areas or sensory breaks with tools like fidget toys, to help children manage sensory overload.

Visual aids play a central role in structured settings. Visual schedules, picture cues, and visual instructions make routines predictable and understandable, supporting children in following activities and transitioning smoothly between tasks. This clear structure not only alleviates stress but also fosters independence and engagement.

### What strategies and components of structured teaching approaches, such as TEACCH and visual supports, promote independence and skill development?

Structured teaching hinges on four fundamental components: the physical environment, visual schedules, visual structure, and work systems.

* **Physical Environment:** Arranged to minimize distractions, with designated areas for different activities, facilitating clarity and focus.
* **Visual Schedules:** Clearly outline daily routines, helping children anticipate what comes next and organize their day.
* **Visual Structure:** Use of cues, color-coding, and pictorial guides to enhance understanding and recall.
* **Work Systems:** Step-by-step visual and physical cues that guide children through tasks, helping them complete activities independently.

By integrating these elements, children grasp routines, understand expectations, and [develop essential skills](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/skill-development) more effectively. The visual focus aligns with many ASD children's learning preferences, promoting mastery of new skills and increasing autonomy.

### Impact of structured teaching methods on developmental and educational outcomes for children with ASD?

Research compiled in a 2018 report by the Autism CRC underscores the positive impact of structured teaching. Studies indicate significant improvements in cognition, motor skills, and social competencies. Children demonstrate increased on-task behavior, meaning they stay engaged longer in learning activities.

Moreover, structured environments have been shown to reduce disruptive behaviors by providing predictability and consistency. These environments also promote inclusion, enabling children with ASD to participate more fully in mainstream classrooms, which enhances their social interactions and acceptance among peers.

Over time, these benefits contribute to better [developmental outcomes](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/skill-development), including independence, communication, and academic achievement, supporting children's overall growth and well-being.

### What evidence-based practices and research support structured teaching techniques?

Structured teaching's effectiveness is bolstered by a substantial body of research—over 150 peer-reviewed studies—that document its benefits. Key findings include improvements in understanding routines, reducing challenging behaviors, and fostering independence.

Organizations like the Autism CRC endorse these practices, emphasizing their reliability in educational settings. They highlight visual supports, organized environments, and routine-based interventions as central to successful implementation.

Professional reviews reveal that when these techniques are tailored to individual needs through proper assessment, their benefits are maximized. They are often combined with other evidence-based practices, such as [Applied Behavioral Analysis (ABA)](https://www.mastermindbehavior.com/in-home-aba-therapy) and social skills training, further enhancing their impact.

### How does structured teaching in inclusive classrooms benefit children with ASD and their peers?

Implementing structured teaching in mainstream settings fosters an inclusive culture. Organized, predictable environments help reduce feelings of marginalization among children with ASD, allowing them to participate meaningfully in group activities.

Such environments promote social interaction and understanding between children with ASD and their neurotypical peers. Structured routines provide shared experiences that encourage peer engagement, social skills development, and mutual respect.

Furthermore, inclusive classrooms equipped with visual supports and clear structure benefit all students—improving overall organization and behavior. They create a respectful atmosphere where diversity is valued and understood, promoting social acceptance and long-term inclusive attitudes.

| Aspect | Benefits | Supporting Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developmental Outcomes | Improved cognition, motor skills, social skills | Autism CRC 2018 report |
| Behavior Management | Increased on-task behavior, decreased disruptive acts | Multiple peer-reviewed studies |
| Inclusion and Social Skills | Better peer interactions, reduced marginalization | Research on inclusive education environments |
| Teacher and Student Satisfaction | Higher engagement, positive classroom climate | Educator reports and learner assessments |

Research continues to affirm that structured teaching strategies promote meaningful learning experiences for children with autism, fostering independence, inclusion, and developmental progress across diverse educational contexts.

## Empowering Inclusion through Organized Education

Structured teaching methods, built on a foundation of research and tailored to each child's needs, have proven to be invaluable in supporting children with ASD. These strategies reduce anxiety, promote independence, and improve academic and social outcomes. args.summary:
This webpage from Mastermind Behavior (a BCBA-owned in-home ABA therapy provider serving New Jersey, Georgia, and North Carolina) explains how structured teaching methods benefit children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). The most well-known approach is TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children), which emphasizes visual schedules, organized spaces, and clear sequences.

Key points about why structure matters for children with ASD:
- Children with ASD experience difficulties with transitions, unpredictable routines, and sensory overload, leading to anxiety and challenging behaviors
- Structure provides predictability, stability, and consistency, helping children feel secure and navigate daily activities with confidence
- Visual aids supplement verbal instructions and provide lasting visual references that reduce confusion

Core principles of structured teaching (TEACCH):
- Leverage the visual processing strengths common in children with ASD
- Establish consistent routines and clear activity sequencing
- Design clear, uncluttered physical environments that minimize distractions
- Use visual cues such as pictures, icons, and written instructions
- Implement individualized work systems so children can complete tasks independently
- Collaborate with families and caregivers to reinforce strategies outside the classroom

The four fundamental components of structured teaching include:
1. Physical Environment - arranged to minimize distractions with designated areas for activities
2. Visual Schedules - outline daily routines to help children anticipate what comes next
3. Visual Structure - cues, color-coding, and pictorial guides to enhance understanding
4. Work Systems - step-by-step visual and physical cues guiding children through tasks

Research evidence:
- A 2018 Autism CRC report documents significant improvements in cognition, motor skills, and social competencies
- Studies show increased on-task behavior and reduced disruptive behaviors through predictability
- Over 150 peer-reviewed studies document the benefits of structured teaching
- Structured environments promote inclusion in mainstream classrooms and benefit all students
- Evidence-based practices include visual supports, structured routines, positive reinforcement, play-based learning, and social skills training
- Guidelines from organizations like NICE endorse play-based learning and social skills training effectiveness

The page concludes by promoting Mastermind Behavior's services, noting their 90%+ staff retention rate, no onboarding waitlist, and that most families begin services within six weeks of initial assessment. Contact number: 732.813.7333.

*   •Effects on communication, ADL, and motor functioning were negligible or small. 
*   •Gains in social and maladaptive behavior were larger but need further replication. 
*   •Our analysis should be considered exploratory owing to the limited data available. 

## Abstract

The intervention program for autism known as Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children (TEACCH) is considered an emerging practice for autism. In the present study we used state-of-the-art meta-analytical procedures to examine the pooled clinical effects of TEACCH in a variety of outcomes. A total of 13 studies were selected for meta-analysis totaling 172 individuals with autism exposed to TEACCH. Standardized measures of perceptual, motor, adaptive, verbal and cognitive skills were identified as treatment outcomes. We used inverse-variance weighted random effects meta-analysis supplemented with quality assessment, sensitivity analysis, meta-regression, and heterogeneity and publication bias tests. The results suggested that TEACCH effects on perceptual, motor, verbal and cognitive skills were of small magnitude in the meta-analyzed studies. Effects over adaptive behavioral repertoires including communication, activities of daily living, and motor functioning were within the negligible to small range. There were moderate to large gains in social behavior and maladaptive behavior. The effects of the TEACCH program were not moderated by aspects of the intervention such as duration (total weeks), intensity (hours per week), and setting (home-based vs. center-based). While the present meta-analysis provided limited support for the TEACCH program as a comprehensive intervention, our results should be considered exploratory owing to the limited pool of studies available.

This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Clinical Psychology Review (Volume 33, Issue 8, December 2013, pages 940-953, DOI: 10.1016/j.cpr.2013.07.005) by Javier Virues-Ortega, Flávia M. Julio, and Roberto Pastor-Barriuso. The study examines the clinical effectiveness of the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children) program for individuals with autism, which is considered an emerging practice for the disorder.

METHODOLOGY: The researchers used state-of-the-art meta-analytical procedures including inverse-variance weighted random effects meta-analysis, supplemented with quality assessment, sensitivity analysis, meta-regression, and heterogeneity and publication bias tests. A total of 13 studies were included, involving 172 individuals with autism exposed to TEACCH. Standardized measures of perceptual, motor, adaptive, verbal, and cognitive skills were identified as treatment outcomes.

RESULTS: The meta-analysis found that TEACCH effects on perceptual, motor, verbal, and cognitive skills were of small magnitude. Effects on adaptive behavioral repertoires including communication, activities of daily living, and motor functioning were in the negligible to small range. However, there were moderate to large gains in social behavior and maladaptive behavior. The effects of TEACCH were NOT moderated by intervention duration (total weeks), intensity (hours per week), or setting (home-based vs. center-based).

CONCLUSIONS: The study provided limited support for the TEACCH program as a comprehensive intervention for autism, though the authors caution that results should be considered exploratory due to the limited pool of studies available. The article has been cited 178 times and has received 16 policy citations, 809 Mendeley readers, and 1 blog mention and 1 news mention.

# 结构化教学（TEACCH）是什么？孤独症视觉支持与家庭实操指南

· 王伟 · 恩启创始人

根据美国北卡罗来纳大学TEACCH项目中心2024年发布的报告，全球已有超过50个国家的康复机构采用TEACCH方法为孤独症儿童提供教育和干预服务。2022年发表在《Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders》上的一项Meta分析显示，**接受TEACCH干预的孤独症儿童在独立完成任务的能力上提升了34%**。在中国，TEACCH的核心理念——视觉支持和结构化环境设计——正在被越来越多的特殊教育机构、康复中心和家庭采纳和应用。本文将为家长系统讲解TEACCH的理论基础、三大核心原则、家庭环境布置的5步实操方法和常见误区，帮助家长快速上手并持续优化和调整。

声明：本文内容基于教育视角，不构成医疗建议。涉及诊断、治疗等医学问题，请咨询专业医生或发育行为儿科专家。

TEACCH与ABA、DIR/地板时光并列为孤独症领域最具影响力的三大干预方法。不同于ABA的回合式教学和DIR的关系导向，TEACCH的核心优势在于：**它不需要孩子具备高水平的语言能力，也不需要密集的一对一教学**。通过环境设计和视觉提示，孤独症儿童可以在相对独立的状态下完成任务，获得成就感和自主性。

## TEACCH到底是什么？它和ABA有什么不同？

TEACCH全称为Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children（孤独症及相关沟通障碍儿童的治疗与教育项目），由美国北卡罗来纳大学Eric Schopler教授于1969年首次开发和推广。根据[北卡罗来纳大学TEACCH项目中心](https://teacch.com/)的介绍，TEACCH的核心理念是：**利用孤独症儿童的视觉学习优势，通过结构化的物理环境和任务设计，帮助他们理解环境期望、独立完成任务**。

### TEACCH vs ABA：两种截然不同的干预哲学

很多家长问”TEACCH和ABA哪个好”。根据[美国国家心理卫生研究所（NIMH）](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/autism-spectrum-disorders-children)的评估，两种方法各有优势，不是替代关系而是互补关系。ABA侧重于通过强化和重复训练建立新技能，需要密集的一对一教学；TEACCH侧重于通过环境设计支持独立行为，更强调孩子的自主性。在恩启的实践中，我们通常将两种方法结合使用——ABA用于技能教学，TEACCH用于技能在日常生活中的泛化和独立应用。

| 对比维度 | TEACCH | ABA |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 核心理念 | 环境适应孩子 | 孩子适应环境要求 |
| 教学形式 | 结构化独立任务 | 回合式一对一教学（DTT） |
| 主要沟通方式 | 视觉支持（图片、实物） | 语言指令+强化 |
| 孩子参与度 | 自主完成任务 | 跟随指令回应 |
| 适合人群 | 语言能力有限、视觉学习者 | 各能力水平的孤独症儿童 |
| 实施场景 | 家庭、学校、社区 | 机构为主，家庭辅助 |
| 培训门槛 | 家长易上手 | 需专业培训和督导 |

在恩启的干预实践中，我们发现一个有趣的现象：**很多在ABA教学中表现优异的孩子，一旦离开教学环境就”不会做”了**。这就是泛化问题。TEACCH恰好弥补了这个短板——通过结构化的环境设计，孩子可以在没有教学者提示的情况下独立完成任务。因此，TEACCH不是ABA的替代品，而是ABA技能泛化的关键桥梁。

## TEACCH的三大核心原则分别是什么？

### 原则一：物理结构化——让环境”会说话”

物理结构化是指通过家具摆放、区域划分和边界设置，让孩子清楚地知道”哪里做什么”。根据[美国CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/autism/hcp-des.html)的家庭支持指南，一个结构化的学习环境可以显著减少孤独症儿童的焦虑和问题行为。具体做法：用书架或地垫划分”学习区””游戏区””休息区”；每个区域只放与该区域活动相关的物品；学习区的桌子面向墙壁（减少视觉干扰），椅子有明确的”坐”的位置标记。

### 原则二：视觉结构化——用”看”代替”听”

孤独症儿童通常是视觉学习者——他们”看到”的理解远好于”听到”的理解。视觉结构化包括三个层面：**视觉日程表**（用图片或文字展示一天的活动顺序）、**视觉工作系统**（用图片/颜色/编号告诉孩子”做什么、做多少、做完了做什么”）、**视觉提示卡**（在特定位置放置提示图片，如洗手台旁贴洗手步骤图）。恩启的干预师通常会在第一次家访时就帮助家庭制作一套基础视觉支持材料。

### 原则三：工作系统——让孩子”独立工作”

工作系统是TEACCH最具特色的实操工具。一个完整的视觉工作系统需要回答4个问题：**①做什么任务？**（从左到右排列的任务篮）**②做多少？**（每个篮子里有固定数量的材料，如3个拼图块）**③怎么知道做完了？**（用绿色”完成”标记或完成盒）**④做完之后做什么？**（视觉日程表上的下一个活动图片）。当这4个问题都被清晰回答时，孩子可以在没有大人提示的情况下独立完成任务。

## 家庭如何布置TEACCH结构化环境？分步实操指南

在恩启15年的家庭干预实践中，我们总结了家庭TEACCH环境布置的5个步骤。这些步骤不需要专业工具或大量费用，普通家庭就可以完成。

1. **第一步：观察孩子的日常动线**。记录孩子一天中在哪些区域活动、每个区域做什么、在哪些环节出现焦虑或问题行为。这些数据是环境调整的基础。
2. **第二步：划分功能区域**。至少划分3个区域：学习区（安静、桌面整洁）、游戏区（玩具分类收纳）、休息区（柔软的垫子或沙发角）。用不同颜色的地垫或家具做物理边界。
3. **第三步：制作视觉日程表**。从最简单的3步日程开始（如”吃点心→玩玩具→看绘本”），用实物照片或简单图片。贴在孩子视线高度的墙上或白板上。每完成一项，让孩子自己取下或翻转图片。
4. **第四步：设计第一个任务篮**。选择孩子已经会做的简单任务（如把积木放进盒子、把袜子配对），放在一个篮子里。旁边放一个”完成盒”。让孩子练习”从左到右完成任务→放入完成盒→看日程表下一个活动”的流程。
5. **第五步：逐步增加任务复杂度**。当孩子能独立完成3-5个简单任务后，开始加入新任务。每次只增加一个新任务，其余保持已掌握的。恩启建议新任务的难度控制在”孩子能完成70%、需要少量帮助30%”的水平。

恩启建议家长在布置环境时拍摄前后对比照片，记录每次调整的内容和原因。这些数据不仅帮助干预师远程指导时快速了解情况，也能让家长看到自己的进步。在恩启的家庭干预用户中，坚持记录环境调整数据的家庭，孩子的独立任务完成率平均提升了25%。

## TEACCH适合什么年龄和能力的孤独症儿童？

TEACCH适用于所有年龄段和能力水平的孤独症儿童。根据[世界卫生组织（WHO）](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders)的建议，结构化环境支持对低龄和语言能力有限的孤独症儿童尤其有效。在恩启的实践中，TEACCH方法被广泛应用于以下场景：

* **2-4岁低龄儿童**：以实物视觉支持为主（如用真实的杯子图片表示”喝水时间”），配合简单的日程板。重点是建立”先做什么、再做什么”的基本概念。
* **4-7岁学龄前儿童**：过渡到图片日程表，开始使用任务篮和工作系统。可以在机构中使用TEACCH结构化的独立工作角，与小组教学交替进行。
* **7-12岁学龄儿童**：使用文字或图文结合的日程表，任务复杂度增加。TEACCH的工作系统可以帮助孩子独立完成家庭作业和生活技能训练。
* **12岁以上青少年**：TEACCH的结构化原则可以转化为自我管理工具——如手机日程提醒、任务清单、时间管理模板。目标是逐步从外部结构化过渡到自我结构化。

无论孩子处于哪个年龄段，TEACCH的核心原则始终不变：**用视觉代替听觉，用结构代替口头指令，用环境设计代替反复催促**。恩启的干预师在制定个别化方案时，会根据孩子的年龄、能力水平和家庭环境，量身定制最适合的结构化支持方案。

## 家长在实施TEACCH时最容易犯的错误有哪些？

1. **环境结构化过度**：有些家长把家里每个角落都贴上标签和图片，反而让孩子信息过载。恩启建议从最关键的1-2个区域开始（通常是学习区和过渡环节），逐步扩展。
2. **视觉材料不匹配孩子能力**：给语言能力很好的孩子用实物照片会显得”幼稚”，给语言有限的孩子用纯文字则无法理解。视觉材料的类型必须匹配孩子的认知水平——实物→照片→简笔画→文字，是一个渐进的谱系。
3. **忽视”完成”信号**：如果孩子不知道”做完了”，会不断重复同一个任务或焦虑地等待。每个任务都必须有明确的完成标记——可以是完成盒、绿色卡片、或日程表上的”✓”。
4. **日程表一成不变**：结构化不等于僵化。日程表中应该包含一些”惊喜”环节（用问号图片表示），帮助孩子接受变化。恩启建议日程表中至少20%的内容是灵活的。
5. **不记录数据**：TEACCH的效果需要通过数据来评估。记录孩子独立完成任务的比例、需要提示的次数、问题行为的发生频率。恩启建议每周至少记录3天，每4周做一次进展评估。

TEACCH的价值不仅在于提升孩子的独立能力，更在于改变家长看待孤独症的方式。当我们不再试图”矫正”孩子，而是调整环境来适应他们的学习方式时，亲子关系中的很多冲突会自然减少。恩启始终相信：**好的干预不是让孩子变得”正常”，而是帮助他们在自己的节奏里发挥最大潜力**。

## 常见问题（FAQ）

### TEACCH和ABA可以一起用吗？

可以，而且推荐结合使用。ABA侧重于通过回合式教学建立新技能，TEACCH侧重于通过结构化环境帮助孩子在日常生活中独立应用这些技能。在恩启的实践中，通常用ABA教新技能（如命名、配对），然后用TEACCH的工作系统让孩子独立完成这些任务，实现技能的泛化。

### TEACCH只适合重度孤独症儿童吗？

不是。TEACCH适用于孤独症谱系上的所有儿童，包括高功能孤独症和阿斯伯格综合征。对于能力较高的孩子，TEACCH的结构化原则可以转化为自我管理工具（如任务清单、时间管理表），帮助他们在学习和生活中更加独立。

### 在家做TEACCH需要买很多专业教具吗？

不需要。TEACCH的核心是环境设计和视觉支持，大部分材料可以自制。任务篮可以用家里的收纳盒，视觉日程表可以用手机拍的照片打印出来，完成盒可以用任何带盖子的盒子。恩启建议家长先从最简单的日程表和1个任务篮开始，不需要一次性投入大量费用。

### TEACCH训练多久能看到效果？

根据恩启的实践数据，坚持每天使用结构化环境的家庭，通常在2-4周内观察到孩子的焦虑水平下降、独立完成任务的时间增加。3个月后，大部分孩子的独立工作能力和任务转换能力有显著提升。但效果的持续性取决于家庭是否坚持使用，以及是否根据孩子的进步逐步调整任务难度。

### 恩启有TEACCH相关的培训或干预服务吗？

恩启的家庭干预服务中包含TEACCH结构化环境的设计和实施指导。干预师会到家访视，帮助家庭评估环境、制作视觉支持材料、设计任务篮和工作系统。家长可以拨打400-606-2105咨询，也可以先使用恩启免费的线上发育筛查工具了解孩子的能力水平。

args.summary:
This webpage is a comprehensive guide from IngCare (恩启), a Chinese autism rehabilitation service founded by author Wang Wei (王伟), explaining the TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and related Communication-handicapped Children) structured teaching method for autism intervention. The article emphasizes that TEACCH is one of the three most influential autism intervention methods alongside ABA and DIR/Floortime, with its core advantage being that it doesn't require high-level language skills or intensive one-on-one teaching—instead using environmental design and visual supports to help children with autism complete tasks independently.

Key statistics cited include: a 2022 meta-analysis in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders showing children receiving TEACCH improved independent task completion by 34%, and more than 50 countries use TEACCH methods per a 2024 report from UNC's TEACCH program center. The article compares TEACCH vs ABA across multiple dimensions (TEACCH adapts the environment to the child while ABA requires the child to adapt to environmental demands; TEACCH uses visual supports and structured independent tasks while ABA uses discrete trial training with language instruction and reinforcement). The author notes TEACCH addresses generalization problems often seen in ABA.

The three core principles are detailed: (1) Physical structuring (using furniture placement and boundaries so children know where to do what, e.g., dividing spaces into study/game/rest areas), (2) Visual structuring (replacing auditory instructions with visual cues including schedules, work systems, and prompt cards), and (3) Work systems (helping children answer four questions: what to do, how much to do, how to know it's done, and what to do next).

A 5-step home setup guide is provided: observe the child's daily routine, divide functional zones, create a visual schedule, design a first task basket, and gradually increase task complexity (maintaining 70% independent/30% assistance ratio for new tasks). The guide reports that families who consistently recorded environmental adjustment data improved independent task completion by an average of 25%.

The article covers age-appropriate applications (2-4 years using physical objects, 4-7 using picture schedules, 7-12 using text-combined schedules and homework support, 12+ transitioning to self-management tools), skills common parent mistakes (over-structuring, mismatched visual materials, neglecting completion signals, rigid schedules—at least 20% should be flexible, and failing to record data), and answers FAQs including that TEACCH and ABA can and should be combined, that TEACCH serves all autism levels including high-functioning individuals, that no expensive teaching tools are needed, and that results typically appear within 2-4 weeks of daily use. The article includes IngCare's contact information (400-606-2105) and links to related articles on ABA, DIR/Floortime, and other autism topics.

## 結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析

[郝佳華](javascript:;)  ；  [吳裕益](javascript:;)

*[《中華民國特殊教育學會年刊》 112年度 (2023/12) Pp. 269-298](javascript:;)*

Download

### Abstracts

---

結構化教學乃因應自閉症光譜障礙者視覺思考方式與優位學習而生的教學法。為瞭解此教學法在我國特殊教育研究上應用成效及實證本位實務水準，本研究採後設分析法，從「全國博碩士論文知識加值系統」、「華藝線上圖書館」二個線上資料庫，以「結構化教學」、「TEACCH」，「視覺提示策略」三個關鍵字，收集後發現各計14篇及89篇研究，合計103篇；再以單一個案研究設計，自閉症光譜障礙症學生為受試對象，經過標題和摘要審視後，「華藝線上圖書館」資料庫符合者一篇，「全國博碩士論文知識加值系統」符合者七篇，共計八篇。經分析此八篇十九位個案研究結果之加權平均Tau-U效果量，對可能影響效果量之研究特徵變項，進行次群體效果量差異顯著性考驗，結果如下：一、效果量部分，達大效果量者有十五個，占了78.95%。固定效果模式與隨機效果模式之加權平均效果量相同，均為.81，屬於「中」效果量。二、結構化教學介入會因應用的對象階段、介入主題與時間、教學要素不同而有成效上的差異，應用於自閉症學生各教育階段、認知／技能與行為上均有中大效果且介入時間越多效果越大。三、目前尚未有足夠之證據支持此四個調節變項對結構化教學介入成效具有調節作用。四、此教學法應用於自閉症之單一個案研究近20年間只有八篇，研究篇數較缺乏；另介入主題以提升認知技能者居多（73.68%），介入時間多為12週（2－3小時／週）且完整使用五個結構化教學要素者較少（僅二篇），多數研究者採視覺提示策略或教材方式介入。最後本研究對此教學法的後續研究設計與應用提出相關建議。

This webpage presents an academic research article titled "結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析" (A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Structured Teaching on Cognition and Behavior of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder), authored by 郝佳華 (Hao Jia-hua) and 吳裕益 (Wu Yu-yi), published in the 《中華民國特殊教育學會年刊》 (Journal of the Special Education Association of the Republic of China), 112年度 (2023), pages 269-298.

**Purpose & Context:** The study examines the effectiveness of structured teaching (結構化教學) as an educational approach tailored to the visual-thinking style and preferred learning methods of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), aiming to evaluate its application effectiveness in special education research in Taiwan and the level of evidence-based practice.

**Methodology:** Using meta-analysis, researchers collected studies from two online databases ("全國博碩士論文知識加值系統" National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations, and "華藝線上圖書館" Airiti Library), searching with three keywords: "結構化教學" (structured teaching), "TEACCH," and "視覺提示策略" (visual cue strategies). A total of 103 studies were collected (14 and 89 respectively). After filtering for single-case research design with ASD students as subjects, 8 studies met the criteria (7 from the theses database, 1 from Airiti), covering 19 individual cases.

**Key Results:**
1. Effect sizes: 15 of the intervention effect sizes (78.95%) reached a large effect size level. The weighted average effect size (Tau-U) was the same (.81) under both fixed-effect and random-effect models, classified as a "medium" effect size.
2. The effectiveness of structured teaching interventions varied based on the students' educational stage, intervention topic/time, and teaching elements used. The approach showed medium-to-large effects across educational stages and on both cognition/skills and behavior, with greater effects from longer intervention times.
3. There is currently insufficient evidence to support that the four moderator variables significantly moderate the intervention effectiveness.
4. Over nearly 20 years, only 8 single-case studies applying this teaching method to autism were found, indicating a lack of research. Intervention topics mostly focused on improving cognitive skills (73.68%), intervention duration was mostly 12 weeks (2-3 hours/week), and only 2 studies fully used all five structured teaching elements; most researchers used visual cue strategies or teaching materials.

**Conclusion:** The study provides recommendations for future research design and application of structured teaching for ASD students.

# Visual Schedules for Autism Classrooms: 7 Reasons Why We Use and Love Them

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: Picture of a single picture schedule on a blurred background.](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-1-768x768.jpg)

So often, those of us who have worked in the field for a while, take the benefits of visual schedules for autism spectrum disorders for granted. We forget that others don’t always know WHY a visual schedule is so important for our students on the spectrum. And frankly how useful they can be for students in special education who have other disabilities.

This post kicks off a series focused on the whys and hows for visual schedules for autism in the classroom. I’ll be talking about types of schedules, how they work and more with lots of pictures and examples of picture schedules, object schedules, and written schedules.

## Table of Contents

## **Visual Schedules for Autism**

We can use visual schedules for autism as a group or individually. And they come in many different formats. Some students benefit from picture schedules. Others can do well with written schedules, and some might need a schedule made of objects.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: Picture of a single picture schedule on a blurred background.](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-1-1024x1024.jpg)

The next few posts will focus on different types of individual schedules, why we need group schedules and when they are appropriate by themselves, the use of first-then schedules, deciding about the form of schedule (e.g., object, picture-symbol, photo or written) and the use of mini-schedules.  We will look at schedules in a variety of settings including self-contained classrooms, inclusion classrooms, work sites, community and home.

For this first post, I want to start with why schedules are important for students with autism and some general thoughts about developing them.

## **Why Use Visual Schedules for Autism**

Visual schedules and visual supports have many benefits for individuals with autism spectrum disorder and other developmental disabilities. Today I’m going to focus on 7 reasons why they can be really helpful for the individual and also for the classroom.

## **#1 Visual Schedules Increase Independence**

The primary reason I see for using visual schedules is that they promote independence in many ways.  If you have a schedule, you can transition and navigate your day without another person having to tell you where to go and what to do.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #1 Build Independence [picture of written and picture schedules]](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-2-1024x1024.jpg)

Students in special education spend a good bit of their time with assistance from teachers, paraprofessionals and even other students. Consequently, it’s critical that we address independence as a life skill for explicit instruction.

Many people worry that picture schedules or written schedules will promote rigidity for the student to get stuck on the schedule cards. I bust this method [in this podcast](https://autismclassroomresources.com/podcasts/visual-schedules-and-autism-busting-5-myths/), but the short version is that it IS a myth. As a quick example. I’m willing to bet that most of you reading have a daily planner. And if we took away the planner, some appointments and tasks would not happen because you didn’t have it to remind you. A visual schedule is no different–it just may take a different form to fit the needs of the student to be able to use it effectively.

## **#2 A Visual Schedule Helps Prevent Power Struggles**

If I have a schedule that tells me what to do, I can’t argue with it.  I can’t tell you how many times I have said, “Schedule says \_\_” and had the student follow the direction; but if I said, “I need you to do \_\_\_” it wouldn’t happen.  The schedule takes the “personal” piece out of it and makes it more objective.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #2 Prevent Power Struggles-picture of first-then schedule](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-3-1024x1024.jpg)

In fact one of the ways you KNOW your student gets how to use the schedule independently is when they start shifting the schedule cards around or crossing things off their written words schedule. When they start thinking they can change what happens in the room, it’s a good sign that the schedule is working for them. And that they know they can’t argue with it. BTW, if that happens, just shift it back to the right schedule and move on.

## **#3 Visual Schedules Provide a Permanent Reminder**

I can leave a schedule with you and you can check it throughout the day.  When the teacher moves on to another student, the activity or the transition doesn’t stop.

If I need to stand next to the student and point to the work he is supposed to be doing, he isn’t working independently. But if he had a list of things to do that he could check off, and could then work with you moving around the room instead of right by him, that permanent reminder helps him be independent.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #3 provide a permanent reminder](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-4-1024x1024.jpg)

It’s like having a to-do list. If I complete the tasks on my to-list on my way, I’m independent. But if I have to keep asking someone “What’s next?” to find out the next thing to do, then I’m not. Then I would need to always be working with someone’s supervision. When you first implement visual schedules, students might need reminders to check their schedule. As they become more independent, you don’t need to be there. They have a visual reminder of their to-do list.

## **#4 Visual Schedules for Autism Reduce Anxiety**

Ever have a student who engages in constant questioning?  Sometimes it’s because they are anxious about what is going to happen next.  A picture schedule (or written or object schedule) allows them to check their schedule instead of checking with you. This is a way we all self-regulate at times.  Reducing anxiety allows them to focus on the task at hand.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #4 They Reduce Anxiety. Picture of written schedules in a notebook](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-5-1024x1024.jpg)

I always think about when I’m taking a flight somewhere. I become a little OCD about when the flight is leaving. But i don’t continually ask for reminders about when the flight is leaving. I check my app and reassure myself that I have time. That visual support of seeing the time my flight is leaving reduce anxiety for me. It helps me self-regulate.

## **#5 They Communicate the Daily Routine and Unexpected Events**

The give students information about what is going to happen and what is expected.  When I check my schedule and it tells me we are going to PE, I know to be prepared to go outside.  If it tells me it’s time for lunch, I know to prepare myself to enter the loud and smelly cafeteria.  This communication also helps students use picture cards receptively to understand upcoming activities. For many kids it builds communication skills as well.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #5 Reduce Surprises [picture of picture schedules on a filing cabinet]](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-6-1024x1024.jpg)

As I mention [**in this post about teaching flexibility**](https://autismclassroomresources.com/visual-schedules/)**,** the schedule doesn’t cause the student to be stuck on the daily sequenced activities and upset when there are unexpected activities. Instead, using positive reinforcement and preferred activities, we can teach students to be more flexible using a visual schedule. It also creates fewer surprises.

## **#6 Individuals with Autism Often Have Better, More Efficient Understanding of Visual Information.**

This isn’t true of all individuals on the spectrum, but for many they comprehend information faster and more easily visually.  So why not use a medium that uses their strengths.

In fact most of us process visual information more efficiently and effectively than auditory cues. As I’ve said, we all use a schedule of some type, most likely a visual schedule like a planner. Why not use what works for you. If you have ever tried to use someone else’s planner system who didn’t think like you, you know how hard that shift can be.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #6 support visual learners [picture of group schedule]](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-7-1024x1024.jpg)

We should always be using the level of information to convey the daily tasks or routine that is easier than what we are capable of understanding. Because when we are stressed, we are likely not able to process at that highest level. That’s when our students with autism spectrum disorder’s visual schedule comes into play.

## **#7 Using a Visual Schedule is an Evidence-based Practice**

There is a ton of research that exists now for using pictures, words, and objects in creating a visual schedule. The [National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence & Practice found visual supports to be an evidence-based practice in 2020](https://ncaep.fpg.unc.edu/) for individuals with ASD from 0-22 years old.  And the [National Standards Project found visual schedules to be an established practice](https://nationalautismcenter.org/national-standards/phase-2-2015/) for 3-9 year old children with autism in 2015.

![7 Reasons to Use Visual Schedules in Autism: #7 Evidence-based practice. Visual supports are an evidence-based practice according to The NCAEP 2020 and an established intervention for the NSP 2nd Report](https://autismclassroomresources.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/05/7-Reasons-to-Use-Visual-Schedules-in-Autism-8-1024x1024.jpg)

## **More Information About Visual Schedules for Autism**

There are several other reasons to use schedules that I talk about in this series.  Over the next posts you’ll find information about:
