Vitae.......................................................................................................................... 1 Chapter One: Introduction and Problem Statement Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) face a variety of challenges. ASD is characterized by social and communication difficulties along with repetitive behaviors and restricted interests (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). These social and communication difficulties can make it difficult to communicate with others face-to-face (Alpern, 2012; Anderson, 2018), such as when working in collaborative groups in the classroom setting. This evaluation study will evaluate the implementation of a digital classroom tool developed to support collaboration and embedded within shared Google Slides to assist all students, including those with ASD, in collaborative activities. Students with ASD may experience a lack of understanding of social cues from others and social rules, which leads to restricted social interactions (Cobb et al., 2002; Simon, 2016; Wang et al., 2017). Children with ASD are often inflexible in their thinking. They may not know social rules or, if they do, may apply those rules in a rigid manner, perhaps being unable to generalize a learned rule past the specific situation in which it was learned, leading to misunderstandings and frustration (Cobb et al., 2002; Moore et al., 2000; Simon, 2016). Social interactions can also be difficult for individuals with ASD due to difficulty interpreting non-verbal cues, social intentions, and the back and forth of conversation (Crooke, Hendrix, & Rachman, 2007). Students with ASD may not be able to make appropriate eye contact with others (Bellini, 2016; Simon, 2016). These difficulties can lead to feelings of isolation, withdrawal from social situations, and even challenging behaviors in the child with ASD (Bellini, 2016; Chandler, 2010; Otten, 2011). These are behaviors learned in response to situations that may be difficult for an individual with ASD and are the individual’s attempt to manage the situation (Glasberg, 2006; Singh, Lancioni, & Winton, 2011). Such behaviors can be 2 a way of communicating discomfort when appropriate communication skills are lacking (Mancil, Conroy, & Haydon, 2008). As a result of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) children identified as needing special-education services are placed in the least-restrictive environment that meets their needs (U.S. Department of Education, 2004). For many children with ASD, this is the general-education classroom, which means classroom teachers need to incorporate methods that will help these students succeed in the classroom. Due to difficulty in social skills and communication and maladaptive behaviors learned in response to these challenges, collaboration can be difficult for those with ASD, but collaborative learning has been established as an effective learning strategy in the general population for over 40 years (Vygotsky, 1978). However, if children with ASD have difficulty with this style of learning, they may find it difficult to experience these benefits or even be excluded from collaborative learning opportunities. Problem Statement A problem exists for children with ASD in the general education classroom who experience difficulty in collaborative learning due to deficits in social skills and communication. These students can miss the powerful learning opportunities available through collaborative activities, and their peers miss the opportunity to collaborate with them. Finally, these missed opportunities may contribute to social isolation already felt by many children with ASD. This study took place in two elementary schools in a public school district in Northern Indiana. Any names used are pseudonyms. Most children with ASD spent 80% or more of their time in their general-education classroom at the time of the study. Most of their services were received during English/Language Arts or Mathematics instruction. Teachers did not generally 3 have extra support from special education teachers during Science or Social Studies. The Science curriculum used at this time included collaborative learning in every unit during a time of day when general-education teachers were most often without push-in support from special-education teachers, meaning that when collaborative learning took place, students with ASD were expected to participate along with their classmates. This left teachers with a need for resources and support. It was hoped that the development of a support for collaborative learning used for all students might allow children with ASD to participate in collaborative learning activities more fully and experience feelings of success, which may also minimize classroom disruptions. The support needed to be easy for teachers to implement with minimal training. Ideally, the support would be used with all children, allowing all students to experience any benefits, using materials with which students were already familiar. Summary of the Study This was an evaluation study to determine whether the use of an online collaboration tool changed the perceptions around collaborative learning for students and teachers using the tool and whether the tool could be used for collaboration. The study sought to answer the research questions: RQ 1: Do teachers perceive that the tool is effective in assisting students with ASD and their classmates to collaborate with their peers? RQ 2: Do students perceive that the tool facilitates their ability to collaborate with their peers? RQ 3: Are students with and without ASD able to use the tool to collaborate with their peers? The ADC tool was implemented in third through fifth-grade classrooms as part of an existing science curriculum that included collaborative learning. Data was collected from artifacts that took the form of edits made within the Google Slides containing the tool, screen 4 recordings, observation notes, discussions with teachers, teacher interviews, and brief surveys of students. This data was analyzed to answer the research questions and to inform improvements to be made for future iterations of the tool. 5 Chapter Two: Literature Review Collaborative learning has long been established as an effective method of learning (Barrera, 2015; Chuang, 2014; Dillenbourg, 1999; Gokhale, 1995; Nokes-Malach, Richey, & Gadgil, 2015; Zhang, L., Ayres, P., & Chan, K., 2010). It affords multiple opportunities for the social construction of knowledge as students work together to learn, discuss, and elaborate and is frequently incorporated in classrooms. In recent years, more children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are being educated in general-education classrooms, but children with ASD experience difficulties with social situations such as collaborative learning which can make engagement in these activities a challenge. A review of why this is challenging as well as successful strategies to assist has informed this evaluation case study. Collaborative Learning Collaborative learning is a term that can be used in different ways and is sometimes used interchangeably with cooperative learning. Both share the commonality of learners working together to build meaning. Because the focus of this study is on helping children with ASD to work with others in a group setting, both types of learning are included without differentiating between the two. This type of learning involves students working together toward a shared learning outcome (Barrera, 2015; Chuang, 2014; Dillenbourg, 1999; Gokhale, 1995; Nokes-Malach, Richey, & Gadgil, 2015; Zhang, L., Ayres, P., & Chan, K., 2010). During collaborative learning, students must be working together to achieve a common goal rather than working separately on a common goal or working together on separate goals. This element of shared responsibility for the outcome can influence group interaction (Dillenbourg, 1999). 6 When students work in collaborative groups rather than as individuals, many positive outcomes occur including improved learning outcomes, the ability to solve more complex problems, and the opportunity to learn through observing group members (Dillenbourg, 1999; Barrera, 2015; Chen, Hernandez, & Dong, 2015; Chuang, 2014; Lin et al., 2015; Nokes-Malach, Richey, & Gadgil, 2015; Hadjerrouit, 2012). Other learning outcomes include increased attention, participation, and learning satisfaction (Chuang, 2014) along with decreased anxiety toward the learning task (Gokhale, 1995). Furthermore, sources such as The Partnership for 21st Century Learning (P21, 2016) and the International Society for Technology in Education (2016) have recognized the importance of collaboration in the 21st Century and have included it as part of their guidelines. Collaboration has even appeared in state academic standards. In their most recent revision of their state academic standards, Indiana has updated the name of a category within English Language Arts to, “Communication and Collaboration,” rather than the former, “Speaking and Listening,” (Indiana Department of Education, 2024). Collaborative learning is becoming more common in classrooms. In particular, the problem-based science curriculum involved in this study includes collaborative learning in most lessons. In order to participate in collaborative learning, children must be able to work together. In their meta-analysis of studies concerning collaborative learning and children with special needs, Murphy, Grey, and Honan (2005) found that successful collaboration included a combination of group interdependence and individual accountability. They also recommended teaching all children the social skills needed to successfully engage in collaborative learning before using it as a strategy (Murphy et al., 2005). Social Skills Challenges in ASD 7 One of the core areas of deficit for children with ASD is a variety of difficulties with social skills (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). During face-to-face communication, nonverbal cues are an important part of exchanges. Children with ASD have difficulty using social skills and interpreting and understanding others’ use of nonverbal social cues (Bellini et al., 2009; Crooke et al., 2007; Simon, 2016). Learning social rules can be difficult, and, due to rigid thinking, students with ASD may be able to apply learned social rules only within the specific context in which they are learned (Cobb et al., 2002; Simon, 2016; Wang et al., 2017). Social skills are affected by the concepts below. Joint attention Joint attention is a construct that is addressed in the literature around ASD and is important to social communication and the development of language (Bruinsma, Koegel, & Kern Koegel, 2004; Mundy et al., 1990; Mundy & Newell, 2007). Joint attention is the ability to attend to items or topics of interest to another person, coordinate attention between the speaker and the object or topic, and to use gestures or eye contact to respond to, initiate, or maintain this attention (Bruinsma et al., 2004; Mundy et al. 1990; Mundy & Newell 2007, Boyle, Arnedillo-Sanchez, & Zahid, 2015). For example, if another person points to an object, a typically developing child will follow the point and attend to the object of interest. Children with ASD often will not do this. They might ignore the gesture completely or glance up briefly only to continue with the previous task. Joint attention plays a key role in social interactions because it is a primary method by which individuals communicate and share experiences with each other (Bruinsma, Koegel, & Kern Koegel, 2004). However, children with ASD can have difficulties both in initiating joint attention and in responding to others’ bids for attention, which can contribute to the social 8 difficulties these children experience (Bruinsma et al., 2004, Mundy & Newell, 2007). Joint attention is important to collaborative work. In order to create a collaborative piece, group members must attend to what other members are discussing, questions they are asking, and points they are trying to make. As a productive collaborative group member, a learner must pay attention to the thoughts and points of others rather than only their own thoughts. Group members must also be able to coordinate their attention between group members and the items or information being discussed (Janssen et al., 2010). Theory of Mind Deficits in Theory of Mind (ToM) often occur in children with ASD. ToM is a theory regarding how individuals understand and acknowledge that other people have thoughts, feelings, intentions, and a perspective unique to their own (Bellini, 2016; Crooke, Hendrix, & Rachman, 2007; Drager, Light, & Finke, 2009; National Research Council, 2001). ToM comes into play when we explain our thoughts or experiences to another person. Thanks to ToM, we know that another person does not have our same background knowledge and experience. We can then judge how much we need to explain to make our ideas or feelings clear. ToM is what allows us to understand that, given the same experience, another person might have a different set of reactions than we have. ToM also plays an important role in social interactions because it motivates us to interact with others (Bellini, 2016). It allows for empathy as we take another’s perspective and imagine what others must be feeling. Lacking the ability to consider another person’s point of view and thoughts or that they might differ from our own means the back and forth of conversation may be difficult or lacking, resulting in one-sided conversations and difficult interactions. 9 Children with ASD have difficulty understanding that other individuals do not have the same background knowledge, thoughts, and feelings as their own. This can cause social problems when a child with ASD does not adequately explain themselves because they do not realize the other person does not have the same background experience or knowledge. Children with ASD might have difficulty understanding the motivations behind another individual’s actions due to lack of ToM. These factors can make collaborative learning more difficult. Communication Challenges in ASD In addition to challenges with social skills, another core area of deficit for children with ASD involves communication difficulties (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Communication impairments may range from mild to severe in children with ASD. Up to one in five children with ASD do not develop adequate functional communication (Drager, Light, & Finke, 2009). When impairment is milder, children may appear to ignore the speaker when they are being spoken to, often because they do not realize the importance of verbal communication for others (Rogers, 2010) or they are simply not socially motivated to participate in communication (Drager et al., 2009). Tone of Voice Tone of voice can convey a large part of verbal communication. Students with ASD can experience difficulty using appropriate tone of voice and understanding others’ tone of voice (Bellini et al., 2009). This contributes to social language difficulties such as when a sarcastic or joking tone might not be understood, and instead the words would be interpreted literally. Literal interpretation of idiomatic expressions might also occur due to lack of understanding of the social rules involved in social language use (Bellini, 2016). Nonverbal Communication 10 Nonverbal communication challenges can impact collaborative learning as well. One example is difficulty making appropriate eye contact with others (Bellini, 2016; Simon, 2016). Lack of eye contact can lead to missed social cues and conversation partners feeling the child with ASD is not attending to the conversation. Understanding body language and gestures can be difficult as well as reading facial expressions and understanding social intentions (Bellini et al., 2009; Crooke et al., 2007). Repetitive or Restricted Behaviors or Interests A final area of deficit for children with ASD that can have an impact on collaborative learning is repetitive or restricted behaviors or interests (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). This can affect social relations and therefore collaborative learning as students may be fixated on a perseverative interest, leading students to take little notice of topics introduced by others (Crooke et al., 2007). Restricted interests can affect relationships and cause students with ASD to appear to lack social reciprocity as they might have one-sided conversations that tend to circle back to the child’s restricted interest without notice of the interest level of a conversation partner (Bellini et al., 2009; Crooke et al., 2007). Cognitive Load Theory Another theory to consider in relation to children with ASD and collaborative learning is cognitive load. This is the amount of working memory being used at any given time. Cognitive load theory states that if cognitive load exceeds the capacity of working memory, the learner will be unable to concentrate on new information (Kirschner et al., 2018, Janssen & Kirschner, 2020). Cognitive load may become too heavy for a learner if the amount of information needing to be processed at any one time becomes too great. The same can be true during collaborative learning. Cognitive load must not be too much for any one learner, as well as for the group as a whole. 11 One advantage of collaborative learning is that cognitive load may be distributed across individual learners (Kirschner et al., 2018; Cai & Gu, 2019; Janssen & Kirschner, 2020); however, cognitive load may increase if learners experience extraneous cognitive load due to ineffective collaboration (Kirschner et al., 2018). Collaborative learning presents a unique situation for children with ASD as they naturally need to process social interactions more so than their peers (Bellini, 2016). For children with ASD, social situations can be challenging, and they can therefore present their own cognitive load as the child with ASD attempts to understand other children’s body language, facial cues, and tones of voice. One method of decreasing cognitive load for all learners when using computers for collaboration is to use scripts to structure collaboration (Kirschner et al., 2018). Supports for Collaborative Learning Given their difficulties with social communication and related skills, children with ASD can experience difficulty when placed in collaborative learning groups. During collaborative learning, groups of students must work together to achieve a common learning goal (Barrera, 2015; Gokhale, 1995; Nokes-Malach et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2010). This means they must be able to communicate with each other and maintain joint attention to the topics relevant to their learning goals (Janssen et al., 2010). Little research exists on supports for children with ASD aimed specifically at collaborative learning; however, there are many supports that have shown success in teaching and supporting the social skills or communication of children with ASD in the school setting. Structure One helpful type of support for children with ASD is any that offers structure (Simon, 2016; Stokes et al., 2017). Children with ASD can become anxious or otherwise experience 12 discomfort in unstructured settings (Simon, 2016; Stokes et al., 2017), so offering support that brings order and predictability to their experience, their surroundings, or the expectations placed on them can help offset this anxiety. One type of structural support that has shown success for a variety of children with special learning needs including ASD while in collaborative groups is graphic organizers (Bryans-Bongey, 2018; Cai & Gu, 2019). These organizers can make information collected by the group more visual, thus structuring the information for children and eliminating the need to hold it in working memory while also concentrating on the collaboration process itself (Cai & Gu, 2019). Students with ASD have relatively strong visual processing skills, which can be supported by visual structural supports (Morlock, 2015; Reavin, 2010). Scripts Social scripts are another tool that has been shown to be successful with children with ASD (Bellini, 2016; Crooke et al., 2007; Rao et al., 2008). Scripts can be prescriptive, with the intent of being used exactly as they are, or they can be simple lists to offer suggestions depending on the child’s needs and the situation (Bellini, 2016; Simon, 2016). Scripts can remove some of the social discomfort felt by children with ASD as they struggle to form an appropriate response to others, especially in new situations (Bellini, 2016). While successful in their own right, these scripts can serve a dual purpose of providing structure because they offer the child with ASD the comfort and structure of a script of verbal remarks to make in a variety of situations (Bellini, 2016). Prompts Prompts can take a variety of forms, but they are intended to remind a child to use a previously-practiced social skill. They can include physical/visual, verbal, modeling, or natural prompting methods (Bellini et al., 2009) and are short reminders (Bellini et al., 2009; Glasberg, 13 2006; Scott, 2008). Visual reminders such as photos or illustrations that provide information about others’ feelings or perspectives have been helpful (Simon, 2016). While working in groups, visual prompts have been used to help with understanding the feelings of others (Simon, 2016). Role play and Rehearsal Role play or rehearsal is another visual and experiential strategy that can help children with ASD to practice and learn social skills for specific situations (Rao, Beidel, & Murray, 2008; Simon, 2016). Role play could be used to model a typical cooperative interaction for the child with ASD in which someone might ask a question to which the child should respond and perhaps follow up with a question or information on the same topic (Simon, 2016). Role play is typically done during a specific social skills intervention and may include typically-developing peers as guides or mentors (Whalon et al., 2015). Role play allows the child to practice or rehearse newly-learned skills without the pressure of an unpredictable social situation (Bellini et al., 2009). Peer-mediated Interventions Peer-mediated interventions of other kinds and those involving peers have also shown success in the classroom setting across studies according to meta-analyses (Bellini et al., 2007; Whalon et al., 2015). These interventions have involved teaching skills to both children with ASD and peers at the same time or teaching skills to peers first accompanied by ways to approach the child with ASD (Whalon et al., 2015). Components of peer-mediated interventions varied including modeling, feedback and praise, and teaching target skills, in addition to role play (Whalon et al., 2015). Feedback and praise or other positive reinforcement have also been used as a successful support for children with ASD as they learn and use social skills (Bellini, 14 2016; National Research Council, 2001; Whalon et al., 2015). Visual feedback may be especially helpful (National Research Council, 2001). Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) is one form collaborative learning can take in which a computer is used to provide support during collaborative learning activities (Janssen & Kirschner, 2020). CSCL takes advantage of the benefits of collaborative learning but extends them by using technology. CSCL has advantages and disadvantages. It affords greater capabilities for collaborative learning when face-to-face learning is difficult or impossible, and it extends the opportunities for collaborative learning past times when individuals are face-to-face. CSCL can have cognitive load implications as using technology can potentially use working memory (Janssen et al., 2010). Technology Supports Technology solutions to support children with ASD during collaborative activities could provide a great benefit in allowing them to collaborate more easily. Technology can help with areas of sensory difficulty such as when children with ASD may prefer typing on a computer to writing by hand (Simon, 2016) or simply have a liking for technology (Boyle, Arnedillo-Sanchez, & Zahid, 2015). Another challenge those with ASD face is that of managing unpredictable environments appropriately (Kandroudi & Brastitsis, 2010). Online environments can be more predictable and allow children to feel more in control because there is some choice in what information to read and respond to and when to do so. Several technology interventions have been used for teaching social skills or collaborative behaviors in children with ASD. These include interventions using smart glasses augmented reality, virtual reality, and interactive tabletop surfaces (Keshav et al., 2018; Boyle et 15 al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2018; Ke & Lee, 2016; Bauminger-Zviely et al., 2013; Mireya Silva, Raposo, & Supolino, 2015). Interactive computer games have also been used to teach social skills (Cobb et al., 2002; Parsons, 2015). These games can provide an opportunity for children to practice social skills without the added pressure of face-to-face interaction with others (van der Aa et al., 2016; Bauminger-Zviely et al., 2013). In addition, offering the support for students inside the general education setting can promote generalization of the collaborative skills learned (Kandroudi & Bratitsis, 2010), which is a challenge for children with ASD as they learn social skills (Bellini, 2016). Advantages of the online environment Research focusing on online communication for adults with ASD found that those with ASD report enjoying online communication due to some of the benefits it offers them over face-to-face communication (van der Aa et al., 2016). For example, many people with ASD find interpreting facial cues and body language to be difficult. Tone of voice may also be confusing for those with ASD. When interacting via technology, facial cues, eye contact, body language, and tone of voice are all removed from communication. This removal of nonverbal cues can allow those with ASD to concentrate on the message of the communication rather than these other signals (Parsons et al., 2000; Rajendran & Mitchell, 2000; van der Aa et al., 2016), which could help those with ASD to communicate more like their peers without ASD. One example showing the effectiveness of these social factors being removed from communication and processing time being added was found by Rajendran & Mitchell (2000). They conducted a study in which teenagers with ASD completed thought bubbles for characters in reaction to a researcher’s entries. The entries were then rated by 33 blinded raters for degrees of emotion, politeness, and how far a topic was pursued. The children with ASD did not rate 16 significantly different from a comparison group of teenagers with other emotional disorders (Rajendran & Mitchell, 2000). Asynchronous Communication Some adults with ASD report that the asynchronous nature of online communication is a benefit for them due to the slower pace of communication, which allows for more time to process information and formulate responses (van der Aa et al., 2016). Those with ASD can find comfort in online communities due to these advantages (Anderson, 2018, van der Aa et al., 2016). Asynchronous communication may hold some benefits for children as well. Kandroudi & Bratitsis (2010) conducted a study with students in a third-grade class including both a child with ASD and typically-developing children to see how using an online discussion tool would affect social interactions. For one phase of the study, the students wrote newspaper-type articles on paper. For the next phase, the students used an online, asynchronous discussion tool for the same task (Kandroudi & Bratitsis, 2010). Through analysis of discussions in the tool, researchers found the child with ASD to be among the most active students in the online discussion tool, and through observations, the child was found to temporarily increase the number of face-to-face social interactions immediately following the online discussion (Kandroudi & Brastitsis, 2010). This temporary increase in social interaction is one possible benefit of using technology in a classroom setting because it increases the chance that skills are generalized to the world outside the technology (Parsons et al., 2000). Google Drive Collaborative Tools Research has found effectiveness for typically-developing middle-school children when engaging in collaborative learning using technology tools. (Barrera, 2015; Chuang, 2014; 17 Hadjerrouit, 2012; Lin et al., 2015; Zhang, Ayres, P., & Chan, K., 2010). In a study of typically-developing students collaborating online through the sharing and commenting tools available in Drawings within Google Drive, Lin et al. (2015) found that students felt both more able to express their suggestions for changes and that the end product reflected more group members’ work when compared to students performing the same task with paper-and-pencil tools. They also had a more positive view of the task and higher motivation toward the learning topic (Lin et al., 2015). While research using technology tools for collaboration among those with ASD is more limited, there has been some research showing benefits for these children. Researchers have found that children with ASD can learn and be supported in collaborative learning skills through the use of interactive, touchscreen, table-top technology (Mireya Silva, Raposo, & Supolino, 2015) as well as the use of interactive games (Cobb et al., 2002; Parsons, 2015; Wang et al., 2017). Universal Design for Learning Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a design theory that applies to learning materials. UDL centers around the thought that design that helps individuals with disabilities or other special needs can also help all students and should therefore be used universally (Strangman, Hall & Meyer, 2003, Bryans-Bogey, 2018). Rather than applying a tool to the few individuals who need it due to special needs, all children in the classroom would receive the tool because it can benefit everyone. In UDL, individuals are not singled out nor given unique accommodations because those same accommodations are given to everyone. Another consideration of UDL is using technology tools to make the curriculum as supportive and 18 flexible as possible (Strangman et al., 2003, Bryans-Bogey, 2018) allowing for different methods of interaction with learning materials or flexible ways to demonstrate what has been learned. 19 Chapter Three: Methodology Introduction This study included the design, implementation, and evaluation of a tool embedded within collaborative Google Slides to promote collaboration abilities among students in a medium-sized school district with and without ASD. The study rested on principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL). According to these design principles, supports that can help students with difficulty in one area can often help many children who do not have an identified need or disability. Therefore, to increase achievement for all and decrease stigma for children identified as having special needs, all children in a classroom utilize the tool or support regardless of identified need. These supports should be designed to be used as flexibly as possible by students with varying abilities (Strangman et al., n.d.). The tool designed for this study was created using Google Slides from Google’s suite of shared tools. This enabled all students in a collaborative group to work inside the same product at the same time, thus having the opportunity to collaborate through technology in addition to traditional face-to-face opportunities. The researcher has co-taught many classes in the school district that include collaboration, and it is uncommon for teachers to speak with children about collaborative learning and how to work well as a group during these lessons. To support all learners as they work collaboratively, scripts or sentence starters were developed. Scripts have been shown to be an effective social-skills intervention for children with ASD (Bellini, 2016; Crooke et al., 2007; Rao et al., 2008). The tool design included scripts for situations that commonly occur during collaborative learning. These included: agreeing with a group member’s idea, disagreeing with a group member’s idea, and suggesting a change to a group member’s idea. 20 Graphic organizers were another component of the support. This tool helps to structure the learning experience for students. Structure is a component of many successful accommodations for children with ASD due to their often-poor executive functioning and organizational skills (Simon, 2016; Stokes et al., 2017). Graphic organizers can also help with storing information generated during collaborative learning. This can help to reduce cognitive load for learners in the group, thus freeing capacity for group thinking and functioning during collaboration (Cai & Gu, 2019). Finally, the organizers fit UDL principles because they can be used flexibly through the inclusion of text, images, and even drawings to represent ideas. Graphic organizers have been tested and found to be used successfully in a UDL context (Strangman et al, n.d.). Graphic organizers were included in the collaborative Google Slides. Specific types and quantity of organizers varied based on the needs of the Science unit being taught. The combination of scripts/prompts and a graphic organizer can offer learners several benefits. First, students can use the scripts as needed for common situations that occur during collaborative learning. This can remove social anxiety for children with ASD (Bellini, 2016) along with all children. Second, these scripted responses support the collaborative learning and work of all students who may find collaborative learning difficult. Third, the graphic organizers allow all members of the group to see a visual representation of their work and progress toward the group learning goal. This visual representation will reduce the amount of information learners attempt to store in working memory, thus reducing cognitive load and allowing students to use working memory for processing the information in the graphic organizer (Cai & Gu, 2019) and to focus on working as a group. The visual nature of the graphic organizer specifically supports those with ASD, as they frequently benefit from visual cues and representations 21 (Bellini, 2016). The use of technology itself can also reduce anxiety for children with ASD as the need to make eye contact and attend to nonverbal communication is reduced when compared to strictly face-to-face communication (van der Aa et al., 2016). The researcher regularly designs similar tools for different purposes on behalf of teachers using this curriculum, so the procedure was not unusual for teachers to follow. The tool used in this study followed similar procedures to those typically used in these cases. The tool was embedded within Google Slides, which is available in Google Workspace for Education, to which all students in the district have access beginning in first grade. All students are issued a Chromebook through the district and regularly use these devices as a learning tool. This was an ideal tool to use in the classrooms in this school district. Students in grades K-12 have their own assigned Chromebook from the school system. Because these devices run on Google’s Chrome operating system, students all have a Google Workspace for Education account and use Google products. Therefore, using a tool inside this platform was a natural fit for which both students and teachers already had background knowledge and relevant previous experience. Collaborative Slides were developed for third through fifth grade. These grade levels do not have specialized science journals included in this science curriculum, so developing these materials to help guide students through the lessons was an extra service and support to accompany the curriculum. In addition, these upper-elementary grade levels have more experience typing and working with technology, which made them an ideal choice. Other factors also made the context of this school district well-suited to the study. Because many children with ASD are learning in the general-education classroom (U.S. Department of Education, 2004), teachers need to incorporate methods that will help them succeed in the classroom. Special-education teachers are often only in classrooms during 22 Mathematics and English/Language Arts classes in this setting, which leaves teachers without additional support for other subjects including Science. All students are expected to participate in classroom activities including collaborative learning. Collaborative learning can be more difficult for children with ASD, which leaves an opportunity for the development of a classroom solution that can be easily implemented and used. At the time of implementation, classroom teachers in grades K-5 were expected to teach two units of the Science curriculum that included collaborative learning, and all teachers and students had access to Google Drive and its online collaborative tools. These factors provided an opportunity for the exploration of the perception of how these tools affected collaborative learning for these classrooms. Research Questions The research questions the evaluation sought to answer were: RQ1: Do teachers perceive that the Slides and tool are effective in assisting students with and without ASD to collaborate with their peers? RQ2: Do students perceive that the Slides and tool facilitate their ability to collaborate with their peers? RQ3: Are students able to use the Slides and tool to collaborate with their pe

This is a doctoral dissertation (Ed.D.) by Tamatha N. Terman May, presented to Indiana University's School of Education in June 2024, titled "Supporting Collaborative Learning for Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder Using a Shared Digital Tool: A Universal Design for Learning Approach." The doctoral committee included Thomas Brush (Chair), Anne T. Leftwich, and Scott Bellini.

**Purpose and Problem:** Students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) face social and communication difficulties that make collaborative learning challenging. Increasingly included in general education classrooms where collaborative learning is expected, these students often miss powerful learning opportunities, and their peers miss chances to collaborate with them. Very little research exists on supports specifically aimed at collaborative learning for children with ASD. The study takes place in two elementary schools in a public school district in Northern Indiana, where most children with ASD spend 80%+ of their time in general education classrooms, and teachers lack specialized support during Science/Social Studies lessons that require collaborative learning.

**Study Design:** This was an evaluation study implementing a digital learning support (the "ADC tool") designed using Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles, embedded within shared Google Slides. The tool combined social scripts/sentence starters (for agreeing, disagreeing, and suggesting changes to group members' ideas) with graphic organizers to provide structure and reduce cognitive load. It was implemented in grades 3-5 as part of an existing science curriculum. Data was collected through surveys, observations, artifact analysis, screen recordings, and teacher interviews, using both qualitative and quantitative methods.

**Research Questions:**
- RQ1: Do teachers perceive that the tool is effective in assisting students with and without ASD to collaborate with their peers?
- RQ2: Do students perceive that the tool facilitates their ability to collaborate with their peers?
- RQ3: Are students able to use the tool to collaborate with their peers?

**Key Findings:** Students were able to use the tool and shared presentations to collaborate. Both teachers and students perceived them to be effective in assisting with collaboration. Teachers found the tool easy to use and would use similar materials again.

**Literature Review highlights:** Collaborative learning has been an effective learning strategy for over 40 years (Vygotsky, 1978). ASD core deficits include social skills challenges (joint attention, theory of mind, communication difficulties including tone of voice and nonverbal communication), and repetitive/restricted behaviors. Cognitive Load Theory suggests that social processing for children with ASD adds cognitive load; scripts can help structure collaboration. Effective supports include structure, graphic organizers, social scripts, prompts, role play/rehearsal, peer-mediated interventions, and technology. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) removes nonverbal cues (facial expressions, eye contact, tone of voice) that are challenging for those with ASD, and asynchronous communication allows more processing time. Research shows children with ASD can be more active in online discussion tools, with temporary increases in subsequent face-to-face interactions. Google Drive collaborative tools have shown positive results with typically-developing students. UDL principles suggest that designs helping those with disabilities can benefit all students and should therefore be applied universally.

<webpage_content>
# TIES Peer Engagement Practice Guides

## A Guide to Implementing Cooperative Learning

**Share this page**

* [Share this page on Facebook.](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fpublications.ici.umn.edu%2Fties%2Fpeer-engagement%2Fpractice-guides%2Fcooperative-learning)
* [Share this page on LinkedIn.](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fpublications.ici.umn.edu%2Fties%2Fpeer-engagement%2Fpractice-guides%2Fcooperative-learning)
* [Share this page via email.](mailto:?&subject=TIES%20Peer%20Engagement%20Practice%20Guides%20%7C%20A%20Guide%20to%20Implementing%20Cooperative%20Learning&body=https%3A%2F%2Fpublications.ici.umn.edu%2Fties%2Fpeer-engagement%2Fpractice-guides%2Fcooperative-learning)

Small group learning, partner discussions, and group projects are a staple of many elementary, middle, and high school classrooms. And this is for good reason. Cooperative learning is beneficial for *all* students, including students with significant cognitive disabilities (Johnson & Johnson, 2009; Kamps et al., 1994; Piercy et al., 2002). Learning together as members of the same general education class can help students with disabilities access and make progress in challenging curriculum. Even more, social interactions that come through cooperative learning can build students’ social and communication skills, promote peer acceptance, and provide shared experiences that support friendships (Biggs & Rossi, 2021; Jackson et al., 2008).

Although many teachers are aware of these benefits, implementing cooperative learning with students can still seem challenging. Teachers may not know how to structure learning activities so that students with and without significant cognitive disabilities remain productive and accomplish shared learning goals. This challenge raises a certain truth—not all groups are cooperative. Seating students together, telling them they are a group, and giving them something to work on does not ensure they will collaborate effectively or learn much from their time together.

The term *cooperation* is commonly defined as working together to accomplish shared goals. Therefore, cooperative learning is evident when students work together to maximize their own and each other’s learning, and when teachers design instruction carefully to support this goal. Research has helped identify five core elements of effective cooperative learning (Johnson & Johnson, 2009):

1. **Positive interdependence:** Students need to believe their success is linked to the success of others in their group. Positive interdependence requires that students feel invested, want to support the learning of their classmates, and [take on roles that contribute to the groups’ success](/ties/peer-engagement/belonging/needed). Therefore, teachers must consider how all students—including students with significant cognitive disabilities—can be full participants. Of course, this does not mean that all students have to participate in exactly the same way.
2. **Individual and group accountability:** All students must be responsible for contributing to the group. The idea of accountability is closely linked with positive interdependence because it is more likely that students will feel responsible for both “carrying their own weight” and supporting other group members if they believe their success is linked to their whole group’s success. Teachers can support individual accountability by ensuring that each student is responsible for contributing to the group and/or knowing the content.
3. **Positive interaction:** The power of cooperative learning happens through social interaction with peers. Some researchers have labeled this essential element “promotive interaction” (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). This means that students should interact with one another in ways that actively *promote* the participation, learning, and contribution of every group member. Promotive interaction is evident when students are seen sharing resources, asking for and giving help, asking questions, providing feedback, giving suggestions, explaining ideas, praising and encouraging one another, listening and exploring one another’s points of view, and keeping stress and anxiety low.
4. **Social skills:** All students benefit from being taught how to cooperate and support one another’s learning. Many different social skills can be strengthened through cooperative learning. For example, students may learn more about how to communicate clearly, accept and support one another, resolve conflicts or misunderstandings, actively listen, share ideas and resources, comment constructively on others’ ideas, and make decisions democratically.
5. **Group processing:** Group processing occurs when the students reflect on their progress and working relationships. For example, they might discuss the following questions: What have we achieved? Are we on track to reach our goals? What do we still need to achieve? How might we do this? What has been helpful or unhelpful to our progress and interactions as a group? During group processing, it is important that students show respect toward all group members. The goal is to reinforce that everyone is a valued group member and to improve how students work together, not to cast blame or identify fault.

### Collaborating

Cooperative learning in inclusive classrooms is typically led by general educators, but that doesn’t mean they need to do it alone. Collaboration should be an everyday part of designing and carrying out cooperative learning, especially when this approach will be used to improve peer engagement and learning outcomes for students with significant cognitive disabilities. Effective collaboration between general and special educators is important so that all students are successfully supported. General and special educators each bring unique strengths to their work together—general educators as experts on their classrooms and curriculum, and special educators as experts on teaching and supporting students with disabilities.

Having the time to collaborate and plan together is often a challenge. One highly recommended practice involves working closely with school administrators before the school year begins to align schedules so that [general and special educators can have protected time to discuss lessons and support for students](https://ici.umn.edu/products/impact/312/Special-Education-Supports/#Special-Education-Supports). However, effective collaboration can happen even if scheduling changes are not possible. When time is limited, effective collaboration requires that teachers [make the most of their time](/ties/building-engagement-with-distance-learning/dl24-the5-15-45-tool-grab-a-partner-and-lets-collaborate). Some teachers find it helpful to use tools like shared cloud-based folders to collaborate asynchronously. For example, a general educator can upload unit and lesson plans with embedded comments or questions for the special educator. The shared folder can also be a place to review student data and track which supports work best for specific students with disabilities.

Specialized instructional support personnel such as speech-language pathologists, physical therapists, or occupational therapists can also be valued collaborators. For example, a speech-language pathologist can suggest [communication](/ties/communicative-competence-tips/cover) [supports](/ties/communicative-competence-tips/cover) [or identify vocabulary words on a student’s speech-generating device](/ties/communicative-competence-tips/cover) that might be helpful for cooperative learning activities. Additionally, [paraprofessionals are sometimes utilized to provide additional support](https://ici.umn.edu/products/impact/312/Paraprofessionals/#Paraprofessionals) within general education classes. Teachers should collaborate with paraprofessionals before, during, and after cooperative learning activities so that their ideas can be incorporated. This also ensures that paraprofessionals understand their roles in supporting peer engagement and learning for all students.

### Planning

Planning for cooperative learning involves (a) identifying the learning goal, (b) deciding on the form for cooperative learning, (c) determining what is expected for all students, and (d) planning class-wide and individualized supports.

#### Identify the Learning Goal

Good teaching is driven by a clear vision for what students should learn. Because cooperative learning can be used to promote both content learning and peer engagement, teachers should identify learning goals in both areas (e.g., a social goal and an academic goal). For example, a teacher might use cooperative learning to help students learn aspects of United States geography, as well as how to share leadership responsibilities or make decisions democratically.

#### Decide on the Form for Cooperative Learning

Cooperative learning can take many different forms. The first consideration is the structure, which can range from informal to formal(Johnson & Johnson, 2009)*. Informal cooperative learning* involves having students work together in brief “ad hoc” groups, which might last anywhere from a few minutes to a class period in length. For example, students might engage in a 5–7 minute “focused discussion” that sets the stage for the start of the lesson by having students discuss their own background knowledge and experiences. On the other hand, *formal cooperative learning* consists of students working together to complete more substantive joint learning tasks such as completing a project, conducting an experiment, researching a topic, writing a report, or developing a presentation. Formal cooperative learning can last anywhere from one class period to several days or weeks (using part of class across several days). Informal and formal cooperative learning are best thought of as two ends of a spectrum; cooperative learning activities can actually fall anywhere in between.

Two other more specific types of cooperative learning arrangements are reciprocal teaching and cooperative base groups. *Reciprocal teaching* describes cooperative learning in which students have opportunities to switch between the roles of the “teacher” and the “learner.” Two examples of different types of reciprocal teaching include classwide peer tutoring and jigsaw arrangements, which are described briefly in Figure 1. *Cooperative base groups* are long-term groups that provide a stable, diverse group of peers who offer one another encouragement, advice, and/or assistance. Typically, cooperative base groups meet regularly (e.g., daily, once per week) throughout the semester or school year. These small groups of 3-4 students might be used to check homework, provide social support, act as a book club, or review previously learned content.

Each of these arrangements for cooperative learning has its own strengths; there is not one right or better approach. Teachers should work to choose which arrangement is best aligned with their learning goal(s), as well as their students, classroom structure, and resources (e.g., amount of instructional time). Several specific examples of different types of cooperative learning activities are described in Figure 1.

Figure 1. **Different Types of Cooperative Learning Activities for Inclusive Classrooms**

* **[Turn and talk](/ties/foundations-of-inclusion-tips/turn-and-talk-in-the-inclusive-classroom):** The teacher poses a very brief question so that students can quickly turn and talk to their neighbor (e.g., repeat a key point, answer a simple question, share background knowledge or experiences that connect with the lesson).
* **Focused discussion:** The teacher poses 1-3 questions to concentrate student discussion in a particular area. Questions can be structured so that students engage more deeply with a particular idea as they move through the different questions.
* **Think-pair-share:**The teacher poses a question to the class. Students are expected to think about or write their answer before turning to a peer to discuss their responses. Partner groups then share their responses with the whole class.
* **Paired reading:**The students read and discuss an assigned text together. The teacher structures paired reading by having the students take on roles such as making predictions, clarifying things that are unclear, asking one another questions, and summarizing information.
* **Paired review:** After completing a task (e.g., solving a problem, taking notes, answering a question), students pair with a classmate to compare or discuss responses. Students can use their discussion to revise their own work.
* **Problem solving/ Task-based:**Students work together to solve problems or complete tasks (e.g., solving math problems, sorting idea cards into categories). After working in small groups, students share their process and results with the whole class.
* **Numbered heads together:** The teacher has students number off (e.g., 1-4) and then asks a question. Students ‘put their heads together’ to answer the question. When a teacher calls a number, all students with that number raise their hands to respond.

* **Talking tokens:** The teacher divides students into small groups (e.g., 4 students), gives each student two “talking tokens,” and poses a discussion topic or question. After instructing students to first think quietly, the discussion begins as each student places a talking token in the center of the table each time they talk. Once all students have used both their tokens, someone in the group can summarize the conversation. This marks the end of the discussion, or the tokens can be divided back up and the conversation can continue.
* **Classwide peer tutoring:** All students are paired and take turns being the tutor or teacher, followed by the tutee or learner. These arrangements should be reciprocal, so that both students in the pair get to be the tutor and the tutee.
* **Jigsaw:** ‘Expert groups’ are first formed. Each group of students is asked to become an expert on a topic, with each group focused on a different topic. Students then re-organize into new groups so that there is one “expert” on each topic in the new group. Students teach the idea to the new group members.
* **Project-based:** Students work in groups to complete a project (e.g., creating a diagram, preparing a presentation). Students may be given specific roles, such as the leader, recorder, material manager, or time keeper.
* **Cooperative base groups:** Students are organized into long-term, heterogeneous groups that meet regularly (e.g., daily, weekly) throughout a semester or year. Students use these groups to do things like check homework, provide social support, discuss readings, or review previously learned content.

Group size is another important factor. Smaller groups generally work better. If groups get too large, students may be less likely to believe that their efforts are important to the group (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). Smaller groups can also help students with complex communication needs participate socially and not be overwhelmed by or left out of interactions. A good rule of thumb is to try to keep cooperative learning groups to about 2-4 students per group. Unlike some other types of small-group instruction, cooperative learning groups should be heterogeneous. This means that each group should be diverse in terms of student strengths and learning needs, as well as things like gender, race/ethnicity, or other characteristics.

#### Determine What Is Expected of All Students

The next step is to clearly delineate expectations and procedures. Teachers should craft their expectations by thinking about students’ learning goal(s) and the five core elements: positive interdependence, individual and group accountability, positive interaction, social skills, and group processing. The amount of planning in each of these areas will vary by the type of cooperative learning. For example, when planning short [“turn and talk” questions](/ties/foundations-of-inclusion-tips/turn-and-talk-in-the-inclusive-classroom) during a lesson, teachers may readily see how they can support individual accountability by asking that each student in the pair have a turn to talk. On the other hand, planning how to ensure both individual and group accountability will take more time for a more formal group project.

#### Plan Class-Wide and Individualized Supports

Students need teachers to actively guide and support their work during cooperative learning. Although students with significant cognitive disabilities may need individualized support, teachers should begin by identifying support that will lead to the success of *all* students at a class-wide level. This approach is directly tied to the idea of [Universal Design for Learning (UDL)](https://ici.umn.edu/products/impact/312/Expert-Learning/#Expert-Learning), which is a framework that guides teachers in designing instruction that supports the diverse learning needs of students in an inclusive classroom. Related specifically to cooperative learning, UDL principles can help teachers overcome barriers that might challenge students’ *engagement* with their peers and with the content, *understanding* of what they are learning (based on how ideas are represented), and *participation and expression* of what they know. For example, teachers can use the UDL principle of student engagement to outline clear expectations for student behavior during cooperative learning groups. This might involve posting visuals at workstations to remind students about these expectations.

Whenever needed, teachers should also [collaborate](/ties/building-engagement-with-distance-learning/dl24-the5-15-45-tool-grab-a-partner-and-lets-collaborate) with other team members to plan individualized support for students with significant cognitive disabilities. This may include [communication](/ties/communicative-competence-tips/cover) or social supports (e.g., a speech-generating device or communication board with picture symbols, social scripts), self-management and behavior supports (e.g., a visual schedule, self-monitoring checklist), learning supports (e.g., manipulatives, visuals, video models), or other supports (e.g., adapted materials). Planning individualized supports should also involve identifying roles within cooperative learning activities that allow students with significant cognitive disabilities to successfully share their strengths, participate in valued ways, and reach their personal learning goals. Teachers often realize that support designed for individual students with disabilities may also be useful for other students in the class. In line with UDL, these can be provided to all students. For example, Figure 2 shows two self-monitoring checklists that could be used as an individualized support or made available to all students.

Figure 2. **Examples of Self-Monitoring Checklists for Partner Reading**

##### During Partner Reading, I:

1. Ask my friend a question about the text or book

**Ideas for What I Can Say:**

* What do you think this will be about?
* What do you think was the main idea?
* Have you had an experience like this story?
* What did you like best about the book?
* What character do you like?

2. Wait and listen when my friend talks

3. Respond with what I think

**Ideas for What I Can Say:**

* I think *\*BLANK\**.
* I agree with you.
* I had a different idea. I thought *\*BLANK\*.*

### Implementing

#### Informal Cooperative Learning

As described previously, informal cooperative learning involves bringing students together to work collaboratively on a task for a short period of time. Collaborative work might include discussing an idea, answering a question, or completing an activity. Although informal cooperative learning can take many different forms (see Figure 1), it is important that teachers always (a) carefully explain the task, and (b) monitor and support students as they work together. Although the word “informal” is used to describe this type of cooperative learning, even simple tasks need to be explained clearly so that students understand expectations, both for the task and for how they need to collaborate. After clearly explaining these directions, teachers and other support staff such as paraprofessionals should move around the room during the activity, offering help and positive feedback (e.g., an encouraging statement, thumb up) as they watch and listen for how students work and interact with one another. When activities are very brief—such as only a few minutes—it is typically better to avoid interrupting students to offer praise. However, if the cooperative activities are longer, simple reinforcing statements can be helpful (e.g., “Great job giving each group member a chance to say what they think.”). Groups that include students with significant cognitive disabilities might need more of this support, at least at the beginning of their work together. Teachers and paraprofessionals can offer support by sharing information, making sure all students have a valued role, teaching or modeling interaction strategies, and providing specific praise statements (e.g., “Let’s be sure that everyone has a chance to share their ideas. Daliah, can you use your communication device to share what you think?”)

To stay on track during cooperative activities, teachers may want to keep a timer nearby. Visual timers can be helpful for many students, including those with disabilities. Because groups may finish their work at different times, teachers should explain what students are to do if they finish early. Since a common goal of cooperative learning is to increase interactions with peers, teachers might want to identify socially-focused activities students can do with extra time that still keep the classroom noise level at a manageable level (e.g., playing an educational game, looking at books with a partner in a class library).

#### Formal Cooperative Learning

Implementing formal cooperative learning has much in common with informal cooperative learning, including the importance of clear expectations for students. Clear directions often become even more important when cooperative learning activities are longer or more complex. Teachers should start by describing the task itself. When expectations have multiple components or are more complex, it can be helpful to break information down into smaller chunks and use multiple ways to communicate ideas (e.g., aloud, written, visuals, videos). Teachers should also explain the cooperative aspects of the activity, making sure that students understand and are excited about supporting one another’s learning. It is important to help students begin to think about how they and their classmates—including classmates with disabilities—each bring different strengths to the group. As part of this, teachers should also describe and teach any cooperative skills that students are expected to use. One great way to do this is to embed social skill “mini-lessons” over time. This involves describing each skill, giving and modeling examples, and giving feedback as students role play the skill.

As students work together, teachers and paraprofessionals should circulate to monitor progress and offer support. Because formal cooperative learning involves longer activities, educators may be able to spend more time with each group than they would during briefer activities. Although it is important that teachers not get in the way of students working together, they should also avoid missing opportunities to step in and support student learning and peer engagement. Teachers should see their role as a facilitator—guiding students rather than simply telling them what they need to know, what they are doing wrong, or how to fix it. Some strategies that teachers and paraprofessionals can use to support cooperative learning include:

* being available to clarify ideas or expectations, review procedures, or answer questions;
* bringing a positive energy to students as they work together, such as by using humor or offering encouragement;
* mediating between students when difficulties arise and seeing these as teaching opportunities;
* asking questions that guide students in planning their next steps or solving their own problems, and;
* sharing ideas so that students with significant cognitive disabilities can contribute to and fully participate in their groups.

Formal cooperative learning activities often conclude with opportunities for students to share what they accomplished or learned with the entire class. There are many different possible ways to do this. Regardless of how students will share what they learned, it is important to plan for how students with disabilities can be full participants (e.g., by using their communication device or using other supports). Some options for sharing include:

* *Some Stay, One Strays:* When it is time to share, one group member rotates to another group to share and listen, while the others stay put, welcoming the member from a different group who joins them. This can repeat for a few rounds so that more students have the chance to “stray.”
* *Stand and Share:* One member of each group can stand and share what they learned with the class, often using visuals.
* *Gallery Walk:* This method of sharing works well when each group has created some type of product (e.g., a poster of their work). Students rotate to explore each poster or product from the other groups. To promote greater engagement, students can leave post-it notes on different posters with comments, questions, or reflections.

### Evaluating Outcomes

Cooperative learning has many benefits for all students. However, it is important that teachers carefully monitor and evaluate students’ progress—both in completing the learning task and in working together. Teachers should gather data to ensure that individual students are accountable for their learning within each group. They can also use data to determine when and how to offer extra support so that every student learns, interacts, and collaborates in effective ways.

#### For Students with Disabilities

Teachers can collect data on student communication and engagement with peers during the cooperative learning activities, both of which can be captured using observation and simple techniques like tallying the frequency of communication, or using a rating scale to evaluate interaction quality. To promote collaboration, it can be helpful for other educational team members (e.g., special educator, related service provider) to observe in the general education classroom and discuss their findings with the teachers. Determining whether any positive changes spill over to other parts of the day is also wise. Prior research shows that well-supported cooperative learning can lead to peer interactions and relationships that extend beyond the classroom (Biggs & Rossi, 2021; Kamps et al., 1994; Piercy et al., 2002). Finally, teachers and other educational team members should collect and reflect on data regarding how cooperative learning helps students with significant cognitive disabilities access and make progress in the general curriculum.

#### For Peers

Being part of cooperative learning with classmates who have significant cognitive disabilities can also positively impact peers without disabilities. Such impact may be evident in changes related to their acceptance of classmates with disabilities, their confidence and skills interacting with classmates with disabilities, and their social relationships. Cooperative learning within inclusive classrooms can also help peers without disabilities learn the academic content better because they have opportunities to explain ideas to their classmates (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). To understand the experiences of peers, teachers can talk with these peers and collect data on their academic progress. In addition, teachers can ask peers about what is good or challenging about the cooperative learning activities, about their relationships with fellow group members, and whether there is anything that could improve the way they learn with their classmates. This input can be used to improve activities in the future.

#### For Others

Carrying out cooperative learning that includes students with and without disabilities can also have a positive impact on educators, such as general educators or paraprofessionals in the classroom. Many general educators already incorporate cooperative learning in their classroom, but learning how to use this practice to support the participation, peer engagement, and academic learning of students with significant cognitive disabilities can be empowering. School teams can try to understand how educators are impacted in these types of ways through informal interviews or questionnaires.

### Sustaining and Expanding

Good teaching does not happen in isolation. Finding ways to help teachers connect more with one another—or even to leverage the connections they already have—can be incredibly helpful for expanding the use of effective cooperative learning to include students with significant cognitive disabilities. At a school level, providing professional development related to cooperative learning in conjunction with UDL can help promote school-wide change. However, *who* teachers know is as important for changing their agency and practice as *what* they know (Baker-Doyle & Yoon, 2020). School teams should think of ways to promote the sharing of ideas and supports across educators related to cooperative learning, whether that is through structural change at the school (e.g., grouping teachers in teams, making time for collaboration), helping teachers become more aware of the importance of their own social networks, or fostering a culture in which collaboration and the sharing ideas or resources is valued and expected.

### Specific Considerations

#### Across Ages and Grades

Cooperative learning can be implemented successfully in inclusive classrooms in all grades—from early elementary years to post-secondary learning. However, it is important for teachers to consider their specific students when planning cooperative learning. For example, younger students, such as those in the lower elementary grades (K-2), will likely need more instruction and support related to using foundational social skills within cooperative learning groups such as taking turns with materials. In contrast, older students may have more experience and confidence working collaboratively in this way, but could benefit from learning other cooperative skills such as making decisions democratically or active listening.

#### Individualized Supports

Teachers should provide individualized support to students with significant cognitive disabilities to promote their learning, participation, and during cooperative learning groups with their peers. This personalized support can take many different forms, including augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) such as speech-generating devices or communication boards if the student has complex communication needs, or adapted materials if the student has a visual impairment or physical disabilities. Collaboration with other team members is important to identify the best individualized support for students with disabilities.

#### Cultural Responsiveness

Culturally responsive teaching requires that teachers work to create equitable classrooms that support the learning of all students from diverse backgrounds. Well-designed cooperative learning can also help students learn to value diversity. It can also strengthen students’ desire and skills to work with peers who come from backgrounds different than their own because it gives them opportunities to know, work with, and interact with classmates at a personal level (Johnson & Johnson, 2009). When students work cooperatively to reach shared goals, they get to see one another’s personal strengths and abilities, rather than stereotypes or labels.

### Case Application

Mrs. Harrison is a 7th grade Life Science teacher at Oakland Middle School. After teaching for 10 years at the school, Mrs. Harrison feels she is a skilled and experienced teacher. She is passionate about helping students engage deeply and critically with understanding key concepts— from systems within single cells to complex ecosystems. This year is the first year that Mrs. Harrison has a student with a significant cognitive disability included in one of her classes. Before the school year begins, Mrs. Harrison doesn’t know all that much about Christiana, who has Down syndrome. But, she does know that she wants to be sure her classroom is a place where Christiana will fully belong—where she is [welcomed](/ties/peer-engagement/belonging/welcomed), involved in every aspect of the class, and [valued](/ties/peer-engagement/belonging/needed) as a member.

Now, about a month into the school year, Mrs. Harrison is getting ready for a 3-week unit on cell structure and function. She already embeds informal opportunities for peer interaction throughout her lessons on a regular basis (e.g., “[turn and talk](/ties/foundations-of-inclusion-tips/turn-and-talk-in-the-inclusive-classroom),” “think-pair-share”). For this unit, Mrs. Harrison has also planned two more formal cooperative learning activities—a jigsaw activity for students to learn about each different part of an animal cell, and a group project that involves creating a 3-D model of a cell to understand how cell parts and their unique functions work together. The jigsaw activity involves groups of four students. Each group is assigned the task of becoming an expert on a certain cell part and its function (e.g., cell membrane, nucleus). Students are then re-grouped so there is one “expert” for each part of the cell in each new group. Using multiple means—like videos, explaining, and pictures—each “expert” student is expected to teach their new groupmates about that part of a cell. Although Mrs. Harrison has used these cooperative learning activities in the past, she wonders how to best support and include Christiana in meaningful ways.

One of the collaboration strategies that Mrs. Harrison had set up with Mr. McLoughlin, the special education teacher, and Ms. Kincaid, a classroom paraprofessional, was meeting together before each new unit. At the meeting for this unit, Mrs. Harrison brought up her questions about supporting Christiana during the cooperative learning activities. Focusing first on the jigsaw activity, Mrs. Harrison, Mr. McLoughlin, and Ms. Kincaid identified several strategies for supporting Christiana well. Since there is an odd number of students in the class, they decided to put Christiana in a group of 5, rather than 4. This would allow her to have a “partner” to work with collaboratively when the students re-grouped to teach one another. Mrs. Harrison and Ms. Kincaid knew that Christiana’s friend Nicki would be the perfect partner. They also wanted Christiana to be able to be in the group focused on becoming experts on the nucleus of the cell. They knew that spending more time learning about the nucleus would set her up well for learning about other key content in the future, like cell division. Mr. McLoughlin agreed to work with Mrs. Harrison over email to develop a visual checklist of expectations for the activity and a communication board to support understanding and use of key vocabulary. They also planned how Mrs. Harrison and Ms. Kincaid would each rotate through student groups to offer support—including Christiana’s group.

This team of educators met again after the lessons with the jigsaw activity were complete. Ms. Kincaid and Mrs. Harrison told Mr. McLoughlin how things went. They were impressed by how well Christiana and Nicki worked together to teach other students about the nucleus. They also discussed a few of the things that seemed to be more challenging, which included that the peers in Christiana’s group tended to try to help her too much. Together, the team decided that Ms. Kincaid and Mrs. Harrison could use times they checked-in with groups to teach peers how to use wait time before offering help. Overall, the team was pleased with how cooperative learning helped all students, including Christiana, engage with the challenging curriculum and with each other.
