--- SOURCE 2: 結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析 ---
URL: https://www.airitilibrary.com/Article/Detail/a0000110-N202401060008-00012

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents an academic research article titled "結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析" (A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Structured Teaching on Cognition and Behavior of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder), authored by 郝佳華 (Hao Jia-hua) and 吳裕益 (Wu Yu-yi), published in the 《中華民國特殊教育學會年刊》 (Journal of the Special Education Association of the Republic of China), 112年度 (2023), pages 269-298.

**Purpose & Context:** The study examines the effectiveness of structured teaching (結構化教學) as an educational approach tailored to the visual-thinking style and preferred learning methods of individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), aiming to evaluate its application effectiveness in special education research in Taiwan and the level of evidence-based practice.

**Methodology:** Using meta-analysis, researchers collected studies from two online databases ("全國博碩士論文知識加值系統" National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations, and "華藝線上圖書館" Airiti Library), searching with three keywords: "結構化教學" (structured teaching), "TEACCH," and "視覺提示策略" (visual cue strategies). A total of 103 studies were collected (14 and 89 respectively). After filtering for single-case research design with ASD students as subjects, 8 studies met the criteria (7 from the theses database, 1 from Airiti), covering 19 individual cases.

**Key Results:**
1. Effect sizes: 15 of the intervention effect sizes (78.95%) reached a large effect size level. The weighted average effect size (Tau-U) was the same (.81) under both fixed-effect and random-effect models, classified as a "medium" effect size.
2. The effectiveness of structured teaching interventions varied based on the students' educational stage, intervention topic/time, and teaching elements used. The approach showed medium-to-large effects across educational stages and on both cognition/skills and behavior, with greater effects from longer intervention times.
3. There is currently insufficient evidence to support that the four moderator variables significantly moderate the intervention effectiveness.
4. Over nearly 20 years, only 8 single-case studies applying this teaching method to autism were found, indicating a lack of research. Intervention topics mostly focused on improving cognitive skills (73.68%), intervention duration was mostly 12 weeks (2-3 hours/week), and only 2 studies fully used all five structured teaching elements; most researchers used visual cue strategies or teaching materials.

**Conclusion:** The study provides recommendations for future research design and application of structured teaching for ASD students.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
本研究採後設分析法，從「全國博碩士論文知識加值系統」、「華藝線上圖書館」二個線上資料庫，以「結構化教學」、「TEACCH」，「視覺提示策略」三個關鍵字，收集後發現各計14篇及89篇研究，合計103篇；再以單一個案研究設計，自閉症光譜障礙症學生為受試對象...共計八篇。
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: 結構教學法對學齡前自閉症兒童學習成效之研究 ---
URL: https://ndltd.ncl.edu.tw/r/04890952828076420124

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a record page from the National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations in Taiwan (臺灣博碩士論文加值系統) for a doctoral dissertation published in 1999.

**Bibliographic Information:**
- **Author:** 倪志琳 (Chi-Lean Ni)
- **Title:** 結構教學法對學齡前自閉症兒童學習成效之研究 (The Effects of TEACCH Structure Teaching Strategies to the Learning Outcome of Preschool Children with Autism)
- **Advisors:** 宋維村 (Soong Wei-Tsuen) and 林幸台 (Lin Hsin-Tai)
- **Degree:** Doctoral (博士)
- **Institution:** National Taiwan Normal University (國立臺灣師範大學), Special Education Research Institute (特殊教育研究所)
- **Field:** Education, Special Education
- **Published:** 1999, Graduation academic year 87; 246 pages; in Chinese
- **Keywords:** 結構教學法 (structure teaching method), 學齡前自閉症兒童 (preschool children with autism), 早期療育 (early intervention)
- **Permanent URL:** https://hdl.handle.net/11296/3sk99c
- **Usage statistics:** Cited 60 times, viewed 1,984 times, bookmarked 7 times

**Study Purpose and Methods:**
The study explored the effects of TEACCH structure teaching strategies (developed by the University of North Carolina) on learning outcomes of preschool children with autism. A single-subject research design with multiple probe design was used. Four children from the Hong-Ai early intervention program participated. Instruments included the Chinese Child Developmental Inventory (CCDI) and PsychoEducational Profile Revised (PEP-R), supplemented by parent/teacher questionnaires and interviews.

**Key Results:**
1. All four children showed overall developmental progress on CCDI and PEP-R. Rate-of-change indicators exceeded 1.0, showing faster development during intervention than before. Children performed better in comprehension-conceptual, situation comprehension, cognitive performance, and imitation than in expressive language and cognitive verbal areas.
2. Except for one child who did not master an imitation goal, all other children achieved their individual learning goals and showed maintenance during follow-up. Children with lower developmental quotients required longer teaching periods for individual goals.
3. Parents reported positive effects on their parenting attitudes, methods, and emotional adjustment. Teachers found structure teaching beneficial to their instructional approaches.
4. The Hong-Ai early intervention program was validated as an effective model when assessed against Powers' (1992) eight essential components of early intervention for children with autism (structured behavioral treatment, parent involvement, early initiation, intensive treatment, generalization planning, social/communication skill development, trained and supervised staff, and integration with typically developing children).

The dissertation contains chapters on introduction, literature review, methodology, results analysis, discussion, and conclusions/recommendations. It includes an extensive reference list of over 150 Chinese and English works on autism research, early intervention, and structured teaching.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"本研究旨在探討結構教學法教導學齡前自閉症兒童學習之成效。由文獻探討可知，美國北卡羅來納大學TEACCH方案所發展的結構教學法對自閉症兒童療育具成效" (This study aims to explore the effectiveness of structure teaching methods on learning outcomes of preschool children with autism, based on the TEACCH program developed by the University of North Carolina).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: 回合式教学法的有效学习: 来自自闭症儿童职前教师的证据 ---
URL: https://journal.psych.ac.cn/xlxb/CN/article/downloadArticleFile.do?attachType=PDF&id=15413

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Acta Psychologica Sinica (2023, Vol. 55, No. 2, pp. 237-256), investigated the effectiveness of different learning material presentation formats on pre-service teachers' self-learning of Discrete Trial Teaching (DTT) for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The researchers conducted three experiments with Chinese pre-service teachers from Northwest Normal University in Lanzhou, China.

Background: ASD prevalence in China is 0.70% (1 in 143 children); the US CDC (2021) estimates 1 in 44 children. More autistic children are entering inclusive education settings, but regular teachers generally lack knowledge of evidence-based interventions. Training pre-service teachers in DTT (an evidence-based intervention) is critical.

Methods: Three experiments compared three learning material formats: (1) real teaching videos (audio-visual dual-channel: subtitle + picture + sound explanation), (2) PowerPoint presentations (visual single-channel: text + image), and (3) Word text documents (visual single-channel). All materials covered the same DTT content (26 teaching trials). Experiments used a self-paced "learning→test→answer→feedback" loop, with learning effectiveness measured by trials needed to reach ≥80% error detection rate. Experiment 3 (6 participants) additionally measured DTT implementation fidelity improvement via role-playing with pre/post tests, using a 21-item DTT fidelity checklist.

Results: 
- Experiment 1 (n=24): Real teaching video required fewest learning sessions (M=3.33) versus PPT (M=4.33) and Word (M=5.17); F(2,23)=8.14, p=0.001.
- Experiment 2 (n=24, different test video assignment): Video (M=4.17) < PPT (M=5.17) < Word (M=8.17); F(2,23)=19.09, p<0.001. PPT significantly outperformed Word here.
- Experiment 3 (n=6): Video (M=2.50) < PPT (M=3.83) < Word (M=5.67); F(2,4)=30.33, p<0.001. Fidelity improvement: video (41.70%) > PPT (30.00%) > Word (26.27%); F(2,4)=38.25, p<0.001.

Conclusions: The modality effect holds for pre-service teachers learning DTT. Audio-visual dual-channel materials (real teaching videos) produce the best learning outcomes in both declarative knowledge and practical implementation fidelity. This extends channel effect research to evidence-based educational interventions for autism. Practical implications include building real teaching video resource libraries, using mastery-based progressive self-learning models, and flipped classroom approaches. Limitations: further research needed on transfer to real autistic children, applicability to parents/teachers, and other evidence-based interventions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"学习内容以视听双通道方式呈现时, 自闭症儿童职前教师的自主学习效果最好" (Learning content presented in audio-visual dual-channel format produces the best autonomous learning outcomes for pre-service teachers of children with autism), 结果证实, 使用基于计算机呈现的、结合了视频示范技术和自我指导技术的视听双通道材料(真实教学视频)呈现方式, 可以更加有效地提高自闭症儿童职前教师DTT 的学习效率和实施忠诚度 (Results confirmed that audio-visual dual-channel materials incorporating video modeling and self-instruction technologies can more effectively improve pre-service teachers' DTT learning efficiency and implementation fidelity).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 5: 适用于自闭症谱系障碍学生的TEACCH教学法 - CinLearn教育首页 ---
URL: https://www.cinlearn.com/%E9%80%82%E7%94%A8%E4%BA%8E%E8%87%AA%E9%97%AD%E7%97%87%E8%B0%B1%E7%B3%BB%E9%9A%9C%E7%A2%8D%E5%AD%A6%E7%94%9F%E7%9A%84teacch%E6%95%99%E5%AD%A6%E6%B3%95

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, published on January 25, 2024, by Shanghai Career Study Technology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai Zhi Xue Ke Ji), explains the TEACCH teaching method ("Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children") designed for students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD/TEA). 

**What is TEACCH?** It is an educational philosophy focused on individual differences in each ASD student, using structured environments, task visualization, and adaptive materials to improve students' abilities, quality of life, and create an inclusive learning atmosphere.

**Benefits of TEACCH:**
- Improves communication skills through visual structuring for students with language difficulties
- Enhances social skills by providing tools to interact more effectively with peers and environment
- Increases autonomy/independence by focusing on functional skills (dressing, eating, time management)
- Reduces anxiety through structured, predictable environments that create safety and comfort

**Classroom implementation strategies:**
1. Task personalization - adapting teaching plans to each student's abilities and preferences
2. Continuous visual support - using diagrams, calendars, and activity boards
3. Consistency and coherence - establishing predictable daily routines with regular activity, rest, and transition times
4. Clear direct communication - using concise, clear language with visual presentation of instructions
5. Sensory-friendly environment - creating comfortable spaces with quiet rest areas and adaptive materials
6. Promoting social interaction - implementing structured activities like role-play and cooperative tasks

The page concludes by recommending relevant master's programs at the European University of Madrid (UEM) for those interested in learning more about ASD education, and promotes following the official WeChat account "UEM Online."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
TEACCH其实是“Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children”（自闭症及相关沟通障碍儿童的治疗和教育）的缩写，这种方法遵循一种教育哲学，专注于每个TEA学生的个体差异。, 通过结构化的环境、任务的可视化和材料的适应性，TEACCH教学法可以提升TEA学生的能力，改善他们的生活质量，并在课堂上中创造一个包容和多元的学习氛围。, 详细的教学计划以及教育工作者、治疗师及家庭之间的有效合作是在课堂上应用TEACCH教学法的必备条件, 通过采用TEACCH教学法，自闭症谱系障碍（TEA）的学生有机会最大限度地发挥他们的潜力，发展关键技能，并充分参与到教育和社交环境中来。
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: 跨学科视角下孤独症学生融合课堂教学策略研究 - 教育研讨 - Full-Text HTML - SCISCAN PUBLISHING LIMITED ---
URL: https://www.sciscanpub.com/index/journals/ainfo/es/8017.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents a research paper titled "Research on Inclusive Classroom Teaching Strategies for Students with Autism from an Interdisciplinary Perspective" (跨学科视角下孤独症学生融合课堂教学策略研究), authored by Li Xiaojuan (李晓娟), published on the International Open Access Journal Platform (SCISCAN). The study addresses the challenge of teaching students with autism in inclusive classrooms, which is framed within China's "14th Five-Year Plan" for special education development promoting integrated education and new curriculum standards requiring cross-disciplinary themed learning.

**Methodology:** The research employed a multi-case embedded research design studying four students with autism (3 boys, 1 girl) in grades 2-4 across four different schools, with mild, moderate, and severe disabilities. Pre-research assessment found classroom participation rates of only 5-10% (2-4 minutes of a 40-minute class) and task completion accuracy of 0-20%. Data was collected through document analysis, participatory observation, and semi-structured interviews with triangular verification.

**Key Results:**
- Student Xiaojun: participation rose from 10% to 87%, with 80%+ accuracy on academic tasks
- Student Xiaolin: participation rose from 5% to 45%, with improved joint attention
- Students Xiaoke and Xiaoduan: participation rose from 45% to 91% and 20% to 65% respectively (in a 7-subject integrated course)
- Overall, autism students' participation increased from 5-10% to 60-90%; voluntary hand-raising increased an average of 415%; behavioral disturbances significantly decreased
- Teachers (from 30 interviews) showed changed attitudes toward inclusive education and began reflecting on their teaching practices

**Five Effective Strategies Identified:**
1. Knowledge/skill integration strategy (connecting multiple disciplines)
2. Emotional environment optimization (safe, positive classroom climate with visual supports)
3. Multi-sensory integration (visual, auditory, and kinesthetic channels)
4. Cognitive pattern adaptation (matching teaching rhythm to brain cognitive principles, progressing from lower to higher-order thinking)
5. Individualized ability supplementation (pre-class preparation, tiered materials, peer support partners, individualized instruction)

**Key Conclusions:** Strategies designed for autism students benefit the entire class—and vice versa. The study recommends holistic class-level instructional design integrating general and special education resources. Limitations include the small sample size affecting generalizability; future research should expand the sample and develop collaborative models between multidisciplinary and special education teachers. The paper includes 8 references on special education, cross-disciplinary methods, and case study research.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"在跨学科融合教育课堂中，适用于普通学生的有效教学策略，在调整细节后同样可有效支持孤独症学生的学习；反之，即使是专为孤独症学生设计的教学方法亦能有效促进普通学生的学习。" (In interdisciplinary inclusive classrooms, effective teaching strategies for regular students can equally support autism students' learning after adjusting details, and vice versa—teaching methods designed specifically for autism students can effectively promote regular students' learning.)

SUMMARY:

This is a news article from China News (中国新闻网), originally sourced from 澎湃新闻 (The Paper), published on March 12, 2021, and authored by reporter 卫佳铭. Key points covered:

**Background and Statistics:**
- According to the 2017 "China Autism Education Rehabilitation Industry Development Report," there are over 10 million people with autism in China, with 2 million+ autistic children aged 0-14, growing at a rate of nearly 200,000 per year.
- Autism (自闭症/孤独症) is a representative pervasive developmental disorder characterized by language/social communication barriers, narrow interests/activities, and repetitive stereotyped behaviors.

**Policy Context:**
- 2014: "Special Education Improvement Plan (2014-2016)" required mildly disabled children to attend regular schools, with "zero rejection" policies adopted in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Xiamen, etc.
- July 2017: The Second Special Education Improvement Plan (2017-2020) further prioritized mainstream school placement for disabled children.
- A 2018 report by the National Alliance of Parents Organizations of People with Mental Disabilities found that only 69% of applicants successfully enrolled in school in 2017.
- 2015 State Council plan promoted inclusive education and building special education resource classrooms (资源教室) in schools with more disabled students.

**Personal Stories:**
- 琪琪 (Qiqi), in Guangzhou, was expelled from school in 2nd grade, then transferred to a more inclusive school. Now in regular junior high, her parents hide her condition and struggle with homework support. Her father 成强 (Cheng Qiang) had to become her "shadow teacher" after hiring an inexperienced college graduate for 5,000 yuan/month.
- 豆豆 (Doudou) in a remote western Guangdong town has been "barely passing time" in mainstream school.
- 小鹿 (Xiaolu), age 7 in Dandong, Liaoning, had her enrollment delayed one year; her mother spent over 1 million yuan on rehabilitation and cannot afford an accompanying assistant (陪读).

**Challenges:**
- Shortage of "shadow teachers" (影子老师/特教助理) - hiring one costs 100,000+ yuan per year per parent reports; many schools refuse to allow them in classrooms.
- Resource classrooms built at cost (e.g., one school spent 200,000 yuan) are often unused due to lack of resource teachers.
- Resource teachers rarely have dedicated staffing positions (编制); most are regular teachers doing double duty.
- Teachers lack special education training; some parents report inappropriate treatment (e.g., harsh criticism that backfired on a girl named 星星/Xingxing who tripped classmates to get attention).
- Special education funding in underdeveloped areas is inadequate; in Bijie, Guizhou, resource classroom construction and teacher training are seriously insufficient.

**Expert Solutions Proposed at 2021 Two Sessions (两会):**
- CPPCC member 邰丽华 (Tai Lihua), head of the China Disabled People's Art Troupe, proposed adding a "one person one plan" (一人一案) approach in the Third Special Education Improvement Plan, allowing schools to hire special education teachers as needed, with an integrated system: "head teacher overall responsibility, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination."
- CPPCC member 黄绮 (Huang Qi), associate professor at Shanghai International Studies University Law School, proposed opening dedicated special education schools for autistic children and including them in compulsory education.

**Science of Assessment and IEP:**
- Current placement in China is based mainly on IQ testing: below 50 suggests special school; 50-70 suggests mainstream school (随班就读).
- IEP (Individualized Education Program) originated in the US in 1975; in the US, a team (school psychologist + learning disability specialists) does comprehensive assessment of intelligence, academics, and social-emotional skills before placement.
- 石荟 (Shi Hui), an inclusive education teacher at New York City and Columbia University early childhood special education graduate, explained US best practices: parents have absolute say in IEPs, teachers cooperate ("regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach"), and IEPs are re-evaluated every 3 months. She believes the best arrangement is one with the least restriction while ensuring effective learning.

The article concludes with optimism that like developed countries, China's special education will improve through continued parental advocacy and policy advancement, though it requires a more inclusive and free social environment. All personal names in the article are pseudonyms.

This webpage from the Calgary CCM Centre (中信卡城中心) is a Chinese-language article (published January 2024) about applying "Visual Strategies" to help children with autism.

The article explains that "visual strategies" is an approach using visual information to help children with autism. Since these children often process visual information better than verbal communication, visual strategies leverage this strength to compensate for difficulties in verbal expression and reception, improving their comprehension, self-expression, self-care, social skills, and behavior/emotion management. Visual strategies can be delivered through text, images, and photos.

The article focuses on how to implement visual strategies at home, detailing five main tools:
1. **Environment arrangement** - Using furniture to divide a learning space into different activity areas with labels, helping children distinguish appropriate activities for different settings (e.g., desk for homework, dining table for meals).
2. **Schedule (日程表)** - Using objects, photos, or pictures with text to show daily activities and their order, allowing children to anticipate changes and reduce anxiety.
3. **Calendar (月曆)** - Placing pictures and text on a calendar to prepare children for upcoming special events or changes (e.g., birthday parties, clinic visits, school holidays), reducing negative emotions from change.
4. **Procedure charts (程序圖)** - Breaking complex tasks into smaller steps displayed with images and text, helping children understand connections between steps and complete tasks more independently.
5. **Communication pictures (溝通圖片)** - Using cards with images of everyday objects/activities to encourage children to actively express their needs, enhancing communication motivation and two-way communication.

Key reminders: Since every autistic child differs in abilities and needs, parents should tailor visual strategies to each child's characteristics and modify them as the child ages.

References cited include resources from Heep Hong Society (協康會), Autism Community Training, and academic research on visual cue strategies. The article states it is for reference only and advises parents to consult therapists or specialists with questions. --- SOURCE 12: Is there science behind that? Antecedent-based interventions ---
URL: https://asatonline.org/for-parents/becoming-a-savvy-consumer/is-there-science-behind-that-antecedent-based-interventions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Association for Science in Autism Treatment (ASAT), authored by Elizabeth Hardesty, MA, BCBA, Breanna Roberts, MA, BCBA, and Thomas Zane, PhD, BCBA-D (Department of Applied Behavioral Science, University of Kansas), examines the evidence base for antecedent-based interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

**Context:** Most children with ASD engage in at least one form of challenging behavior. These behaviors are often triggered by specific antecedents (events occurring before the behavior), such as loud noises, healthcare appointments, instructions, chores, academic/hygiene tasks, and novel foods. Antecedent-based interventions aim to change these environmental triggers to decrease challenging behavior and increase socially appropriate behavior.

**Core Intervention Types:** Antecedent-based interventions typically include one or more of: (a) stimulus fading or graduated exposure, (b) noncontingent reinforcement (providing reinforcement on a time-based schedule rather than contingent on behavior), (c) advanced notice (warnings before transitions), (d) choice-making, and (e) demand fading (reducing task difficulty).

**Research Evidence:**
- Kupzyk & Allen (2019): Review of 32 studies on graduated exposure for medical/dental procedures; 96% reported effectiveness in reducing challenging behavior and increasing compliance (72% included consequent-based interventions).
- Abdel-Jalil et al. (2024): Graduated exposure increased completion of medical procedures in 70% of participants; combined with other interventions in 87.1% of applications.
- Chazin et al. (2021): Meta-analysis of 39 studies (79 participants) on challenging behaviors related to nonpreferred activities; antecedent-only interventions were effective in 67.5% of applications. Noncontingent reinforcement was effective in 50% of applications (12 of 24); demand fading and advanced notice were effective 100% of the time (across two participants each).
- Tereshko et al. (2021): Systematic review of 21 articles on antecedent-based feeding interventions for food selectivity; stimulus fading was categorized as highly effective, but 67% of studies used treatment packages combining antecedent and consequent interventions.
- The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice (Steinbrenner et al., 2020) found antecedent-based interventions strongly supported by 49 articles. The National Standards Project (2009) also classified antecedent packages as evidence-based.
- Kamana et al. (2023): Trained ~150 group home/day service staff on a prevention package (positive interactions every ~5 min, promoting engagement, clear instructions, reducing reinforcement after challenging behavior); staff acquired skills but effects on challenging behavior were not directly evaluated.

**Caveats:** Most studies combined antecedent-based interventions with consequent-based interventions (e.g., differential reinforcement of alternative behavior), so it is unknown if consequences need to be changed for similar outcomes. More research is needed on optimal fading strategies, which intervention combinations are most effective, caregiver acceptance, and whether antecedent-only packages can prevent challenging behavior.

**Conclusion:** There is a large body of research supporting antecedent-based interventions as evidence-based across various applications and settings, though more research is needed on the conditions under which specific interventions (e.g., stimulus fading for food acceptance vs. graduated exposure for medical procedures) are most effective.
</summary>

"Antecedent-based interventions include an 'arrangement of events or circumstances that precede an activity or demand in order to increase the occurrence of an alternative socially appropriate behavior or lead to the reduction of challenging/interfering behavior'" (Steinbrenner et al., 2020).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 14: The role of antecedent strategies in behavior management ---
URL: https://www.skillbuildersaba.com/blog/the-role-of-antecedent-strategies-in-behavior-management

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an educational article from Skill Builders ABA (SkillBuildersABA.com) about the role of antecedent strategies in behavior management, with a focus on proactive approaches for optimizing classroom behaviors.

**Core Concepts:**
- Antecedent strategies are proactive techniques used to influence behavior before it occurs by changing the environment or context to prevent undesired behaviors and encourage positive actions.
- They involve manipulating environmental conditions (rather than reacting after behavior occurs) to create a supportive environment where desirable behaviors are more likely to occur.
- These strategies can reduce the motivation for challenging behaviors by altering reinforcing factors.

**Types of Antecedent Strategies (with examples):**
1. Signaling consequences - using cues like hand signals to indicate what behaviors will be reinforced
2. Providing choices - offering students choices of activities to boost motivation
3. Non-contingent reinforcement (NCR) - giving reinforcement independently of behaviors
4. Manipulating motivating events - altering environment to lessen triggers
5. High-probability request sequences - requesting easy tasks first to build compliance momentum
6. Stimulus control strategies - pairing stimuli with reinforcement
7. Demand fading - gradually adjusting task difficulty

**The ABC Model (Antecedent, Behavior, Consequence):**
- Antecedents are events occurring before behavior that signal reinforcement availability
- The behavior is the observable action; consequences follow and influence future likelihood
- Functional Behavioral Assessment (FBA) is used to identify antecedents and behavior functions (attention-seeking, escape, tangible access)
- The model incorporates motivating operations (MOs) and stimulus control

**Practical Implementation Methods:**
- Environmental modifications (classroom layout, lighting, noise reduction)
- Visual supports and cues (schedules, cue cards, prompts)
- Behavioral momentum and priming (high-probability requests, countdowns)
- Offering choices
- Non-contingent reinforcement
- Task interspersion and demand fading
- Environmental enrichment and stimulus control

**Research Evidence:**
- Meta-analyses and systematic reviews confirm antecedent-based interventions significantly reduce problematic behaviors, especially for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)
- Cited researchers include Kupzyk and Allen (2019), Chazin et al. (2021), and Tereshko et al. (2021)
- Interventions studied include non-contingent reinforcement, demand fading, advanced notice, and graduated exposure
- Combining antecedent strategies with techniques like extinction improves treatment outcomes

**Functional Behavioral Assessments (FBAs):**
- FBA identifies the purpose/function behind behaviors (attention, escape, tangible items)
- FBA data enables function-based, targeted antecedent interventions
- Components include data collection, observation, and hypothesis testing

**Key Conclusions:**
- Antecedent strategies shift focus from reacting to behaviors to preventing them
- They reduce reliance on reactive discipline which is often less effective and more disruptive
- Strategies are simple to implement, adaptable across settings, and effective for behaviors of all severities
- These approaches are especially beneficial for learners with ASD, ADHD, and other behavioral challenges
- They are foundational components of positive behavioral frameworks and comprehensive behavior intervention plans

The article includes references from IRIS Center, Autism Speaks, n2y, Baylor College of Medicine, and Indiana state resources, and promotes Skill Builders ABA services for ABA therapy.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Bridging the Gap Between Evidence-Based Practice in ASDs and the Classroom - Autism Spectrum News ---
URL: https://autismspectrumnews.org/bridging-the-gap-between-evidence-based-practice-in-asds-and-the-classroom

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Autism Spectrum News (July 1, 2015) addresses the gap between evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) and their implementation in classrooms. As ASD prevalence increases, more students receive services in public school settings, and legislation (IDEIA 2004, No Child Left Behind 2001) mandates educators implement evidence-based programs. However, many interventions are based on anecdotal reports, case studies, or non-referred journals rather than empirical evidence, and a third of interventions teachers report using have limited research support.

Key barriers to implementing EBPs identified in the literature include teacher training, administrative support, time for planning, and clear role definitions. A systems perspective is needed to move evidence-based practices into daily education.

The article highlights the National Professional Development Center on Autism Spectrum Disorders (NPDC), a collaboration among the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, the Waisman Center at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and the MIND Institute at UC-Davis. The NPDC has established criteria for determining if an intervention is evidence-based:
1. Two high-quality experimental or quasi-experimental group design studies by at least two different researchers, OR
2. Five high-quality single-subject studies by three investigators with at least 20 total participants, OR
3. A combination: one high-quality group design study plus at least three high-quality single-subject studies by three different investigators.

The NPDC has identified 27 evidence-based practices for teaching children with ASDs. Since the literature rarely describes implementation in enough detail, the NPDC created step-by-step guidelines, checklists, and web-based modules (developed with the Ohio Center for Autism and Low Incidence Disabilities, available at autisminternetmodules.org) containing evidence bases, procedural details, data collection methods, case examples, videos, and resources.

The authors recommend that teachers use the NPDC modules to learn EBPs and implement them with fidelity. School leaders, curriculum selectors, and teacher recruitment/evaluation professionals should receive training to ensure effective strategies are used. Teacher preparation programs should prepare future educators to evaluate research, identify EBPs, and stay informed of new research. School systems must encourage professional development. The authors conclude that moving from science to practice remains a clear challenge but is a critical next step for the field.

The article was written by Jill Krata, PhD (Program Coordinator of Autism BrainNet at Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, with over 15 years of experience in ASDs and intellectual disabilities) and Patrick R. Hof, MD (Irving and Dorothy Regenstreif Research Professor of Neuroscience and Vice-Chair of the Fishberg Department of Neuroscience at Icahn School of Medicine, Director of the Seaver Autism Center Tissue Program since 2014). References cited include works by Boutot & Myles (2011), Hess et al. (2008), Odom et al. (2010), Perry & Weiss (2007), Simpson (2005), and Wong et al. (2015).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Autism And The Impact Of Environmental Noise On Learning ---
URL: https://www.allaboutaba.com/blog/autism-and-the-impact-of-environmental-noise-on-learning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article (published October 1, 2025) examines the impact of environmental noise on learning for children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) and provides strategies for creating inclusive classrooms and educational environments.

**Key findings:**
- Children with ASD often experience hyper-reactivity to sounds that neurotypical children ignore, turning ordinary classroom noises (chatter, footsteps, equipment hums) into sources of distress and distraction.
- Noise sensitivity impairs focus, comprehension of spoken instructions, and speech/language abilities, especially in noisy environments.
- Poor classroom acoustics (excessive reverberation, echoes, and external noise) weaken communication channels and elevate stress, hindering emotional regulation and attention.
- Scientific research shows increased ambient noise leads to longer reaction times, more errors in cognitive tasks, and reduced attentional capacity. Many existing school and cafeteria spaces do not meet the acoustic needs of autistic children without acoustic treatments.
- Environmental noise from traffic, airplanes, and indoor sources disrupts sleep (increased night waking, bedtime resistance), increases daytime irritability and hyperactivity, and triggers stress responses.

**Noise types:**
- White noise (all frequencies at equal intensity): masks sudden sounds; may be calming or overwhelming depending on sensitivity.
- Pink noise (balanced frequencies emphasizing lower tones): suitable for relaxation and sleep; often soothing.
- Brown noise (deep, low frequencies): grounding and calming, particularly for those sensitive to sharp sounds.
- Individual sensitivities vary greatly, so a personalized approach is recommended.

**Recommended strategies:**
- Installing sound-absorbing materials (acoustic tiles, carpets, draperies) to reduce reverberation.
- Designing classrooms with soundproof walls and windows to minimize external noise.
- Using noise-canceling headphones, earplugs, and personal listening devices.
- Implementing quiet zones or retreat rooms for overwhelmed students.
- Employing steady background sounds (white, pink, brown noise) to mask disruptive noises.
- Modifying lighting and visual clutter to reduce overall sensory overload.

The article concludes that managing environmental noise through thoughtful design and sound treatments, and updating acoustic standards, is essential for fostering equitable, supportive learning environments for autistic learners. References include studies from UCL, NIH, ScienceDirect, Nature, and the American Academy of Pediatrics.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 8: Implications of Sensory Processing and Attentional Differences Associated With Autism in Academic Settings: An Integrative Review ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8430329

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific review article published in Frontiers in Psychiatry (2021 Aug 27;12:695825, doi:10.3389/fpsyt.2021.695825) by Courtney Mallory and Brandon Keehn, examining sensory processing and attentional differences in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and their implications for academic settings.

**Background and Purpose:** The article addresses how classroom environments impact student engagement and academic performance, particularly for students with ASD who exhibit atypical sensory processing and attentional impairments. These differences may explain why students with ASD show discrepancies between intellectual ability and academic performance. The review has three objectives: (1) review current literature on sensory processing and attention in ASD, (2) examine how these functions affect academic outcomes, and (3) suggest accommodations/interventions. ASD prevalence has increased from 1 in 150 to 1 in 54 children since 2000, with 27-44% having average or above-average intelligence.

**Sensory Processing:** Dunn's Model of Sensory Processing describes four patterns based on sensory threshold (habituation vs. sensitization) and behavioral regulation: poor registration, sensitivity to stimuli, sensation seeking, and sensation avoiding. Sensory differences between ASD and TD groups are consistent across studies, with extreme sensory symptoms present in ~95% of children (ages 3-6) and adults with ASD. First-person accounts describe heightened senses, difficulty ignoring background noises, and noise as a major classroom concern. Sensory dysfunction correlates with restricted/repetitive behaviors, social impairments, and poorer communication outcomes.

**Attention:** Attention is organized into three networks per Petersen and Posner: alerting (tonic and phasic), orienting (disengaging, shifting, reengaging), and executive control (inhibition, conflict resolution, planning, cognitive flexibility). Individuals with ASD show impairments in each network—particularly orienting deficits, set shifting, and difficulty filtering irrelevant distractors. Some research suggests this may relate to increased perceptual capacity, which can enhance visual search but increase distraction.

**Classroom Impact:**
- Auditory: Signal-to-noise ratios are often below recommended levels; students with ASD show the greatest negative impact from auditory stimuli. Noise correlates with increased repetitive behaviors and stress.
- Visual: Natural/combination lighting benefits learning; LED outperforms fluorescent (especially for students with developmental delays). Heavily decorated classrooms reduce attention and learning.
- Tactile: Touch is the second-highest rated sensory modality negatively affecting students with ASD.
- Attention: Alerting, orienting, and executive functions are predictive of academic achievement across grades. For students with ASD, attention-switching difficulties link to poorer math and reading outcomes; divided attention correlates with math achievement.

**Key Findings:** 60% of students with ASD perform below predicted achievement based on intellectual ability (Estes et al.). Students with ASD are less likely to complete postsecondary degrees than students with other disabilities. Over half of students with ASD were rated as under-achieving academically with difficulty maintaining attention. The article concludes with recommendations for sensory accommodations based on Universal Design principles to decrease attentional and sensory demands while supporting all students.
</summary>

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with atypical sensory processing and attentional impairments, which may lead to challenges in successfully accessing educational material within these settings."

--- SOURCE 10: 6 Classroom Accommodations to Support Children with Sensory Processing Challenges ---
URL: https://blog.kaplanco.com/6-classroom-accommodations-to-support-children-with-sensory-processing-challenges

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Latoya Torrance (published November 30, 2025, in Kaplan Early Learning Company's Learning Center blog) provides guidance for early childhood educators on supporting children with sensory processing challenges through classroom accommodations. 

Key background information:
- Sensory processing disorder (SPD) is the brain's inability to process sensory information effectively, differing from normal sensory preferences.
- SPD affects at least 1 in 20 children ages 4-8, including those without autism, ADHD, or learning disabilities.
- Not every child with sensory needs has a formal diagnosis.
- Sources cited include Christy Isbell, PhD, OTR/L (co-author of "Sensory Integration: A Guide for Preschool Teachers") and Keriann Wilmot, OTR/L (author of "Wired Differently: A Teacher's Guide to Understanding Sensory Processing Challenges").

Signs of sensory processing challenges include: difficulty settling down or sitting still, trouble with transitions, over-sensitivity to bright lights/loud noises/unexpected sounds, frustration shown through pushing/hitting/biting/screaming, fidgeting, and bolting away from activities or teachers.

The article presents six classroom accommodations:

1. **Reduce visual clutter** - Store toys/materials in labeled bins and low open shelves, cover materials with sheets when unused, minimize wall decorations, use natural/soft lighting, and fill space with neutral natural tones.

2. **Use flexible seating options** - Balance/exercise balls, active seat cushions, cozy couches, wiggle seats, and stools. Chairs should allow children to plant feet firmly on the floor with knees bent at 90 degrees.

3. **Provide easy access to fidgets** - Stress balls, tangle toys, slime, textured balls, and fidget spinners placed at desks, tables, or in a designated fidget zone/sensory bin.

4. **Designate spaces for quiet and movement** - A quiet cozy corner with plush carpets, soft surroundings, tunnels/arches, and noise-reduction headphones; plus a movement corner with an obstacle course format (e.g., downward dog for 10 seconds, 5 jumping jacks, push the wall for 10 seconds, 10 frog jumps, 5 sit-ups).

5. **Stock the classroom with weighted items** - Blankets, lap pads, and stuffed animals that use deep pressure to activate the body's "rest and digest" system. Weighted items should be no more than 5-10% of the child's body weight, used for no longer than 20 minutes at a time, with adult supervision.

6. **Add sensory tables and bins to learning centers** - Kinetic sand, play dough, tactile toys, and water to help calm children and improve focus. The author warns against overuse, as too much stimulation can lead to meltdowns; include variety of textures, tools (tweezers, shovels, sifters), and plastic gloves to avoid overwhelming sensitive children.

The article concludes that proper accommodations help children with sensory needs learn and grow alongside their peers, and promotes Kaplan's sensory product collection for creating sensory-friendly classrooms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
There is a difference between "typical" sensory issues and sensory processing disorder (SPD). According to Christy Isbell, PhD, OTR/L... we're all sensitive to particular sensory input. Yet, sensory preferences are different from sensory processing disorder, which is the brain's inability to process sensory information in an effective way., Sensory processing disorders are also relatively common, affecting at least 1 in 20 children ages 4-8., As Wilmot states in Wired Differently, they're most often overreacting to sensory input from the environment. Their sensory issues hinder their ability to learn and participate in the classroom. And these barriers frequently manifest as bad or defiant behavior., These items use deep pressure to activate the body's "rest and digest" system. Turning on this system releases "feel-good" chemicals that produce a calming effect., But Wilmot warns against overusing this approach. Too much stimulation can quickly lead to a meltdown or tantrum, especially for children who are more sensitive to touch.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: Sensory Diets: What They Are and What the Evidence Shows ---
URL: https://www.drsensory.com/spd/sensory-diet-strategies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page from DrSensory.com provides an expert-reviewed, evidence-based guide to sensory diets for children (last updated August 6, 2026, reviewed by Dr. Eva Lassey, PT, DPT). A sensory diet is a planned set of sensory activities scheduled through the day—movement (swinging, jumping, spinning), deep pressure (squeezes, weighted items, burrowing), heavy work (carrying, pushing, climbing), and tactile/oral/calming input—to help a child stay regulated. The term has nothing to do with food; it borrows the idea of regular nourishment. Plans are highly individualized, as an activity that regulates one child can dysregulate another.

Evidence assessment: Sensory diets fall under sensory-based interventions, which have weaker evidence than Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI), a manualized approach delivered by trained occupational therapists. Per the 2025 Acuña et al. systematic review, ASI has strong evidence from randomized trials for helping children meet individualized goals but only moderate evidence of no benefit for behaviors of concern. Weighted vests have repeatedly been found to have no effect on claimed outcomes (Stephenson & Carter, 2009). A 2018 systematic review (Bodison & Parham) found moderate evidence for sensory environmental modifications to clinical settings but only limited evidence for weighted vests—suggesting reducing environmental load is usually cheaper and easier than adding activities. The recommended framing: sensory diets are a low-risk, individualized strategy many families find helpful, but not an established treatment; change the plan rather than intensifying it if not working.

Building a plan with an OT should involve assessment first, functional goals, realistic scheduling, and a review point (a useful question: "what would prompt a change of approach?"). Without a therapist, families can use movement breaks before demanding tasks, heavy work before transitions, noticing what precedes dysregulation and adjusting the environment, and building activities into existing routines. Oral sensory input (chewable jewelry, chew tools, straw drinking) is reasonable; however, this is not eating advice—restricted diets, texture difficulties, or mealtime distress warrant a feeding assessment by a speech-language pathologist or occupational therapist rather than a sensory activity plan. School integration is emphasized since most demands occur there. The page includes FAQs on weighted vests, timelines, and starting at home (start small with one or two activities, keep consistency between home and school via a shared log, and use low-cost everyday options like carrying groceries or pushing a laundry basket). Three peer-reviewed references are cited.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"A sensory diet is a planned set of sensory activities scheduled through the day to help a child stay regulated. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with food."

--- SOURCE 12: Is There Science Behind That? Sensory Diets ---
URL: https://asatonline.org/for-parents/becoming-a-savvy-consumer/is-there-science-behind-that-sensory-diets

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Association for Science in Autism Treatment (ASAT), authored by Kathleen M. Holehan, MA, BCBA, LBA, and Thomas Zane, PhD, BCBA-D (University of Kansas Department of Applied Behavioral Science), critically examines whether there is scientific evidence supporting sensory diets for individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

HISTORICAL BACKGROUND: Patricia Wilbarger proposed sensory diets in 1995, based on Jean Ayers' Sensory Integration (SI) theory (1972) and Winnie Dunn's sensory processing theory (1997). Sensory diets involve schedules of sensory-based activities (e.g., brushing, joint compression, climbing, weighted vests) provided across environments to maintain a "regulated behavioral state." A high percentage (80-90%) of individuals with ASD reportedly display sensory processing disorders, leading many occupational therapists to recommend sensory diets.

EVIDENCE STATUS: Sensory processing disorder is not recognized in the DSM-V; the American Psychiatric Association Board of Trustees rejected its inclusion due to insufficient research. Research specifically on sensory diets is sparse - only one case study (Stagnitti et al., 1999) was found, which showed initial improvements but had significant methodological limitations (including non-systematic data, anecdotal parent reports, and confounding interventions). Multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews of SI interventions (Ottenbacher 1982, Polatajko 1992, Hoehn & Baumeister 1994, May-Benson & Koomar 2010, Baranek 2002, Case-Smith et al. 2014) found mixed results, with SI showing no greater effectiveness than other interventions and lacking rigorous methodology.

POSITION STATEMENTS: The American Academy of Pediatrics (2012) concluded sensory processing disorder should not be diagnosed and there is limited evidence of effectiveness. The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice (Steinbrenner et al., 2020) found no empirical studies on sensory diets published since 2011 and recommends caution.

BOTTOM LINE: The authors conclude that "there have not been a sufficient amount of empirical studies conducted showing effectiveness for consumers and service providers to conclude that SI procedures are effective. The evidence that exists, at best, is mixed, mostly showing ineffectiveness." They argue that "until an empirical consensus is reached regarding the effectiveness of sensory diets and SI interventions, they should not be used," citing an ethical responsibility to use evidence-based interventions. The article includes extensive references and links to related ASAT articles, research synopses, and media watch letters.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"sensory diets, which continue to lack empirical support but are popular for individuals with ASD (Barton et al., 2015; Case-Smith & Arbesman, 2014)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Sensory-based interventions ---
URL: https://www.autismcrc.com.au/interventions-evidence/category-overview/sensory

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Autism CRC provides an overview of evidence for sensory-based interventions for autistic children, drawn from the report "Interventions for children on the autism spectrum: A synthesis of research evidence" (Whitehouse et al., 2020). Notably, the page includes a February 2023 update noting that Autism CRC released a new "National Guideline for supporting the learning, participation, and wellbeing of autistic children and the families in Australia" on 16 February 2023, which supersedes the information in this report.

**Background and theory:** Sensory-based interventions rest on the premise that sensory functions are fundamental building blocks of all developmental skills, and that differences in sensory processing among autistic children may produce cascading effects on skill acquisition and behavioural development. These interventions aim to change how children process sensory stimuli temporarily or permanently, with downstream therapeutic effects on attention and self-regulation.

**Clinical practice:** Application typically involves assessing the child's sensory functioning. Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) Therapy uses assessment to develop individually-tailored, sensory-rich programs, typically conducted in clinic settings with specialised equipment (e.g., suspended equipment, scooter boards). Other approaches target specific sensory modalities and may be delivered in natural environments, including auditory integration approaches, music therapy, weighted blankets, swinging, brushing, deep pressure, massage, joint compression, and vestibular stimulation. These may be combined into a 'sensory diet.'

**Core principles (from Parham et al.):** Ten elements for sensory integration therapies include providing tactile/proprioceptive opportunities, challenging sensory systems at a 'just right' level, collaborating on activity choice, teaching self-organisation, supporting optimal arousal, using play as learning context, maximising success, ensuring physical safety, arranging the room to encourage interaction, and fostering therapeutic alliance.

**Evidence summary (from systematic reviews since 2010, rated by effect type and quality H/M/L):**
- **Assorted sensory-based interventions (3 reviews):** Null effects on communication and general outcomes.
- **Auditory Integration Therapy (3 reviews):** Null effects on communication and general outcomes.
- **Ayres Sensory Integration (4 reviews):** Inconsistent effects on overall autistic characteristics, social-communication, sensory behaviours, communication, adaptive behaviour, and general outcomes; Positive effects on cognition, motor, social-emotional/challenging behaviour, academic skills, and community participation; Null effect on play.
- **Environmental enrichment (1 review):** Null effect on expressive language; Positive effect on cognition.
- **Music therapy (4 reviews):** Positive effects on social-communication, communication, motor, social-emotional/challenging behaviour, play, school/learning readiness, quality of life, and caregiver social-emotional wellbeing; Inconsistent effects on adaptive behaviour and general outcomes.
- **Sensory diet (1 review):** Null effect on general outcomes.

Most evidence is rated low-to-moderate quality, with many outcome cells having no available evidence. The page includes links to the full evidence report and seven other intervention category overviews (behavioural, developmental, NDBI, technology-based, animal-assisted, cognitive behaviour therapy, and TEACCH).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Sensory-based interventions are based on the theoretical premise that sensory functions are a fundamental building block of all developmental skills, and that differences in how children on the autism spectrum process sensory information may produce cascading effects on skill acquisition and behavioural development across a range of domains, including core autism characteristics, 2. On 16 February, 2023, Autism CRC released a new guideline... --- SOURCE 15: Sensory Integration Therapy: Everything You Need to Know ---
URL: https://soundsory.com/sensory-integration-therapy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Soundsory.com provides a comprehensive overview of Sensory Integration Therapy (SIT) for children. Written by Rachel Ann Melegrito, a licensed occupational therapist, the article was published February 21, 2024.

Key definitions and concepts covered:
- Sensory integration (SI) was defined by Jean Ayres as "organization of sensation for use" - how a child selects, organizes, and reacts to sensory information from the environment.
- The terms "sensory integration" and "sensory processing" are now used interchangeably, though "sensory processing disorder" was first used in Dr. Lucy Miller's model based on Ayres' theory.
- Sensory integration therapy is a one-on-one intervention program provided by trained occupational therapists, now trademarked as Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI).

Prevalence statistics:
- Approximately 5 to 16.5% of the general population have some form of sensory processing difficulty.
- Around 90 to 95% of children with autism have sensory processing difficulties.
- Up to 40% of children with ADHD also have SPD.

Sensory processing difficulties fall into three categories: sensory modulation problems, sensory registration problems, and sensory-based motor disorder. Common in children with ASD, ADHD, and Auditory Processing Disorder (APD).

The therapy uses play-based sensory-motor activities targeting auditory, vestibular, and tactile input, using equipment like balance beams, trampolines, swings, sensory brushes, weighted vests, and activities like playing with shaving cream.

Evidence base: A 2010 systematic review found SIT to be evidence-based; however, the American Academy of Pediatrics stated effectiveness in autism is inconclusive and limited. ASI has been included as an evidence-based intervention for children with ASD in the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice.

The article compares several sensory integration programs in detail:
- MNRI (Masgutova Neurosensorimotor Reflex Integration): $200-$500/session, 60-minute sessions
- Brain Balance: $29-$49 online assessment, $199-$299 full assessment, >1hr/day 5 days/week for 3 months minimum
- Interactive Metronome: equipment costs ~$6,000, 12-15 one-hour sessions
- Brain Gym: 26 physical movements; limited research showing no significant results
- Play Attention: $995 basic package, $2,495 professional package, 10 minutes daily
- Forbrain: $299, 20 minutes daily for 6 weeks, bone-conduction headphone technology

The article also promotes Soundsory, a home-based program integrating music therapy and movement exercises based on the Tomatis Method, involving a 40-day regimen of daily 30-minute music listening with movement exercises, using dynamic filter and bone conduction technology to stimulate auditory and vestibular systems.

Research evidence for SIT across populations includes studies from 2013-2023 showing benefits such as improved independence, reduced stereotypic behaviors, improved balance and executive functions (ASD); reduced attention deficit, hyperactivity, and impulsivity (ADHD); and reduced auditory sensitivity (APD).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Sensory integration therapy (SIT) is a one-on-one intervention program trained occupational therapists provide to children with problems with sensory integration (SI). This program is individually tailored to improve the SI problems that interfere with a child's participation in everyday activities..."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: 自闭症儿童的感觉统合障碍怎么干预？ - ALSOLIFE ---
URL: https://www.alsolife.com/column/art/1460561738753572865

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from alsolife.com is an educational article (published March 8, 2022, by ALSO孤独症) about how to intervene in sensory integration disorders (感觉统合障碍) in children with autism. 

Key points include:
- Sensory integration disorder (also called sensory processing disorder or 感统失调) is common among children with autism.
- Sensory integration (感统) refers to the brain's process of interpreting and unifying sensory information from visual, auditory, tactile, taste, olfactory, vestibular, and proprioceptive channels. Sensory integration disorder means a person cannot properly integrate information or respond appropriately.
- Specific manifestations of sensory integration disorder include:
  - **Vestibular dysfunction**: hyperactivity, inattention, restlessness in class, difficulty getting along with others, delayed language development, late talking, difficulty expressing.
  - **Visual integration disorder**: can watch cartoons/play toys for long periods but cannot read fluently, learning difficulties.
  - **Auditory integration disorder**: appears not to hear others, forgetful, loses things, forgets what others say.
  - **Proprioceptive integration disorder**: lacks confidence, passive/withdrawn, poor balance, clumsy, cannot roll, tie shoelaces, etc.
  - **Tactile integration disorder**: abnormal touch sensitivity, sluggish response to hot/cold/pain, easily nervous, unsociable, picky eating, irritable, fears unfamiliar environments, frequently sucks fingers or bites nails.
- Sensory integration disorder usually appears as a comorbid condition; doctors must consider other childhood developmental and behavioral disorders, especially autism spectrum disorder (ASD), ADHD, and developmental coordination disorder (DCD).
- A professional evaluation by a doctor is required before deciding whether a child with autism should undergo sensory integration training. If sensory integration disorder exists, sensory integration training (感统训练) is needed to improve symptoms.
- Sensory integration training is a necessary aid that helps adjust sensory input and emotional state, but it is NOT the primary rehabilitation method.
- Sensory integration training is typically conducted in game form. Parents can use toys and facilities for parent-child games, including:
  - Ball throwing/catching: exercises hand-eye coordination and arm flexibility.
  - Climbing stairs: builds courage and leg strength.
  - Pushing/pulling objects while walking: develops gross motor skills and hand-eye-leg coordination.
  - Walking backward: develops spatial concepts and body coordination.
  - Kicking a ball: develops gross motor skills including leg extension and eye-leg coordination.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
感觉统合障碍又称感觉处理障碍，即人们常说的感统失调。孩子接受感统训练的前提是确实存在感统失调，关于自闭症儿童要不要做感统训练，需由专业人士的评估，每一项干预手段的运用都要从孩子的特点出发。
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: 无处安放的自闭症“星娃”：高质量融合教育还有多远-中新网 ---
URL: https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2021/03-12/9430467.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from China News (中国新闻网), originally sourced from 澎湃新闻 (The Paper), published on March 12, 2021, and authored by reporter 卫佳铭. The article investigates the state of "high-quality inclusive/integrated education" (融合教育) for children with autism ("星娃" or "star children") in China.

Key points covered:

**Background and Statistics:**
- According to the 2017 "China Autism Education Rehabilitation Industry Development Report," there are over 10 million people with autism in China, with 2 million+ autistic children aged 0-14, growing at a rate of nearly 200,000 per year.
- Autism (自闭症/孤独症) is a representative pervasive developmental disorder characterized by language/social communication barriers, narrow interests/activities, and repetitive stereotyped behaviors.

**Policy Context:**
- 2014: "Special Education Improvement Plan (2014-2016)" required mildly disabled children to attend regular schools, with "zero rejection" policies adopted in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Xiamen, etc.
- July 2017: The Second Special Education Improvement Plan (2017-2020) further prioritized mainstream school placement for disabled children.
- A 2018 report by the National Alliance of Parents Organizations of People with Mental Disabilities found that only 69% of applicants successfully enrolled in school in 2017.
- 2015 State Council plan promoted inclusive education and building special education resource classrooms (资源教室) in schools with more disabled students.

**Personal Stories:**
- 琪琪 (Qiqi), in Guangzhou, was expelled from school in 2nd grade, then transferred to a more inclusive school. Now in regular junior high, her parents hide her condition and struggle with homework support. Her father 成强 (Cheng Qiang) had to become her "shadow teacher" after hiring an inexperienced college graduate for 5,000 yuan/month.
- 豆豆 (Doudou) in a remote western Guangdong town has been "barely passing time" in mainstream school.
- 小鹿 (Xiaolu), age 7 in Dandong, Liaoning, had her enrollment delayed one year; her mother spent over 1 million yuan on rehabilitation and cannot afford an accompanying assistant (陪读).

**Challenges:**
- Shortage of "shadow teachers" (影子老师/特教助理) - hiring one costs 100,000+ yuan per year per parent reports; many schools refuse to allow them in classrooms.
- Resource classrooms built at cost (e.g., one school spent 200,000 yuan) are often unused due to lack of resource teachers.
- Resource teachers rarely have dedicated staffing positions (编制); most are regular teachers doing double duty.
- Teachers lack special education training; some parents report inappropriate treatment (e.g., harsh criticism that backfired on a girl named 星星/Xingxing who tripped classmates to get attention).
- Special education funding in underdeveloped areas is inadequate; in Bijie, Guizhou, resource classroom construction and teacher training are seriously insufficient.

**Expert Solutions Proposed at 2021 Two Sessions (两会):**
- CPPCC member 邰丽华 (Tai Lihua), head of the China Disabled People's Art Troupe, proposed adding a "one person one plan" (一人一案) approach in the Third Special Education Improvement Plan, allowing schools to hire special education teachers as needed, with an integrated system: "head teacher overall responsibility, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination."
- CPPCC member 黄绮 (Huang Qi), associate professor at Shanghai International Studies University Law School, proposed opening dedicated special education schools for autistic children and including them in compulsory education.

**Science of Assessment and IEP:**
- Current placement in China is based mainly on IQ testing: below 50 suggests special school; 50-70 suggests mainstream school (随班就读).
- IEP (Individualized Education Program) originated in the US in 1975; in the US, a team (school psychologist + learning disability specialists) does comprehensive assessment of intelligence, academics, and social-emotional skills before placement.
- 石荟 (Shi Hui), an inclusive education teacher at New York City and Columbia University early childhood special education graduate, explained US best practices: parents have absolute say in IEPs, teachers cooperate ("regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach"), and IEPs are re-evaluated every 3 months. She believes the best arrangement is one with the least restriction while ensuring effective learning.

**Benefits of Good Inclusive Education:**
- Experts 石荟 and 刘丽 (Liu Li, who works in multiple Beijing mainstream schools) argue that good inclusive education benefits both special needs children and ordinary children - helping typical children learn about diversity and how to respect and treat others well.
- The article highlights bullying incidents (e.g., a boy taping "I have autism" on 琪琪's back) and teacher bias cases.
- 刘丽 shared a positive example: classmates spontaneously leaving red teaching aids for autistic child 天天 (Tiantian) because they knew he liked red.

The article concludes with optimism that like developed countries, China's special education will improve through continued parental advocacy and policy advancement, though it requires a more inclusive and free social environment. All personal names in the article are pseudonyms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"特殊需要孩子也是孩子，他是一个生命，可以享受他/她应有的受教育权利。" (Special needs children are also children; they are lives that can enjoy their right to education. - 菲菲妈妈/Fifi's mother), "好的融合教育一定是让特殊需要儿童和普通儿童双方受益的，它不仅能让特殊需要儿童学习社会规范、早日回归主流，同时能让普通孩子通过和特殊需要孩子相处，了解世界的多元，学会如何尊重和善待他人。" (Good inclusive education must benefit both special needs and ordinary children... - 石荟/Shi Hui), "普通教师决定教什么，特殊教师决定怎么教。" (Regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach. - 石荟 on US IEP practice), "班主任全面负责儿童发展，特教教师入班支持，资源教师总体统筹协调" (Head teacher overall responsible for child development, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination - 邰丽华's proposal), "来自同龄人欺凌的伤害给家长的触动太大了。" (The hurt from peer bullying touches parents too deeply. - 成强/Cheng Qiang)
</key_excerpts>

This is a Chinese-language article (originally written in English and translated) about autism awareness in China, written by Sihan Yang, a graduate student, for Stages Learning on December 10, 2016. Key points include: The first autism case in China was diagnosed at Nanjing Brain Hospital in the early 1980s, but 30+ years later, most people still view it as a rare condition. The article highlights Beijing Starry Rain (北京星星雨) Education Institute, an NGO offering resources, diagnostic information, parent training courses, and support platforms. The author participated in Stages Learning's global autism awareness project with students from Pakistan. The article mentions World Autism Awareness Day (April 2, 2016 was the 8th) and Autism Speaks' Light It Up Blue campaign. It concludes with links to Stages Learning, the Language Builder app, and Autism Speaks, along with academic references.

- Sensory integration involves registering, modulating, and discriminating sensory input from visual, auditory, gustatory, olfactory, tactile, proprioceptive, and vestibular systems to produce purposeful, adaptive behaviors. Dysfunction can limit a child's ability to make coordinated movements, plan new tasks, develop social relationships, and care for themselves.
- ASI intervention plans include nine core elements: delivery under direct supervision of qualified therapists (occupational, physical, or speech-language); family-centered planning with input from significant others; safe environments with equipment for vestibular, proprioceptive, and tactile stimulation; adaptive responses to challenges; child-centered activities; rich sensory stimulation especially vestibular, tactile, and proprioceptive input integrated with other senses; tasks requiring planning and successful execution; special equipment (hanging devices, scooters, balls) for posture control and balance; and activities that adjust difficulty to ensure success.

Critical conclusion: Sensory integration training is controversial despite being EBP-supported. Being evidence-based does not mean a method is "best." For children with sensory integration dysfunction, sensory training is a good supplementary intervention but cannot replace core ABA (Applied Behavior Analysis) therapy. Autism's two core deficits—social communication impairments and restricted/repetitive behaviors—are not caused by sensory integration dysfunction, so sensory integration training targets children with sensory integration disorder specifically, not autism generally.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Studies show fidgets and stress balls can increase focus, attention, and serve as stress management tools, but teachers have had mixed results introducing them.
- Not all fidgets are equal: a systematic review found that "fidget spinners negatively influence young children with ADHD's attentional functioning." Fidgets that demand visual attention or have game components (matching, unlocking, solving) are poor choices for boosting on-task behavior.
- Movement as small as squeezing a ball to robust exercise can increase on-task behavior and attention, working especially well with students who have significant attention challenges. Fidgets become valuable intervention tools when frequent movement breaks aren't possible.

RECOMMENDED CLASSROOM FIDGETS:
Good classroom fidgets are quiet, discreet, have interesting textures, and allow for lots of finger/hand movement. Recommended items include: Squigglet Bracelet, Stress-less Gel Ball, Tangle Toy, Pencil Fidget Toppers, Inside Out Ball, and Squeeze Star.

EFFECTIVE FIDGETING ALTERNATIVES:
Fidgeting doesn't have to be a specific toy - effective options include allowing students to stand at their desk, using alternative seating (therapy balls, wiggle seats), using a kick/bouncy band on chairs, or sticking Velcro on the desk.

TIPS FOR INTRODUCING FIDGETS:
1. Frame fidgets as learning tools, not toys - they provide a movement break so students can learn.
2. Use a strengths/weaknesses discussion (comparing what subjects are easy/hard to paying attention being hard).
3. Create simple fidget rules (e.g., "I use fidgets to help me pay attention," "I keep fidgets on my desk or in my hands," "I don't show other students my fidget," "I always put away my fidget when I am done").
4. Wait until novelty wears off before using fidgets as focus tools.
5. For students who mouth things, ensure fidgets are sturdy without breakable pieces.
6. Consider individual student texture preferences; offer a fidget set for selection.
7. Give the strategy time before deeming it ineffective.

The page also lists 11 academic references supporting these claims and promotes the company's fidget products (Fidget Set, Stress-Less Gel Ball, Tangle Relax, Squigglets Sensory Bracelet) with free U.S. shipping on orders over $89.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 16: Benefits and Uses of Weighted Vests for Autism – SensorySouk.com ---
URL: https://www.sensorysouk.com/blogs/community/benefits-and-uses-of-weighted-vests-for-autism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Sensory Souk (a Qatar-based retailer) discusses the benefits and uses of weighted vests for children with autism. Weighted vests provide deep touch pressure that helps children relax and focus during classroom activities, potentially reducing anxiety and increasing attentiveness. While there is no solid scientific evidence they reduce stereotypy/stimming, a 2001 study by VandenBerg showed an 18-25% increase in on-task completion of fine motor activities for children wearing weighted vests. However, conflicting research (Stephenson & Carter, 2009) found that four out of seven similar studies concluded weighted vests had no positive or negative effects.

The article outlines several key practical guidelines:
- Weight should be 5-10% of the child's body weight (up to 12% for adults)
- No clear rules on wearing duration; consult a therapist for a wearing schedule (some recommend no more than an hour, others allow full school days)
- Material and design matter for child's sensory sensitivity and willingness to wear the vest

Weighted vests provide proprioceptive input through deep pressure, sending signals to the brain that promote calm and focus. Reported benefits include calmness, increased focus, decreased stimming, reduced anxiety, better body awareness, and self-regulation.

Two main types exist: compression vests (combining weight with tightness) and deep pressure vests. Weighted vests are part of sensory integration therapy, which also includes sensory/motor activities, noise-canceling headphones, sensory diets, and environment modifications.

Important warnings: The Oxford Health NHS Foundation does not endorse weighted or compressive products, warning against use for children with respiratory problems, cardiac/heart problems, serious hypotonia, skin allergies, circulatory problems, or physical impairment preventing self-removal.

Weighted vests can serve as a calming tool for emotional episodes and meltdowns. Notable references include Temple Grandin's book "Emergence: Labeled Autistic" describing how deep pressure helped her overcome severe anxiety. The article is by Kim Barloso, originally from Autism Parent Magazine.
</summary>

"Therapists have noted a decrease in this behavior (stimming) when a weighted vest is worn... a study showed that children with autism who wore weighted vests had an 18 to 25 percent increase in on-task completion of fine motor activities (VandenBerg, 2001)."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 17: Research Roundup: Weighted Vests - Apply EBP ---
URL: https://www.applyebp.com/ask-applyebp/research-roundup-weighted-vests

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Apply EBP's "Research Roundup" series addresses the question of whether weighted vests work and what weight should be used, compiling peer-reviewed research relevant to OT, PT, and SLP practice. The overall conclusion (the "Big Picture") indicates that numerous studies, mostly with small participant numbers (including autistic children, children with ADHD, and developmental delays), found no significant change between wearing weighted vests and baselines, or no significant difference compared to no vest or unweighted vests. Studies typically used 5-10% of body weight (some up to 15%). A small number of low-to-moderate quality studies with children with ADHD showed improvement in some outcome measures. Apply EBP's take is to use other evidence-based strategies for student goals.

**Systematic Reviews findings:**
- Ouellet et al. (2021): Mixed results, with some significant improvements in task engagement in low-to-moderate quality ADHD studies, but no differences in most ASD studies.
- Barton et al. (2015): "All 6 studies examining weighted vests documented no behavioral differences in conditions with or without the weighted vests."
- Case-Smith et al. (2015): Among seven single-subject studies applying a weighted vest, only one demonstrated positive effects; findings suggest weighted vests do not result in improved behavior.
- Taylor et al. (2017): "The results of the review show that the use of WV [weighted vests] with individuals with ASD is not an evidence-based practice."
- Quigley et al. (2011): No functional relationship between 5% or 10% weighted vests and challenging behaviors.
- Stephenson & Carter (2009): On balance, "indications are that weighted vests are ineffective."

**Non-systematic studies (since 2010) findings:**
- Macphee et al. (2019, ADHD): Medication, but not weighted vests or stability balls, improved following classroom rules and academic productivity.
- Lin et al. (2014, ADHD, 110 children): Significant improvement in three attentional variables and three of four on-task behaviors, but no significant improvements in impulse control.
- Davis et al. (2013, autism): No functional relationship between weighted vest use and challenging behavior.
- Hodgetts et al. (2011 - two studies, autism): No objective improvements in some children; others still had high off-task behavior rates; use of weighted vests to decrease stereotyped behaviors or arousal was not supported.
- Collins & Dworkin (2011): "Weighted vests were not effective in increasing time on task."
- Leew et al. (2010, toddlers with ASD): No replicated effects on competing behaviours or joint attention, though mothers experienced increased morale.
- Reichow et al. (2010): "The results showed no differentiation in engagement between conditions for any of the participants" (comparing 5% weighted vest, unweighted vest placebo, and no vest baseline).

The page also promotes Apply EBP's educational offerings (symposiums, webinars, callback to join their Facebook group for a PDF version) and an article titled "4 Tips When Considering Interventions with Insufficient Evidence."
</summary>
