## Introduction

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a set of neurodevelopmental disorders characterised by a deficit in social communication, social behaviours and restrictive and repetitive behaviours, activities, or interests (American Psychiatric Association [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR3 "American Psychiatric Association. (2013). Diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders (DSM-5). Arlington, Virginia: American Psychiatric Publishing.")). Based on epidemiological studies conducted over the past 40 years, the prevalence of ASD appears to be increasing globally (WHO [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR73 "WHO (2020). Autism spectrum disorders. Retrieved 25 June 2020, from 
                  https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/autism-spectrum-disorders
                  
                .")). Recent studies indicate that ASD has an estimated prevalence rate of 1 in 54, with 4.3 of these being male for every one female diagnosed, among children aged 8 years in the USA (Maenner et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR34 "Maenner, M. J., Shaw, K. A., Baio, J., et al. (2020). Prevalence of autism spectrum disorder among children aged 8 years. Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network, 11 Sites, United States, 2016. MMWR Surveillance Summaries, 69(SS-4), 1–12.")).

Autism has a significant and persistent impact on the lives of those receiving a diagnosis as well as their families (Begum and Mamin [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR6 "Begum, R., & Mamin, F. A. (2019). Impact of autism spectrum disorder on family. Autism-Open Access, 9(04).")). Also, in financial terms, the cost of supporting children with ASDs is estimated to be £2.7 billion each year in the UK alone (Knapp et al. [2009](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR27 "Knapp, M., Romeo, R., & Beecham, J. (2009). Economic cost of autism in the UK. Autism, 13(3), 317–336.")). The financial demands, as well as the persistent and the pervasive impact of ASD on a person’s current and future well-being, highlight the importance of providing support, and Social Stories™ is a widely used intervention that is liked by professionals and acceptable to children on the autism spectrum and their families.

### Social Stories

The Social Story™ (SS) intervention was developed for, and is used frequently to assist, children with autism spectrum disorder (Kokina and Kern [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR28 "Kokina, A., & Kern, L. (2010). Social Story interventions for students with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis. Journal of Autism & Developmental Disorders, 40(7), 812–826."); Pane et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR42 "Pane, H. M., Sidener, T. M., Vladescu, J. C., & Nirgudkar, A. (2015). evaluating function-based Social Stories™ with children with autism. Behavior Modification, 39(6), 912–931.")). SS are narratives consisting of personalised text and illustrations. The intervention was introduced by Gray and Garand ([1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR21 "Gray, C. A., & Garand, J. D. (1993). Social Stories: Improving responses of students with autism with accurate social information. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 8(1), 1–10.")) to provide individuals with ASD with the information they may need to learn new information and to understand and function appropriately in different social situations. Gray and Garand ([1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR21 "Gray, C. A., & Garand, J. D. (1993). Social Stories: Improving responses of students with autism with accurate social information. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 8(1), 1–10.")) originally recommended Social Stories™ to be used only with higher functioning verbal pupils and that the entire story should be presented on a single sheet of paper without other visual distractions. Over time, some of these recommendations, particularly related to story style and format, have changed (Gray [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR16 "Gray, C. (1998). Social Stories and comic strip conversations with students with Asperger syndrome and high-functioning autism. In E. Schopler, G. Mesibov, & L. Kunce (Eds.), Asperger Syndrome or High-Functioning Autism? (pp. 167–198). Springer US."), [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR18 "Gray, C. (2004). Social Stories™ 10.0: The new defining criteria and guidelines. Jenison Autism Journal, 15(4), 2–21."), [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR19 "Gray, C. (2010). The new Social Story™ book: Revised and expanded 10th anniversary edition. Arlington, TX: Future Horizons."), [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR20 "Gray, C. (2015). The new Social StoryTM book revised and expanded 15th anniversary edition. Texas: Future Horizons Inc.."); Gray and Garand [1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR21 "Gray, C. A., & Garand, J. D. (1993). Social Stories: Improving responses of students with autism with accurate social information. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 8(1), 1–10.")). Social Stories have become a widely used intervention due to their low cost and accessibility, as well as their capacity to address parents’ support needs, such as managing challenging behaviour (Derguy et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR11 "Derguy, C., Michel, G., M’Bailara, K., Roux, S., & Bouvard, M. (2015). Assessing needs in parents of children with autism spectrum disorder: A crucial preliminary step to target relevant issues for support programs. Journal of Intellectual and Developmental Disability, 40(2), 156–166."); Wahman et al. [2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR71 "Wahman, C. L., Pustejovsky, J. E., Ostrosky, M. M., & Santos, R. M. (2019). Examining the effects of Social Stories™ on challenging behavior and prosocial skills in young children: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Topics in Early Childhood Special Education.")). Given the widely used nature of the intervention, as well as the variability in the recommendations for how the intervention should be delivered over the 25 years since it was developed, professionals must follow evidence-based practice and recommendations. This should ensure that the intervention is sound, and delivered appropriately (Suhrheinrich et al. [2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR68 "Suhrheinrich, J., Hall, L. J., Reed, S. R., Stahmer, A. C., & Schreibman, L. (2014). Evidence based interventions in the classroom. In L. Wilkinson (Ed.), Autism spectrum disorder in children and adolescents: Evidence-based assessment and intervention in schools (pp. 151–172). Washington: American Psychological Association."); Will et al. [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR74 "Will, M. N., Currans, K., Smith, J., Weber, S., Duncan, A., Burton, J., Kroeger-Geoppinger, K., Miller, V., Stone, M., Mays, L., Luebrecht, A., Heeman, A., Erickson, C. & Anixt, J. (2018). Evidenced-based interventions for children with autism spectrum disorder. Current Problems in Pediatric and Adolescent Health Care, 48(10), 234–249.")). However, despite decades of research, there is still a question as to whether or not SS interventions should be considered an evidenced-based practice (e.g. Test et al. [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR69 "Test, D. W. R. S, Knight, V., Spooner, F. (2011). A comprehensive review and meta-analysis of the Social Stories literature. 26(1), 49–62.")).

### Evidence-Based Practice

Intervention literature moves quickly, and so does evidence-based practice, which is an active and dynamic concept (Wong et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR75 "Wong, C., Odom, S. L., Hume, K. A., Cox, A. W., Fettig, A., Kucharczyk, S., Schultz, T. R., et al. (2015). Evidence-based practices for children, youth, and young adults with autism spectrum disorder: A comprehensive review. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 45(7), 1951–1966.")). The Canadian Psychological Association Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice of Psychological Treatments (Dozois et al. [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR12 "Dozois, D., Mikail, S., Alden, L., Bieling, P., Bourhon, G., Clark, D. A., et al. (2012). Evidence-based practice of psychological treatments: A Canadian perspective. Report of the CPA Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice of Psychological Treatments Canadian Psychological Association (CPA) 
                  https://cpa.ca/docs/File/Practice/Report_of_the_EBP_Task_Force_FINAL_Board_Approved_2012.pdf
                  
                . Accessed 20 June 2020.")) defines evidence-based practice (EBP) as the conscientious, explicit and judicious application of the best available research evidence to inform clinical practice and service delivery. Contrariwise, the use of treatments that are based on poor-quality research tend to waste time and money, and “prey upon the emotional vulnerability of parents and caregivers” (Zane et al. [2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR76 "Zane, T., Davis, C., & Rosswurm, M. (2008). The cost of fad treatments in autism. Journal of Early and Intensive Behavior Intervention, 5(2), 44–51."), p. 44). Reports by the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice Review Team (Odom et al. [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR41 "Odom, S., Collet-Klingenberg, L., Rogers, S., & Hatton, D. (2010). Evidence-based practices in interventions for children and youth with autism spectrum disorders. Preventing School Failure, 54, 275–282."); Steinbrenner et al. [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR66 "Steinbrenner, J. R., Hume, K., Odom, S. L., Morin, K. L., Nowell, S. W., Tomaszewski, B., Szendrey, S., McIntyre, N. S., Yücesoy-Özkan, S., & Savage, M. N. (2020). Evidence-based practices for children, youth, and young adults with Autism. The University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, Frank Porter Graham Child Development Institute, National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice Review Team.")), which aimed to document possible new EBPs whilst continuing to validate existing EBPs, failed to define the SS intervention as an EBP. However, they placed Social Narratives within the EPB category. In this case, Social Narratives were defined as “interventions that describe social situations in order to highlight relevant features of a target behaviour” (p. 29). Here Social Narratives were not considered “tantamount” to Carol Gray’s Social Stories™ ([1993](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR21 "Gray, C. A., & Garand, J. D. (1993). Social Stories: Improving responses of students with autism with accurate social information. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 8(1), 1–10.")); rather, they were defined as a distinct type of narrative. Nevertheless, they were deemed to “fit” within the Social Narratives category. Nonetheless, these conclusions were challenged by Zimmerman and Ledford ([2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR77 "Zimmerman, K. N., & Ledford, J. R. (2017). Beyond ASD: Evidence for the effectiveness of social narratives. Journal of Early Intervention, 39(3), 199–217.")) who report variable outcomes and absence of a sufficient number of rigorous studies on Social Narratives. They also advocate for professionals to be cautious with the use of social narratives in isolation for children.

### Purpose of the Current Review

Clinical observation, qualitative research, single-subject research (SSR), and randomised control trials (RCTs) are amongst the research designs that can contribute towards an “evidence base” (APA [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR4 "American Psychological Association, Presidential Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice. (2006). Evidence-based practice in psychology. American Psychologist, 61(4), 271–285.")). However, most of the published research on SSs that has been undertaken has been within “the constraints of a wholly positivist or quantitative paradigm” (Styles [2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR67 "Styles, A. (2011). Social Stories: Does the research evidence support the popularity? Educational Psychology in Practice, 27(4), 415–436."), p.424). Very few descriptive and qualitative research designs have been published. Studies such as Sandt ([2008](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR56 "Sandt, D. (2008). Social stories for students with autism in physical education. Journal of Physical Education, Recreation & Dance (JOPERD), 79(6), 42–45."))—who presents a descriptive report that explains how the author used a SS to help students with autism participate in physical education (PE) lessons—or Smith ([2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR63 "Smith, C. (2001). Using social stories to enhance behaviour in children with autistic spectrum difficulties. Educational Psychology in Practice, 17, 337–345."))—who examined the impact on children’s social behaviour of a two-session workshop for groups of parents and teacher—provide descriptive evidence about the effectiveness of SSs. Nevertheless, although useful, such evidence could be considered anecdotal, particularly when considering the effectiveness—i.e. the degree of beneficial effect in real world clinical practice (Godwin et al. [2003](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR15 "Godwin, M., Ruhland, L., Casson, I., MacDonald, S., Delva, D., Birtwhistle, R., Seguin, R., et al. (2003). Pragmatic controlled clinical trials in primary care: The struggle between external and internal validity. BMC Medical Research Methodology, 3(1)."))—of the intervention.

Several reviews of literature, in the form of systematic reviews, meta-analysis, and narrative reviews, have been published, all of which contribute towards the current knowledge base on SSs. An increase in the quality of the experimental research over time has been noted by a number of these reviews, such as Test et al. ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR69 "Test, D. W. R. S, Knight, V., Spooner, F. (2011). A comprehensive review and meta-analysis of the Social Stories literature. 26(1), 49–62.")). However, the extent, range, and nature of research activity remains unclear, whist the question of efficacy remains unanswered, especially because of the high variability in research quality that these reviews have identified. Thus, the purpose of the current review was to provide up-to-date information about the current state of SS research, with a specific focus on the effectiveness of SS interventions and factors which influence outcomes. In turn, outcomes of these findings could contribute further to the debate of whether or not SSs should be considered an EBP.

## Method

As reviews of SS already exist, the aim of the present study was not to conduct yet another literature review of one form or another, but rather to conduct a scoping review of the existing reviews. A scoping review is an exercise in mapping the existing literature (Ehrich et al. [2002](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR13 "Ehrich, K., Freeman, G., Richards, S., Robinson, I., & Shepperd, S. (2002). How to do a scoping exercise: Continuity of care. Research Policy Planning, 20, 25–29.")). An adapted version of the scoping process outlined by Arksey and O’Malley ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR5 "Arksey, H., & O’Malley, L. (2005). Scoping studies: towards a methodological framework. International Journal of Social Research Methodology, 8(1), 19–32.")) was utilised for this review. This entailed (1) the identification of the research aims; (2) the searching for relevant studies; (3) the systematic selection of studies; (4) the charting of the data; and (5) the presentation of the results.

### Identifying Relevant Studies

The electronic databases searched were CINAH EBSCO, A+Eductaion (Informit), ERIC, Education Source, PsyINFO, PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Web of Science, and ABI Inform Global. The search was limited to English language publications. Search terms used were “Social Story” and “Social Stories”. The terms were combined using the Boolean operand “OR” and across strings using the Boolean operand “AND”. The publication date was not restricted. The search results were managed and analysed using EndNote™ X9 (Endnote [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR14 "EndNote. (2013). EndNote (Version EndNote X9) [64 bit]. Philadelphia: Clarivate.")).

### Study Eligibility and Selection

The objective of the initial search was to investigate the current state of research on SS. The search that was informed by this goal yielded 459 citations following the removal of duplicates and the exclusion of citations that were not in English, were not peer-reviewed, were not related to ASD, and that were not about SS research. Titles and keywords of the remaining articles were further screened in more detail. Autism was not included in the original search terms as there are a wide range of potential variations and reading the titles and keywords ensured that the relevant studies were not erroneously excluded. This resulted in 119 full-text articles. The reading of these articles highlighted that they were already included in several reviews of literature that ranged from synthesis of literature; systematic reviews; meta-analyses; comparative reviews; and descriptive reviews. The publication dates of these articles ranged from 2004 to 2019. Thus, this scoping review included exclusively peer-reviewed reviews of literature. The final number of articles that met the inclusion criteria, and that were included in the current scoping review, was 17. The study search and selection process are presented in Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Fig1).

**Fig. 1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1007%2Fs40489-020-00235-6/MediaObjects/40489_2020_235_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6/figures/1)

PRISMA flow diagram for scoping review

### Analysis

The search results were analysed in terms of the aims identified for this scoping review. An inductive, data-driven, analysis was carried out to identify themes that could appraise the current state of SS research. A deductive analysis, which aimed to map the elements reported in the reviews of literature that specifically focused on outcomes (i.e. effectiveness of SS interventions) and factors which influence outcomes, was also carried out. NVIVO-12 software (QRS International [1999](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR47 "QSR International (1999) NVivo Qualitative Data Analysis Software [Software]. Available from 
                  https://qsrinternational.com/nvivo/nvivo-products
                  
                .")) was employed for this stage of the review, whilst a semantic content analysis of the data, as described by Braun and Clarke ([2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR8 "Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101.")), led to the coding of data according to the pre-defined research aims. Descriptive characteristics including title, author(s), year of publication, type of review, inclusion criteria, and the number of studies included in the review were extracted and organised. Also, key findings and conclusions, as well as recommendations for future research, were added to descriptive information to create detailed extraction tables (Tables[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Tab1), [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Tab2), [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Tab3), and [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Tab4)).

## Results

The 17 reviews included in this scoping study reported on a total of 120 individual studies focusing on SSs, which were conducted from 1995 to 2018. Some of these articles are included in more than one of the research syntheses included in this scoping review. Two themes were identified, as a result of the deductive analysis, whilst a further 3 themes were identified as a result of the inductive analysis of the 17 articles. The themes are (1) research design of SS research, (2) effectiveness of SS, (3) factors influencing outcomes of SSs, (4) social validity of goals of SS interventions, and (5) maintenance and generalisation of SS intervention outcomes. The “factors influencing outcomes” category consist of 2 further subthemes, which are (3.1) environmental factors and (3.2) within-child factors. These themes and subthemes are organised in hierarchical order (see Fig.[2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Fig2)) which illustrates their relevance in relation to the research objectives of this scoping review.

### 1) Research design

The research design most frequently encountered in SS research is single-subject research (Ali and Frederickson [2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR2 "Ali, S., & Frederickson, N. (2006). Investigating the evidence base of social stories. Educational Psychology in Practice, 22(4), 355–377."); Bucholz [2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR10 "Bucholz, J. L. (2012). Social Stories™ for children with autism: A review of the literature. Journal of Research in Education, 22(2), 48–73.")). The only exception to this is Karkhaneh et al.’s ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR26 "Karkhaneh, M., Clark, B., Ospina, M. B., Seida, J. C., Smith, V., & Hartling, L. (2010). Social Stories[TM] to improve social skills in children with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism: The International Journal of Research and Practice, 14, 641–662.")) review where only randomised control trials (RCTs) and controlled clinical trials (CCT) are included. Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#Tab2) presents an overview of the different research designs that have been included in the reviews. AB designs (where “A” describes a baseline phase and “B” an intervention phase) feature regularly in reviews conducted before 2012. After 2012, the reviews highlight the recurrent use of studies that, unlike AB designs, could see threats to internal validity, such as variations of ABAB designs, alternating treatment designs, and multiple-baseline designs (which involves the concurrent measurement of two or more behaviours in a baseline condition, followed by the application of the treatment variable to one of the behaviours).

The single-case research design quality utilised in SS research has been a persistent concern (McGill et al. [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR37 "McGill, R. J., Baker, D., & Busse, R. T. (2015). Social Story™ interventions for decreasing challenging behaviours: a single-case meta-analysis 1995–2012. Educational Psychology in Practice, 31(1), 21–42.")). The quality of individual studies included in any review will determine the quality of the outcomes of a review, and will consequently impact the strength and validity of the claims made by that review (Schlosser et al. [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR59 "Schlosser, R. W., Wendt, O., & Sigafoos, J. (2007). Not all systematic reviews are created equal: Considerations for appraisal. Evidence-Based Communication Assessment and Intervention, 1(3), 138–150.")). The quality of single-case research should be rigorously analysed for conclusions on causal relationships among interventions and outcomes to be determined. Tools for quality appraisal of single-case research guides are relatively novel (Lobo et al. [2017](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR33 "Lobo, M. A., Moeyaert, M., Baraldi Cunha, A., & Babik, I. (2017). Single-case design, analysis, and quality assessment for intervention research. Journal of Neurologic Physical Therapy, 41(3), 187–197.")), but are available in the works of Horner et al. ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR23 "Horner, R. H., Carr, E. G., Halle, J., McGee, G., Odom, S., & Wolery, M. (2005). The use of single-subject research to identify evidence-based practice in special education. Exceptional Children, 71(2), 165–179.")) and What Words Clearinghouse Standards (Kratochwill et al. [2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR30 "Kratochwill, T. R., Hitchcock, J. H., Horner, R. H., Levin, J. R., Odom, S. L., Rindskopf, D. M., & Shadish, W. R. (2013). Single-case intervention research design standards. Remedial and Special Education, 34(1), 26–38.")).

From the 17 reviews selected, only 8 used quality appraisal criteria of studies they reviewed. Reynhout and Carter ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR50 "Reynhout, G., & Carter, M. (2011). Evaluation of the efficacy of Social Stories[TM] using three single subject metrics. Research in Autism Spectrum Disorders, 5(2), 885–900.")), Test et al. ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR69 "Test, D. W. R. S, Knight, V., Spooner, F. (2011). A comprehensive review and meta-analysis of the Social Stories literature. 26(1), 49–62.")), and Mayton et al. ([2013](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR36 "Mayton, M. R., Menendez, A. L., Wheeler, J. J., Carter, S. L., & Chitiyo, M. (2013). An analysis of Social Stories TM research using an evidence-based practice model. 13(3), 208–217.")) utilised Horner et al. ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR23 "Horner, R. H., Carr, E. G., Halle, J., McGee, G., Odom, S., & Wolery, M. (2005). The use of single-subject research to identify evidence-based practice in special education. Exceptional Children, 71(2), 165–179.")) criteria. McGill et al. ([2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR37 "McGill, R. J., Baker, D., & Busse, R. T. (2015). Social Story™ interventions for decreasing challenging behaviours: a single-case meta-analysis 1995–2012. Educational Psychology in Practice, 31(1), 21–42.")) and Qi et al. ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR46 "Qi, C. H., Barton, E. E., Collier, M., Lin, Y.-L., & Montoya, C. (2018). A systematic review of effects of social stories interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 33(1), 25–34.")) utilised What Works Clearinghouse Standards (WWC). Karal and Wolfe ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR25 "Karal, M. A., & Wolfe, P. S. (2018). Social Story effectiveness on social interaction for students with autism: A review of the literature. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 53(1), 44–58.")) and Aldabas ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR1 "Aldabas, R. (2019). Effectiveness of social stories for children with autism: A comprehensive review. Technology and Disability, 31(1-2), 1–13.")) used National Autism Centre’s (NAC [2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR39 "National Autism Center. (2015). Findings and conclusions: National standards project Phase 2. Randolph: Author.")) Scientific Merit Rating Scale (SMRS) as a means of objectively assessing if the methods used in each study were sufficiently rigorous to determine whether or not SS intervention was effective for participants on the autism spectrum. Karkhaneh et al. ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR26 "Karkhaneh, M., Clark, B., Ospina, M. B., Seida, J. C., Smith, V., & Hartling, L. (2010). Social Stories[TM] to improve social skills in children with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review. Autism: The International Journal of Research and Practice, 14, 641–662.")) only reviewed RCT and CCTs, and thus utilised the Jadad Scale (Jadad et al. [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR24 "Jadad, A. R., Moore, R. A., Carroll, D., Jenkinson, C., Reynolds, D. J., Gavaghan, D. J., & McQuay, H. J. (1996). Assessing the quality of reports of randomized clinical trials: is blinding necessary? Controlled Clinical Trials, 17(1), 1–12.")) which is a validated scale that is used for assessing the quality of reports of RCTs.

Nine studies failed to evaluate the methodological quality of the studies that were included in the review. These included Sansosti et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR58 "Sansosti, F., Powell-Smith, K., & Kincaid, D. (2004). A research synthesis of social story interventions for children with autism spectrum disorders. Focus on Autism & Other Developmental Disabilities, 19(4), 194–204.")); Kokina and Kern ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR28 "Kokina, A., & Kern, L. (2010). Social Story interventions for students with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis. Journal of Autism & Developmental Disorders, 40(7), 812–826.")); Reynhout and Carter ([2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR49 "Reynhout, G., & Carter, M. (2006). Social Stories for children with disabilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 36(4), 445–469.")); Styles ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR67 "Styles, A. (2011). Social Stories: Does the research evidence support the popularity? Educational Psychology in Practice, 27(4), 415–436.")); Bucholz ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR10 "Bucholz, J. L. (2012). Social Stories™ for children with autism: A review of the literature. Journal of Research in Education, 22(2), 48–73.")); Rhodes ([2014](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR52 "Rhodes, C. (2014). Do Social Stories help to decrease disruptive behaviour in children with autistic spectrum disorders? A review of the published literature. Journal of Intellectual Disabilities, 18(1), 35–50.")); Saad ([2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR55 "Saad, M. A. E. (2016). The effectiveness of social stories among children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorders: Meta-analysis. Online Submission, 5(2), 51–60.")); and Rodríguez et al. ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR53 "Rodríguez, M. G., Pastor-Cerezuela, G., Tijeras-Iborra, A., & Fernandez-Andres, M. I. (2019). Effectiveness of social stories in intervention in autistic spectrum disorder: A review. Papeles del Psicologo, 40(3), 217–225.")).

With the introduction of standards in 2005 (Horner et al. [2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR23 "Horner, R. H., Carr, E. Remedial and Special Education, 34(1), 26–38.")), an increase in study quality has been reported. Social Story™ interventions for decreasing challenging behaviours: a single-case meta-analysis 1995–2012. Educational Psychology in Practice, 31(1), 21–42.")) review, the authors explain how only one study, published from 1995 to 2004 included in their review, met all seven of WWC’s design standards. In contrast, eight studies published from 2005 to 2012 met all seven of the design standards. Overall, the 15% increase in average indicators met as well as the nominal increase in the number of studies meeting all of the standards across the periods provides some evidence of systematic improvements in single-case research quality over time.

### 2) Effectiveness of SS

The main focus of the reviews of literature that were included in this scoping study was to investigate the effectiveness of SS intervention. Sansosti et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR58 "Sansosti, F., Powell-Smith, K., & Kincaid, D. (2004). A research synthesis of social story interventions for children with autism spectrum disorders. Focus on Autism & Other Developmental Disabilities, 19(4), 194–204.")) concluded that the empirical foundation regarding the effectiveness of Social Stories is limited (Sansosti et al. [2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR58 "Sansosti, F., Powell-Smith, K., & Kincaid, D. (2004). A research synthesis of social story interventions for children with autism spectrum disorders. Focus on Autism & Other Developmental Disabilities, 19(4), 194–204.")). Kokina and Kern ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR28 "Kokina, A., & Kern, L. (2010). Social Story interventions for students with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis. Journal of Autism & Developmental Disorders, 40(7), 812–826.")) argue that their findings are indicative of questionable effectiveness of Social Story interventions for students with ASD (Kokina and Kern [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR28 "Kokina, A., & Kern, L. (2010). Social Story interventions for students with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis. Journal of Autism & Developmental Disorders, 40(7), 812–826.")). Reynhout and Carter ([2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR49 "Reynhout, G., & Carter, M. (2006). Social Stories for children with disabilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 36(4), 445–469.")); Sansosti et al. ([2004](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR58 "Sansosti, F., Powell-Smith, K., & Kincaid, D. (2004). A research synthesis of social story interventions for children with autism spectrum disorders. Focus on Autism & Other Developmental Disabilities, 19(4), 194–204.")); and Bucholz ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR10 "Bucholz, J. L. (2012). Social Stories™ for children with autism: A review of the literature. Journal of Research in Education, 22(2), 48–73.")) argue that the effects of SS are highly variable. More recent reviews, such as Karal and Wolfe ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR25 "Karal, M. A., & Wolfe, P. S. (2018). Social Story effectiveness on social interaction for students with autism: A review of the literature. Education and Training in Autism and Developmental Disabilities, 53(1), 44–58.")); Qi et al. ([2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR46 "Qi, C. H., Barton, E. E., Collier, M., Lin, Y.-L., & Montoya, C. (2018). A systematic review of effects of social stories interventions for individuals with autism spectrum disorder. Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, 33(1), 25–34.")); and Aldabas ([2019](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR1 "Aldabas, R. (2019). Effectiveness of social stories for children with autism: A comprehensive review. Technology and Disability, 31(1-2), 1–13.")), indicate the SS research published since 2013 has increased in quality and has also reported relatively higher effectiveness ratings.

Mean difference effect size statistic was used to interpret outcome of intervention using group designs (0.80 = large effect size, 0.50 = moderate, and 0.20 = small). Visual analysis ratings (VARs) (+ 2 significant decrease in target behaviours from baseline, + 1 moderate decrease in target behaviours from baseline, 0 little to no decrease in target behaviours from baseline, − 1 moderate increase in target behaviours from baseline, − 2 significant increases in target behaviours from baseline), percentage of non-overlapping data (PND) statistic (PNDs > 80 are indicative of a strong effect, 60 to 79 is a moderate effect, and PNDs < 60 indicate negligible effect), improvement rate difference (IRD) (range 0 to 1.00, > 0.75 indicate very large effect sizes, scores between 0.70 and 0.75 indicate large, scores between 0.51 and 0.70 indicate moderate, and scores less than 0.50 indicate small effect sizes), and points exceeding the median (PEM) (range 0 to 1. < 0.7 reflects an intervention that is not effective, PEM of 0.7 to 0.9 reflects moderate effectiveness, PEM of 0.9 to 1 reflects a highly effective treatment) were used to interpret the efficacy of SS intervention in single-case experimental designs. Whilst it is claimed that the IRD metric is the strongest validated metric, when compared to PND and PEM (Parker et al. [2007](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR43 "Parker, R. I., Hagan-Burke, S., & Vannest, K. (2007). Percentage of all non-overlapping data (PAND). The Journal of Special Education, 40(4), 194–204.")), nevertheless, IRD seems to have been employed to a limited extent whilst PND is the most used metric in the reviews.

Reynhout and Carter ([2006](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR49 "Reynhout, G., & Carter, M. (2006). Social Stories for children with disabilities. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 36(4), 445–469.")) obtained a Mean PND of 43 (range 16–95) which indicates that SS intervention is ineffective according to PND evaluative criteria (refer to Scruggs and Mastropieri [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR60 "Scruggs, T. Behavior Modification, 22, 221–242."), [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR61 "Scruggs, T. E., & Mastropieri, M. A. (2001). How to summarize single-participant research: Ideas and applications. Exceptionality, 9, 227–244."); Scruggs et al. [1987](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR62 "Scruggs, T. E., Mastropieri, M. A., & Casto, G. (1987). The quantitative synthesis of single-subject research: Methodology and validation. Remedial and Special Education, 8, 24–32.")). Kokina and Kern ([2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR28 "Kokina, A., & Kern, L. (2010). Social Story interventions for students with autism spectrum disorders: A meta-analysis. Journal of Autism & Developmental Disorders, 40(7), 812–826.")) report a mean PND score of 60% (range, 11–100%) for SS interventions. This score places SS in the low/questionable effectiveness category according to Scruggs and Mastropieri ([1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR60 "Scruggs, T. E., & Mastropieri, M. A. (1998). Synthesizing single subject research: Issues and applications. Behavior Modification, 22, 221–242.")). Reynhout and Carter ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR50 "Reynhout, G., & Carter, M. (2011). Evaluation of the efficacy of Social Stories[TM] using three single subject metrics. On the other hand, the PEM metric resulted in a mean score of 72% (range 0–100, SD 26), which is indicative of moderate effectiveness.

In Test et al.’s ([2011](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40489-020-00235-6#ref-CR69 "Test, D. W. R. S, Knight, V., Spooner, F. (2011). This is a scoping review published in the Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2022, Volume 9, pages 21-38) titled "Autism Spectrum Disorder and Social Story Research: a Scoping Study of Published, Peer-Reviewed Literature Reviews" by Louis John Camilleri, Katie Maras, and Mark Brosnan. The article is open access, published February 24, 2021, with 20k accesses and 18 citations.

**Purpose and Background:** Social Stories (SS) is a widely used intervention for children on the autism spectrum, introduced by Gray and Garand (1993) to help individuals with ASD understand and function in social situations. The intervention was originally recommended only for higher functioning verbal pupils with stories on a single sheet. The question of whether SS should be considered an evidence-based practice (EBP) remains debated—the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice classified Social Narratives as EBP but did not define Social Stories™ as an EBP.

**Method:** Rather than conducting another literature review, the authors conducted a scoping review of existing reviews. They searched 10 databases (CINAH EBSCO, A+Education, ERIC, Education Source, PsycINFO, PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Web of Science, ABI Inform Global), yielding 459 citations, then 119 full-text articles, finally including 17 peer-reviewed literature reviews published between 2004 and 2019. These reviews covered synthesis of literature, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, comparative reviews, and descriptive reviews.

**Results:** The 17 reviews reported on 120 individual SS studies (conducted 1995-2018). Five major themes were identified: (1) research design, (2) effectiveness of SS, (3) factors influencing outcomes (with subthemes of environmental and within-child factors), (4) social validity, and (5) maintenance and generalization.

Key findings on research design: Single-subject research is the most common design. Reviews after 2012 highlighted improved designs (ABAB, alternating treatment, multiple-baseline) compared to earlier AB designs. Only 8 of 17 reviews used quality appraisal criteria (Horner et al. criteria, WWC Standards, NAC Scientific Merit Rating Scale, Jadad Scale). Nine studies failed to evaluate methodological quality. Research quality has improved over time—in McGill et al. (2015), only 1 study from 1995-2004 met all seven WWC design standards, versus 8 studies from 2005-2012.

Key findings on effectiveness: Results on SS effectiveness are mixed. Older reviews found limited or questionable effectiveness (Sansosti et al. 2004; Kokina & Kern 2010 reported mean PND of 60%, indicating low/questionable effectiveness). Reynhout and Carter (2006) obtained a mean PND of 43 (ineffective), while their 2011 review reported PND mean 51 and IRD mean 0.57 (mildly effective) and PEM mean 72% (moderate effectiveness). More recent reviews (Karal & Wolfe 2018; Qi et al. 2018; Aldabas 2019) indicate research published since 2013 has increased in quality and reported relatively higher effectiveness ratings.

The authors conclude that despite decades of research, the question of SS interventions as evidence-based practice remains unanswered, with high variability in research quality across reviews.

## Social Stories™ to alleviate challenging behaviour and social difficulties exhibited by children with autism spectrum disorder in mainstream schools: design of a manualised training toolkit and feasibility study for a cluster randomised controlled trial with nested qualitative and cost-effectiveness components.

# Chapter 1Introduction

## Background

### Autism spectrum disorders and challenging behaviour

Children with autism spectrum disorders (ASDs) are less able to learn social rules, conventions and behaviours by intuition compared with their typically developing peers. This may impact upon social interaction, social integration, learning and mental health and on occasions may lead to high levels of anxiety and or challenging behaviours.[1](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib1) Both parents and teachers report more behaviour problems in children with ASD than in typically developing children.[2](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib2) Many children with ASD therefore need additional support to understand and adopt social behaviours that are helpful to them. Social Stories™ (Carol Gray) are a non-intrusive, child-focused intervention designed to fill in the gaps of the child’s social understanding with the intention of helping them develop constructive behaviours and coping strategies.

### Social Stories

Social Stories are short stories characterised by 10 predefined criteria developed by their original creator, Carol Gray.[3](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib3) These criteria both define and guide story development. They ensure that the story structure and content is descriptive, meaningful and safe for its audience. In particular, the content is tailored to the specific needs of each individual child, which can usually be incorporated into the story.

For the purposes of this study we are referring to Social Stories (using upper case letters) when these 10 criteria are adhered to (described more fully in the next section). A wider literature exists using stories in a range of ways to support children’s learning (e.g. generic stories about starting school or going to the dentist) but without adhering to these principles and we will refer to these as social stories (using lower case letters).

### The ten criteria of Social Stories

Gray’s 10 criteria must be adhered to for a story to be considered a Social Story™.[3](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib3) The criteria give clear guidance on the elements that make a Social Story what it is and the process of researching, writing and formatting or illustrating one. They lead a Social Story to be developed and delivered in a certain way and consider the specific qualities of children with ASD. To give the later chapters the appropriate context, each of these criteria is described below using Gray’s original terminology as headings.[3](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib3)

#### One goal

The first criterion emphasises the main purpose and overall tone of Social Stories. It states that the goal of a Social Story is to share accurate, socially meaningful information in a positive and reassuring way. Although they are often used in response to challenging behaviour, the focus of the content of the story would not be on that particular behaviour. The focus of the Story is usually provision of social information with the expectation that it will bring about changes in behaviour that benefit the child. Having one clear and shared goal enables those around the child to support them in a co-ordinated and supportive way.

#### Two-step discovery

This criterion emphasises the importance of gathering information before developing the story. This is an essential, non-negotiable part of developing a Social Story. It is the process by which the child and their needs are better understood. For example, ‘why is the child frustrated?’ or ‘what is it they do not understand?’. It is suggested that people who know the child best will be the best source of information for this stage. This criterion discourages ‘off the peg’ stories being used that are only partially suitable to the situation or the child.

#### Three parts and a title

The third criterion simply states that a Social Story is a story and needs a title describing the content, a beginning (introduction), a middle (body) and an end (conclusion). A good title should be clear to the child and easy to understand. It describes what the story is about.

#### Four-mat

The fourth criterion details four characteristics of the child which should be considered to ensure the story is appropriate for their cognitive ability. This criterion emphasises the importance of tailoring the Social Story to the child. The factors to be considered are their learning style, attention span, comprehension level and reading ability.

#### Five factors define voice and vocabulary

This criterion recognises the importance of the use of language and how the story is told. It details five separate rules when selecting the language used that are important in providing the story with the appropriate tone. The main emphasis is for the language to be positive and for the information presented to be accurate. The five rules are:

#### Six questions guide story development

The sixth criterion ensures that the appropriate content and information relevant to the situation is presented in the story. It encourages the writer to ask the six questions (who, what, where, when, why and how) about the situation that provides in-depth information about the child, and what needs to be explained in the Story to help the child. The questions are intended to explore the gaps in information for the child as the story is developed. For example, where and when does the issue occur? Who does it involve?

#### Seven types of sentences

The seventh criterion describes how the information included in a story should be presented by detailing seven types of sentence. Each sentence type has a different function in a story. The following are the common different types of sentences used.

#### A gr-eight formula

The eighth criterion defines the structure of the story by examining the balance of sentence types. It states that for something to be considered a Social Story, coaching sentences must amount to less than one-third of the total number of sentences in the story.

#### Nine makes it mine

This criterion emphasises the importance of using the child’s interests (e.g. trains or superheroes) in the story. A story should be written with knowledge of the child’s personal interests and preferences in an effort to make Stories more interesting and fun to read.

#### Ten guides to editing and implementation

The tenth criterion details the best practice for finalising and delivering the intervention. It emphasises the need to monitor and edit the story when necessary and the importance of having a quiet safe place to deliver it.

#### Evidence for the effectiveness of Social Stories

Social Stories can be effective in tackling challenging behaviour when they set out to explicitly teach social skills.[4](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib4) Until recently, research exploring efficacy and outcome has been confined to single-case studies. These case reports in children with ASD have suggested improvements in social interactions,[5](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib5),[6](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib6) choice making in an educational setting,[6](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib6) voice volume in class[7](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib7) and meal time skills.[8](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib8) Success has also been reported in addressing disruptive behaviours, including reducing tantrums[9](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib9),[10](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib10) and behaviours associated with frustration.[11](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib11) Non-comparative research has examined Social Story use in special education,[12](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib12) mainstream education settings[13](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib13) and within the home.[14](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib14)

Two previous systematic reviews of Social Story effectiveness[4](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib4),[15](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib15) identified largely single-case designs and a paucity of good quality, comparative evidence on Social Stories. Both suggest further research, especially with the use of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) to evaluate whether or not positive outcomes seen in case series can be replicated.

Although Social Stories have much potential to improve behaviour, the comparative evidence base is limited and attributed levels of effect are based mostly on single-case research. A well-designed RCT is required to address this important gap in our knowledge, and a feasibility RCT is required to plan the appropriate experimental design. Evidence suggests that Social Stories delivered in a general education setting produced significantly larger effect sizes on behaviour than those implemented at home or in self-contained settings, such as separate schools or self-contained classrooms.[4](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib4) Therefore, this study specifically focuses on the feasibility of assessing Social Stories delivered within a mainstream schooling system.

## Overview

Social Stories for children with ASD represents a complex, individualised intervention. With this in mind the feasibility of conducting a full RCT must be examined. Our aim in this study was to develop a UK-accessible, manualised Social Stories training intervention for teachers of children with ASD in mainstream schools and to explore the effect of this on reducing challenging behaviour or other social difficulties. We conducted a feasibility study to inform the design of a full RCT, including a justification and description of appropriate costs, outcomes and parameters to include cost-effectiveness. The study was carried out in three phases, following the guidelines set out by the Medical Research Council in their framework for development and evaluation of RCTs for complex interventions to improve health.[16](/books/n/ukhta2006/ref1/#ref1-bib16)

### Theoretical phase

The initial pre-clinical phase was to conduct a systematic review of the current literature on social stories (including stories following Gray’s criteria). *[Chapter 2](/books/n/ukhta2006/s2/)* details the findings of this systematic review. It included studies using social stories in all settings but paid particular attention to those used in mainstream schools. The review had two broad aims: firstly to provide a comprehensive description of how they have been used in education and clinical practice, and secondly to provide a quantitative estimate of the effectiveness of these interventions.

### Phase 1

*[Chapters 3](/books/n/ukhta2006/s3/)* to *[6](/books/n/ukhta2006/s6/)* detail phase 1 of the study. The aim of this phase was to develop a toolkit for writing Social Stories more accessible to a UK audience. It included a qualitative element to help develop the intervention and a small pilot study to refine it. This process was informed by patient and public involvement (PPI) on the study team who gave in depth advice for the qualitative interviews including assistance in the development of the topic guides and in supporting the research team in understanding the family perspective. *[Chapter 3](/books/n/ukhta2006/s3/)* gives an overview of the development process as a whole. This process had strong PPI, including parent and teacher involvement and interviews with young people on the autism spectrum. *[Chapter 4](/books/n/ukhta2006/s4/)* details the qualitative element in which interviews and focus groups were conducted with people with experience of using Social Stories. The aim of this process was to gather information relating to the optimum design and use of Social Stories, and to explore whether or not the intervention can feasibly be delivered in this particular context. *[Chapter 5](/books/n/ukhta2006/s5/)* describes the progress at each stage of the developmental process for the intervention to be used in the feasibility study. Finally, *[Chapter 6](/books/n/ukhta2006/s6/)* details the final stage of development of the intervention; a pilot study conducted with a small number of participants to examine the acceptability of the intervention before using it in the feasibility study.

### Phase 2

*[Chapters 7](/books/n/ukhta2006/s7/)* to *[9](/books/n/ukhta2006/s9/)* detail phase 2 of the study, the feasibility trial. *[Chapter 7](/books/n/ukhta2006/s7/)* reports on the findings of the feasibility RCT and the considerations for conducting a full-scale trial. *[Chapter 8](/books/n/ukhta2006/s8/)* details the health economic component of the study. Finally, *[Chapter 9](/books/n/ukhta2006/s9/)* describes the findings of an additional qualitative component which consisted of interviews with the participating parents, teachers and children after they had completed their involvement with the feasibility trial. This additional component was suggested by our PPI representatives to give a richer quality of information to inform a fully powered trial.

### Discussion

*[Chapter 10](/books/n/ukhta2006/s10/)* attempts to bring together the conclusions from the previous chapters into a general discussion that critically evaluates the findings against the proposed objectives and makes recommendations for a future trial.

## Objectives

This webpage is the Introduction chapter (Chapter 1) of a NIHR Health Technology Assessment report published in January 2016, describing a feasibility study for a cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) evaluating Social Stories™ as an intervention for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in mainstream UK schools. The report is available on NCBI Bookshelf.

Key content:
- Background: Children with ASD are less able to learn social rules intuitively, leading to social interaction problems, anxiety, and challenging behaviours. Social Stories™ (created by Carol Gray) are a non-intrusive, child-focused intervention designed to fill gaps in social understanding and help develop constructive behaviours.

- The ten criteria of Social Stories™ are described in detail: (1) One goal - share accurate, socially meaningful information positively; (2) Two-step discovery - gather information before developing the story; (3) Three parts and a title - beginning, middle, end; (4) Four-mat - consider child's learning style, attention span, comprehension, reading ability; (5) Five factors define voice and vocabulary; (6) Six questions (who, what, where, when, why, how) guide story development; (7) Seven types of sentences; (8) A gr-eight formula - coaching sentences must be less than one-third of total sentences; (9) Nine makes it mine - use the child's personal interests; (10) Ten guides to editing and implementation.

- Evidence for effectiveness: Research has been mostly single-case studies showing improvements in social interactions, choice making, voice volume, and meal time skills, as well as reductions in tantrums and frustration-related behaviours. Two systematic reviews found largely single-case designs with a paucity of good quality comparative evidence, calling for RCTs. Evidence suggests Social Stories in general education settings produce larger effect sizes than those at home or in self-contained settings.

- Study overview: The three-phase study followed MRC guidelines for complex interventions. The theoretical phase (systematic review - Chapter 2), Phase 1 (developing a UK-accessible manualised training toolkit with qualitative elements - Chapters 3-6), and Phase 2 (feasibility trial including health economics and qualitative interviews - Chapters 7-9). Chapter 10 provides discussion and recommendations for a future full trial. The study had strong patient and public involvement (PPI).

### **摘要**

**目的** 探讨基于结构化教学法(TEACCH)的小组训练对学龄前孤独谱系障碍(ASD)儿童的训练效果,为TEACCH本土化训练模式提供参考。**方法** 将武汉市精神卫生中心2018年1月— 2021年10月的60例ASD儿童进行康复训练,随机分为TEACCH组和对照组各30例,分别比较两组在训练前、训练后、训练后6个月随访和1年随访时评估康复效果各项得分的变化,采用PEP-3进行康复效果的评估。**结果** TEACCH组和对照组在训练前基线得分差异均无统计学意义(*P*>0.05)。在所有评估项目中时间主效应均显著(*P*<0.001),TEACCH组在语言表达、语言理解、小肌肉、社交互动、问题行为、个人自理和适应行为得分均高于对照组,差异具有统计学意义(*F*=4.159、10.447、4.556、4.666、12.922、4.199、8.484,*P*<0.05),组间和时间交互效应在情感表达、问题行为、个人自理差异具有统计学意义(*F*=3.919、5.071、9.689,*P*<0.05)。TEACCH组的语言表达、问题行为、个人自理在训练后、6个月随访和1年随访前后测差值均高于对照组,差异有统计学意义(*P*<0.05),情感表达、社交互动仅在训练后和6个月随访时前后测差值高于对照组,差异有统计学意义(*P*<0.05),语言理解、小肌肉、适应行为仅在训练后和1年随访时前后测差值高于对照组,差异有统计学意义(*P*<0.05)。**结论** 基于TEACCH的小组训练,对于学龄前ASD儿童语言、小肌肉、情感、社交、行为方面均有促进作用。

### **Abstract**

**Objective** To explore the effect of treatment and education of autistic and communication handicapped children (TEACCH) group training in preschool children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), in order to provide reference for localization of the training mode of TEACCH. **Methods** Totally 60 preschool children with ASD in Children's Rehabilitation Department of Wuhan Mental Health Center from January 2018 to October 2021 were enrolled in this study, and were randomly assigned to the TEACCH group (*n*=30) and the control group (*n*=30).The Chinese version of Psycho-Educational Profile, 3rd ed(PEP-3) was used to assess treatment effects at baseline, posttest, 6-month follow-up and 1-year follow-up after training. **Results** No significant difference was found between the two groups at baseline (*P*>0.05). Time effect was significant for all indicators (*P*＜0.001). The scores of expressive language, receptive language, fine motor, social reciprocity, problem behavior, personal self-care and adaptive behavior in the TEACCH group were significantly improved than those of the control group (*F*=4.159, 10.447, 4.556, 4.666, 12.922, 4.199, 8.484, *P*<0.05). The interaction effects between time and group were significant in affective expression, problem behavior and personal self-care scores (*F*=3.919, 5.071, 9.689, *P*<0.05). The change scores of expressive language, problem behavior and personal self-care in the TEACCH group were significantly higher than those of the control group at posttest, 6-month follow-up and 1-year follow-up (*P*<0.05). The change scores of emotional expression and social interaction in the TEACCH group were significantly higher than those of the control group only at posttest and 6-month follow-up (*P*<0.05). The change scores of receptive language, fine motor and adaptive behavior in the TEACCH group were significantly higher than those of the control group only at posttest and 1-year follow-up (*P*<0.05). **Conclusion** Group training based on TEACCH can promote the language, fine motor, emotion, social interaction and behavior of preschool ASD children.

This is a scientific research article published in the Chinese Journal of Child Health Care (中国儿童保健杂志), Vol. 31, Issue 5, 2023, pages 564-569 (DOI: 10.11852/zgetbjzz2022-0839). The study, titled "基于结构化教学法的小组训练对学龄前孤独谱系障碍儿童的疗效分析" (Effect of group training based on TEACCH on preschool children with autism spectrum disorder), was authored by ZENG Hongling, ZHOU Yi, XIE Jun, DAI Lisha, and TANG Jun from the Children's Rehabilitation Department, Wuhan Mental Health Center, Wuhan Hospital for Psychotherapy, Hubei, China.

**Objective:** To explore the effect of group training based on Structured Teaching (TEACCH - Treatment and Education of Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children) on preschool children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), providing reference for the localization of the TEACCH training model.

**Methods:** Sixty preschool children with ASD at the Wuhan Mental Health Center (January 2018 to October 2021) were randomly assigned to a TEACCH group (n=30) and a control group (n=30). The Chinese version of the Psycho-Educational Profile, 3rd edition (PEP-3) was used to assess treatment effects at baseline, posttest, 6-month follow-up, and 1-year follow-up.

**Results:** No significant baseline differences existed between groups (P>0.05). Time effects were significant for all indicators (P<0.001). The TEACCH group scored significantly higher than the control group on expressive language, receptive language, fine motor, social reciprocity, problem behavior, personal self-care, and adaptive behavior (F=4.159, 10.447, 4.556, 4.666, 12.922, 4.199, 8.484, P<0.05). Interaction effects between time and group were significant for affective expression, problem behavior, and personal self-care (F=3.919, 5.071, 9.689, P<0.05). The change scores for expressive language, problem behavior, and personal self-care remained significantly higher at posttest, 6-month, and 1-year follow-up; emotional expression and social interaction change scores were higher only at posttest and 6-month follow-up; receptive language, fine motor, and adaptive behavior change scores were higher only at posttest and 1-year follow-up.

**Conclusion:** Group training based on TEACCH promotes language, fine motor, emotion, social interaction, and behavior in preschool ASD children.

**Timeline/History:** Submitted 2022-07-12; revised 2022-11-24; published 2023-05-10 (published online 2023-05-06).

**Funding:** Wuhan Health and Family Planning Scientific Research Projects (WX17Q29, WX18Q19); Wuhan Fourth Batch of Public Health Key Discipline Projects (Child and Adolescent Mental Health).

**Classification:** R493, R749.94. The article belongs to the "适宜技术" (Appropriate Technology) category and includes 27 references, including earlier related studies in the same journal (e.g., Zhang et al. 2019, Cheng et al. 2019, Jiang et al. 2006).

--- SOURCE 1: Research | TEACCH® Autism Program ---
URL: https://teacch.com/research

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage presents the current research projects of the UNC TEACCH® Autism Program, a part of the UNC School of Medicine, focused on community dissemination and implementation of intervention and professional development programs to improve the quality of life for autistic individuals. The research team is interdisciplinary, comprising faculty, postdoctoral fellows, clinical psychology interns, and graduate students from the School of Medicine and the Department of Psychology and Neurosciences. Key current research projects include:

- **AASET-MHTP**: A first large-scale head-to-head comparison of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) versus mindfulness-based therapy (MBT), both delivered via telehealth, to improve mental health and quality of life among autistic adults with anxiety or depression. Supported by a PCORI Award (IDD-2022C1-26372).
- **AASET-SP**: A study comparing two suicide prevention strategies tailored for autistic individuals—the Safety Planning Intervention tailored for Autistic individuals (SPI-A) and SPI-A plus structured follow-up care (SPI-A+). Supported by PCORI Award (SP-2020C3-20951).
- **ASAP-Autism**: Compares two school-based programs (Zones of Regulation and Facing Your Fears-School Based) to help autistic youth decrease anxiety and regulate emotions. Funded by PCORI.
- **Long-term Adult Outcomes**: Following 300 autistic adults in their 40s–60s who were seen at TEACCH as children, examining developmental trajectories and adult needs. --- SOURCE 2: The effectiveness of TEACCH-based interventions in improving adaptive skills in children with autism spectrum disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12771134

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: TEACCH-Based Interventions for Children with ASD

**Publication details:** Published in Translational Pediatrics (2025 Dec 24;14(12):3263), PMID: 41502886, PMCID: PMC12771134, DOI: 10.21037/tp-2025-466. Received July 15, 2025; accepted November 3, 2025.

**Authors:** Junmin Li, Ming Chen (Education University of Hong Kong), Raffy C. F. Chan, Jacqueline L. M. Chan, Xiao Liang (Hong Kong Polytechnic University), and Lulu Wang (corresponding author, Hubei Provincial Hospital of Traditional Chinese Medicine).

### Background
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) affects approximately 1–2.5% of children globally (WHO: 1 in 100 children), with males affected 3–4 times more often than females. The TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication Handicapped Children) program, developed by Schopler et al., emphasizes structured educational environments, visual learning, and organizational support. The program focuses on: (I) physical environment organization with visual cues; (II) visual arrangements for schedules/routines; and (III) physical or visual work/activity systems to foster independence. Approximately 15.7% of ASD families use TEACCH.

### Methods
- Protocol registered in PROSPERO (No. CRD42024554992)
- Databases searched: PubMed, Embase, MEDLINE, APA PsycInfo, Scopus, Web of Science (from inception to May 10, 2024)
- Inclusion criteria: ASD diagnosis per professional criteria (DSM-IV/DSM-IV-TR/DSM-V) or school report; age ≤18 years; explicit TEACCH-based interventions; outcomes measured with validated instruments; RCTs or nonrandomized controlled studies (NRSs)
- From 1,522 initial articles and 1,019 after duplicate removal, **20 studies (920 children)** were included in the review; **16 in the meta-analysis**
- STATA 18.0 used; Hedges method for standardized mean differences; random-effects model; quality assessed via PEDro scale
- Kappa coefficient for reviewer agreement: 0.83

### Results
**Primary outcomes (adaptive skills):**
- **Communication skills:** significant small positive effect (g=0.21; 95% CI: 0.03–0.39; P=0.02); low heterogeneity (I²=35.4%)
- **Daily living skills:** significant small positive effect (g=0.39; 95% CI: 0.04–0.75; P=0.03); moderate heterogeneity (I²=54.2%)
- **Motor skills:** significant small positive effect (g=0.19; 95% CI: 0.00–0.38; P=0.05); moderate heterogeneity (I²=51.8%)
- **Social skills:** significant moderate positive effect (g=0.75/0.76; 95% CI: 0.32–1.18; P=0.001); high heterogeneity (I²=79.4%)

**Secondary outcomes:**
- **ASD symptom severity:** significant large reduction (g=–0.89/–0.91; 95% CI: –1.61 to –0.17; P=0.04)
- **Cognitive functioning:** significant small positive effect (g=0.30; 95% CI: 0.06–0.53; P=0.01); low heterogeneity (I²=0%)
- **Parental stress:** significant small reduction (g=–0.40; 95% CI: –0.74 to –0.06; P=0.02); low heterogeneity (I²=0%)

### Key Subgroup Findings
- **Age:** School-age children (6–12 years) benefited significantly more than preschool children across communication, daily living, motor, and social skills (e.g., social skills: school-age g=1.30 vs. preschool g=0.20)
- **Educational setting:** Clinical settings produced significant effects for communication (g=0.40) and motor skills (g=0.35); home and school settings largely nonsignificant
- **Parental involvement:** Significantly enhanced daily living skills (g=0.62 with parent participation vs. g=0.12 without) and motor skills (g=0.28 vs. 0.13)
- **Region:** European studies showed significant effects for communication (g=0.39), daily living (g=0.35), motor (g=0.33), and social skills (g=0.88); US studies generally nonsignificant
- **Intervention duration:** 6–12 months optimal for motor skills (g=0.36); social skills showed largest effects with <6 months duration (g=1.65)
- **Study design:** RCTs showed larger effects than NRS for daily living (g=0.90 vs. 0.25), motor (g=0.39 vs. 0.16), and social skills (g=1.14 vs. 0.40)

### Meta-regression
Age significantly predicted improvements in communication, motor skills, and social skills (school-age children benefiting more). Country significantly associated with communication outcomes; intervention setting significantly associated with motor skill outcomes.

### Quality & Limitations
- Overall quality fair: mean PEDro score 5.05 (range 2–8)
- Few studies incorporated blinding or intent-to-treat analysis (only 2 studies)
- Studies published 1998–2023; 12 reported significant positive effects, 3 nonsignificant effects (attributed to methodological variations or small sample sizes)
- 4 pre-post design studies included only in systematic review, not meta-analysis

### Conclusions
TEACCH-based interventions significantly enhance communication, daily living, motor, and social skills, reduce ASD symptom severity, improve cognition, and decrease parental stress in children with ASD. Optimal outcomes occur with **structured clinical environments, medium-term implementation periods (6–12 months), and intentional parent participation**. Cultural considerations are important, particularly in Asian contexts where multigenerational caregiving and stigma affect engagement. Future research should prioritize large-scale RCTs and long-term follow-up. Data/code available on OSF (https://osf.io/eync2/).
</summary>

This webpage is a Chinese-language educational resource about Evidence-Based Practices (EBPs) for autism intervention, based on the Autism Focused Intervention Resources & Modules (AFIRM) program. The site addresses why EBPs matter, what they are, how to learn them, and how to select them.

**Why EBPs:** No single intervention method (ABA, TEACCH, ESDM, PRT, etc.) can meet the diverse developmental needs of autistic children at different ages and domains. High-quality intervention requires integrating multiple EBPs based on individual needs (Hyman et al., 2020; Rogers et al., 2020). Currently, no medical intervention effectively improves core ASD symptoms (CDC, 2019), and many complementary/alternative treatments lack scientific support (American Academy of Pediatrics, 2020). This site focuses on non-medical educational interventions.

**What EBPs are:** Two categories exist:
- Comprehensive Treatment Models (CTMs): Combinations of interventions built on a theoretical framework with standardized procedures (e.g., UCLA Young Autism Program, TEACCH, LEAP, Denver Model). They have high frequency, long duration (1+ years), and broad goals.
- Focused Intervention Practices (FIPs): Specific methods targeting one skill (e.g., Discrete Trial Training, visual supports, prompting). EBPs are FIPs that meet evidence standards.

The NPDC's 2014 second edition report reviewed 29,105 studies (1990-2011), selected 427, and approved 27 EBPs. The 2020 third edition added 31,779 studies (2012-2015), selected 545, and cumulatively analyzed 972 studies (1990-2017), approving 28 EBPs.

**How to learn:** The site offers online learning materials (overview, evidence base, step guides, tables, professional prompts, parent guides, additional resources, references) for each EBP, an EBPs comprehensive modular training course, and content based on the 2020 third edition report (updated as research advances).

**Who should learn:** Professionals (teachers, special educators, therapists, counselors) and parents/family members.

**The 28 EBPs** are listed with brief descriptions: AAC (Augmentative and Alternative Communication), ASI (Ayres Sensory Integration), BMI (Behavioral Momentum Intervention), DI (Direct Instruction), MMI (Music-Mediated Intervention), ABI (Antecedent-based Intervention), CBI (Cognitive Behavioral Intervention), DR (Differential Reinforcement), DTT (Discrete Trial Training), ECE (Exercise), EXT (Extinction), FBA (Functional Behavior Assessment), FCT (Functional Communication Training), MD (Modeling), NI (Naturalistic Intervention), PII (Parent Implemented Intervention), PMII (Peer-mediated Instruction and Intervention), PP (Prompting), R+ (Reinforcement), RIR (Response Interruption and Redirection), SM (Self-management), SN (Social Narratives), SST (Social Skills Training), TA (Task Analysis), TAII (Technology-aided Instruction and Intervention), TD (Time Delay), VM (Video Modeling), and VS (Visual Supports). Four methods (PECS → AAC, PRT → NI, Structured Play Groups → PMII, Scripting → VS) were folded into broader categories in the third edition.

**Choosing methods:** An EBPs matrix shows which of the 28 methods are evidence-supported across 3 age groups (0-5, 6-14, 15-22) and 12 target domains.

**Copyright:** The EBPs Guide originates from AFIRM (UNC), with Chinese translation rights held by 星之光盐 (Starlight Salt) Fan Yuebo team. The Chinese version was translated by multiple individuals and reviewed by 于洛迪 and 何昕劼.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 14: Visual Activity Schedules ---
URL: https://asatonline.org/for-parents/learn-more-about-specific-treatments/activity-schedules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Association for Science in Autism Treatment (ASAT) provides a comprehensive treatment summary of Visual Activity Schedules for individuals with autism, authored by Lisa Tereshko, PhD, BCBA-D of Endicott College (published in Science in Autism Treatment, Vol. 20, Issue 6, 2023).

**Description:** Visual activity schedules are arrangements of pictures or words that display a sequence of upcoming events (e.g., getting dressed, packing lunch, cooking dinner). They encompass three evidence-based strategies: antecedent interventions (presented before task initiation to cue expectations and reduce challenging behaviors), prompting (support to increase success completing tasks), and visual supports (reducing reliance on others for assistance). Visual schedules are particularly beneficial for autistic individuals who may display prompt dependency and have difficulty processing auditory information (Koyama & Wang, 2011; Knight et al., 2015).

**Formats:** Schedules can be displayed linearly (vertical or horizontal), in small books with icons moved to a "done" column, or using actual objects for individuals who struggle with pictures. They can also use narrative/word formats for readers. Technological options include videos, tablets, smartphones, and smart watches (e.g., iPad-based schedules for community shopping skills per Burckley et al., 2015; smart watch schedules for play skills per Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2021).

**Research Summary:** The National Standards Project: Phase 2 (2015) identifies schedule use as an established intervention for increasing independence and event planning. Hume et al. (2021) identified visual supports as an evidence-based practice. Two systematic reviews support this: Koyama and Wang (2011) reviewed 23 peer-reviewed studies (69 total participants across preschool [24.6%], school-aged [30.4%], and adults [23.2%], with 59.4% having an autism diagnosis), and Knight et al. (2014) reviewed 31 articles confirming effectiveness for teaching diverse skills across the lifespan. Visual schedules have successfully taught toothbrushing (Moran et al., 2022), medical exam cooperation (Chebuhar et al., 2013), bedtime routines (Hart Barnett et al., 2022), leisure/play skills, physical activity compliance (Becerra et al., 2021), appropriate feeding (Kirkpatrick et al., 2019), academic task engagement, choice-making (Deel et al., 2021), vocational tasks (Lora et al., 2020; Sances et al., 2019), transitions (Pierce et al., 2013), and social skills (Osos et al., 2021).

**Cautions/Limitations:** Knight et al. (2014) found that nearly all studies combined visual schedules with other systematic instruction (graduated guidance, reinforcement, prompting), which may have enhanced effects. Maintenance and generalization research is limited but promising (e.g., MacDuff et al., 1993 demonstrated generalization to novel pictures and activities).

**Recommendations:** Teams should decide interventions based on the individual's skills (symbolic representation, receptive language, reading/comprehension) and personal preference for modality. Giles et al. (2017) found similar acquisition rates between static pictures and tablet-based formats, with idiosyncratic preferences. Learner assent should be regularly assessed, and component skills (choice-making, stamina, social engagement, self-monitoring) can be built incidentally. Continued research should explore long-term effects, generalization, and technology's role in reducing social stigma.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Visual activity schedules are an arrangement of pictures or words used to display a sequence of upcoming events."
</key_excerpts>
