SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is an official notice from the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government Office (issued April 10, 2023, published April 12, 2023) regarding the issuance of the "Shenzhen Special Education Development and Enhancement Action Plan (2023-2025)" (Document No. 深府办函〔2023〕21号). The plan aims to implement national policies from the State Council (国办发〔2021〕60号) and Guangdong Province (粤府办〔2022〕20号) to safeguard the educational rights of persons with disabilities and develop special education.

**Overall Goals by 2025:**
- Establish a high-quality special education system
- Achieve 100% enrollment rate for school-age disabled children in compulsory education
- Achieve over 90% enrollment rate for disabled children in preschool (three years)
- Significantly increase high school admission opportunities for disabled students
- Promote 15-year free education for disabled students
- Advance integrated (inclusive) education across ordinary education, vocational education, medical rehabilitation, and information technology

**Key Measures (17 items across 5 sections):**

1. **Improving the Special Education System:**
- Adhere to "full coverage, zero rejection" principle for compulsory education
- Maintain educational placement model: mainstreaming (following classes) as the main body, special education schools as backbone, home-based education as supplement
- Control home-based teaching recipients to under 10% of school-age disabled students by 2025
- Develop preschool and high school special education, including vocational education-focused high school programs
- Expand special education services to children with learning difficulties, emotional and behavioral disorders
- Support construction of autism education departments in special education schools

2. **Promoting Integrated (Inclusive) Education Development:**
- Promote integrated school grouping (集团化办学) between special and ordinary schools
- Transform special education schools into special education resource/guidance centers
- Establish Shenzhen Special Education Alliance, promote Hong Kong-Shenzhen "sister schools" cooperation
- Integrate vocational education with special education; explore "3+2 split" training models
- Implement "assistive devices into schools" project, free assistive devices for compulsory education stage
- Provide "rehabilitation services to schools" for children aged 7-17
- Build digital special education course and teaching resource platforms, establish lifelong electronic learning files

3. **Improving Special Education Safeguard Mechanisms:**
- **Funding:** Public funds for compulsory and high school special education schools, attached special education classes, mainstreamed students (including those with learning/emotional disorders), and home-based students shall be allocated at 10 times the ordinary school public fund standard
- High school disabled students exempt from tuition; subsidy standard at no less than 1.1 times the ordinary secondary vocational school exemption subsidy
- **School Places:** Support construction of 15-year special education schools (kindergarten through high school); Futian, Luohu, Yantian, Longgang, Longhua, Pingshan, and Guangming districts must complete one independent comprehensive special education school meeting national standards
- Districts with over 200,000 population encouraged to build dedicated preschool education institutions for disabled children
- **Facilities:** Ordinary schools enrolling 5+ disabled students should fully build resource classrooms with full-time resource teachers
- **Teachers:** Strengthen special education teaching staff, improve salaries and treatment

4. **Curriculum, Quality Evaluation, Family and Community Support:**
- Municipal research institutions to have 1+ full-time special education researcher; district-level 1+ full-time or part-time
- Pilot special education quality evaluation
- Establish home-school cooperation service mechanisms, expand family professional support
- Integrate "children and youth growth support services" into community party-masses service center social work mandatory projects

**Implementation guarantees** include strengthening organizational leadership ("special education handled specially"), supervision and evaluation, and broad public awareness campaigns.
</summary>

This is an official notice from the Nanjing Municipal Government (issued by the General Office of the Nanjing Municipal People's Government) publishing the "Nanjing 14th Five-Year Plan for Special Education Development and Enhancement Action Plan" (Document No. 宁政办发〔2023〕5号), dated February 5, 2023, and released on the government website on March 27, 2023. The plan was developed to implement national (国办发〔2021〕60号) and Jiangsu provincial (苏政办发〔2022〕56号) special education development plans.

The plan's main objectives are to build a high-quality special education system by 2025 with targets including: preschool special-needs children enrollment rate reaching 85%+, compulsory education enrollment maintained at 99%+, and high school special-needs student education rate reaching 80%+. Free education continues from preschool through high school for special-needs children.

Key tasks across five areas:
1. Improving the education system: Expand preschool special education (each special education school needs a preschool department), strengthen compulsory education placement (home-based teaching limited to no more than 5% of eligible students), develop high school vocational education (all special education schools to open vocational departments by 2025), and enhance higher education/continuing education opportunities.
2. Deepening integrated education: Promote regular-special school integration (pairing mechanisms), vocational-special integration (vocational expert committees, skills certificates), medical-education integration (monthly collaborative activities, medical personnel participation), special education research, curriculum reform, and information technology integration (smart campuses, AI/big data).
3. Optimizing institutional mechanisms: Strengthen the special education leadership system (annual star evaluations of district guidance centers from 2023), professional guidance mechanisms, and special-needs children enrollment systems (midterm exam reform exploration, separate testing database).
4. Strengthening teacher teams: Special education teachers need 72+ continuing education hours annually, staffing ratios (1 full-time special education teacher per 5 special-needs students in regular schools, per 3 in kindergartens), performance pay increases, and preferential title/title-promotion policies.
5. Enhancing support guarantees: Per-student public funding at 8 times or more the standard for regular schools at the same level, designated medical insurance coverage, and disabled employment fund allocation for special education vocational training.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 2: 特殊幼儿随班就读的内涵、困境及支持策略探究 ---
URL: https://pdf.hanspub.org/ae2024149_781167401.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic paper by Pan Ying (Guizhou Minzu University) examines the connotation, predicaments, and support strategies for special children "learning in regular classes" (随班就读, suiban jiudu) in China - the practice of placing children with disabilities in mainstream classrooms. Published in Advances in Education (教育进展), Vol. 14, No. 9 (September 2024), pp. 512-518.

**Context and Significance:** The paper is grounded in several Chinese policy initiatives including the 2022 "14th Five-Year Plan for Special Education Development and Improvement," the 2023 Basic Education Expansion and Quality Improvement Action Plan, and "China's Education Modernization 2035." Statistics show in 2023 China had 912,000 special education students, with 57.08% (570,800) studying in regular schools (up from 2022), marking a trend away from segregated special schools.

**Two Major Predicaments:**
1. **Peer relationship marginalization**: Special children are often socially isolated, viewed as "perfect targets for teasing," seen as "game breakers" or "invaders," becoming "invisible people" or marginalized figures in class social networks. Children lack mutual social skills without teacher guidance.
2. **Teacher guidance inefficacy**: While teachers generally hold positive attitudes toward inclusive education, they lack special education training (pre-service preparation is nearly blank), behavioral management skills, and individualized teaching capacity, creating feelings of helplessness.

**Proposed Support Strategy: "One Dimension, Three Levels, Four Roles" (一维三层四者):**
- **One Dimension**: Uphold humanistic (Rogerian) thought - implementing "同感理解" (empathic understanding), sincerity, and unconditional positive regard to cultivate the "whole person"
- **Layer 1 - Empathy**: Build positive teacher-child interactions, remove stereotypes of special children as "slow students" or "problem children," use diagnostic results, home/personal interviews, and daily life records to understand children as "understanding the child's body and mind"
- **Layer 2 - Planning**: Develop Individualized Education Programs (IEPs) in two phases (analysis/evaluation then formulation/implementation), balancing "adaptation" and "development" principles with knowledge, skills, and emotion competency goals across time periods, as "supporting the child's body and mind"
- **Layer 3 - Environment**: Build positive behavioral support environments through pre-entry preparation (introducing "a special friend" to the class), "leading one to lead many" (以一带多) peer mentoring, and creating loving, inclusive classroom environments to eliminate the "otherness" (异己感) that causes rejection, as "healing and comforting the child's body and mind"

The paper concludes that teachers are crucial to improving the quality of inclusive education in regular classrooms and must break through traditional segregated education paradigms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"特殊幼儿随班就读是中国式现代化融合教育的重要表现形式，也是确保特殊幼儿享有公平教育权的主要实施途径" (Special children learning in regular classes is an important manifestation of Chinese modern integrated education and the main implementation way to ensure special children's right to fair education).
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: 无处安放的自闭症“星娃”：高质量融合教育还有多远-中新网 ---
URL: https://www.chinanews.com/gn/2021/03-12/9430467.shtml

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a news article from China News (中国新闻网), originally sourced from 澎湃新闻 (The Paper), published on March 12, 2021, and authored by reporter 卫佳铭. The article investigates the state of "high-quality inclusive/integrated education" (融合教育) for children with autism ("星娃" or "star children") in China.

Key points covered:

**Background and Statistics:**
- According to the 2017 "China Autism Education Rehabilitation Industry Development Report," there are over 10 million people with autism in China, with 2 million+ autistic children aged 0-14, growing at a rate of nearly 200,000 per year.
- Autism (自闭症/孤独症) is a representative pervasive developmental disorder characterized by language/social communication barriers, narrow interests/activities, and repetitive stereotyped behaviors.

**Policy Context:**
- 2014: "Special Education Improvement Plan (2014-2016)" required mildly disabled children to attend regular schools, with "zero rejection" policies adopted in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Xiamen, etc.
- July 2017: The Second Special Education Improvement Plan (2017-2020) further prioritized mainstream school placement for disabled children.
- A 2018 report by the National Alliance of Parents Organizations of People with Mental Disabilities found that only 69% of applicants successfully enrolled in school in 2017.
- 2015 State Council plan promoted inclusive education and building special education resource classrooms (资源教室) in schools with more disabled students.

**Personal Stories:**
- 琪琪 (Qiqi), in Guangzhou, was expelled from school in 2nd grade, then transferred to a more inclusive school. Now in regular junior high, her parents hide her condition and struggle with homework support. Her father 成强 (Cheng Qiang) had to become her "shadow teacher" after hiring an inexperienced college graduate for 5,000 yuan/month.
- 豆豆 (Doudou) in a remote western Guangdong town has been "barely passing time" in mainstream school.
- 小鹿 (Xiaolu), age 7 in Dandong, Liaoning, had her enrollment delayed one year; her mother spent over 1 million yuan on rehabilitation and cannot afford an accompanying assistant (陪读).

**Challenges:**
- Shortage of "shadow teachers" (影子老师/特教助理) - hiring one costs 100,000+ yuan per year per parent reports; many schools refuse to allow them in classrooms.
- Resource classrooms built at cost (e.g., one school spent 200,000 yuan) are often unused due to lack of resource teachers.
- Resource teachers rarely have dedicated staffing positions (编制); most are regular teachers doing double duty.
- Teachers lack special education training; some parents report inappropriate treatment (e.g., harsh criticism that backfired on a girl named 星星/Xingxing who tripped classmates to get attention).
- Special education funding in underdeveloped areas is inadequate; in Bijie, Guizhou, resource classroom construction and teacher training are seriously insufficient.

**Expert Solutions Proposed at 2021 Two Sessions (两会):**
- CPPCC member 邰丽华 (Tai Lihua), head of the China Disabled People's Art Troupe, proposed adding a "one person one plan" (一人一案) approach in the Third Special Education Improvement Plan, allowing schools to hire special education teachers as needed, with an integrated system: "head teacher overall responsibility, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination."
- CPPCC member 黄绮 (Huang Qi), associate professor at Shanghai International Studies University Law School, proposed opening dedicated special education schools for autistic children and including them in compulsory education.

**Science of Assessment and IEP:**
- Current placement in China is based mainly on IQ testing: below 50 suggests special school; 50-70 suggests mainstream school (随班就读).
- IEP (Individualized Education Program) originated in the US in 1975; in the US, a team (school psychologist + learning disability specialists) does comprehensive assessment of intelligence, academics, and social-emotional skills before placement.
- 石荟 (Shi Hui), an inclusive education teacher at New York City and Columbia University early childhood special education graduate, explained US best practices: parents have absolute say in IEPs, teachers cooperate ("regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach"), and IEPs are re-evaluated every 3 months. She believes the best arrangement is one with the least restriction while ensuring effective learning.

**Benefits of Good Inclusive Education:**
- Experts 石荟 and 刘丽 (Liu Li, who works in multiple Beijing mainstream schools) argue that good inclusive education benefits both special needs children and ordinary children - helping typical children learn about diversity and how to respect and treat others well.
- The article highlights bullying incidents (e.g., a boy taping "I have autism" on 琪琪's back) and teacher bias cases.
- 刘丽 shared a positive example: classmates spontaneously leaving red teaching aids for autistic child 天天 (Tiantian) because they knew he liked red.

The article concludes with optimism that like developed countries, China's special education will improve through continued parental advocacy and policy advancement, though it requires a more inclusive and free social environment. All personal names in the article are pseudonyms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"特殊需要孩子也是孩子，他是一个生命，可以享受他/她应有的受教育权利。" (Special needs children are also children; they are lives that can enjoy their right to education. - 菲菲妈妈/Fifi's mother), "好的融合教育一定是让特殊需要儿童和普通儿童双方受益的，它不仅能让特殊需要儿童学习社会规范、早日回归主流，同时能让普通孩子通过和特殊需要孩子相处，了解世界的多元，学会如何尊重和善待他人。" (Good inclusive education must benefit both special needs and ordinary children... - 石荟/Shi Hui), "普通教师决定教什么，特殊教师决定怎么教。" (Regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach. - 石荟 on US IEP practice), "班主任全面负责儿童发展，特教教师入班支持，资源教师总体统筹协调" (Head teacher overall responsible for child development, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination - 邰丽华's proposal), "来自同龄人欺凌的伤害给家长的触动太大了。" (The hurt from peer bullying touches parents too deeply. - 成强/Cheng Qiang)
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: 自闭症儿童的融合教育不能“形合神不合”-中青在线 ---
URL: http://zqb.cyol.com/html/2021-03/30/nw.D110000zgqnb_20210330_2-08.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Chinese news article from 中国青年报 (China Youth Daily), published March 30, 2021, ahead of World Autism Day (April 2). The article features an interview with 黄伟合 (Huang Weihe), an internationally certified doctoral-level behavior analyst who worked for many years at an autism clinic in California, USA.

**Key Topic**: The article discusses the challenges and proper approaches to education and intervention for children with autism in China, where it is estimated there are 3-5 million autistic children. Autism has no known cause and no effective drug cure; the only widely recognized improvement method is "scientific intervention."

**Main Points:**

1. **Child-centered intervention**: Huang emphasizes that educational intervention must be based on the child's actual needs, not parents' wishes, which may be influenced by comparing with other children. He cites an example of a mother who insisted her severely autistic daughter learn to write essays for university, which far exceeded the girl's capacity and led to aggressive behavior. Professional institutions should conduct qualitative diagnosis and quantitative evaluation of both abilities and problem behaviors to set appropriate individual goals.

2. **Three principles: Functionality, initiative, flexibility**:
   - Functionality: Teach useful functional language (e.g., expressing desires about toys or food) rather than mere polite greetings.
   - Initiative: Help children actively care about others and ask questions, illustrated by a case where a boy earned game time by collecting marks for asking questions, eventually developing social friendships.
   - Flexibility: Break rigid stereotyped behaviors (e.g., a boy who only played with toy cars was guided to explore different toys through a self-management reward system). Huang notes flexibility is crucial even for adults, and recommends Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) for parents unable to accept their child's autism diagnosis.

3. **University participation needed**: Huang found universities in China have been largely absent from autism intervention research over the past 20 years, though universities like Peking University, Beijing Normal University, Qingdao University, and Tsinghua University have recently begun offering behavioral analysis courses to train expert rehabilitation personnel. He compares this to the US, where research is university-based (UCLA, UC Santa Barbara, Stanford).

4. **Importance of early intervention**: In California, families, the Department of Developmental Services, and school districts share responsibility. Schools adopt a "zero rejection" policy. Statistics: intervention before age 3 gives a 90% chance of developing spoken language; at age 3-5, 80-90%; after age 6, only ~20%.

5. **Problems in China**: Parents bear the education burden alone. Many schools refuse autistic children, normal children's parents resist integration, and even when accepted, schools lack trained teachers, resulting in "形合而神不合" (form without substance) integration education. Huang recommends legal guarantees for enrollment and top-down training of special teachers.

6. **Evidence-based intervention standards**: Since 2020, an international health outcomes measurement consortium (autism spectrum branch), involving dozens of countries' experts (including Huang), has been working to establish objective standards for what constitutes "proven effective" intervention, to help parents select qualified service providers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"在对自闭症儿童进行教育干预时，不能仅仅从家长的愿望出发，而要把重点放在自闭症儿童本身。有时候家长的想法也许会受与其他孩子攀比等主观因素影响，而并不符合孩子发展的客观需求。干预团队要理解自闭症儿童的真正需求，以他们的需求为本，来帮助他们提升自己的能力。" (When intervening educationally with autistic children, we cannot start only from parents' wishes but must focus on the children themselves... The intervention team must understand the true needs of autistic children and help them improve their abilities based on those needs.)

URL: https://www.chinalawtranslate.com/regulation-on-education-for-persons-with-disabilities%EF%BC%882017-edition%EF%BC%89

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from China Law Translate presents the full Chinese text of the 2017 edition of China's "Regulations on Education for Persons with Disabilities" (残疾人教育条例). The regulation was originally issued on August 23, 1994, via State Council Order No. 161, revised on January 8, 2011, and re-adopted at the 161st executive meeting of the State Council on January 11, 2017. It was promulgated by State Council Order No. 674 and took effect on May 1, 2017.

Key provisions of the regulation include:
- **General Principles (Chapter 1):** Guarantees equal educational rights for persons with disabilities and prohibits disability-based educational discrimination. Emphasizes "inclusive education" (融合教育), prioritizing ordinary educational methods over special education when possible. Mandates government leadership, financing, and supervision of disability education.
- **Compulsory Education (Chapter 2):** Requires governments to ensure school-age disabled children receive compulsory education. Establishes special education resource classrooms in ordinary schools and requires expert committees for assessing disabled children's educational capacity. Provides for placement in ordinary schools (with support), special education schools, or home/remote instruction for those needing special care.
- **Vocational Education (Chapter 3):** Focuses on developing secondary vocational education, accelerating higher vocational education, and providing skills training. Ordinary vocational schools cannot refuse qualified disabled applicants.
- **Preschool Education (Chapter 4):** Encourages integrating disabled children into ordinary preschools and requires combining education with care and rehabilitation, emphasizing early detection, rehabilitation, and education.
- **Higher Education and Continuing Education (Chapter 5):** Ordinary high schools, universities, and continuing education institutions must admit qualified disabled candidates. Promotes distance education and flexible models to support disabled learners.
- **Teachers (Chapter 6):** Requires special education teachers to hold teaching qualifications and special education training, with sign language and Braille standards for teachers of hearing-/vision-impaired students. Provides special allowances and preferential treatment for special education teachers.
- **Conditions and Safeguards (Chapter 7):** Requires funding, special education schools, barrier-free campus environments, tuition waivers for economically disadvantaged disabled students, reasonable accommodations for national examinations, and support for private special education institutions.
- **Legal Liability (Chapter 8):** Prescribes penalties (including administrative discipline and criminal liability) for refusing to admit qualified disabled students, discriminating against or harming disabled students, and failing to waive fees for disadvantaged students.
- **Supplementary Provisions (Chapter 9):** Defines "inclusive education" as maximally integrating disabled students into ordinary education, and "special education resource classrooms" as dedicated classrooms in ordinary schools equipped with special education and rehabilitation facilities.

The regulation is the primary national legal framework governing disability education rights in China, spanning compulsory through higher education, with strong emphasis on inclusive education, teacher training, and adequate funding and facilities.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 7: 教育部关于加强残疾儿童少年义务教育阶段随班就读工作的 ... ---
URL: https://www.shanghai.gov.cn/cjrqygjj/20230627/d6d1d734341b4d40aa784a9e5e213e5b.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the official Guiding Opinion (指导意见) issued by China's Ministry of Education on June 17, 2020, concerning the strengthening of "learning in regular classes" (随班就读) — the practice of placing children with disabilities in regular compulsory education classrooms alongside their peers in mainstream schools. The policy addresses key problems including unsound working mechanisms, incomplete support conditions, and low levels of special education expertise among classroom teachers.

The document sets out seven major sections with 16 specific measures:

1. **Overall Requirements**: Adhere to scientific assessment, "should be included, all included" (应随尽随), respect differences, teach according to aptitude, and promote integration of special education with ordinary education for fair and quality development.

2. **Scientific Assessment Mechanisms**: Before the end of April each year, county-level education departments must work with disabled persons federations and street/township governments to register all school-age children with disabilities. Before the end of May, county-level expert committees must assess whether each child is suitable for integrated learning. Work ledgers must be established, with strict confidentiality of student information.

3. **Placement Systems**: County education departments must ensure school places for integrated learners, prioritizing nearby enrollment in the same school district, and may designate higher-quality schools as fixed-point schools.

4. **Resource Support Systems**: Schools enrolling 5 or more students with disabilities must establish dedicated special education resource classrooms with facilities and resource teachers; province/city/county resource centers must be fully established.

5. **Special Educational Care**: Emphasis on curriculum adaptation, "one student, one plan" (一人一案) individualized education plans, comprehensive evaluation that goes beyond academic achievement alone, and campus culture that prohibits educational discrimination and promotes peer assistance.

6. **Teacher Professional Capacity**: Assign caring teachers with special education literacy, provide training through the national training plan and continuing education, and establish classification-based evaluation in the teacher title/promotion system with appropriate preferences and special post subsidies for resource teachers.

7. **Organizational Implementation**: Multi-department collaboration (development and reform, civil affairs, finance, health, disabled persons federations), inclusion in compulsory education efforts and annual school evaluations, sufficient per-student public funding, and strengthened home-school cooperation.

The policy also stipulates that ordinary education institutions at non-compulsory education stages (kindergartens, regular high schools, vocational schools, and higher education institutions) may implement integrated learning with reference to these guidelines.
</summary>

KEY TARGETS BY 2025:
- Compulsory education enrollment rate for school-age children with disabilities to reach 97%.
- Every city (prefecture) and qualified county to have a secondary vocational education department (class) for persons with disabilities; each province to establish at least one well-run secondary vocational school and one school for blind/deaf senior high school.

1. Expanding service at all education stages: Improve compulsory education enrollment mechanisms at county level; encourage counties with populations over 200,000 to run a standard special education school; layout special schools for children with autism in provincial capitals, separately listed cities, and larger cities; strengthen door-to-door teaching (送教上门) services; develop preschool special education; support ordinary kindergartens and special education schools adding preschool sections; develop vocational-education-focused senior high special education; steadily develop higher special education and continue education channels.

2. Promoting inclusive (integrated) education: Explore integration models for disabled and ordinary children; pair special education and general schools; complete curriculum and textbook compilation for special education compulsory education by 2023; establish teaching assistant/companion reading systems for autistic children; promote national sign language and Braille; integrate vocational education; develop professional programs for intellectual/multiple disabilities and autism; pilot "academic certificate + multiple vocational skill level certificates"; integrate medical rehabilitation and IT — implement assistive devices in schools, apply AI, cloud, big data, VR technologies, and smart campuses.

3. Strengthening support and guarantee mechanisms: Improve facilities and accessibility; build special education resource centers at national, provincial, city, county, and school levels; raise per-student public funding for compulsory special education to at least 7,000 yuan per student per year by 2025; central funding to support central/western regions; continue free senior high education for economically disadvantaged disabled students; expand special education teacher training programs, include special education in teacher qualification exams and continued education; implement special education teacher allowances and tilt awards, promotions, and performance pay toward special education teachers.

IMPLEMENTATION: Strengthen Party leadership; build multi-department coordination mechanisms (education, development reform, civil affairs, finance, HRSS, health, disabled persons' federations); incorporate special education development into provincial government education responsibility evaluations and compulsory education quality supervision; include implementation in municipal/county government performance assessments with incentive and accountability mechanisms.

--- SOURCE 1: How to Use Universal Design for Learning (UDL) in Autism: A Comprehensive Guide for Educators | Links ---
URL: https://linksaba.com/how-to-use-universal-design-for-learning-udl-in-autism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This educational guide from Links ABA Therapy Solutions explains how educators can use Universal Design for Learning (UDL) to support students with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). The article begins with recent statistics: about 1 in 31 (3.2%) children aged 8 are identified with ASD per CDC estimates (based on 2022 medical records), a significant increase from 1 in 54 in 2016 and 1 in 150 in 2000. Boys are three times more likely than girls to be diagnosed, and diagnoses are more common among Black and Hispanic children. Additionally, 8% of autistic students don't finish high school versus 5% of all students.

The content explains that UDL is an evidence-based framework originally developed by the Center for Applied Special Technology (CAST), grounded in neuroscience, and built on three core principles: Multiple Means of Engagement (building interest/motivation through leveraging intense interests and offering choices), Multiple Means of Representation (visual and multimodal support, comprehension aids, language adaptations), and Multiple Means of Action and Expression (alternative assessment methods, executive function supports, communication pathways).

Research evidence cited includes a meta-analysis with total effect sizes of 3.56, and findings that implementing all three UDL principles together produces higher positive educational gains than using one or two in isolation. Intervention studies confirmed the effectiveness of UDL-based tools (digital environments, e-books, shared stories, audio systems, software, videos, and classroom management systems) across academic, social, and behavioral outcomes.

The article provides practical strategies for engagement, representation, and action/expression, plus professional development guidance (studies conducted across six countries). It references Thomas Tobin and Kirsten Behling's book "Reach Everyone, Teach Everyone: Universal Design for Learning in Higher Education" for implementation planning. Culturally responsive practices are discussed given the demographic shifts, noting multicultural students with autism face challenges in communication, social skills, behavioral repertoires, and culture. The conclusion frames UDL as a paradigm shift from "fixing the student" to "improving the learning environment," and includes a practical implementation checklist for educators.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In a classroom using universal design for learning, there are no students with limitations, only students who accomplish the same tasks and learn the same information with different methods."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: UDL as a Framework for Inclusion: Bridging Neurodiversity and Learning through Sensory-Responsive Design — SENcastle ---
URL: https://www.sencastle.com/blog/universal-design-for-learning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Mateja Vukasinec (published on the SENcastle website) explores how Universal Design for Learning (UDL) serves as a framework for inclusion by bridging neurodiversity and learning through sensory-responsive design, specifically through the SENcastle multimodal device.

**UDL Overview:** UDL is an evidence-based educational framework developed by CAST that designs flexible learning environments enabling access and progress for all students regardless of cognitive, sensory, motor, or communication abilities. It is grounded in neuroscience and describes three key learning networks: affective (why we learn), recognition (what we learn), and strategic (how we learn). The latest UDL guidelines (version 3.0, 2024) emphasize removing learning barriers using flexible methods and technologies.

**UDL's Three Principles:**
1. Multiple means of engagement (motivation, choice, relevance, adjusted challenges)
2. Multiple means of representation (content access through visual, auditory, and tactile modalities)
3. Multiple means of action and expression (students demonstrate knowledge in different ways via assistive technology and alternative communication)

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** Guo and Wang (2025) report a 37.4% increase in academic achievement in high-UDL-implementation environments, with greatest benefits for students with lower baseline engagement. UDL is effective in improving academic, social, and behavioral outcomes for learners with intellectual and developmental disabilities, especially when digital and multisensory tools are used consistently (AlRawi and AlKahtani, 2021).

**SENcastle System:** SENcastle is a multimodal device developed with therapists providing controlled, adaptable input to five sensory systems: visual, auditory, tactile, proprioceptive, and vestibular. Features include adjustable-color light elements, message/sound recording and playback, vibratory and proprioceptive components, and customizable sensory scenes. It is particularly suitable for children with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and sensory integration difficulties.

**UDL-SENcastle Alignment:** 
- Supports multiple means of representation through combined visual, auditory, and tactile stimuli with adjustable intensity
- Enhances engagement through tailored, predictable, motivating sensory activities, flexible breaks, proprioceptive deep input, and calming scenes (beneficial for ADHD and autism learners)
- Enables action and expression through touch, movement, cause-and-effect interactions; SENcastle Access model supports wheelchair users with switch and eye-gaze control

**Future Outlook:** Integration of UDL and SENcastle represents a modern inclusive approach where sensory-educational tools become standard for all learners, not exclusively those with disabilities, promoting equitable education and reducing stigma. Further longitudinal research is needed, though existing evidence strongly supports SENcastle's role in implementing UDL principles.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Universal Design for Learning (UDL) represents the foundation of inclusive education. It is an evidence-based educational framework that focuses on designing flexible learning environments that enable access, participation, and progress for all students, regardless of their cognitive, sensory, motor, or communication abilities or individual differences." "Guo and Wang (2025) report a 37.4% increase in academic achievement among students in environments with high UDL implementation, with the greatest benefits observed among students with lower baseline engagement." "SENcastle is a multimodal device developed in collaboration with therapists to provide controlled, adaptable input to five sensory systems: visual, auditory, tactile, proprioceptive, and vestibular." "Integrating SENcastle within a UDL approach supports the development of independence, a sense of competence, and social skills, which are among the key goals of inclusive education (AlRawi and AlKahtani, 2021)." "The integration of UDL and the SENcastle system represents a modern, inclusive approach in which sensory-educational tools are not intended exclusively for students with developmental disabilities but are instead a standard part of the educational environment for all learners."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: What Universal Design for Learning principles, guidelines, and checkpoints are evident in educators’ descriptions of their practice when supporting students on the autism spectrum? ---
URL: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0883035519327120

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a research article published in the International Journal of Educational Research (Volume 102, 2020, Article 101583) by Suzanne Carrington, Beth Saggers, Amanda Webster, Keely Harper-Hill, and Julie Nickerson. The study examines whether Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles, guidelines, and checkpoints are evident in educators' descriptions of their practice when supporting students on the autism spectrum.

**Key details:**
- UDL is a comprehensive framework developed by researchers (Rose & Meyer, 2002) at the Center for Applied Special Technology (CAST), based on neuroscience research that assumes variability in life and learning. The framework has three guiding principles supporting all learners by providing multiple ways of engaging.
- Data was collected from 20 teaching and specialist personnel in Australia using semi-structured interviews (10 teachers and principals, 10 specialist personnel).
- A social constructionist lens was used to highlight educators' individual realities.
- Findings showed that all three UDL principles, all nine guidelines, and many of the checkpoints were evident in the educators' descriptions of practice.
- The study was financially supported by the Cooperative Research Centre for Living with Autism (Autism CRC), supported under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program (Project 2.009).

**Background context:** Australian teachers must meet educational needs of all students consistent with the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 and Disability Standards for Education 2005. Schools must report data on students with disabilities and adjustments to the Nationally Consistent Collection of Data on School Students with Disability (NCCD).

**Evidence on UDL effectiveness:** A meta-analysis by Capp (2017) examined 18 peer-reviewed studies (2013-2016) using pre/post-testing and concluded UDL is an effective teaching methodology for improving the learning process for all students, though its impact on educational outcomes was not clearly demonstrated.

**Limitations:** Small sample size (20 educators, self-selected from Australia) with potential bias toward educators committed to meeting needs of students on the autism spectrum.

**Metrics:** The article has been cited 53 times (including 2 policy citations) and has 177 Mendeley readers. Citing works include research on implementing Universal Design through augmented-reality game-based learning, student voices on UDL in higher education, and inclusive education policy in Australia.
</summary>

"Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is a comprehensive framework that supports teachers to address diversity of learning in the classroom.", "Findings show that all three principles of UDL, all nine guidelines, and many of the checkpoints were evident in the descriptions of practice.", "Capp concluded that UDL is an effective teaching methodology for improving the learning process for all students, but noted that the impact on educational outcomes was not clearly demonstrated.", "This study is informed by the theory of social constructionism, which suggests that knowledge is developed from the interconnection of individuals' perspectives (Burr, 1995).", "The research (Project 2.009) was financially supported by the Cooperative Research Centre for Living with Autism (Autism CRC), established and supported under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program."

--- SOURCE 4: CAST Universal Design for Learning Guidelines ---
URL: https://udlguidelines.cast.org

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from CAST presents the Universal Design for Learning (UDL) Guidelines 3.0, an educational framework designed to ensure all learners can access and participate in meaningful, challenging learning opportunities. The goal of UDL is learner agency that is purposeful & reflective, resourceful & authentic, strategic & action-oriented.

UDL Guidelines 3.0 was released on July 30, 2024, following an update process launched in 2020. This iteration responds to calls from practitioners and researchers to address critical barriers rooted in biases and systems of exclusion for learners with and without disabilities. The Guidelines are based on scientific insights into how humans learn and are supported by evidence to benefit learners of all ages.

The framework organizes design options into three main principles:

1. **Engagement** - The "why" of learning, including:
   - Welcoming Interests & Identities (Guideline 7): Optimize choice and autonomy (7.1), relevance/value/authenticity (7.2), joy and play (7.3), address biases/threats/distractions (7.4)
   - Sustaining Effort & Persistence (Guideline 8): Clarify meaning/purpose of goals (8.1), optimize challenge and support (8.2), foster collaboration/interdependence (8.3), foster belonging and community (8.4), offer action-oriented feedback (8.5)
   - Emotional Capacity (Guideline 9): Recognize expectations/beliefs/motivations (9.1), develop awareness of self and others (9.2), promote reflection (9.3), cultivate empathy and restorative practices (9.4)

2. **Representation** - The "what" of learning, including:
   - Perception (Guideline 1): Customize display (1.1), multiple ways to perceive (1.2), represent diverse perspectives (1.3)
   - Language & Symbols (Guideline 2): Clarify vocabulary/symbols (2.1), support decoding (2.2), understand languages/dialects (2.3), address language biases (2.4), illustrate through multiple media (2.5)
   - Building Knowledge (Guideline 3): Connect prior knowledge (3.1), highlight patterns/features (3.2), multiple ways of knowing (3.3), maximize transfer/generalization (3.4)

3. **Action & Expression** - The "how" of learning, including:
   - Interaction (Guideline 4): Vary methods for response/navigation (4.1), optimize access to assistive technologies (4.2)
   - Expression & Communication (Guideline 5): Multiple media for communication (5.1), multiple tools for construction (5.2), build fluencies with support (5.3), address expression biases (5.4)
   - Strategy Development (Guideline 6): Set meaningful goals (6.1), anticipate/plan for challenges (6.2), organize information (6.3), monitor progress (6.4), challenge exclusionary practices (6.5)

The Guidelines support educators, curriculum developers, learning designers, researchers, and parents. Resources include webinars for UDL Guidelines 3.0, a Spanish version (DUA en español), PDF graphic organizers available for download, translations in over 20 languages, and professional development opportunities for PreK-12, Postsecondary, and Workforce/CTE audiences.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The CAST UDL Guidelines™ are a tool that can be applied in any discipline or domain to ensure that all learners are able to access and participate in meaningful, challenging learning opportunities."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Frontiers | Teachers’ knowledge and attitudes toward inclusive education for children with autism in mainstream schools ---
URL: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1630710/full

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an original research article published in Frontiers in Education (Vol. 10, 2025) by Mohammed Abdulrhman Alassaf of Imam Mohammad ibn Saud Islamic University (IMSIU), Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study assessed the knowledge and attitudes of special education teachers in Riyadh toward inclusive education for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in mainstream schools, and identified demographic predictors of these variables.

**Study Design and Methods:** A descriptive cross-sectional design was used with 321 special education teachers recruited via convenience sampling. Data were collected using a structured self-administered Arabic questionnaire comprising three sections: sociodemographic data, a 15-item knowledge scale, and a 15-item attitude scale (both using 5-point Likert scales). The sample included 62.6% female and 37.4% male teachers, with 77.9% holding bachelor's degrees, 56.7% having received prior autism training, and 46.1% teaching at primary level. Validity was established via expert panel review, and reliability was confirmed with Cronbach's alpha of 0.87 (knowledge) and 0.91 (attitudes). Analyses used SPSS including t-tests, ANOVA, and multiple linear regression with significance at p < 0.05.

**Key Results:** Teachers demonstrated moderate levels of knowledge (M = 3.29) and attitudes (M = 3.48) toward inclusive education. Significant differences were found based on gender, educational qualification, teaching experience, and previous autism training (but not age). Female teachers scored higher than males on both knowledge (p = 0.032) and attitudes (p = 0.045). Regression analyses showed that female gender, higher educational qualifications, longer teaching experience, and prior autism training were significant predictors of both higher knowledge and more positive attitudes. Prior autism training was the strongest predictor (β = 0.31 for knowledge, β = 0.29 for attitudes, p < 0.001).

**Strengths and Gaps:** Teachers scored highest on items about peer-mediated strategies (M = 3.65) and awareness of routine-change struggles (M = 3.56), but showed gaps in understanding autism as a neurological (not mental) condition (M = 2.83) and in familiarity with Individualized Education Plans (M = 2.93). Teachers strongly endorsed inclusion's social benefits (M = 3.89) and willingness to attend more training (M = 3.89), but expressed lower confidence in supporting students with autism (M = 3.12).

**Conclusions:** While teachers hold generally supportive views, key knowledge gaps and structural challenges remain. The study recommends targeted, autism-specific professional development and stronger institutional support (addressing overcrowded classrooms, lack of teaching assistants, and limited resources) to enhance inclusive practices. Limitations include the cross-sectional design, self-report data with potential social desirability bias, and restriction to special education teachers in Riyadh, limiting generalizability.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Findings revealed that teachers demonstrated a moderate level of knowledge (M = 3.29) and attitudes (M = 3.48) toward inclusive education. Significant differences were observed based on gender, age, educational qualification, teaching experience, and previous autism-related training.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Shaping Inclusive Classrooms: Key Factors Influencing Teachers’ Attitudes Toward Inclusion of Students with Special Needs ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/5/541

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific research article published in the MDPI journal *Education Sciences* (Volume 15, Issue 5, Article 541) on April 27, 2025, with the DOI 10.3390/educsci15050541. The study, "Shaping Inclusive Classrooms: Key Factors Influencing Teachers' Attitudes Toward Inclusion of Students with Special Needs," was authored by Carmit Gal, Chen Hanna Ryder, Shani Raveh Amsalem, and Oshrat On, affiliated with Western Galilee College (Israel), Sha'anan Academic Teacher's College, and Gordon College of Education.

**Context/Background:** Israel has undergone significant educational reforms toward inclusive education, beginning with the 1988 Special Education Law, followed by a major 2018 amendment emphasizing the right of students with special needs to be educated in regular settings with a new funding model. The Ministry of Education launched a five-year Inclusion Implementation Plan (2020-2025) aiming to increase inclusion rates from 60% to 80% by 2025; by 2024, approximately 70% of students with special needs were educated in mainstream settings. All teacher training institutions are now required to include special education and inclusive practice courses.

**Methodology:** The study employed an interpretive phenomenological approach using semi-structured interviews with 40 female mainstream Israeli teachers (aged 27-49) who had recently attended a special education training workshop. Participants included kindergarten, elementary, middle, and high school teachers. Notably, 66% were interns, 27% held B.Ed. certificates, and 7% held M.Ed. certificates. 63% reported no prior training in special education/inclusion, 49% had no inclusion experience, and only 12% had over 4 years of experience. Data was analyzed using Braun and Clarke's (2006) thematic analysis with six phases; two researchers independently coded data to ensure reliability.

**Key Findings - Four Main Themes:**
1. **Nuanced Support for Inclusive Education:** Teachers generally supported inclusion as a societal goal but with awareness of implementation challenges. Support varied by educational level (kindergarten teachers emphasized early socialization; high school teachers focused on academic preparation).
2. **Factors Influencing Self-Efficacy:** Three subthemes emerged: (a) lack of adequate training and preparation, (b) insufficient institutional support, and (c) fear of negative outcomes.
3. **Key Determinants of Successful Inclusion:** Four subthemes: (a) student-teacher ratio (large classes of 30+ students viewed as making inclusion impossible), (b) support from educational staff and administration, (c) need for proper training and knowledge, and (d) parental cooperation.
4. **Acceptance Challenges Based on Disability Severity:** Teachers' attitudes varied based on the nature and severity of students' disabilities.

**Conclusions:** The study finds general support for inclusive education but significant concerns about teacher preparedness, institutional support, and managing diverse needs. It emphasizes the need for comprehensive training, adequate institutional backing, and teacher self-efficacy. Recommendations include targeted professional development, collaborative approaches, and systemic policy alignment. The article highlights that Israel represents a case of accelerated policy transformation that provides unique insights for other educational systems undertaking similar rapid reforms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We, as a society have to promote the concept of inclusion. Only then, we can all feel equal." — Shani; "I want to do it; however, I do not feel skilled or trained to meet the special needs of these students… therefore, for now, I prefer not to…" — Ester; "I am the only teacher in my school who agreed to try… I do not feel like I am succeeding in helping him…. I have little support from the school… it's very hard" — Rina; "It's almost impossible to be there for 30+ students as well as for the students with special needs… We must reduce the size of inclusive classrooms. Otherwise, there's no chance in my opinion" — Sharon; "Cooperation with the parents of integrated children is very important and can determine whether the inclusion will be successful or a nightmare…" — Tamar
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: Effective Teaching Practices and Inclusion of Students with Special Needs in Regular Classrooms: Examining Teachers’ Attitudes and Knowledge toward Special Needs Minorities | IntechOpen ---
URL: https://www.intechopen.com/online-first/1211970

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access, peer-reviewed chapter published on IntechOpen (April 15, 2025) from the edited volume "Inclusive Special Education - Research to Practice." Written by Awal Mohammed Alhassan (Norwegian Centre for Learning Environment and Behavioral Research in Education, University of Stavanger, Norway), the study (DOI: 10.5772/intechopen.1009987) examines how principals' expectations, teachers' attitudes, and knowledge of special education influence inclusive teaching practices for minority students with special needs in Norwegian secondary classrooms.

**Methodology:** A cross-sectional survey of 330 educators (10 principals, 320 teachers) from 10 secondary schools in Oslo and Rogaland counties, plus 48 classroom observations. Participants were 64% female, aged 26-65; 43% had formal special education training, 42% had prior SEN experience. Four validated instruments were used: ATIES (attitudes, Cronbach's α=0.87), KIES (knowledge, α=0.82), PES (principals' expectations, α=0.83), and ETPC (30-item effective teaching checklist). The study integrated Ajzen's Theory of Planned Behavior and Allport's Intergroup Contact Theory.

**Key Findings:**
- Principals held high expectations for collaboration/teamwork, assessments, differentiated instruction, co-teaching, and adapting materials, but LOW expectations for individualization tasks including multi-level teaching, individual performance standards, and IEPs.
- Teachers consistently demonstrated classroom management and lesson presentation behaviors, but rarely used adaptive teaching practices (IEPs, multi-level teaching, adapting instructional materials, assistive technology).
- Multiple regression found no significant correlation among attitudes, knowledge, and principal expectations with teaching practices.
- Training in special education significantly predicted use of peer tutoring/cooperative learning (t=-3.38, p=.002) and differentiated class activities (t=-2.05, p=.048).
- Experience with SEN students emerged as the strongest predictor of adaptive instructional practices, explaining 10.8% of variance (adjusted R²=.108, F=5.36, p=.027).

**Key context:** Nearly 48% of SEN students in Norway are taught in segregated settings despite national policies. Effective strategies identified include differentiated instruction, culturally relevant pedagogy, family involvement, and peer support/cooperative learning. The study recommends enhanced professional development and adaptive teaching to address resource gaps. Limitations include cross-sectional design and small sample size. The chapter has 240 downloads and 1 citation.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an open-access systematic review paper published on January 19, 2022, in the Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (Volume 10, pages 477-491, 2023), titled "Educator Attitudes Towards the Inclusion of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorders in Mainstream Education: a Systematic Review." The authors are Amy Russell, Aideen Scriney, and Sinéad Smyth.

The review is the first to focus solely on educator attitudes towards the inclusion of students with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) in mainstream education, since attitudes differ depending on the special educational needs (SEN) cohort. Seven databases (PsycINFO, CINAHL Complete, British Education Index, Education Research Complete, UK and Ireland Reference Centre, PsycArticles, and Web of Science) were searched, yielding 13 relevant articles involving 3,247 educators (sample sizes ranged from 72 to 863, including general education, special education, and physical education teachers, principals, and instructors).

Key findings:
- The majority of studies reported positive educator attitudes towards ASD inclusion, but with considerable variety in the measures used.
- There were mixed findings regarding the impact of training and experience on attitudes.
- Where measured, higher self-efficacy was related to positive attitudes.

The review highlights the need for more homogeneous attitudinal measures and further research to aggregate data on attitudes towards SEN cohorts other than those with ASD. The study was conducted using PICOSS framework for eligibility criteria, with quality assessed using the Quantitative Quality Appraisal Tool. The review included studies published up to March 2021 (searches conducted March 5-19, 2021).

Background context: The paper notes that inclusive education is recognized as a human rights issue under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and UNESCO guidelines. ASD affects about 1-2% of children worldwide, and students with ASD are more likely to be excluded from school than most other groups. Two-thirds of teachers reported lacking confidence and being apprehensive about teaching a student with ASD. Educators have more positive attitudes towards inclusion of students with physical or mild learning disabilities compared to those with emotional disorders, cognitive impairments, or behavioural issues. The review notes that teaching students with ASD presents significant instructional challenges, and mainstream teachers report inadequate preparation and lack of ASD-specific training. Factors influencing attitudes include resources/staffing concerns, self-efficacy, training, and experience.

The paper has 36k accesses, 58 citations, and 3 Altmetric mentions.

This is a systematic review published in Autism & Developmental Language Impairments (September 21, 2022) by Linda Petersson-Bloom and Mona Holmqvist from Malmö University, Sweden, examining strategies for supporting inclusive education for autistic students through qualitative research.

**Background and Aim:** The review identifies qualitative research results on adaptation and modification strategies to support inclusive education for autistic students at school and classroom levels in mainstream education.

**Method:** Four databases were searched (ERIC, Medline, PsycINFO, Web of Science) following PRISMA guidelines. Journal articles published in English between 1990-2018 were included. Searching retrieved 10,863 records; after screening, 108 studies met inclusion criteria. Studies focused on students with ASD aged 5-19 years attending mainstream schools, with interventions in learning contexts (social, pedagogical, physical).

**Key Results:**
- Only 16 studies were at the classroom level, 89 at school level, and 3 were uncategorized.
- Four categories of research focus were identified: Didactical perspective, Attitudes and views, Environmental sensitivity, and Social skills focus.
- Most studies (80) included views/attitudes of teachers or paraprofessionals. Teachers' attitudes were found crucial for inclusive education success.
- Limited professional development and knowledge about autism was identified as a major challenge in 31 studies.
- After professional development, teachers showed more positive attitudes and increased self-efficacy.
- Only 6 studies investigated environmental sensitivity (sensory processing difficulties), identified as insufficient.
- Only 10 studies focused on didactical/content knowledge development.
- Only 1 study included students with learning difficulties or intellectual disabilities combined with autism.
- Studies came from 17 countries, predominantly English-speaking (USA: 37, UK: 34, Australia: 12).
- Only 12 articles focused solely on autistic students' perspectives.

**Classroom-level findings:** Research showed need for adjusting sound and light aspects of the environment, noise-attenuating headphones increased participation, visual support and structured timetables improved learning outcomes, and assistive technologies (tablets, laptops, computerized devices) supported reading and writing development.

**Conclusions:** Professional development that includes autism-specific understanding and strategies for adjustment is essential. The review identified research gaps regarding: autistic students' own perspectives, environmental adaptations for sensory difficulties, and didactic perspectives on content instruction and knowledge development. --- SOURCE 2: Circle of Friends: A Complete Guide for Teachers ---
URL: https://www.structural-learning.com/post/circle-friends-complete-teachers-guide-peer

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive teacher's guide on implementing "Circle of Friends" interventions to support socially isolated learners in schools. The approach was created by Jack Pearpoint, Marsha Forest, and Judith Snow in Canada in the early 1990s, and was popularised in the UK by Newton, Taylor, and Wilson during the 1990s. Circle of Friends differs from adult-led interventions by empowering classmates to become active agents in befriending and problem-solving for a "focus child."

**Core Philosophy:** The approach is grounded in full inclusion for all children, the importance of relationships for learning, and the powerful influence of peers (which exceeds what adult support can achieve alone). Both the focus learner and peer volunteers benefit—volunteers gain empathy and leadership skills.

**Who Benefits:** Learners with autism, SEMH needs, learning/behavioural/physical challenges, newly arrived students, those returning after long absences, and children whose behaviour led to social rejection.

**Four Circles Model:** A visual tool mapping relationships in concentric rings: (1) Circle of Intimacy (family/anchors), (2) Circle of Friendship (close friends/allies), (3) Circle of Participation (classmates, club members), and (4) Circle of Exchange (paid professionals like teachers/doctors). The goal is to move peers from Circle 3 into Circle 2.

**Setup Steps (2-3 weeks preparation):** (1) Identify a suitable focus child with parental consent, (2) Recruit a consistent facilitator, (3) Select 4-8 empathetic, reliable peer volunteers (including children who've experienced social difficulties themselves), (4) Hold an initial class session without the focus child using the Four Circles model, (5) First circle meeting with the focus child (max 20 minutes, focusing on rapport).

**Session Structure (30-45 minutes weekly):** Check-in round (5 min), celebration of successes (10 min), identification of challenges (10 min), problem-solving with specific achievable strategies (10 min), and close (5 min). Facilitators guide rather than direct and must monitor volunteer wellbeing.

**Evidence Base:** Frederickson and Turner (2003) found boosted acceptance and self-esteem across 20 schools after one term; Whitaker et al. (2002) found autistic learners had more social contact at breaks; Kalyva and Avramidis (2005) showed circle members became more accepting of difference. Critically, Taylor and Burden (2002) noted poor facilitation can worsen a learner's sense of difference.

**Troubleshooting:** Address lack of commitment, gossip/negativity (with clear consequences), unrealistic expectations, conflict within the circle, and focus child resistance (allow observation time before active participation).

**15 strategies** are provided covering consent, volunteer selection, training, ground rules, regular meetings, skilled facilitation, achievable goals, celebrating wins, group problem-solving, unstructured time, wellbeing monitoring, parent communication, transition planning, review/adaptation, and planning for ending.

**Comparison Table:** Circle of Friends is compared to Social Stories (Carol Gray, 1991), LEGO Therapy (Daniel LeGoff, 2004), and Peer Mediation—differing in developer, primary focus, group size, session frequency, staff training needed, evidence base, and cost. These interventions complement each other rather than compete.

The article was written by the Structural Learning Research Team, reviewed by Paul Main (Founder & Educational Consultant), published January 16, 2026, and updated August 17, 2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The children in your classroom have the capacity to be one another's most powerful source of support. Circle of Friends gives them the structure and permission to do exactly that., A teaching assistant sitting with a child at lunch is not the same as a classmate choosing to sit with them., Circle of Friends fundamentally redefines inclusion by empowering learners to create supportive peer networks, Training is a key factor: the approach trains classmates to be active agents in befriending and problem-solving, cultivating a more inclusive school environment., Research indicates that participation can lead to increased self-esteem, improved social skills, and a reduction in experiences of bullying and loneliness for the focus child (Cowie, 2000)., Good facilitation decides if circles work or not (Taylor & Burden, 2002).
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from SCISCAN PUBLISHING LIMITED's International Open Access Journal Platform (based in Hong Kong, China), featuring a scholarly review article in the "Education Study" category. The article, titled "孤独症谱系儿童家长参与的融合教育研究进展" (Research Progress on Inclusive Education Involving Parents of Children with ASD), is authored by 薛佳玲, 黄美琳, 陈洁, 王海霏, 罗国予, 唐瑶, and 杜亚松. The paper is indexed by CNKI (中国知网) and Crossref.

Key content of the review article:
- **Background**: ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder in early childhood characterized by social/communication deficits, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors. US CDC 2023 data shows ASD prevalence of 1/36 among 8-year-olds. In China, 0.7% of children aged 6-12 have ASD (about 2 million children aged 0-14). There is no specific medication; rehabilitation training is the main intervention.

- **Concepts**: Inclusive education (proposed at the 1994 World Conference on Special Education) places children with special needs in regular classrooms. Parental involvement in inclusive education encompasses parent training (institution-centered) and parent-child activities (family-centered), including observing children's growth, collaborating with teachers, and learning training skills.

- **Current status**: A five-year Beijing study of ~500 schools found 79.4% of ASD children improved in proactively completing homework/learning tasks and 77.9% improved academically in inclusive settings. However, ASD children face challenges including low academic quality, social marginalization, higher risk of bullying, and limited peer popularity. Parental involvement levels are generally low; some parents feel excluded, helpless, and frustrated, treated only as "recipients" of education.

- **Roles/effects of parental involvement**: 
  1. Reduces core ASD symptoms (e.g., a study by Strain et al. showed symptom reduction in 6 children; 5 successfully entered regular elementary schools).
  2. Improves social functioning (e.g., "interaction handbooks" made by mothers helped typical children understand ASD peers; parent training plus parent-child games improved social skills).
  3. Increases appropriate behaviors (a study by Wang Shuqin et al. showed a year of parent training reduced leaving-seat and saliva-playing behaviors from week 4 onward, generalizing to other classes).
  4. Enhances parenting efficacy, reduces parental stress and depression, improves mental health and family functioning, creating a positive feedback cycle benefiting child recovery.

- **Future directions**: Calls for more evidence-based research on parental involvement, more studies on language, stereotyped behaviors, narrow interests, and emotional instability (which are currently under-researched), and inclusion of multiple stakeholders with other effective interventions.

The article includes 40 references from both Chinese and international sources.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage, published by 恩启 IngCare (authored by founder 王伟), is a comprehensive guide for parents on how to implement inclusive education (融合教育) and help children with special needs adapt to elementary school. It covers four main dimensions: policy framework, school readiness, application process, and campus support.

**Key statistics:**
- According to the Ministry of Education's 2024 statistical bulletin, 97.3% of children with disabilities in China have access to compulsory education, with over 55% studying in regular schools (随班就读)
- UNESCO's 2023 Global Education Monitoring Report shows only about 52% of countries worldwide have clear inclusive education policies
- As of 2025, over 20 provinces have issued provincial-level implementation rules for 随班就读
- China Disabled Persons' Federation 2023 data: about 918,000 children with disabilities in compulsory education, over 50% in regular classes
- 2024 data: approximately 876,000 disabled students in regular schools, accounting for 55.2% of disabled students in compulsory education
- Schools must provide at least 1 full-time resource teacher and develop IEPs within 10 working days of placement

**Policy framework:** China's inclusive education is primarily implemented through the 随班就读 (learning in regular classes) system. Key regulations include the 1994 trial measures, the 2017 revised 《残疾人教育条例》 (Regulations on Education of Persons with Disabilities, State Council Order No. 674), and the 2020 Ministry of Education guidance establishing a "regular school + special education school + special education resource center" three-in-one support system. The 2020 guidance requires full coverage of provincial, municipal, and county-level special education resource centers by the end of 2025.

**Difference between inclusive and special education:** Comparison table highlights differences in environment, teacher-student ratio (regular ~1:45 vs special ~1:4-8), curriculum, teacher qualifications, social development, academic pace, professional support, and policy basis.

**School readiness checklist (3 dimensions):**
- Social/behavioral: sit quietly 15-20 minutes, raise hand to speak, express needs verbally
- Learning adaptation: follow 2+ step instructions, focus 10-15 minutes on tasks, recognize one's name and classroom signs
- Self-care: independent toileting, organizing backpack/school supplies, dressing/undressing; parents should begin training 3-6 months before school entry

**5-step application process:**
1. Professional evaluation (at tertiary hospital developmental behavior or child health departments)
2. Submit application to district/county education authority (typically March-May window)
3. Educational placement assessment by special education expert committee
4. School placement, with IEP development within 10 working days
5. Continuous tracking with at least one IEP evaluation and adjustment per semester

**School support framework (3 levels):**
- Institutional: fusion education leadership group, resource classrooms, at least 1 full-time resource teacher
- Teacher: differentiated assignment adjustments, visual cue cards, peer assistance, recording classroom performance
- Peer: "buddy" assistance systems, themed class meetings, integration activities; systemically supported classes can improve peer acceptance by over 40% and reduce bullying

**Common misconceptions addressed (4):**
1. Inclusive education requires no extra support (harmful myth - it requires systematic professional support)
2. All children with special needs are suitable for inclusive education (not true for those needing intensive support)
3. Only special needs children benefit (regular students also benefit from empathy, tolerance, and collaboration skills)
4. Parental involvement ends after enrollment (parents must remain deeply involved)

The article includes references to government regulations, UNESCO, WHO, and recommends related reading on special education policies, ABA vs ESDM intervention comparison, early autism signs, ADHD parent guides, and speech/language development. Contact information: 400-606-2105, with a disclaimer that content is for education/reference only and not medical advice.

URL: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/2331186X.2023.2218191

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed, open-access systematic review and meta-analysis published in Cogent Education (Volume 10, 2023, Issue 1) examining "The effectiveness of universal design for learning: A systematic review of the literature and meta-analysis." The article was authored by Qais I. Almeqdad, Ali M. Alodat, Mahmoud F. Alquraan, Mohammad A. Mohaidat, and Alaa K. Al-Makhzoomy from Yarmouk University (Jordan) and Al Ain University (UAE). It was received January 10, 2023, accepted May 14, 2023, and published online May 29, 2023. The study has 107,775 views and 144 CrossRef citations.

The study examined the effectiveness of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) framework principles in inclusive educational settings. UDL is a philosophical framework based on cognitive neuroscience research, organized by the Center for Applied Special Technology (CAST) into three main principles: Representation (aligning with recognition networks, the "what" of learning), Action and Expression (aligning with strategic networks, the "how"), and Engagement (aligning with affective networks, the "why"). CAST includes nine guidelines and 31 checkpoints under these principles.

METHODOLOGY: The authors used the PRISMA-P checklist and searched seven databases (ERIC, ProQuest, Science Direct, Directory of Open Access Journals, PsychInfo, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost) in both English and Arabic. The initial search identified over 26,000 potential records (about 22,000 were removed as duplicates, no full text, irrelevant, or other languages). An additional search identified 925 more studies, plus 10 from snowballing methods. After screening, 3,114 studies were identified, 304 advanced to final screening, and ultimately 13 studies met all inclusion criteria (empirical, peer-reviewed, English/Arabic, published 2015-2021, K-12 through university level, with pre-post test designs). Of these, 10 were one-group pre-post design studies and 3 were experimental-control two-group design studies (yielding 39 total effect sizes calculated using the metafor R package).

KEY FINDINGS: Descriptive findings showed the studies were conducted across 6 countries: 8 in the USA, 1 in Canada, 2 in Saudi Arabia, 1 in Malaysia, and 1 in Turkey. No experimental studies were found in Europe, Africa, or Australia. Eight studies investigated teachers' implementation of UDL, and studies targeted either K-12 or higher education levels, generally implementing all UDL principles through professional development programs or school interventions, mostly using one-group quantitative research design. The meta-analysis found the total effect size across studies was 3.56 with considerable heterogeneity. Statistically significant effect sizes were found for one-group studies, student participants, specific domains, and quantitative research designs.

CONCLUSION: The findings suggest UDL can improve student learning, especially in particular domains and when applied through professional development initiatives or classroom interventions, but more research is needed to ensure broad applicability. The public interest statement notes consequences for educators, decision-makers, and academics working to make schools more diverse and egalitarian.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 20: UDL as a Framework for Inclusion: Bridging Neurodiversity ... ---
URL: https://www.sencastle.com/blog/universal-design-for-learning

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post by Mateja Vukasinec (published on the SENcastle website) explores how Universal Design for Learning (UDL) serves as a framework for inclusion by bridging neurodiversity and learning through sensory-responsive design, specifically through the SENcastle multimodal device.

**UDL Overview:** UDL is an evidence-based educational framework developed by CAST that designs flexible learning environments enabling access and progress for all students regardless of cognitive, sensory, motor, or communication abilities. It is grounded in neuroscience and describes three key learning networks: affective (why we learn), recognition (what we learn), and strategic (how we learn). The latest UDL guidelines (version 3.0, 2024) emphasize removing learning barriers using flexible methods and technologies.

**UDL's Three Principles:**
1. Multiple means of engagement (motivation, choice, relevance, adjusted challenges)
2. Multiple means of representation (content access through visual, auditory, and tactile modalities)
3. Multiple means of action and expression (students demonstrate knowledge in different ways via assistive technology and alternative communication)

**Evidence of Effectiveness:** Guo and Wang (2025) report a 37.4% increase in academic achievement in high-UDL-implementation environments, with greatest benefits for students with lower baseline engagement. UDL is effective in improving academic, social, and behavioral outcomes for learners with intellectual and developmental disabilities, especially when digital and multisensory tools are used consistently (AlRawi and AlKahtani, 2021).

**SENcastle System:** SENcastle is a multimodal device developed with therapists providing controlled, adaptable input to five sensory systems: visual, auditory, tactile, proprioceptive, and vestibular. Features include adjustable-color light elements, message/sound recording and playback, vibratory and proprioceptive components, and customizable sensory scenes. It is particularly suitable for children with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and sensory integration difficulties.

**UDL-SENcastle Alignment:** 
- Supports multiple means of representation through combined visual, auditory, and tactile stimuli with adjustable intensity
- Enhances engagement through tailored, predictable, motivating sensory activities, flexible breaks, proprioceptive deep input, and calming scenes (beneficial for ADHD and autism learners)
- Enables action and expression through touch, movement, cause-and-effect interactions; SENcastle Access model supports wheelchair users with switch and eye-gaze control

**Future Outlook:** Integration of UDL and SENcastle represents a modern inclusive approach where sensory-educational tools become standard for all learners, not exclusively those with disabilities, promoting equitable education and reducing stigma. Further longitudinal research is needed, though existing evidence strongly supports SENcastle's role in implementing UDL principles.
</summary>
