--- SOURCE 6: 早期介入丹佛模式的密集训练结合家长培训对孤独症谱系障碍儿童疗效及其对父母育儿压力的影响 ---
URL: https://www.zgddek.com/CN/abstract/html/2020-2-158.htm

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in the Chinese Journal of Contemporary Pediatrics (2020, Vol. 22, Issue 2, pp. 158-163, DOI: 10.7499/j.issn.1008-8830.2020.02.014) from the Department of Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics, First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China. The study investigated whether Early Start Denver Model (ESDM)-based parental training combined with intensive training improves outcomes for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and reduces parenting stress, compared to ESDM intensive training alone.

**Objective:** To explore the effect of ESDM-based parental training combined with intensive training on children with ASD aged 2-5 years and its impact on parenting stress.

**Methodology:** Seventy children aged 2-5 years diagnosed with ASD (August 2018-January 2019) were randomly divided into two groups (35 each): an ESDM group receiving only ESDM intensive training (2 hours/day, 6 days/week for 3 months), and a parental training group receiving the same ESDM intensive training plus 10 weekly parental skill training sessions (1 per week, 3.5 hours each) comprising theoretical instruction and home video review/coaching. Four participants dropped out, leaving 33 per group. Assessments using Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), and Parenting Stress Index-Short Form (PSI-SF) were conducted before and after 3 months of intervention.

**Key Results:**
- Both groups showed significant improvements in core ASD symptoms: ABC, CARS, and ATEC total scores decreased significantly after 3 months in both groups (P < 0.001). No significant between-group differences were found in these scores before or after treatment, nor in the magnitude of change between groups.
- Both groups showed reduced total PSI-SF parenting stress scores (P < 0.05). However, improvements differed: the ESDM group showed reduction only in the "difficult child" sub-scale, while the parental training group showed significant reductions across all three sub-scales (parent distress, parent-child dysfunctional interaction, and difficult child).
- The parental training group showed significantly larger changes in total PSI-SF score and in the parent distress and difficult child sub-scales compared to the ESDM group (P < 0.05), demonstrating the parental training group had significantly more relief of parenting stress.
- No significant differences were found between groups for the parent-child dysfunctional interaction sub-scale change (P > 0.05).

**Conclusions:** Both ESDM intensive training combined with parental training and ESDM intensive training alone can improve core symptoms in children with ASD aged 2-5 years and relieve parenting stress. However, ESDM intensive training combined with parental training was significantly more effective in relieving parenting stress, particularly in the domains of parent distress and difficult child. The authors suggest parental training helps parents acquire interaction skills, gain more emotional feedback and confidence, and better manage challenging behaviors. The study was funded by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (81973054), the Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Program (2016YFC1306204), and the First Hospital of Jilin University Translational Fund (JDYYZH-1902034). Limitations noted include small sample size, short intervention duration, and lack of formal assessment of home intervention content implemented by parents.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"ESDM密集训练结合家长培训及单纯ESDM密集训练均可改善2~5岁ASD儿童的核心症状，同时缓解父母育儿压力；但ESDM密集训练结合家长培训对缓解父母育儿压力的效果更为显著。" (Both ESDM intensive training combined with parental training and ESDM intensive training alone can improve core symptoms of 2-5 year old ASD children and relieve parenting stress; however, the former is more effective in relieving parenting stress.)

--- SOURCE 7: Preliminary application of Early Start Denver Model in children with autism spectrum disorder - PMC ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7389043

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed scientific article published in the Chinese Journal of Contemporary Pediatrics (中国当代儿科杂志) on October 25, 2018 (DOI: 10.7499/j.issn.1008-8830.2018.10.002), authored by Hong-Hua LI and colleagues from the Department of Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics, First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun, China. The article is in Chinese with an English abstract, reporting a preliminary application study of the Early Start Denver Model (ESDM) in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).

**Background:** ASD is a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by social communication deficits, restricted interests, and repetitive behaviors, with prevalence reaching 1/68 in the US. ESDM is a comprehensive intensive intervention model developed by Rogers and Dawson in 2010 for children aged 1-3 years (extendable to 4-5 years). It is based on normal social-communication development patterns, is child-centered, emphasizes caregiver-child relationships, and uses play-based learning strategies.

**Methods:** Forty children aged 2-5 years diagnosed with ASD (per DSM-5 criteria, confirmed by ADOS) from September 2017 to January 2018 were enrolled and randomly divided into a conventional intervention group (n=20) and ESDM intervention group (n=20). Due to attrition (5 dropouts), the final samples were 18 (conventional; 15 boys, 3 girls; mean age 39±11 months) and 17 (ESDM; 14 boys, 3 girls; mean age 38±11 months). The conventional group received language training, cognitive training, occupational therapy, and sensory integration training (6 days/week, 4 sessions of 30 min daily). The ESDM group received ESDM-delivered interventions (6 days/week, 1 session of 2 hours daily) focusing on joint attention, language, social, cognitive, and motor skills through interest-led play. Both groups received 2 hours of daily home intervention. Assessments used the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (ABC), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Clinical Global Impression-Severity (CGI-S), and CGI-Improvement (CGI-I).

**Key Results:**
- After 3 months, both groups showed significantly decreased total ABC and CARS scores (P<0.01)
- The conventional group significantly improved on ABC social withdrawal and hyperactivity subscales (P<0.01)
- The ESDM group significantly improved on 4 ABC subscales (mood swings, social withdrawal, hyperactivity, and stereotyped behavior) (P<0.01)
- The ESDM group showed significantly greater improvements in ABC total score, 3 ABC subscales (mood swings, social withdrawal, hyperactivity), and CARS total score compared with the conventional group (P<0.05)
- CGI-I showed significantly better overall improvement in the ESDM group (65% "significant improvement" vs 28% in conventional group; P=0.035)

**Conclusions:** Both conventional and ESDM interventions improve social withdrawal and hyperactivity in ASD children aged 2-5 years, but ESDM is significantly more effective in improving aberrant behaviors, particularly emotional instability and social withdrawal. The authors note limitations including short intervention duration, small sample size, baseline differences in some ABC subscales, and lack of standardization of home interventions. The study was funded by the Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Program (2016YFC1306204) and Jilin Provincial Education Department projects. The authors recommend larger-sample, longer-term follow-up studies to further validate ESDM effectiveness for Chinese children with ASD.
</summary>

"Early intervention... Both conventional intervention and ESDM intervention can improve the social withdrawal and hyperactivity in children with ASD aged 2 to 5 years, but ESDM is more effective in improving the aberrant behavior of children with ASD." (English abstract conclusion)

--- SOURCE 15: Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions: Empirically Validated Treatments for Autism Spectrum Disorder ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4513196

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a scientific article from the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (2015) titled "Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions: Empirically Validated Treatments for Autism Spectrum Disorder." The article, authored by Laura Schreibman, Geraldine Dawson, Aubyn C. Stahmer, Rebecca Landa, Sally J. Rogers, Gail G. McGee, Connie Kasari, Brooke Ingersoll, Ann P. Kaiser, Yvonne Bruinsma, Erin McNerney, Amy Wetherby, and Alycia Halladay, discusses NDBIs as empirically supported autism interventions that merge applied behavioral and developmental sciences.

Key points:
- NDBIs are implemented in natural settings, involve shared control between child and therapist, utilize natural contingencies, and use behavioral strategies to teach developmentally appropriate skills.
- Historical context: Prior to the 1960s, many believed children with ASD were unlikely to respond to treatment. Early work by Ferster and DeMyer (1961-62) demonstrated children with autism could acquire skills via operant discrimination. Ivar Lovaas's 1987 autism treatment study showed significant IQ gains and success in typical school placements for nearly half of treated children with up to 25-40 hours per week of intervention.
- Lovaas's study led to two trends: increased parental advocacy for early intensive behavioral intervention (resulting in educational policy and insurance reform), and increased popularity of discrete trial training (DTT).
- DTT limitations included failure to generalize skills, escape/avoidance behaviors, lack of spontaneity, and overdependence on prompts.
- Developmental principles from Piaget, Bruner, Vygotsky, Snow, and Gibson informed NDBIs, emphasizing active participation, developmentally appropriate learning, meaningful contexts, and the "zone of proximal development."
- NDBIs emerged from efforts to improve DTT effectiveness through natural rewards, child-preferred materials, reinforcement of approximations, and naturalistic contexts.
- Core components of NDBIs: (1) nature of intervention targets (integrating skills across developmental domains, focusing on precursors like joint attention and imitation), (2) nature of learning contexts (emotionally meaningful social interactions, natural contingencies), and (3) nature of development-enhancing strategies (modeling, shaping, chaining, prompting, differential reinforcement).
- Examples of NDBIs include Incidental Teaching (IT), Pivotal Response Training (PRT), Early Start Denver Model (ESDM), Enhanced Milieu Teaching (EMT), Reciprocal Imitation Training (RIT), Project ImPACT, JASPER, SCERTS, and Early Achievements.
- Common features include: basis in ABA principles with a three-part contingency (antecedent-response-consequence), manualized practices, and fidelity of implementation criteria.
- No large-scale RCTs have compared DTT versus NDBI or two different NDBIs, though such trials are underway. The article notes DTT remains appropriate for certain skills and some children may learn better with structured approaches.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Teachers’ Familiarity, Confidence, Training, and Use of Problem Behavior Interventions for Learners with Autism Spectrum Disorder in School Settings ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9638298

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article published in the Journal of Developmental and Physical Disabilities (Nov 4, 2022; DOI: 10.1007/s10882-022-09885-2) examining special education teachers' familiarity, confidence, training, and use of problem behavior interventions for learners with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in school settings. Authors: Laura C. Chezan (Old Dominion University), Meka N. McCammon (University of South Florida), Katie Wolfe and Erik Drasgow (University of South Carolina), and Lucia M. Tabacu (Old Dominion University). PMCID: PMC9638298, PMID: 36373127.

METHOD: 80 special education teachers (from a pool of 191 who accessed the survey) from South Carolina and Virginia completed a 44-question survey covering six sections: behavioral assessment, antecedent-based interventions, instruction-based interventions, reinforcement-based interventions and extinction, punishment-based interventions, and demographics. A total of 35 assessments/interventions were rated. Most participants were female (88.75%), White Non-Hispanic (76.25%), held master's degrees (56.25%), had more than 10 years of experience (55%), and 80% had taken behavior-analytic courses. Data analysis used descriptive statistics, Spearman rank-order correlations, Wald-Type Statistics (WTS), and thematic analysis.

KEY RESULTS:
- The four highest-ranked interventions in familiarity, confidence, and use were prompting, modeling, direct instruction, and providing choices.
- Positive significant correlations were found: familiarity-confidence (φ=0.980), familiarity-use (φ=0.838), training-familiarity (φ=0.902), training-confidence (φ=0.914), and training-use (φ=0.861), all p<0.001.
- No significant group differences based on education or graduation year; however, teachers with 3 or fewer years of experience reported significantly lower familiarity and confidence than teachers with 4-10 years and 11+ years of experience.
- Descriptive FBA had the highest familiarity (91.25%), confidence (80%), use (32.5%), and training (61.25%) in behavioral assessment, yet FA was rarely used (20%) despite 75% familiarity.
- Punishment-based interventions had low use rankings (RIRD highest at 43.75% use; positive practice overcorrection lowest at 28.75%).
- Mand training received the lowest rankings for familiarity (76.25%), confidence (32%), training (51.25%), and use (37.5%) in instructional-based interventions.

QUALITATIVE FINDINGS: Five main themes identified as barriers limiting use of interventions: expertise (lack of knowledge/training), resources (limited material/human resources, competing responsibilities, time), relationships (lack of communication/support from families), prioritization (based on severity of behavior, e.g., dangerous behaviors prioritized), and implementation (inconsistent implementation across staff, fidelity issues).

DISCUSSION/CONCLUSIONS: Training increases familiarity and confidence, which leads to more frequent use, highlighting the need for teacher preparation programs and professional development. The low use of FBA is concerning given evidence that assessment-driven interventions are more effective. The low use of punishment-based interventions is encouraging given ethical concerns. The authors recommend future research with larger, more diverse samples.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Data revealed positive and significant correlations between familiarity, confidence, and use of problem behavior interventions suggesting that when teachers are more familiar with problem behavior interventions, they are more confident in implementing these interventions (φ = 0.980, p< 0.001***), and more likely to use them frequently in their classrooms (φ = 0.838, p< 0.001***).", "Overall, teachers with 3 or less years of experience rated their familiarity and confidence in using problem behavior interventions significantly lower than teachers with 4 to 10 years of experience and teachers with 11 or more years of experience.", "Many teachers need more training on why and how behavioral assessments are used. Some do not understand the purpose.", "A large body of empirical evidence has documented that problem behavior interventions derived from assessment data are more effective than problem behavior interventions that are not data-based driven when addressing problem behavior in learners with disabilities", "Because of the side effects associated with the use of punishment, such as emotional and aggressive reactions, and escape and avoidance, and their long-lasting effect and possible psychological harm for the learner, it is recommended that teachers and other school professionals consider first reinforcement-based interventions prior to using punishment (Cooper et al., 2020)."

--- SOURCE 3: Antecedent Interventions in ABA: Complete Guide (2026) | CertifyndABA ---
URL: https://certifyndaba.com/blog/clinical-skills/antecedent-interventions-aba-guide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from CertifyndABA is a comprehensive guide to antecedent interventions in Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA). Antecedent-based interventions (ABIs) are proactive strategies that modify events, environments, and motivating operations preceding a behavior to prevent challenging behavior and promote appropriate responses. They are classified as an established evidence-based practice for individuals aged 0-22 by the AFIRM program at UNC-Chapel Hill and are codified in Section D of the BACB's RBT Task List.

**Two Categories of ABIs:**
- Contingency-dependent: Require learner response before reinforcement (prompting, modeling, high-probability sequences); best for skill acquisition
- Contingency-independent: Deliver reinforcer on time-based schedule regardless of behavior (noncontingent reinforcement, scheduled breaks, environmental enrichment); best for safety-critical behavior reduction

**The 8 Core Antecedent Interventions:**
1. Noncontingent Reinforcement (NCR) – reinforcers delivered on fixed/variable schedules regardless of behavior
2. High-Probability Request Sequence (Behavioral Momentum) – 3-5 easy requests before the difficult target
3. Environmental Modifications – layout, lighting, noise, sensory adjustments
4. Visual Supports – first-then boards, schedules, token boards, social stories
5. Priming – advance preview of tasks/transitions
6. Choice-Making – offering 2-3 acceptable options
7. Demand and Task Modification – task interspersal, demand fading, task chunking
8. Errorless Learning and Antecedent Prompting – prompts delivered early and systematically faded (most-to-least, time delay)

**Function-first matching:** ABIs must be matched to FBA-identified behavioral functions: attention-maintained (NCR with attention), escape-maintained (demand fading, choice-making, high-p sequence), tangible-maintained (NCR with preferred item), and automatic/sensory (environmental enrichment). The Competing Behavior Pathway model (O'Neill et al., 1997) formalizes this approach.

**6-Step Implementation Process:** (1) Complete/review FBA, (2) Select 1-2 function-matched ABIs, (3) Operationalize in BIP, (4) Train implementers via behavioral skills training, (5) Collect baseline and ongoing data, (6) Evaluate and adjust with visual analysis after 2-3 weeks.

**Data standards:** Event/frequency, duration, latency, and ABC narrative recording plus treatment fidelity checklists. Minimum 80% treatment fidelity and interobserver agreement benchmarks are standard.

**Ethical considerations (BACB Ethics Code 2022):** Code 2.14 requires selecting evidence-based interventions minimizing risk; Code 2.15 requires continual evaluation and fading interventions. Cultural responsiveness, learner assent, and dignity are emphasized.

ABIs work best when combined with differential reinforcement (DRA/DRI/DRO), extinction (reducing extinction burst intensity), and skill acquisition programs. Well-matched ABIs often produce observable change within 5-10 sessions at high fidelity; contingency-independent strategies like NCR can show effects within the first session. Common mistakes include selecting ABIs without an FBA, overusing visual supports, failing to fade NCR schedules, skipping implementer training, ignoring setting events, and treating ABIs as permanent accommodations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The most powerful behavior change in ABA often happens before the behavior occurs, not after it."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: Antecedent-Based Interventions - Evidence-Based Practices ---
URL: https://docs.autismspeaks.org/evidence-based-practices/antecedent-based-interventions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage provides an overview of Antecedent-Based Interventions (ABIs), which are strategies that manipulate the environment prior to the occurrence of target behavior. ABIs include noncontingent reinforcement (NCR), manipulation of motivating events, antecedent exercise, environmental enrichment, high-probability sequences/behavioral momentum, stimulus control strategies, and demand/stimulus fading.

Key sections covered:

1. **Intervention type**: ABIs can be used as standalone treatments or as components in larger treatment packages. For example, NCR can be used alone to treat attention-maintained behavior, while demand fading can be part of a larger package combining antecedent intervention with differential reinforcement.

2. **Behavioral mechanisms**: Two likely mechanisms explain ABI effects — motivating operations (MOs), which impact reinforcer value by increasing (establishing) or decreasing (abolishing) it (most antecedent interventions decrease reinforcer value), and stimulus control, where specific stimuli are paired with consequences to gain discriminative control (requiring consequence-based procedures during pairing, but functioning as antecedent interventions afterward).

3. **Severity and function considerations**: ABIs fall into two categories — default interventions (not reliant on identifying maintaining variables, e.g., environmental enrichment) and function-based interventions (rely on identifying the functional reinforcer, e.g., NCR). They can be used for all behavioral functions and are good options for very severe behaviors, especially when extinction is not safe or feasible.

4. **Caregiver, context, and practical considerations**: Antecedent interventions are easy to implement across various settings and caregivers, work well when consequence-based interventions (like extinction) are not possible, combine well with other components such as differential reinforcement, and can increase the likelihood of individuals contacting differential reinforcement.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Antecedent-Based Interventions are strategies that manipulate the environment prior to the occurrence of the target behavior and include treatments such as: noncontingent reinforcement (NCR), manipulation of motivating events, antecedent exercise, environmental enrichment, high-probability sequences/behavioral momentum, stimulus control strategies, demand/stimulus fading.
</key_excerpts>

URL: https://caltan.info/resources/documents/antecedent-based-intervention-ebp-for-asd-brief-packet-ma-final.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is an evidence-based practice brief packet on Antecedent-based Intervention (ABI) for learners with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), developed by the National Professional Development Center on ASD at the University of North Carolina's FPG Child Development Center (2016).

**What is ABI?** Derived from applied behavior analysis, ABI addresses both interfering behaviors (e.g., repetitive, disruptive) and on-task behaviors (e.g., engagement in tasks). ABI focuses on identifying events that occur immediately before (antecedents) and after (consequences) an identified interfering behavior. **List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

The researcher conducted three rounds of Tavily web searches:

**Round 1 (3 queries, parallel):**
1. "TEACCH structured teaching model autism effectiveness research evidence Journal of Autism Developmental Disorders"
2. "TEACCH 结构化教学 自闭症谱系障碍 中国特殊教育 效果"
3. "visual schedules social stories autism evidence-based practice NPDC National Standards Project"

**Round 2 (3 queries, parallel):**
1. "中国特殊教育 孤独症 结构化教学 TEACCH 期刊论文 效果 2020"
2. "自然发展行为干预 NDBI 孤独症 早期介入丹佛模式 ESDM 循证 中国"
3. "naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions autism evidence Schreibman 2015 review ESDM Dawson randomized"

**Round 3 (3 queries, parallel):**
1. "antecedent-based interventions autism evidence review Kern Clemens classroom behavior modification task interspersal"
2. "social stories autism evidence review randomized controlled trial 2020 2021 effectiveness"
3. "TEACCH 结构化教学 应用研究 孤独症 小学 期刊 知网"

**Note:** Round 3 returned no results (all three queries produced empty search returns). Therefore, no sources were gathered specifically on antecedent-based interventions, task modification, or recent social stories RCTs; the researcher's findings on these topics come only from sources surfaced in Rounds 1 and 2 (e.g., NCAEP 28-EBP list, NDBI literature, TEACCH reviews).

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children) Model

### 1.1 Model Description and History

- TEACCH stands for "Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children." It is a structured form of visual learning specifically designed for children with autism spectrum disorder. It was developed at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill by Drs. Robert Reichler and Eric Schopler in the 1960s (developed 1966–1972) [2][4].
- TEACCH is described as one of the three most influential autism intervention methods alongside ABA and DIR/Floortime, with its core advantage being that it does not require high-level language skills or intensive one-on-one teaching—instead using environmental design and visual supports to help children with autism complete tasks independently [6].
- The method is based on the "culture of autism" concept—understanding autism as a different way of thinking—and is built on five principles: understanding the culture of autism, collaborative partnership with families (parents as co-therapists), individualization, visual structure and predictability, and a developmental perspective [4].
- TEACCH combines diagnosis, assessment, early education, school education, family education, and vocational training with the goal of promoting independent living for autistic children. It leverages the visual strengths of autistic children by organizing the educational environment and training procedures to improve comprehension, communication, perception, and motor skills [10].
- TEACCH is effective across all autism severity levels and can be tailored to individual needs, complementing other therapies like speech therapy. It applies to individuals of varying ages and skill levels, emphasizing individualized instruction. Implementation involves a multidisciplinary team including psychologists, special education teachers, speech therapists, social workers, and residential care providers. Certification is available through the TEACCH Autism Program in North Carolina, offering two levels: Practitioner and Advanced Consultant [2].
- More than 50 countries use TEACCH methods per a 2024 report from UNC's TEACCH program center [6].
- Two assessment tools are associated with the model: the Psychoeducational Profile (PEP-3) and the TEACCH Transition Assessment Profile (T-TAP, for adolescents and adults). Before receiving an individualized education plan (IEP), children undergo PEP assessment, and programs are designed based on results given the developmental delays and imbalances typical of autism [10].
- TEACCH can be combined synergistically with ABA, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and social skills interventions, with approximately 78% of school-based autism programs using TEACCH alongside other practices [4]. The Chinese source 恩启 notes "TEACCH不是ABA的替代品，而是ABA技能泛化的关键桥梁" (TEACCH is not a substitute for ABA, but a key bridge for generalization of ABA skills), addressing generalization problems often seen in ABA—many children who perform well in ABA teaching settings "cannot do it" once they leave the teaching environment [6].
- A comparison study (Khafaie, 2016) in Iran found TEACCH more effective than Sensory Integration Therapy (SIT); a study by Callahan et al. (2010) found no clear provider preference between ABA and TEACCH models; while some studies suggest ABA may be more effective, TEACCH provides comparable outcomes, especially in natural settings [1].

### 1.2 TEACCH Evidence Base

**Virues-Ortega et al. (2013) meta-analysis (Clinical Psychology Review)** [5]:
- Peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Clinical Psychology Review (Volume 33, Issue 8, December 2013, pages 940–953, DOI: 10.1016/j.cpr.2013.07.005) by Javier Virues-Ortega, Flávia M. Julio, and Roberto Pastor-Barriuso.
- Used inverse-variance weighted random effects meta-analysis, supplemented with quality assessment, sensitivity analysis, meta-regression, and heterogeneity and publication bias tests.
- Included 13 studies involving 172 individuals with autism exposed to TEACCH.
- **Findings:** TEACCH effects on perceptual, motor, verbal, and cognitive skills were of small magnitude. Effects on adaptive behavioral repertoires (communication, activities of daily living, motor functioning) were in the negligible-to-small range. However, there were moderate to large gains in social behavior and maladaptive behavior.
- Effects were NOT moderated by intervention duration (total weeks), intensity (hours per week), or setting (home-based vs. center-based).
- Conclusion: "limited support for the TEACCH program as a comprehensive intervention for autism," with results considered exploratory due to the limited pool of studies. Cited 178 times.

**Pastor-Cerezuela (2018) review study** [1]:
- Review of 14 studies evaluating TEACCH effectiveness for children with ASD (DOI: 10.23923/PAP.PSICOL2018.2851).
- All 14 reviewed studies reported developmental improvements following TEACCH intervention; 11 of 14 demonstrated statistically significant improvements in child development metrics.
- 5 of 7 studies assessing stress found significant reductions in stress for parents and teachers.
- Interventions varied in duration from 5 sessions to 3 years; sessions ranged from 30 minutes to 7 hours per day; implemented by parents or teachers in home and/or school contexts.
- Methodological limitations identified: shortage of RCTs, small sample sizes, variability complicating generalization. Future research recommended with larger samples including ASD severity and comorbid disorders.
- A meta-analysis cited within this review (Virues-Ortega et al., 2013) found TEACCH had small effects on perceptual, motor, verbal, and cognitive skills.

**Chinese-language meta-analysis (Taiwan) — 郝佳華 & 吳裕益 (2023)** [8]:
- Title: 《結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析》(A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Structured Teaching on Cognition and Behavior of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder), published in 《中華民國特殊教育學會年刊》(Journal of the Special Education Association of the Republic of China), 112年度 (2023), pages 269–298.
- Collected 103 studies from two online databases (「全國博碩士論文知識加值系統」National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations, and 「華藝線上圖書館」Airiti Library) using keywords "結構化教學" (structured teaching), "TEACCH," and "視覺提示策略" (visual cue strategies); 14 and 89 studies respectively.
- After filtering for single-case research design with ASD students as subjects, 8 studies met criteria (7 theses, 1 from Airiti), covering 19 individual cases.
- **Key results:** 15 of the intervention effect sizes (78.95%) reached a large effect size level. Weighted average effect size (Tau-U) was .81 under both fixed-effect and random-effect models, classified as a "medium" effect size. Medium-to-large effects across educational stages and on both cognition/skills and behavior, with greater effects from longer intervention times. Insufficient evidence that the four moderator variables significantly moderate intervention effectiveness.
- Over nearly 20 years, only 8 single-case studies applying this teaching method to autism were found, indicating a lack of research. Intervention topics mostly focused on improving cognitive skills (73.68%); intervention duration was mostly 12 weeks (2–3 hours/week); only 2 studies fully used all five structured teaching elements; most researchers used visual cue strategies or teaching materials.

**Chinese doctoral dissertation (Taiwan) — 倪志琳 (1999)** [17]:
- 《結構教學法對學齡前自閉症兒童學習成效之研究》(The Effects of TEACCH Structure Teaching Strategies to the Learning Outcome of Preschool Children with Autism), doctoral dissertation, National Taiwan Normal University, Special Education Research Institute, advisors 宋維村 (Soong Wei-Tsuen) and 林幸台 (Lin Hsin-Tai), 246 pages, permanent URL: https://hdl.handle.net/11296/3sk99c; cited 60 times.
- Single-subject multiple probe design; four children from the Hong-Ai early intervention program; instruments included Chinese Child Developmental Inventory (CCDI) and PsychoEducational Profile Revised (PEP-R), supplemented by parent/teacher questionnaires and interviews.
- **Results:** (1) All four children showed overall developmental progress on CCDI and PEP-R; rate-of-change indicators exceeded 1.0, showing faster development during intervention than before; children performed better in comprehension-conceptual, situation comprehension, cognitive performance, and imitation than in expressive language and cognitive verbal areas. (2) Except for one child who did not master an imitation goal, all children achieved their individual learning goals and showed maintenance during follow-up; children with lower developmental quotients required longer teaching periods. (3) Parents reported positive effects on parenting attitudes, methods, and emotional adjustment; teachers found structure teaching beneficial. (4) The Hong-Ai early intervention program was validated against Powers' (1992) eight essential components of early intervention for autism (structured behavioral treatment, parent involvement, early initiation, intensive treatment, generalization planning, social/communication skill development, trained and supervised staff, integration with typically developing children).

**Additional evidence claims from lay/clinical sources:**
- A 2022 meta-analysis in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (cited by 恩启) reportedly showed children receiving TEACCH improved independent task completion by 34% [6]. *(Note: this specific meta-analysis was not independently located in the search results; reported via the Chinese source.)*
- A 2018 Autism CRC report documents significant improvements in cognition, motor skills, and social competencies; over 150 peer-reviewed studies document the benefits of structured teaching [3].
- A 2018 systematic review across 28 studies (cited by Kids Club ABA) found improvements in adaptive skills and reduced challenging behaviors; a four-year longitudinal study found a 57% reduction in challenging behaviors and 64% increase in functional communication; a meta-analysis of 13 studies found structured work systems improved on-task behavior by 78% on average; a 2019 study of 45 classrooms found a 42% increase in independent task completion and 38% decrease in challenging behaviors; in home settings, structured teaching can reduce family stress by up to 30%; in vocational settings, 62% of adults with autism maintained competitive employment for over one year (vs. 29% national average); early intervention leads to a 45% greater likelihood of inclusion in general education; transition-age youth achieved 72% success in post-secondary goals (vs. 48% for traditional services); adults with TEACCH supports were 3.2 times more likely to report high life satisfaction [4]. *(Note: these statistics are reported by a commercial ABA provider blog and were not verified against primary sources in the searches.)*

### 1.3 Core Components of Structured Teaching (TEACCH)

The four fundamental components of structured teaching [3][4][9]:

1. **Physical Structure/Environment Organization (物理环境/环境结构化):** Arranged to minimize distractions with designated areas for activities; clear boundaries, minimized distractions, designated areas (e.g., dividing spaces into study/game/rest areas); creating clear zones in the teaching environment (e.g., reading area, activity area) to help children become familiar with the classroom and provide security [3][4][6][9].

2. **Visual Schedules (视觉时间表/日程表):** Outline daily routines to help children anticipate what comes next; object, picture, written schedules, and first-then boards [3][4].

3. **Work Systems (工作系统):** Step-by-step visual and physical cues guiding children through tasks; task organization, quantity indicators, completion signals. A complete visual work system answers four questions: ①What task to do? ②How much to do? ③How do I know when it's finished? ④What to do next? (做什么任务？做多少？怎么知道做完了？做完之后做什么？) [4][6].

4. **Visual Structure of Materials/Tasks (视觉结构/视觉指令):** Cues, color-coding, and pictorial guides to enhance understanding; visual instructions, organization, clarity, and completed models [3][4].

The Chinese source ALSOLIFE describes four steps of structured teaching: (1) Arrange training spaces according to different training content, with emphasis on visual cues and special placement of toys and items; (2) Establish training schedules/programs emphasizing procedural consistency; (3) Define training content including imitation, gross and fine motor skills, perception, cognition, hand-eye coordination, language comprehension and expression, self-care, social skills, and emotional regulation; (4) Use language, body posture, cues, labels, charts, and text to enhance understanding; apply behavioral reinforcement and behavior modification to reduce abnormal behaviors [10].

The Macau 展智服務協會 (citing 協康會 Heep Hong Society) outlines five core teaching principles: (1) Individualized Education Plan (IEP); (2) Structured Teaching—structured environments and activity arrangements using picture flowcharts and labels for clear guidance and predictability; (3) Visual Prompts—pictures to help autistic children understand and express ideas and aid in planning/organization; (4) Environmental Zoning—clear zones in the teaching environment (e.g., reading area, activity area); (5) Autonomy—encouraging children to actively participate and providing appropriate choice opportunities to build confidence and independence [9].

### 1.4 TEACCH vs. ABA

恩启 compares TEACCH vs. ABA across multiple dimensions: TEACCH adapts the environment to the child while ABA requires the child to adapt to environmental demands; TEACCH uses visual supports and structured independent tasks while ABA uses discrete trial training with language instruction and reinforcement. TEACCH addresses generalization problems often seen in ABA [6].

---

## 2. Visual Supports (视觉支持)

### 2.1 Definition and Rationale

- Visual supports are broadly defined as "tools presented visually that support an individual as he or she moves through the…day" (Hume, 2008), including photographs, icons, written words, objects, schedules, maps, labels, and scripts [13]. They gained popularity following Temple Grandin's 1995 book "Thinking in Pictures" [13].
- Visual supports address core ASD features (social interaction, communication, restricted interests/repetitive behaviors) and align with underlying cognitive traits: enhanced perceptual functioning ("thinking in pictures"), weak central coherence (bias toward local processing), and executive dysfunction (impairments in planning and organizing) [13].
- Visual aids supplement verbal instructions and provide lasting visual references that reduce confusion. As Leslie Broun noted, "Auditory information is transient – visual information can be fixed and permanent" [14].
- Research shows that 85% of children with autism process visual information more effectively than auditory information [4].
- Many individuals with autism process visual information more efficiently than auditory cues, making visual schedules align with their strengths [11].

### 2.2 Evidence Base for Visual Supports

- Visual supports are recognized as an evidence-based practice by the National Professional Development Center (NPDC) and schedules are deemed an established treatment by the National Autism Center's National Standards Project (NSP) [13].
- The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence & Practice (NCAEP) found visual supports to be an evidence-based practice in 2020 for individuals with ASD from 0–22 years old [11].
- The National Standards Project found visual schedules to be an established practice in 2015 for children aged 3–9 with autism [11].
- Visual supports meet NPDC criteria as evidence-based for young children with ASD, but have NOT been identified as evidence-based for the 0–2 population. The NPDC's broad definition includes maps, labels, timelines, and graphic organizers—but individual supports may not each independently qualify as evidence-based [13].
- Visual supports can attract and hold children's attention, are fairly nonintrusive, and provide concrete representation appropriate for young children. Selection should depend on developmental level and sociocultural context, with decisions made by a team including practitioners and family. Emerging use of technology (computers, handheld devices) should follow developmental guidelines and assistive technology best practices [13].
- Visual supports are often components of broader models (TEACCH, LEAP) and other focused interventions; further research is needed on young children, particularly the toddler population and pictorial scripts [13].

### 2.3 Specific Visual Supports and Their Evidence

**Environmental/learning environment organization:** Visual boundaries (colored rugs, tape, low furniture) help segment space. Three studies directly examined organized physical space with visual supports for students with ASD (Duker & Rasing 1989; Hirasawa et al. 2009; Nordquist et al. 1991—the only study with young children) [13].

**Visual Schedules:** Support transitions between activities; distinguish between-activity (visual schedules) vs. within-activity (activity schedules) support, though terms are now used interchangeably [13].

**Visual Instructions:** Interactive 2D/3D visuals during storybook reading increased engagement (Carnahan et al. 2009); product samples, picture dictionaries, jigs, and color coding increased independent activity for 7-year-olds (Mavropoulou et al. 2011) [13].

**Structured Work Systems:** TEACCH-developed visual organizational systems communicating what to do, how much work, when finished, and what to do next. Evidence-based per NPDC; studies with preschoolers and elementary students increased on-task behavior and decreased adult support (Hume & Odom 2007; Bennett et al. 2011; Mavropoulou et al. 2011) [13].

**Scripts:** Taught phrases for conversation, often with script-fading. Audiotaped scripts used with preschoolers (Betz et al. 2011); pictorial scripts increased play behavior and play-related language (Ganz & Flores 2008; Murdock & Hobbs 2011). Most appropriate for verbal children [13]. (Note: NCAEP 2020 reclassified Scripting into Visual Supports [12].)

**Social Narratives (including Social Stories):** Describe social situations with pictures/visual aids. Two comprehensive reviews (Karkhaneh et al. 2010; Test et al. 2011) concluded **insufficient evidence exists to support social stories as an evidence-based practice** [13].

### 2.4 Visual Schedules — Detailed Evidence and Implementation

**The 7 reasons visual schedules are used (Autism Classroom Resources)** [11]:
1. **Increase independence** — students navigate their day without constant adult direction; independence is a critical life skill.
2. **Prevent power struggles** — schedules make expectations objective rather than personal; "The schedule takes the personal piece out of it and makes it more objective."
3. **Provide a permanent reminder** — function like a to-do list students can check independently.
4. **Reduce anxiety** — students check their schedule instead of constantly questioning what comes next.
5. **Communicate daily routines and unexpected events** — help students prepare for transitions like going to PE or navigating a loud cafeteria.
6. **Align with visual processing strengths** — many individuals with autism process visual information more efficiently than auditory cues.
7. **Evidence-based practice** — NCAEP (2020) found visual supports evidence-based for ages 0–22; National Standards Project (2015) found visual schedules established for ages 3–9.

**Evidence from Links ABA guide** [14]:
- Visual schedules are recognized by the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice as one of 28 evidence-based practices for autism, with 31 studies reviewed and 16 meeting quality criteria.
- Research findings: improvements in academic on-task behavior (six studies met strong criteria), behavioral outcomes, and long-term benefits (seven studies reported social validity, six programmed generalization, four reported maintenance).
- Family/home implementation showed statistically significant improvements in parent-reported quality of life (t28=3.09, p=0.005) and parent-reported perception of autism-specific difficulties (t28=2.99, p=0.006).
- Visual schedules reduce anxiety and increase predictability; 1 in 36 children is now diagnosed with autism (CDC 2023); number of individuals with autism receiving IDEA services grew from 93,000 in 2001 to 803,000 in 2020 (1.6% of special education students).
- Five types of schedules: object, photograph, picture symbol, written, and digital.
- **CHECK implementation method:** Choose format, Honor needs, Establish expectations, Create consistency, Keep simple.
- Visual schedules can reduce transition anxiety by up to 65% [4].
- Common myths: the misconception that schedules promote rigidity is countered by noting even neurotypical adults use planners [11].

---

## 3. Structured Routines and Predictable Classroom Procedures

- Children with ASD experience difficulties with transitions, unpredictable routines, and sensory overload, leading to anxiety and challenging behaviors. Structure provides predictability, stability, and consistency, helping children feel secure and navigate daily activities with confidence [3].
- Studies show increased on-task behavior and reduced disruptive behaviors through predictability; structured environments promote inclusion in mainstream classrooms and benefit all students [3].
- Core principles of structured teaching: leverage the visual processing strengths common in children with ASD; establish consistent routines and clear activity sequencing; design clear, uncluttered physical environments that minimize distractions; use visual cues such as pictures, icons, and written instructions; implement individualized work systems so children can complete tasks independently; collaborate with families and caregivers to reinforce strategies outside the classroom [3].
- CinLearn classroom implementation strategies: (1) Task personalization—adapting teaching plans to each student's abilities and preferences; (2) Continuous visual support—diagrams, calendars, and activity boards; (3) Consistency and coherence—establishing predictable daily routines with regular activity, rest, and transition times; (4) Clear direct communication—concise, clear language with visual presentation of instructions; (5) Sensory-friendly environment—comfortable spaces with quiet rest areas and adaptive materials; (6) Promoting social interaction—structured activities like role-play and cooperative tasks [7].
- TEACCH improves communication skills through visual structuring for students with language difficulties; enhances social skills by providing tools to interact more effectively with peers and environment; increases autonomy/independence by focusing on functional skills (dressing, eating, time management); reduces anxiety through structured, predictable environments that create safety and comfort [7].

## 4. Evidence-Based Practices (EBP) Framework — NCAEP 2020 (Hume et al. 2021)

The third-generation systematic review of EBPs for autistic children, youth, and young adults (birth to 22), conducted by the National Clearinghouse for Autism Evidence and Practice (NCAEP) at UNC-Chapel Hill, updating Wong et al. (2015), published in the **Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders** (2021), authored by Kara Hume, Jessica R. Steinbrenner, Samuel L. Odom, and colleagues [12]:
- Included only peer-reviewed, English-language studies using behavioral, developmental, and/or educational focused intervention practices, participants aged birth to 22 diagnosed with ASD; search covered nine databases yielding 61,147 initial articles, reduced to 31,779 after deduplication; 972 acceptable articles analyzed. Both group designs (RCTs, quasi-experimental, SMART, regression discontinuity) and single case experimental designs (SCD) were included; a national panel of 221 trained reviewers conducted quality appraisals.
- **To qualify as evidence-based, a practice needed (a) two high quality group studies by two independent research groups, (b) five high quality SCD studies by three independent groups involving 20 participants, or (c) one group study plus three SCD studies by two independent groups.**
- **Twenty-eight practices met the criteria as evidence-based.** Five new EBPs were identified: **Behavior Momentum Intervention, Direct Instruction, Music-Mediated Intervention, Sensory Integration®** (the specific model developed by Jean Ayres), **and Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC)**.
- Reclassifications: PECS® merged into AAC; **Pivotal Response Training into Naturalistic Interventions; Scripting into Visual Supports**; Peer-Mediated Intervention and Structured Play Groups merged into Peer-Based Intervention and Instruction.
- Ten Manualized Interventions Meeting Criteria (MIMCs) were also identified, including Project ImPACT.
- Key data: SCD made up 83% of studies, group designs 17% (group designs increased from 9% in 1990–2011 to 23% in 2012–2017). Most studies involved preschool (43%) and elementary-aged children (57%). Of studies reporting gender, 84% male; 59% White, 10% Black, 9% Asian, 8% Hispanic/Latino. Research staff implemented interventions in 52% of studies, educators/service providers 20%, parents 10%. Educational settings hosted 48% of interventions. Communication, social, and challenging/interfering behavior were the most commonly addressed outcomes. 23 EBPs impact seven or more outcome categories; 16 impact nine or more.
- Note on methodology: "When excluding SCD research, researchers are ignoring the admonition by Sackett et al. (1996): '… if no randomised trial has been carried out for our patient's predicament, we must follow the trail to the next best external evidence and work from there (p. 72).'"
- Notably, "Sensory Integration® refers explicitly to the therapy model developed by Jean Ayres (2005) and not to a variety of interventions that address sensory issues but have been found to be unsupported" [12].

**National Autism Center National Standards Project, Phase 2 (April 2015)** [15]:
- Systematic review of ASD interventions updating the 2009 National Standards Report, reviewing studies published 2007–February 2012 for children and youth under 22, and the first-ever systematic evaluation of interventions for adults (22+). For adults, only 27 studies met inclusion criteria, resulting in just one Established and one Emerging intervention for adults.
- Reinforced Phase 1 findings showing even more empirical support for behaviorally based interventions for children and adolescents under 22.
- Used the Scientific Merit Rating Scale (SMRS), Intervention Effects Ratings, and Strength of Evidence Classification System. Combining NSP1 and NSP2 produced the largest compilation of studies ever reviewed.
- The NSP (Phases 1 and 2) is among seven nationally recognized systematic reviews of ASD interventions. Notably, the NPDC and CMS (which used NSP's classification system) included single-subject research and reached similar findings, while the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality did not include most single-subject studies.

## 5. Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions (NDBI)

### 5.1 Definition and Core Components

- NDBIs "are implemented in natural settings, involve shared control between child and therapist, utilize natural contingencies, and use a variety of behavioral strategies to teach developmentally appropriate and prerequisite skills" (Schreibman et al., 2015, Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders) [28].
- NDBIs fuse the teaching principles of applied behavior analysis (ABA) with a developmental, relationship-based approach appropriate for very young children with ASD. Hallmarks include intervention delivered in settings typical of early childhood, incorporation of child choice and following the child's motivation, and use of behavioral teaching principles [27].
- Historical context: Prior to the 1960s, many believed children with ASD were unlikely to respond to treatment. Early work by Ferster and DeMyer (1961–62) demonstrated children with autism could acquire skills via operant discrimination. Ivar Lovaas's 1987 study showed significant IQ gains and success in typical school placements for nearly half of treated children with up to 25–40 hours per week of intervention. This led to increased parental advocacy for early intensive behavioral intervention and increased popularity of DTT [28].
- DTT limitations: failure to generalize skills, escape/avoidance behaviors, lack of spontaneity, and overdependence on prompts. NDBIs emerged from efforts to improve DTT effectiveness through natural rewards, child-preferred materials, reinforcement of approximations, and naturalistic contexts [28].
- Core components: (1) nature of intervention targets (integrating skills across developmental domains, focusing on precursors like joint attention and imitation); (2) nature of learning contexts (emotionally meaningful social interactions, natural contingencies); (3) nature of development-enhancing strategies (modeling, shaping, chaining, prompting, differential reinforcement) [28].
- Examples of NDBIs: Incidental Teaching (IT), Pivotal Response Training (PRT), Early Start Denver Model (ESDM), Enhanced Milieu Teaching (EMT), Reciprocal Imitation Training (RIT), Project ImPACT, JASPER, SCERTS, and Early Achievements [28]. The 2024 review adds Early Social Interaction (ESI) and LEAP to the list of NDBI examples [24][26].
- Common features: basis in ABA principles with a three-part contingency (antecedent-response-consequence), manualized practices, and fidelity of implementation criteria. No large-scale RCTs have compared DTT versus NDBI or two different NDBIs. DTT remains appropriate for certain skills and some children may learn better with structured approaches [28].

### 5.2 NDBI Evidence Base

**Schreibman et al. (2015), JADD** [28]: The foundational review paper establishing NDBIs as empirically validated treatments for ASD; authored by Laura Schreibman, Geraldine Dawson, Aubyn C. Stahmer, Rebecca Landa, Sally J. Rogers, Gail G. McGee, Connie Kasari, Brooke Ingersoll, Ann P. Kaiser, Yvonne Bruinsma, Erin McNerney, Amy Wetherby, and Alycia Halladay.

**Network meta-analysis (2025), Research in Autism** [26]:
- "The effects of naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions in young children with autism spectrum disorder: A systematic review and network meta-analysis" by LI Dan, HUANG Yaping, CUI Xiaobing, BING Jiaojiao, SHEN Youhong, and YIN Huazhan (Volume 126, August 2025, Article 202656, DOI: 10.1016/j.reia.2025.202656). PROSPERO registered (CRD42024518553), PRISMA-NMA guidelines.
- 29,125 records retrieved; 41 studies met inclusion criteria; 2,781 participants (children up to 8 years old); six distinct intervention methods; efficacy assessed across five domains: receptive language, expressive language, cognitive development, reduction of ASD symptoms, and social skills.
- **Results: ESDM was identified as the most effective intervention for improving receptive language, expressive language, and cognitive development. LEAP was most likely the most effective intervention for alleviating ASD-related symptoms. ESI appeared to be the optimal intervention for enhancing social skills.**
- Background: ASD prevalence reached 2.76% among 8-year-olds by 2020 (approximately 1 in 36) per CDC; traditional DTT has limitations including limited generalizability, lack of spontaneity, excessive reliance on prompts, and negative emotional responses; NDBIs integrate behavioral and developmental strategies and are considered best practice for early ASD intervention.
- This is the first network meta-analysis of NDBIs for ASD, directly comparing multiple NDBIs rather than only comparing NDBIs to non-NDBI approaches.

**Parent-mediated NDBI systematic review (2024), Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders** [24]:
- "Parent-Mediated Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions for Young Autistic Children: A Systematic Literature Review of Single-Case Research" by Lauren van Noorden, Siobhan Gardiner, and Hannah Waddington (published March 12, 2024; open access).
- 353 articles screened; 17 single-case studies eligible (6 unpublished theses, 11 peer-reviewed articles; 27 group-design studies set aside for separate review). Studies involved 69 children (9 girls, 13.0%) aged 15–94 months, and 69 parents (15 males, 21.7%).
- Child outcome measures included engagement, joint attention, language/communication, imitation, and compliance/avoidance.
- Most studies found positive effects for at least some children on at least one measure, but no consistently positive effects across studies. Most parents increased their NDBI fidelity, but many did not reach specified fidelity criteria. Only three studies met all Council for Exceptional Children (CEC) quality indicators.
- **Conclusion: "Parent-mediated NDBIs are a promising approach to supporting young autistic children, but more high-quality research is needed."**
- Background: NDBIs are based on both behavioral and developmental principles, using behavioral teaching to integrate developmentally appropriate learning targets into daily routines. Parent inclusion in early support is considered best practice. Search covered ProQuest, ERIC, Scopus, PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science (April 12, 2023); inclusion criteria: English publications 2014–2023, children average age ≤8, majority diagnosed with autism or high-likelihood, NDBI classified per Schreibman et al. (2015), parents as sole implementers, quantitative outcomes, experimental single-case designs.

**NDBI book (2019/2020, Paul H. Brookes Publishing)** [25]:
- "Naturalistic Developmental Behavioral Interventions for Autism Spectrum Disorder" (1st ed., ISBN 168125204X/9781681252049), 464 pages, edited by Yvonne Bruinsma, Ph.D., BCBA-D; Mendy B. Minjarez, Ph.D.; Laura Schreibman, Ph.D.; and Aubyn C. Stahmer, Ph.D., BCBA-D. LCCN 2019001591.
- 17 chapters in four sections: (I) Overview (Understanding NDBI; Considering NDBI Models—ESDM, Enhanced Milieu Teaching, Incidental Teaching/Walden Toddler Program, JASPER, PRT, Project ImPACT); (II) Core Concepts and Foundational Principles (Selecting Meaningful Skills; Empowering Parents Through Parent Training and Coaching; Fostering Inclusion With Peers and in the Community); (III) NDBI Strategies (Implementing Motivational Strategies; **Applying Antecedent Strategies**; Implementing Instructional Cues and Prompting Strategies; Using Consequence Strategies; Guiding Meaningful Goal Development); (IV) Applications (Targeting Communication Skills; Improving Social Skills and Play; Supporting Behavior, Self-Regulation, and Adaptive Skills; **Implementing NDBI in Schools**; Collecting Data in NDBI; Identifying Quality Indicators of NDBI Programs; Future Directions).
- Foreword notes approximately 66,000 children are born each year in the US who will have autism; 50% of children with autism are diagnosed after age 4–5 years; children from underserved populations (minorities, low income, rural) are diagnosed later still.
- Note: This book's Section III includes "Applying Antecedent Strategies" as a core NDBI strategy chapter—relevant to the user's request on antecedent-based interventions, though no standalone ABI evidence review was located in the searches.

**Community-based NDBI program (Autism Spectrum News, 2016)** [27]:
- Center for Autism and the Developing Brain (CADB) early intervention program at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital delivers NDBIs (ESDM and Early Social Interaction/ESI) in a public community setting, free through the New York State Early Intervention Program (EIP) within a focused 6-month period.
- Components: group classroom (6 children, 6 hours/week, small and large group activities with individualized objectives embedded; multidisciplinary team; parents observe through one-way mirror); individual intervention (parents spend 3 hours/week in coaching sessions with therapist and child in clinic and home, learning to embed naturalistic teaching into daily routines like mealtimes, bath time, book reading, outdoor play); family components (weekly parent support group and psychoeducational sessions covering ASD symptoms, intervention options, visual supports, managing challenging behavior, advocacy skills).
- Pilot data show treatment effects in all child developmental domains, with the largest gains in language, play, and behavioral regulation.

### 5.3 ESDM — Chinese Research Evidence

**Chinese RCT: ESDM parental training + intensive training (2020), Chinese Journal of Contemporary Pediatrics (中国当代儿科杂志)** [19]:
- Published 2020, Vol. 22, Issue 2, pp. 158–163, DOI: 10.7499/j.issn.1008-8830.2020.02.014, from Department of Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics, First Hospital of Jilin University, Changchun.
- Seventy children aged 2–5 years with ASD (August 2018–January 2019) randomly divided into two groups (35 each): ESDM group receiving only ESDM intensive training (2 hours/day, 6 days/week for 3 months); parental training group receiving the same ESDM intensive training plus 10 weekly parental skill training sessions (1 per week, 3.5 hours each) comprising theoretical instruction and home video review/coaching. Four dropped out, leaving 33 per group. Assessments: Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), Parenting Stress Index-Short Form (PSI-SF).
- **Results:** Both groups showed significant improvements in core ASD symptoms (ABC, CARS, ATEC total scores decreased significantly after 3 months in both groups, P < 0.001); no significant between-group differences in these scores. Both groups showed reduced total PSI-SF parenting stress scores (P < 0.05). However, the ESDM group showed reduction only in the "difficult child" sub-scale, while the parental training group showed significant reductions across all three sub-scales (parent distress, parent-child dysfunctional interaction, and difficult child). The parental training group showed significantly larger changes in total PSI-SF score and in the parent distress and difficult child sub-scales compared to the ESDM group (P < 0.05).
- **Conclusions:** Both ESDM intensive training combined with parental training and ESDM intensive training alone can improve core symptoms in children with ASD aged 2–5 years and relieve parenting stress; however, ESDM combined with parental training was significantly more effective in relieving parenting stress, particularly in parent distress and difficult child domains.
- Funded by National Natural Science Foundation of China (81973054), Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Program (2016YFC1306204), First Hospital of Jilin University Translational Fund (JDYYZH-1902034).

**Chinese RCT: Preliminary application of ESDM (2018), Chinese Journal of Contemporary Pediatrics** [20]:
- Published October 25, 2018 (DOI: 10.7499/j.issn.1008-8830.2018.10.002), authored by Hong-Hua LI et al., First Hospital of Jilin University.
- Forty children aged 2–5 years diagnosed with ASD (DSM-5, confirmed by ADOS), September 2017–January 2018, randomly divided into conventional intervention group (n=20; final 18; 15 boys, 3 girls; mean age 39±11 months) and ESDM group (n=20; final 17; 14 boys, 3 girls; mean age 38±11 months).
- Conventional group: language training, cognitive training, occupational therapy, sensory integration training (6 days/week, 4 sessions of 30 min daily). ESDM group: ESDM-delivered interventions (6 days/week, 1 session of 2 hours daily) focusing on joint attention, language, social, cognitive, and motor skills through interest-led play. Both groups received 2 hours of daily home intervention. Assessments: ABC, CARS, CGI-S, CGI-I.
- **Results:** After 3 months, both groups showed significantly decreased total ABC and CARS scores (P<0.01). Conventional group significantly improved on ABC social withdrawal and hyperactivity subscales (P<0.01). ESDM group significantly improved on 4 ABC subscales (mood swings, social withdrawal, hyperactivity, stereotyped behavior) (P<0.01). ESDM group showed significantly greater improvements in ABC total score, 3 ABC subscales (mood swings, social withdrawal, hyperactivity), and CARS total score compared with conventional group (P<0.05). CGI-I showed significantly better overall improvement in ESDM group (65% "significant improvement" vs 28% in conventional group; P=0.035).
- **Conclusions:** Both conventional and ESDM interventions improve social withdrawal and hyperactivity in ASD children aged 2–5 years, but ESDM is significantly more effective in improving aberrant behaviors, particularly emotional instability and social withdrawal. Funded by Ministry of Science and Technology National Key R&D Program (2016YFC1306204) and Jilin Provincial Education Department.

## 6. Direct Instruction and Other EBPs

- **Direct Instruction** was identified as one of five new EBPs in the NCAEP 2020 review (Hume et al., 2021) [12]. No further standalone Direct Instruction studies were located in the searches.
- **Behavior Momentum Intervention** was also identified as a new EBP in the NCAEP 2020 review [12].
- **Discrete Trial Teaching (DTT)** context: A Chinese study in Acta Psychologica Sinica (2023, Vol. 55, No. 2, pp. 237–256) from Northwest Normal University, Lanzhou, investigated the effectiveness of different learning material formats on pre-service teachers' self-learning of DTT for children with ASD [16]:
  - ASD prevalence in China is 0.70% (1 in 143 children); US CDC (2021) estimates 1 in 44 children. More autistic children are entering inclusive education settings, but regular teachers generally lack knowledge of evidence-based interventions.
  - Three experiments compared real teaching videos (audio-visual dual-channel: subtitle + picture + sound), PowerPoint presentations (visual single-channel), and Word text documents (visual single-channel), all covering the same DTT content (26 teaching trials).
  - Experiment 1 (n=24): Video required fewest learning sessions (M=3.33) vs. PPT (M=4.33) vs. Word (M=5.17); F(2,23)=8.14, p=0.001. Experiment 2 (n=24): Video (M=4.17) < PPT (M=5.17) < Word (M=8.17); F(2,23)=19.09, p<0.001. Experiment 3 (n=6): Video (M=2.50) < PPT (M=3.83) < Word (M=5.67); F(2,4)=30.33, p<0.001. Fidelity improvement: video (41.70%) > PPT (30.00%) > Word (26.27%); F(2,4)=38.25, p<0.001.
  - Conclusion: Audio-visual dual-channel materials (real teaching videos) produce the best learning outcomes in both declarative knowledge and practical implementation fidelity for pre-service teachers learning DTT.

### 7.3 Chinese Clinical/Practitioner TEACCH Guidance (恩启 IngCare) [6]
- A 5-step home setup guide: observe the child's daily routine, divide functional zones, create a visual schedule, design a first task basket, and gradually increase task complexity (maintaining 70% independent/30% assistance ratio for new tasks).
- Families who consistently recorded environmental adjustment data improved independent task completion by an average of 25%.
- Age-appropriate applications: 2–4 years using physical objects; 4–7 using picture schedules; 7–12 using text-combined schedules and homework support; 12+ transitioning to self-management tools.
- Common parent mistakes: over-structuring, mismatched visual materials, neglecting completion signals, rigid schedules (at least 20% should be flexible), and failing to record data.
- FAQs: TEACCH and ABA can and should be combined; TEACCH serves all autism levels including high-functioning individuals; no expensive teaching tools are needed; results typically appear within 2–4 weeks of daily use.
- Three core principles: physical structuring (furniture placement and boundaries so children know where to do what); visual structuring (replacing auditory instructions with visual cues including schedules, work systems, and prompt cards); work systems (answering four questions: what to do, how much to do, how to know it's done, what to do next).

## 8. Evidence Strength Ranking (as derivable from located sources)

Based on the sources gathered, the following ranking by evidence strength can be constructed:

1. **NDBI (as a category)** — supported by the foundational Schreibman et al. (2015) JADD paper, the 2025 network meta-analysis (ESDM most effective for receptive/expressive language and cognitive development; LEAP for symptom reduction; ESI for social skills), two Chinese RCTs of ESDM (2018, 2020 in 中国当代儿科杂志), and a 2024 parent-mediated NDBI single-case systematic review (promising but needing more high-quality research) [24][26][28][19][20].

2. **TEACCH** — supported by one meta-analysis (Virues-Ortega et al., 2013, Clinical Psychology Review: small effects on perceptual/motor/verbal/cognitive skills; moderate-to-large gains in social and maladaptive behavior; exploratory due to limited studies), one review of 14 studies (Pastor-Cerezuela, 2018: all 14 showed developmental improvements, 11 statistically significant), and Chinese single-case meta-analytic evidence (郝佳華 & 吳裕益, 2023: Tau-U = .81, medium effect; 78.95% of effect sizes large) [5][1][8].

3. **Visual supports** — identified as an evidence-based practice by NCAEP (2020, ages 0–22) and NPDC; visual schedules established by NSP (2015, ages 3–9); 31 studies reviewed with 16 meeting quality criteria for visual schedules [11][12][13][14].

4. **Social stories/social narratives** — **insufficient evidence** per two comprehensive reviews (Karkhaneh et al., 2010; Test et al., 2011); not identified as evidence-based [13].

5. **Direct Instruction and Behavior Momentum Intervention** — newly identified as EBPs in NCAEP 2020 [12].

6. **Structured work systems** — evidence-based per NPDC; studies with preschoolers and elementary students increased on-task behavior and decreased adult support (Hume & Odom 2007; Bennett et al. 2011; Mavropoulou et al. 2011) [13].

## 9. Classroom Implementation Steps by Age/Level and Context (as gathered)

### Preschool/Early Childhood (2–6 years)
- Use physical objects for visual schedules at ages 2–4; picture schedules at ages 4–7 [6].
- Use visual boundaries (colored rugs, tape, low furniture) to segment space; the only young-children study of organized physical space is Nordquist et al. (1991) [13].
- Audiotaped scripts with preschoolers (Betz et al., 2011); pictorial scripts increased play behavior and play-related language (Ganz & Flores 2008; Murdock & Hobbs 2011) [13].
- NDBI/ESDM delivery in preschool: interest-led play focusing on joint attention, language, social, cognitive, and motor skills; parent coaching embedded in daily routines (mealtimes, bath time, book reading, outdoor play) [20][27].
- ESDM group model: 6 children, 6 hours/week in small and large group activities with individualized objectives embedded into developmentally appropriate activities (art, gym, snack, toy play); multidisciplinary team; parents observe through one-way mirror [27].
- TEACCH with preschoolers: the 倪志琳 (1999) dissertation applied TEACCH structure teaching strategies to four preschool children with positive results on CCDI and PEP-R [17].

### Elementary School (6–12 years)
- Picture schedules transitioning to text-combined schedules and homework support at ages 7–12 [6].
- Product samples, picture dictionaries, jigs, and color coding increased independent activity for 7-year-olds (Mavropoulou et al., 2011) [13].
- Visual schedules support transitions between activities and reduce anxiety; use individual vs. group schedules, first-then schedules, mini-schedules [11][14].
- Work systems communicate what to do, how much work, when finished, and what to do next; studies with elementary students increased on-task behavior and decreased adult support (Hume & Odom 2007; Bennett et al. 2011) [13].
- CHECK method for visual schedules: Choose format, Honor needs, Establish expectations, Create consistency, Keep simple [14].

### Middle/High School (12+)
- Transition to self-management tools at 12+ [6].
- TEACCH Transition Assessment Profile (T-TAP) for adolescents and adults [10].
- Vocational applications: TEACCH-based vocational training (62% of adults maintained competitive employment over one year vs. 29% national average per Kids Club ABA) [4].

### Mainstream Inclusive Classroom vs. Special Education Setting
- Structured environments promote inclusion in mainstream classrooms and benefit all students [3].
- Visual schedules can be individual or group schedules used across self-contained classrooms, inclusion classrooms, work sites, community, and home [11].
- Educational settings hosted 48% of EBP interventions in the NCAEP review; educators/service providers implemented 20% of interventions [12].
- NDBIs are implemented in natural settings typical of early childhood (home, playground, preschool) [27][28].
- TEACCH can be used in hospitals, rehabilitation centers, and home interventions [10].
- The NDBI book includes a chapter on "Implementing NDBI in Schools" [25].

You are a research supervisor. Your job is to conduct research by calling the "ConductResearch" tool. For context, today's date is Sun Aug 23, 2026.

<Task>
Your focus is to call the "ConductResearch" tool to conduct research against the overall research question passed in by the user. 
When you are completely satisfied with the research findings returned from the tool calls, then you should call the "ResearchComplete" tool to indicate that you are done with your research.
</Task>

<Available Tools>
You have access to three main tools:
1. **ConductResearch**: Delegate research tasks to specialized sub-agents
2. **ResearchComplete**: Indicate that research is complete
3. **think_tool**: For reflection and strategic planning during research

**CRITICAL: Use think_tool before calling ConductResearch to plan your approach, and after each ConductResearch to assess progress. Do not call think_tool with any other tools in parallel.**
</Available Tools>

<Instructions>
Think like a research manager with limited time and resources. Follow these steps:

1. **Read the question carefully** - What specific information does the user need?
2. **Decide how to delegate the research** - Carefully consider the question and decide how to delegate the research. Are there multiple independent directions that can be explored simultaneously?
3. **After each call to ConductResearch, pause and assess** - Do I have enough to answer? What's still missing?
</Instructions>

<Hard Limits>
**Task Delegation Budgets** (Prevent excessive delegation):
- **Bias towards single agent** - Use single agent for simplicity unless the user request has clear opportunity for parallelization
- **Stop when you can answer confidently** - Don't keep delegating research for perfection
- **Limit tool calls** - Always stop after 3 tool calls to ConductResearch and think_tool if you cannot find the right sources

**Maximum 3 parallel agents per iteration**
</Hard Limits>

<Show Your Thinking>
Before you call ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to plan your approach:
- Can the task be broken down into smaller sub-tasks?

After each ConductResearch tool call, use think_tool to analyze the results:
- What key information did I find?
- What's missing?
- Do I have enough to answer the question comprehensively?
- Should I delegate more research or call ResearchComplete?
</Show Your Thinking>

<Scaling Rules>
**Simple fact-finding, lists, and rankings** can use a single sub-agent:
- *Example*: List the top 10 coffee shops in San Francisco → Use 1 sub-agent

**Comparisons presented in the user request** can use a sub-agent for each element of the comparison:
- *Example*: Compare OpenAI vs. Anthropic vs. DeepMind approaches to AI safety → Use 3 sub-agents
- Delegate clear, distinct, non-overlapping subtopics

**Important Reminders:**
- Each ConductResearch call spawns a dedicated research agent for that specific topic
- A separate agent will write the final report - you just need to gather information
- When calling ConductResearch, provide complete standalone instructions - sub-agents can't see other agents' work
- Do NOT use acronyms or abbreviations in your research questions, be very clear and specific
</Scaling Rules>

I would like to research effective strategies to enhance classroom participation and engagement for autistic (autism spectrum disorder) students. Please identify and detail the most effective, evidence-based strategies and interventions that teachers and educators can use to increase classroom participation for students with autism. 

Specifically, please cover the following dimensions (treating each as open-ended unless otherwise specified):
1. Classroom/environmental modifications and sensory-friendly accommodations
2. Instructional strategies (e.g., visual supports, structured teaching/visual schedules, TEACCH, structured routines)
3. Inclusive education practices and peer-mediated or social-support strategies
4. Motivation and engagement techniques (e.g., special interests, choice-making, reinforcement)
5. Assistive technology and communication supports (e.g., AAC, augmentative communication)
6. Behavioral and positive reinforcement approaches
7. Collaboration with parents, para-educators, and support staff
8. Differentiated approaches for varying ages/developmental levels and for students with non-speaking or minimally verbal autism

Please organize the strategies by effectiveness where possible, cite the evidence base and research supporting each strategy, and provide practical implementation guidance for educators. Address the age/grade levels and contexts (mainstream inclusive classrooms vs. special education settings) where applicable. Prioritize academic and scientific sources—link directly to original research papers, official journal publications, and guidelines from reputable organizations (e.g., research journals on autism education, official education/special needs authorities). Since the inquiry is in Chinese, please prioritize sources published in Chinese where available, while also including authoritative English-language sources when they are the primary origin. Provide concrete, actionable strategies that can be immediately applied in classroom settings.

The user is Chinese-speaking, so prioritize Chinese-language academic sources (e.g., 《中国特殊教育》, Chinese journal articles on 自闭症谱系障碍 感统训练, 随班就读) where available, but include authoritative English sources (e.g., Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, Focus on Autism and Other Developmental Disabilities, Research in Autism Spectrum Disorders, National Autism Center / National Professional Development Center on ASD reports). Research evidence-based instructional strategies that enhance classroom participation and engagement for students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), with emphasis on structured teaching.
