**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

Four rounds of web searches were conducted via the Tavily search tool (15 queries total), covering:

1. "evidence-based practices for autism classroom environmental modifications National Professional Development Center NPDC report"
2. "classroom sensory accommodations autism spectrum disorder evidence lighting noise visual clutter"
3. "sensory integration therapy sensory diet school evidence review autism"
4. "中国特殊教育 自闭症谱系障碍 感统训练 课堂 研究 期刊"
5. "自闭症 随班就读 感觉统合训练 循证研究 环境创设 教室"
6. "fidget tools fidget spinners classroom attention evidence research autism"
7. "weighted vests autism classroom evidence research review Stephenson Carter"
8. "中国特殊教育 孤独症 课堂 环境创设 视觉支持 转衔 融合教育 研究"
9. "visual supports visual schedules autism classroom transitions evidence based practice research"
10. "flexible seating classroom choice autism on-task behavior research evidence"
11. "movement breaks physical activity classroom autism attention behavior evidence review"
12. "physical exercise intervention children autism on-task behavior classroom meta-analysis Lang Bremer evidence"
13. "Barrett Clever Classrooms sensory design study SEN students classroom physical environment learning"
14. "感统训练 自闭症 儿童 干预 研究 硕士 论文 中国 特殊教育 效果 随机"
15. "autism classroom lighting fluorescent noise reduction accommodation special education research study"

Note: One search result returned an HTTP 500 error page from the Chinese journal 《心理学报》(Acta Psychologica Sinica) website (journal.psych.ac.cn) — no usable content. A separate, valid Acta Psychologica Sinica article on Discrete Trial Teaching was retrieved and is included below.

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. Evidence-Based Practice (EBP) Frameworks and Definitions

**National Professional Development Center on ASD (NPDC) / NCAEP framework.** The NPDC's goal was to "promote the use of evidence-based practices (EBPs) for autistic children and youth, birth to 22 years of age." An EBP is defined as "an instructional/intervention procedure or set of procedures for which researchers have provided an acceptable level of research that shows the practice produces positive outcomes for autistic children, youth, and/or adults" [1]. The NPDC was funded by the Office of Special Education Programs in the US Department of Education from 2007–2014, and created resources used in its work with 12 states [2]. The NPDC (collaboration of UNC Chapel Hill, the Waisman Center at UW-Madison, and the MIND Institute at UC-Davis) established criteria for determining if an intervention is evidence-based: (1) Two high-quality experimental or quasi-experimental group design studies by at least two different researchers, OR (2) Five high-quality single-subject studies by three investigators with at least 20 total participants, OR (3) A combination: one high-quality group design study plus at least three high-quality single-subject studies by three different investigators [5]. Using rigorous criteria, the NPDC classified 27 focused interventions as EBPs in 2014; the systematic review was later updated through 2017 by the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice (NCAEP), which identified **28 evidence-based practices** in a systematic review of literature published 1990–2017 [2][3]. The NPDC created the **AFIRM (Autism Focused-Intervention Resources and Modules)** online modules for each EBP, plus virtual certification training for the Autism Program Environment Rating Scale (APERS) for preschool, elementary, middle, and high school settings [2]. "By law, teaching practices must be based on evidence of effectiveness" (IDEIA 2004; No Child Left Behind 2001 mandate educators to implement evidence-based educational programs) [3][5].

**The "Foundational Five" EBPs.** The VCU Autism Center for Education identified five practices integral to high-quality instructional environments — "The Foundational Five EBPs" — which serve as building blocks for implementing additional strategies: **antecedent-based intervention, visual supports, systematic instruction, reinforcement, and social communication instruction** [4]. The National Autism Center (offering the National Standards Report and school-based guides) and the NPDC's free AFIRM modules are flagged as key national resources; Autism Internet Modules (50 free self-paced modules) and OCALI are also listed [4].

**Implementation barriers.** A third of interventions teachers report using have limited research support. Key barriers to implementing EBPs include teacher training, administrative support, time for planning, and clear role definitions. The literature rarely describes implementation in enough detail, so the NPDC created step-by-step guidelines, checklists, and web-based modules (developed with the Ohio Center for Autism and Low Incidence Disabilities, at autisminternetmodules.org) containing evidence bases, procedural details, data collection methods, case examples, videos, and resources. Recommended steps: teachers should use NPDC modules to learn EBPs and implement them with fidelity; school leaders and teacher preparation programs should receive training; school systems must encourage professional development [5].

## 2. (a) Physical Classroom Layout and Seating Arrangements

**General classroom design evidence (whole-population).** The landmark University of Salford HEAD ("Holistic Evidence and Design") study assessed 153 classrooms across 27 UK primary schools (Blackpool, Hampshire, Ealing), involving 3,766 pupils aged 5–11. Environmental factors account for roughly 10% of total variability in pupil progress per subject (9.3% for reading, 8.4% for writing, 11.7% for math); classroom design accounts for **16% of the variation in students' academic progress** [61][62][63][7]. The three design principles were: **Naturalness** (light, temperature, air quality, links-to-nature), **Individualization** (ownership, flexibility, connection), and **Level of Stimulation** (complexity, color). Light and Flexibility were significant across all three subjects; Flexibility had a particularly strong correlation with math progress (coefficient = 0.197); "corridor libraries" were associated with significantly higher reading progress (4.18 vs. 3.90 NC points); Links-to-Nature was significant only for writing. Color and Complexity were curvilinear — mid-levels of visual stimulation were optimal, while overly sparse or overly cluttered rooms scored poorly [62][63]. The Clever Classrooms project confirms "differences in the physical design of a classroom explain 16% of the variation in the learning" [60]. Research also shows: assigned seating can forge new friendships while separating close friends reduces disruptions by up to 70%; the best arrangement matches the learning task (clusters for collaboration, rows for independent work); a 2019 study supports creating multiple learning zones (main teaching space plus smaller rotating areas), and a 2020 study of 610 classrooms found learning zones improve transitions and facilitate differentiated instruction [63].

**Seating for students with ASD (therapy balls/dynamic seating).** A 2017 peer-reviewed study in the Iranian Journal of Child Neurology tested 15 students with ASD (aged 7–10) at Tabasom School, Mashhad, Iran, using a single-case multiple treatment A1-B-A2-C crossover design comparing regular chairs, therapy balls (45cm Gymnic balls), and Disc 'O' Sit air cushions. Results: **significant increases in in-seat behavior in 86.7% (13/15) of students when seated on therapy balls (P<0.001)**, with in-seat mean scores rising from 40.1±19.6 (baseline) to 51.2±13.6; on-task behavior improved in 53.3% (8/15) of students on therapy balls; air cushions showed no statistically significant effect on in-seat or on-task behaviors (P=0.82); GARS II scores significantly decreased from 43.4±11.7 to 39.5±10.07 (P=0.017), indicating reduced autism-related behaviors including decreased stereotyped movements and increased communication/social skills. Teachers preferred therapy balls and air cushions over regular chairs and reported students were calmer. The authors conclude that ball seating provides dynamic sitting that stimulates proprioceptive and vestibular systems, helping normalize arousal levels, though individual students showed unique responses; air cushions provide a more stable surface with insufficient sensory stimulation [46]. A 2020 master's thesis on flexible seating options for students with ADHD and Autism examined on-task behavior changes during instruction [45]. A 2020 literature review found three studies showing therapy balls help boost behavior and engagement for students with autism [44]. Three additional studies (Bloom-Williams, 2023) demonstrated all participants showed improvements in in-seat behavior using both types of alternative seating compared to standard classroom chairs (kindergarteners) [48]. The NEA reports practitioner evidence that flexible seating (wobble stools, exercise balls, standing desks, floor seating) decreased behavior issues and increased engagement, with particular benefits for students with ADHD, anxiety, depression, and dyslexia; 78% of college students agreed they could concentrate with flexible seating, 64% said it helped them participate more, and 88% of students reporting mental health challenges reported improved concentration. Implementation guidance: train students on the seating system, establish rules (e.g., no bouncing, only back-and-forth movement), give warnings before moving students back to standard chairs, assign seats to specific desks with a daily position chart, start with what you have, and test your own tolerance for movement [47].

**Practical seating/layout guidance from practitioner sources.** Recommended: seat students away from doors, windows, or buzzing lights; ensure properly fitted chairs with feet planted firmly on floor and knees bent at 90 degrees; use inflated seat cushions, beanbag chairs, or therapy balls as options; clearly defined workstations with visual labels; flexible seating options (balance/exercise balls, active seat cushions, cozy couches, wiggle seats, stools) [7][9][10]. DYNSEO's Chinese-language guide recommends structuring the physical environment with quiet locations, reduced visual clutter, quiet corners, appropriate lighting, defined activity zones, and visual schedules [24]. The Chinese case study of "Small Y" (a 12-year-old autistic girl transitioning to a Shanghai junior high) included "physical environment adjustments (visual cues, strategic seating) and human environment adjustments (integration partners, 'rotating integration partners' method)" [35]. A Guangming Daily article recommends priority seating as a classroom support for autistic students in inclusive settings [37].

## 3. (b) Sensory-Friendly Accommodations: Lighting, Noise, Visual Clutter, Quiet/Sensory Break Spaces

**Lighting.** Natural/combination lighting benefits learning; LED outperforms fluorescent lighting, especially for students with developmental delays [8]. A 2018 doctoral dissertation (Stickney, Trevecca Nazarene University) used a mixed-methods single-subject design with five middle school students with ASD and specific learning disabilities: during baseline phases fluorescent lighting was used; during treatment phases the classroom was lit with floor lamps using incandescent light bulbs. Using a Wilcoxon Signed Rank Test, the researcher found a statistical difference among the subjects, and student perceptions were affected by the lighting changes [68]. A 2022 case study in Frontiers in Psychiatry surveyed 87 parents/caretakers of autistic children aged 6–16 in Northern India (45 males, 42 females, mean age 8.7): "Autistic children did not prefer harsh lights, fluorescent tubes, bright lights, below-eye-level windows, flickering lights, dark lights, or dark spaces. Flickering fluorescent lights were identified as stress-producing and could hurt eyes and cause headaches. Lights should be easy to control with dimmer switches... Natural daylight is preferable, and direct lighting should be present but glare avoided. Children had difficulty with reading and language activities under low light conditions, losing concentration and becoming flustered." Color findings: "Neutral tones and mellow shades were found to be calming and soothing (autism-friendly), while bright, bold, and intense colors were over-stimulating and could cause tension and aggression... Red and yellow can be problematic as they may agitate, depress, or confuse autistic children." The article also recommends sound levels below 50 dB (above 60 dB inappropriate), reducing echoes, and wayfinding elements like color-coded paths and landmarks [70]. Practitioner sources add: replace flickering fluorescent bulbs; use warmer recessed lighting, dimmer switches, full-spectrum bulbs, and affordable light filters placed under fluorescent fixtures; a case example of a nonverbal autistic student who struggled with his visual communication device due to glare from fluorescent lighting on laminated white pages — solved by a visor and printing images on blue paper; fluorescent bulbs "have been shown to increase feelings of anxiety and induce headaches among some students" [7][20][72]. NCAEP noted heavily decorated classrooms reduce attention and learning; natural light improves students' working speed and productivity, but too much direct sun impairs test scores, so glare control via shades is needed [63]. The Kaplan article recommends natural/soft lighting and neutral natural tones [10].

**Noise.** Children with ASD "often face heightened sensitivities to sounds that most neurotypical children may ignore or barely notice. This sensory processing challenge can turn ordinary classroom noises — like chatter, footsteps, or equipment hums — into sources of distress and distraction" [6]. Noise sensitivity impairs focus, comprehension of spoken instructions, and speech/language abilities; poor classroom acoustics (excessive reverberation, echoes, external noise) weaken communication and elevate stress; scientific research shows increased ambient noise leads to longer reaction times, more errors in cognitive tasks, and reduced attentional capacity [6]. Background noise in occupied classrooms averages 50 decibels (vs. WHO recommended maximum of 35 dB), with research measuring a mean noise level of 76 dB(A) in classrooms [7]. Typical primary classroom background noise runs 55–75 dB (comparable to a busy restaurant); acoustic panels on two walls can reduce reverberation by 40% (Shield and Dockrell, 2008) [59]. A 2023 study found students in open classrooms read half as fast as peers in traditional classrooms due to acoustical chaos requiring higher listening effort; quiet spaces are essential for deep focus [63]. Strategies: installing sound-absorbing materials (acoustic tiles, carpets, draperies), soundproofing walls/windows, noise-canceling headphones, earplugs, personal listening devices, quiet zones/retreat rooms, and steady background sound (white, pink, brown noise) to mask disruptive noises; individual sensitivities vary greatly so a personalized approach is recommended [6]. Additional strategies include using noise-level monitoring apps, warning students about loud noises, classroom amplification systems for students who have trouble filtering background noise, sound-absorbing acoustic panels as portable room partitions, sound shell chairs for sensory corners, and noise-reduction devices that allow self-management without blocking all sound [7][72]. In the Mallory & Keehn integrative review, auditory findings: signal-to-noise ratios are often below recommended levels; students with ASD show the greatest negative impact from auditory stimuli; noise correlates with increased repetitive behaviors and stress [8].

**Visual clutter.** "Heavily decorated classrooms reduce attention and learning" [8]. Students are more frequently off task when visual clutter overwhelms their developing ability to ignore distractions; research points to a middle ground — classrooms should not be too cluttered or too austere; avoid extreme wall colors (black, neon green); use a neutral base with splashes of brightness [63]. For the approximately one in three students with disabilities who have sensory or executive function issues, colorful environments may be "visual noise"; recommendations include aligning wall displays with current topics, using the front wall for daily materials, creating distinct activity areas, and managing glare [63]. Practical strategies: minimize wall decorations near work areas, use neutral colors, organize spaces, store toys/materials in labeled bins and low open shelves, cover materials with sheets when unused [7][10].

**Quiet/sensory break spaces.** Designated calm-down zones with soft lighting, comfortable seating, weighted blankets, and sensory-blocking tools like noise-canceling headphones [7]. Recommendations include a quiet cozy corner with plush carpets, soft surroundings, tunnels/arches, and noise-reduction headphones, plus a movement corner with an obstacle course format (e.g., downward dog for 10 seconds, 5 jumping jacks, push the wall for 10 seconds, 10 frog jumps, 5 sit-ups) [10]. Retreat/regulation spaces with calming materials (weighted pads, stress balls) are recommended for preventing and managing difficult behaviors [24]. The fundamental distinction: "'time-out' removes a learner from the group as a consequence. 'Take-a-break' allows a learner to self-select a regulation strategy before they reach crisis point" [59]. Chinese sources (Guangming Daily) describe resource classrooms (资源教室) serving multiple roles: academic support stations, emotional rest stops, and coordination hubs for IEP implementation [37]. An audit-based approach (Structural Learning) covers five domains — sensory processing, physical layout and accessibility, visual supports, communication-friendly spaces, and emotional regulation zones — with a three-tier action plan (Tier 1 changes under £50; Tier 2 at £50–300; Tier 3 at £300+); many fixes cost under £200 (replacing fluorescent tubes with LED panels ~£15 each, tennis balls on chair legs £5, acoustic panels ~£30), and it recommends "auditing with learners, not just for them" [59].

## 4. (c) Evidence on Sensory Integration Therapy and Sensory Diets

**Sensory integration therapy (SIT/ASI) — mixed-to-weak evidence.** The Chinese translation/adaptation (Hao Yan, East China Normal University Special Education Department) of the Lang et al. (2012) systematic review published in Research in Autism Spectrum Disorders analyzed 25 studies (217 children with ASD; 176 male, 31 female, 10 unknown; ages 2–12, mean 5.9). Results: **14 studies (56%) reported SIT had no benefit, with 4 of these reporting SIT may have increased stereotyped and problem behaviors**; 8 studies reported mixed results; only 3 studies reported SIT was effective, and ALL 3 were classified at the "suggestive" (lowest) evidence level. Of the no-benefit studies with "decisive" evidence, all 5 used weighted vests. The review found methodological problems in the 3 "effective" studies: Fazlioglu (2008) combined SIT with ABA (effectiveness likely reflects ABA); Linderman (1999) subjects received language therapy after baseline; Thompson (2011) did not report specific ANOVA results. The review's conclusion: "The current evidence-base does not support the use of SIT in the education and treatment of children with autism spectrum disorders (ASD), and practitioners and agencies serving children with ASD should not use SIT outside of carefully controlled research," and recommends avoiding large-scale implementation of SIT in public schools funded by federal money [21]. ASAT similarly concludes: multiple meta-analyses and systematic reviews of SI interventions (Ottenbacher 1982, Polatajko 1992, Hoehn & Baumeister 1994, May-Benson & Koomar 2010, Baranek 2002, Case-Smith et al. 2014) found mixed results, with SI showing no greater effectiveness than other interventions; "there have not been a sufficient amount of empirical studies conducted... The evidence that exists, at best, is mixed, mostly showing ineffectiveness"; the American Academy of Pediatrics (2012) concluded sensory processing disorder should not be diagnosed and there is limited evidence of effectiveness [12].

**Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) specifically.** More recent evidence is somewhat more favorable: "Per the 2025 Acuña et al. systematic review, ASI has strong evidence from randomized trials for helping children meet individualized goals but only moderate evidence of no benefit for behaviors of concern" [11]. The Autism CRC evidence synthesis (Whitehouse et al., 2020) found for ASI (4 reviews): inconsistent effects on overall autistic characteristics, social-communication, sensory behaviors, communication, adaptive behaviour, and general outcomes; positive effects on cognition, motor, social-emotional/challenging behaviour, academic skills, and community participation; null effect on play. For assorted sensory-based interventions (3 reviews): null effects on communication and general outcomes. For Auditory Integration Therapy (3 reviews): null effects. Environmental enrichment (1 review): null effect on expressive language; positive effect on cognition. Sensory diet (1 review): null effect on general outcomes. Most evidence rated low-to-moderate quality [13]. Soundsory notes a 2010 systematic review found SIT to be evidence-based, but the American Academy of Pediatrics stated effectiveness in autism is inconclusive and limited; ASI has been included as an evidence-based intervention for children with ASD in the National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice [15]. ASI is a manualized approach delivered by trained occupational therapists, containing (per Parham et al.) ten core elements: providing tactile/proprioceptive opportunities, challenging sensory systems at a 'just right' level, collaborating on activity choice, teaching self-organisation, supporting optimal arousal, using play as learning context, maximising success, ensuring physical safety, arranging the room to encourage interaction, and fostering therapeutic alliance [13][15].

**Sensory diets.** A sensory diet is "a planned set of sensory activities scheduled through the day to help a child stay regulated. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with food" [11][14]. Activities include movement (swinging, jumping, spinning), deep pressure (squeezes, weighted items, burrowing), heavy work (carrying, pushing, climbing), and tactile/oral/calming input. Evidence assessment: **sensory diets fall under sensory-based interventions, which have weaker evidence than Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI)**; a 2018 systematic review (Bodison & Parham) found moderate evidence for sensory environmental modifications but only limited evidence for weighted vests — "suggesting reducing environmental load is usually cheaper and easier than adding activities." Sensory diets are "a low-risk, individualized strategy many families find helpful, but not an established treatment; change the plan rather than intensifying it if not working." Building a plan with an OT should involve assessment first, functional goals, realistic scheduling, and a review point (useful question: "what would prompt a change of approach?"). Without a therapist, families can use movement breaks before demanding tasks, heavy work before transitions, and building activities into existing routines. Oral sensory input (chewable jewelry, chew tools, straw drinking) is reasonable; restricted diets, texture difficulties, or mealtime distress warrant a feeding assessment by an SLP or OT rather than a sensory activity plan. Start small with one or two activities, keep consistency between home and school via a shared log, and use low-cost everyday options like carrying groceries or pushing a laundry basket [11]. ASAT is far more critical: Patricia Wilbarger proposed sensory diets in 1995, based on Jean Ayres' Sensory Integration theory (1972) and Winnie Dunn's sensory processing theory (1997); a high percentage (80–90%) of individuals with ASD reportedly display sensory processing disorders. Research specifically on sensory diets is sparse — only one case study (Stagnitti et al., 1999) was found, with significant methodological limitations. Sensory processing disorder is not recognized in the DSM-V (rejected by the APA Board of Trustees due to insufficient research). The National Clearinghouse on Autism Evidence and Practice (Steinbrenner et al., 2020) found no empirical studies on sensory diets published since 2011 and recommends caution. ASAT's position: "until an empirical consensus is reached regarding the effectiveness of sensory diets and SI interventions, they should not be used" [12]. A practitioner summary notes research suggests sensory diets are beneficial when tailored to the child's individual sensory profile and guided by an occupational therapist, with effectiveness depending on consistency, correct activity selection, and ongoing adjustments [14].

**Chinese-language sources on 感统训练 (sensory integration training).** The ALSOLIFE platform (Chinese autism support organization) explains: sensory integration disorder (感觉统合障碍/感统失调) is common among children with autism; 感统 refers to the brain's process of interpreting and unifying sensory information from visual, auditory, tactile, taste, olfactory, vestibular, and proprioceptive channels. Manifestations include vestibular dysfunction (hyperactivity, inattention, restlessness in class, delayed language), visual integration disorder (cannot read fluently despite being able to watch cartoons), auditory integration disorder (appears not to hear others, forgetful), proprioceptive integration disorder (poor balance, clumsy), and tactile integration disorder (abnormal touch sensitivity, picky eating, irritability, fears unfamiliar environments, finger-sucking). Sensory integration training is "a necessary aid that helps adjust sensory input and emotional state, but it is NOT the primary rehabilitation method"; a professional evaluation is required before deciding, and intervention must be based on the child's characteristics [16]. A second ALSOLIFE article notes that while sensory integration training has been included among the 28 EBPs per US NCAEP reports, "it is not universally applicable to every child with autism": "感觉统合训练只针对于有感统失调的孩子，而不针对自闭症" (sensory integration training only targets children with sensory integration disorder, not autism). ASI intervention plans include nine core elements (delivery under direct supervision of qualified therapists; family-centered planning; safe environments with vestibular/proprioceptive/tactile equipment; adaptive responses; child-centered activities; rich sensory stimulation; tasks requiring planning; special equipment like hanging devices, scooters, balls; difficulty-adjusted activities). Three criteria to judge a training institution: ① practitioner qualifications/systematic training; ② complete evaluation, intervention planning, and data recording systems; ③ whether the intervention embodies core sensory integration elements. Being evidence-based does not mean a method is "best"; sensory training cannot replace core ABA therapy [22]. A Taiwan master's thesis (Tsai Pei-shan, National Taichung University of Education, 2006, 126 pages) — "The Effects of Sensory Integration Therapy on the Improvement of Motor and Socially Interactive Abilities by Preschool Children with Autism" — used a single-subject multiple-probe design with three preschool children with autism; therapy occurred twice weekly for 11 weeks. Results: all three subjects showed significant and sustained improvements in "postural movement" abilities; all three showed significant and sustained improvements in "bilateral integration sequencing" abilities; subjects 2 and 3 showed significant and sustained effects on verbally expressive behavior; all three showed significant and sustained increases in nonverbal expressive behavior [64].

## 5. (d) Classroom-Wide Sensory Supports: Fidget Tools, Weighted Items, Movement Breaks

**Fidget tools — mixed/contradictory evidence.** Evidence AGAINST fidget spinners: Three studies argue against fidget spinners in classrooms: (1) a study published online Oct. 26, 2019 in the Journal of Applied Cognitive Psychology ("Putting a negative spin on it," UC Santa Cruz) found college students randomly given fidget spinners while watching educational videos scored worse on subsequent memory tests, even among students who thought the spinners were helpful; (2) a German study (January 2019) found both fidget spinners and doodling impaired memory, while stress balls neither negatively affected memory nor helped; (3) Paulo Graziano's study in the Journal of Attention Disorders ("To Fidget or Not to Fidget, That is the Question") tested fidget spinners on preschoolers with ADHD — children given spinners displayed more moments of inattentiveness, and although initially less hyperactive, that behavioral benefit disappeared four weeks later. Graziano: "Kids with ADHD get distracted. And having something that occupies their attention is likely going to take away from them listening to the teacher and doing their work." Evidence-based alternatives include seating restless children in front of the class, positive reinforcement, and active classroom jobs [26]. The Shaping Minds article cites: Driesen et al. (2023) — tested over 200 primary students; fidget spinners consistently negatively impacted academic performance, bouncy bands slightly better but still net negative; Trout et al. (2020) — multisite study showing clear decrease in performance for students using spinners; Graziano et al. (2020) — small behavioral benefits (reduced outbursts, increased compliance) but fidget spinners nearly doubled attention disruptions for both user and nearby students; Reichow et al. (2015) — systematic review of sensory interventions (weighted vests, textured seats, hand-held fidgets) finding no reliable evidence of improved academic outcomes and some negative effects. Many pro-sensory-toy studies relied on weaker self-reported measures or clinical one-on-one settings. Recommendation: avoid sensory toys in mainstream classrooms wherever possible, or choose the least distracting option [25].

Evidence FOR fidgets in specific populations: Aspiranti & Hulac (Behavior Analysis in Practice, 2021) used a concurrent multiple-baseline across-students design with three second-grade students with ADHD in a general education classroom. Five rules preceded the intervention (two fingers on the spinner at all times; use only during work/listening; eyes on work/teacher; use quietly; only user). Results: Allison baseline M=27% to intervention M=79% (NAP=1.0, large effect); Ben M=25% to M=67% (NAP=.85); Carl M=34% to M=55% (NAP=.90). Interobserver agreement averaged 98.5%; procedural integrity 100%. However, the teacher strongly disagreed with acceptability items, stating students were quieter and looked at their work but "did not actually complete the assignments." No habituation effect was observed; the spinner may function as a motivating operation providing an appropriate replacement for disruptive movements (DRA framework) [28]. Roche, Back, & Van Herwegen (Current Psychology, 2023; 129 parents: 53 autistic, 76 neurotypical children, ages 3–16) found parents of autistic children perceived fidget toys and spinners as overall more beneficial than NT parents, especially for reducing anxiety (fidget toys beneficial χ²(4)=26.456, p<.001; anxiety χ²(4)=17.478, p=.002) and improving concentration (χ²(4)=16.148, p=.003); autistic children had significantly higher sensory-seeking scores (M=51.19, SD=17.02) vs. NT (M=24.02, SD=18.15), t(77)=6.834, p<.001; "the perceived benefits of fidget toys depends on the sensory processing style of the child as well as the type of sensory toy involved." Safety concerns: nickel/cobalt allergic contact dermatitis from spinners and ingestion hazards [27]. Practitioner guides recommend: good classroom fidgets are quiet, discreet, have interesting textures, and allow lots of finger/hand movement (Squigglet Bracelet, Stress-less Gel Ball, Tangle Toy, Pencil Fidget Toppers, Inside Out Ball, Squeeze Star — per National Autism Resources); fidgeting need not be a toy — standing at desk, alternative seating, kick/bouncy bands, Velcro on desk; establish fidget rules ("I use fidgets to help me pay attention," "I keep fidgets on my desk or in my hands," "I don't show other students my fidget," "I always put away my fidget when I am done"); wait until novelty wears off; consider texture preferences; give the strategy time; for students who mouth things, ensure fidgets are sturdy without breakable pieces [29]. Kaplan recommends easy access to fidgets — stress balls, tangle toys, slime, textured balls, fidget spinners placed at desks or in a designated fidget zone/sensory bin [10].

**Weighted items (vests, blankets, lap pads) — consistently weak evidence.** The Stephenson & Carter (2009) review in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders (Vol. 39, pp. 105–114): "Signs are that weighted vests are ineffective and there may be an arguable case for continued research on this intervention, but they cannot be recommended for clinical application at this point" [33]. Taylor et al. (2017, Research in Autism Spectrum Disorders, Vol. 37, pp. 49–60), a systematic review using What Works Clearinghouse standards: **"Weighted vests are a frequently recommended practice for students with autism spectrum disorder... An examination of research for quality using What Works Clearinghouse standards indicates that weighted vests for students with autism spectrum disorder is not an evidence-based practice"** [34]. Apply EBP's Research Roundup compiles: Barton et al. (2015): "All 6 studies examining weighted vests documented no behavioral differences in conditions with or without the weighted vests"; Case-Smith et al. (2015): among seven single-subject studies, only one demonstrated positive effects; Taylor et al. (2017): WV use not an EBP; Quigley et al. (2011): no functional relationship between 5% or 10% weighted vests and challenging behaviors; Stephenson & Carter (2009): "indications are that weighted vests are ineffective"; Macphee et al. (2019, ADHD): medication, but not weighted vests or stability balls, improved following classroom rules and academic productivity; Lin et al. (2014, ADHD, 110 children): significant improvement in three attentional variables and three of four on-task behaviors, but no significant improvements in impulse control; Davis et al. (2013): no functional relationship; Hodgetts et al. (2011, two studies): no objective improvements; Collins & Dworkin (2011): "Weighted vests were not effective in increasing time on task"; Leew et al. (2010, toddlers): no replicated effects on competing behaviors or joint attention; Reichow et al. (2010): "no differentiation in engagement between conditions for any of the participants" (comparing 5% weighted vest, unweighted vest placebo, no vest baseline). Typical weight: 5–10% of body weight (some up to 15%) [31]. ASAT treatment summary (Gasiewski, 2024, Science in Autism Treatment 21(6)): Watling & Hauer (2015): evidence does not support weighted vests; Bodison & Parham (2018): limited and insufficient evidence; Grajo et al. (2020): low evidence for targeting educational participation; Cahill & Beisbier (2020): use with caution with close monitoring; Battin et al. (2020): "strong and sufficient evidence AGAINST weighted vests; designated vests as 'a red-light procedure'." Weight is generally distributed at 10% of body weight (research range 4–10%); no exact protocol exists; existing research reports no adverse effects [32]. The Semantic Scholar citation record for Stephenson & Carter shows follow-up studies reinforcing the finding, including Quigley et al. (2011), Leew et al. (2010), Hodgetts et al. (2011) ("The results do not support the use of weighted vests in isolation to improve attention to task or sitting in children with autism in the classroom setting"), Davis et al. (2013), Losinski et al. (2016, deep touch pressure interventions of generally poor quality), Lang et al. (2012) [33]. One retailer claims a 2001 study by VandenBerg showed an 18–25% increase in on-task completion of fine motor activities, but conflicting research (Stephenson & Carter, 2009) found four of seven similar studies concluded weighted vests had no effects; safety warnings: Oxford Health NHS Foundation does not endorse weighted/compressive products, warning against use for children with respiratory problems, cardiac problems, serious hypotonia, skin allergies, circulatory problems, or physical impairment preventing self-removal [30]. For weighted blankets/lap pads, the Kaplan guide advises: use deep pressure to activate the body's "rest and digest" system, releasing "feel-good" chemicals; **weighted items should be no more than 5–10% of the child's body weight, used for no longer than 20 minutes at a time, with adult supervision**; Wilmot warns against overusing this approach — too much stimulation can quickly lead to a meltdown [10].

**Movement breaks and physical activity — moderately strong evidence.** A study published in the International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education (December 2016, Vol. 9, Issue 2, pp. 405–418) examined adult-directed physical activities during circle time on the on-task behavior of three male kindergarteners with ASD (Paul 5y10m; Nate 6y1m; Liam 6y3m) during a subsequent journal-writing activity, using an alternating treatment design (yoga = mild, dance party = moderate, book reading = sedentary control). Results: Paul: baseline 53% → yoga 92%, dance 83%, book 45%; Liam: baseline 44% → 55%, 66%, 42%; Nate: baseline 48% → 73%, 79%, 45%. All 29 kindergarten students surveyed preferred movement activities (19 chose dance party, 9 yoga, 1 book reading); teachers rated ease of use 4/5 and all planned to use it again. Conclusion: "Students with ASD demonstrate increased on-task behavior following brief bouts of embedded physical activity. More vigorous activity (dance party) may have greater effects, possibly serving as a more fulfilling sensory experience"; implications include embedding multiple bouts of adult-led planned physical activity across the instructional day [57]. A Frontiers in Psychology (2016) study with 92 children aged 11–12 used a 2×2 design (physical exertion × cognitive engagement) with four conditions (combo, cognition, physical, control) over a 10-minute intervention: **"physical exertion had no effect on any measure of children's attentional performance. Cognitive engagement was the crucial factor leading to increased focused attention and enhanced processing speed"** — high CE conditions outperformed low CE conditions in focused attention [F(4,87)=4.19, p=0.044, ηp²=0.046]; changes in positive affect mediated the effect between cognitive engagement and focused attention (indirect effect β=−0.03, p=0.020) and processing speed (β=−0.04, p=0.033) [50]. A 2024 meta-analysis (Frontiers in Psychology, Koh) of 16 studies (51 cases) on physical exercise interventions and social skills in children with ASD found overall significant moderate improvement (SMD=−0.54, 95% CI [−0.63; −0.44]), low heterogeneity (I²=19.8%); social cognition showed the largest effect (ES=−0.82); autistic mannerisms (−0.72), social responsiveness (−0.64), irritability (−0.58), social communication (−0.52), social motivation (−0.46), social awareness (−0.37); age was the only significant moderator (p=0.034): children under 7 showed larger effects (ES=−0.65) than children 7+ (ES=−0.46); interventions lasting 12+ weeks showed larger effects (ES=−0.62); exercise types included horseback riding (n=5), mini-basketball (n=3), swimming (n=2), combined training (n=2), karate, yoga, mind-body exercise, outdoor adventure; fail-safe N=2,427 [54]. A 2026 MDPI systematic review of RCTs (16 studies, 465 participants, ages 6–11): physical activity interventions positively influenced motor coordination with **81.2% of studies reporting beneficial effects**, particularly in balance, motor coordination, and overall motor proficiency; land-based programs more accessible and feasible; aquatic programs offered additional sensory-motor benefits; interventions lasted 7 weeks to nearly one year, 2–4 sessions/week, 25–60 minutes [55]. Understood.org/Reading Rockets "brain breaks" guidance: quick structured breaks (1–5 minutes) using physical movement, mindfulness, or sensory activities; plan a break before fatigue sets in, "This may be after 10 to 25 minutes of intensive work"; start with a visual timer; "read the room" and adjust; wrap up with countdown; research shows exercise increases blood flow to the brain — in one study students learned vocabulary words 20 percent faster after exercising; brain breaks reduce stress, anxiety, and frustration; best for grades K-5 (aligned with CASEL Core SEL Competencies: Self-management); provide a nonverbal signal for students opting out [51][52]. Movement breaks should make learning more efficient, increase oxygen to the brain, interrupt negative patterns, provide sensory breaks, and support self-regulation; even 5 minutes between lessons can have a huge impact; proprioception activities ("heavy work" like carrying books, pushing carts, passing out supplies) and vestibular stimulation activities (head movements, bending over, "Head, Shoulders, Knees and Toes") are recommended [53]. Teachers building in brain breaks and movement stations with 4–5 sequenced activities is also recommended [7].

## 6. (e) Transition Support via Environmental Cues: Visual Supports and Visual Schedules

**Visual supports as an EBP.** Visual Supports (VS) are "objects or pictures/symbols that can be seen and/or held, which are used to provide information visually to enhance an individual's understanding of: the physical environment; people and the social environment... and more abstract concepts, such as the passage of time, a sequence of events, or socially abstract concepts such as emotions." Visual supports are among the 28 NCAEP-identified EBPs and are one of VCU's "Foundational Five" [4][43]. They can be low-tech (objects, photos, pictures, symbols, written words) or high-tech (electronic devices). They increase understanding of expectations, reduce anxiety, facilitate participation, support communication, and increase independence, reducing the risk of challenging behavior. VS include pictures, written lists, or timers as reminders of pending transitions; choice boards; first-then boards; visual schedules; social stories. VS are preventive (antecedent) strategies; interventions typically include systematic prompting and graduated guidance. VS are appropriate for mild to moderate challenging behavior; published studies addressed behavior maintained by escape/task avoidance. VS are low cost, adaptable, portable, applicable across contexts, and have been used successfully by caregivers and school staff [43]. This is why visual supports are ranked as one of the highest-confidence, well-established classroom environmental strategies.

**Visual schedules: evidence base.** The ASAT treatment summary (Tereshko, 2023): Visual activity schedules are "an arrangement of pictures or words used to display a sequence of upcoming events." They encompass three EB strategies: antecedent interventions, prompting, and visual supports. They are beneficial for autistic individuals "who may display prompt dependency and have difficulty processing auditory information" (Koyama & Wang, 2011; Knight et al., 2015). The **National Standards Project: Phase 2 (2015) identifies schedule use as an established intervention** for increasing independence and event planning. Hume et al. (2021) identified visual supports as an EBP. Two systematic reviews support this: Koyama and Wang (2011) reviewed 23 peer-reviewed studies (69 participants: preschool 24.6%, school-aged 30.4%, adults 23.2%; 59.4% with autism diagnosis); Knight et al. (2014) reviewed 31 articles confirming effectiveness across the lifespan. Visual schedules have successfully taught toothbrushing (Moran et al., 2022), medical exam cooperation (Chebuhar et al., 2013), bedtime routines (Hart Barnett et al., 2022), leisure/play skills, physical activity compliance (Becerra et al., 2021), appropriate feeding (Kirkpatrick et al., 2019), academic task engagement, choice-making (Deel et al., 2021), vocational tasks (Lora et al., 2020; Sances et al., 2019), **transitions (Pierce et al., 2013)**, and social skills (Osos et al., 2021). Caution: Knight et al. (2014) found nearly all studies combined visual schedules with other systematic instruction, which may have enhanced effects. Formats: linear displays (vertical/horizontal), small books with icons moved to a "done" column, object schedules, narrative/word formats, and technological options (iPad-based schedules, smart watches per Jimenez-Gomez et al., 2021); Giles et al. (2017) found similar acquisition rates between static pictures and tablet-based formats with idiosyncratic preferences; teams should decide based on the individual's skills (symbolic representation, receptive language, reading) and preference [40]. The Liang, Lee, Zuo & Liang (2024) literature review in the International Journal of Developmental Disabilities on visual schedules to increase academic-related on-task behaviors: 10 peer-reviewed studies (31 participants aged 4–19, mean age 10, mostly elementary schoolers; nine of ten school-based); all used single-case designs; formats included photographs, pictures, text, video via albums, workbooks, task lists, schedule books, folders, binders, iPads/iPods; all studies combined VS with other strategies (least-to-most prompting n=6; reinforcement n=6); all reported positive outcomes, though one found VS alone insufficient without other components; six studies programmed for generalization, four reported maintenance, seven reported social validity; by Reichow's standards, six studies rated strong, one adequate, three weak. Background context: individuals with autism receiving IDEA services increased from 93,000 in 2001 to 803,000 in 2020 (1.6% of special education students); academic difficulties link to executive functioning deficits, auditory processing weaknesses, and stimulus over-selectivity. Conclusion: visual schedules, combined with prompting and reinforcement, can effectively increase academic-related on-task behaviors [39]. The Links ABA guide adds: visual schedules are recognized by NCAEP as one of 28 EBPs (31 studies reviewed, 16 meeting quality criteria); types include object, photograph, picture symbol, written, and digital; the CHECK implementation method (Choose format, Honor needs, Establish expectations, Create consistency, Keep simple); the intervention led to statistically significant improvement in parent-reported quality of life (t28=3.09, p=0.005) and parent-reported perception of autism-specific difficulties (t28=2.99, p=0.006); "Auditory information is transient – visual information can be fixed and permanent" (Leslie Broun) [41]. For transitions specifically: visual schedules help because they provide predictability and structure, support visual learning strengths, encourage independence and self-management, reduce behavioral challenges by setting clear expectations, and help students understand the flow of the school day; types include First–Then boards, picture schedules, written schedules, and portable schedules; "Anticipation is the key to successful transitions" [24][42].

**DYNSEO Chinese-language transition guidance.** Transition is often difficult for autistic students because they need predictability and struggle with change; key strategies: advance notice with time markers, visual/auditory timers, consistent transition routines, and assigning students specific roles during transitions; "Time is often a limiting factor for autistic students... Always give an additional third of the time"; the behavioral challenges observed "are usually expressions of stress, misunderstanding or sensory overload" [24]. The Mallory & Keehn review also notes visual supports (visual schedules, visual cues in the environment) as a recommended classroom accommodation to reduce attentional and sensory demands [8].

**Chinese-language sources on visual supports/structured teaching (TEACCH).** The ALSOLIFE article on structured teaching (结构化教学) describes the TEACCH program (Treatment and Education for Autistic and Communication Handicapped Children) developed by Professor Eric Schopler at UNC Chapel Hill, which combines diagnosis, assessment, early education, school education, family education, and vocational training. "结构化教学的原理是充分利用自闭症儿童的视觉优势安排教育环境和训练程序" (the principle of structured teaching is to fully use the visual strengths of autistic children to arrange the educational environment and training procedures). Four steps: (1) arrange training spaces according to training content with visual cues; (2) establish training schedules/programs emphasizing procedural consistency; (3) define training content (imitation, gross/fine motor, perception, cognition, hand-eye coordination, language, self-care, social skills, emotional regulation); (4) use language, body posture, cues, labels, charts, and text to enhance understanding, plus behavioral reinforcement. Assessment tools: Psychoeducational Profile (PEP-3) and TEACCH Transition Assessment Profile (T-TAP for adolescents/adults); IEPs are designed from PEP results. Visual reminders of progress help children complete work according to event sequence and logical structure [23].

## 7. Chinese-Language Context: Inclusive Education (随班就读/融合教育), Policy, and Implementation

**Policy and statistics.** According to the 2017 "China Autism Education Rehabilitation Industry Development Report," there are over 10 million people with autism in China, with 2 million+ autistic children aged 0–14, growing at nearly 200,000 per year [17]. China's incidence rate of autism among school-age children is 0.7%, global prevalence ~1%, US rate 2.8% (per Guangming Daily / Li Yinghui) [37]. A Chinese case study article states ASD prevalence reached 1/44 with a male-to-female ratio of about 4.2:1, and China has over 2 million ASD children under 14 [20]. An Acta Psychologica Sinica study states China's ASD prevalence is 0.70% (1 in 143), while the US CDC (2021) estimates 1 in 44 [65]. Policy milestones: 2014 Special Education Improvement Plan (2014–2016) required mildly disabled children to attend regular schools with "zero rejection" policies in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Xiamen; July 2017 Second Special Education Improvement Plan (2017–2020) prioritized mainstream placement; 2015 State Council plan promoted inclusive education and building special education resource classrooms (资源教室); the 2019 "Education Modernization 2035" (《中国教育现代化2035》) called for "全面推进融合教育" (comprehensively advancing integrated education); the 2021 "Fourteenth Five-Year Plan to Improve Special Education" promotes integration of regular and special education; the 2022 "14th Five-Year Plan for Special Education Development and Improvement Action Plan" emphasizes comprehensive and appropriate inclusive education [17][20][36][37]. "Learning in Regular Class" (随班就读) is a Chinese educational policy from the 1980s; Inclusive Education (全纳教育) was formally proposed in the 1994 Salamanca Statement [20]. The Guangming Daily article argues three foundational works are needed: (1) clarify the core concept of inclusive education — students with autism fully integrated with special support, including IEPs, classroom supports (audiobooks, auxiliary graphics, priority seating), and extracurricular supports (resource classrooms, specialized tutoring, psychological support); (2) build a complete support system — each student with an IEP should have a resource teacher as case manager; plans jointly developed by resource teachers, subject teachers, behavior analysts, psychology teachers, language therapists, and occupational therapists; resource classrooms serve as academic support stations, emotional rest stops, and coordination hubs; (3) strengthen home-school-community coordination — for transitioning students (transfers or graduation), schools should establish referral systems, adjust/transfer IEPs, and introduce social resources including employment guidance, vocational skills training, and adaptive training [37].

**Challenges in Chinese mainstream schools.** A China News article (2021, from The Paper, reporter 卫佳铭) documented that only 69% of applicants successfully enrolled in school in 2017 (National Alliance of Parents Organizations of People with Mental Disabilities report); shortage of "shadow teachers" (影子老师/特教助理) — hiring one costs 100,000+ yuan/year per parent reports, and many schools refuse to allow them in classrooms; resource classrooms built at cost (one school spent 200,000 yuan) are often unused due to lack of resource teachers; resource teachers rarely have dedicated staffing positions (编制); teachers lack special education training; special education funding in underdeveloped areas is inadequate (e.g., Bijie, Guizhou). Expert proposals (2021 Two Sessions): CPPCC member 邰丽华 proposed "一人一案" (one person one plan) with an integrated system: "班主任全面负责儿童发展，特教教师入班支持，资源教师总体统筹协调" (head teacher overall responsibility, special education teacher in-class support, resource teacher overall coordination); CPPCC member 黄绮 proposed dedicated special education schools for autistic children. Current placement in China is based mainly on IQ testing: below 50 suggests special school; 50–70 suggests mainstream school (随班就读). US best practices (per 石荟/Shi Hui): parents have absolute say in IEPs; "普通教师决定教什么，特殊教师决定怎么教" (regular teacher decides what to teach, special teacher decides how to teach); IEPs re-evaluated every 3 months. Expert view: "好的融合教育一定是让特殊需要儿童和普通儿童双方受益的" (good inclusive education must benefit both special needs and ordinary children). The article documented bullying incidents (e.g., a boy taping "I have autism" on 琪琪's back) but also positive examples (classmates leaving red teaching aids for autistic child 天天 because they knew he liked red) [17].

**Chinese case study of inclusive practice.** Liu Ninghuan's 2024 case study (Advances in Education/教育进展) of "Xiaoxiao," an autistic boy (born 2014, diagnosed May 2016, >6 years rehabilitation) in a Chengdu primary school, implemented three strategies: (1) equal acceptance and mutual respect — daily 5-minute sitting practice for all students, respecting privacy by not disclosing his condition to classmates; (2) multi-force collaboration — daily documented communication with parents, coordination with subject teachers, peer intervention through desk-mate arrangements and a "class-wide administrator" system where Xiaoxiao self-elected as "uniform manager," plus four safety monitors; (3) friendly harmony — encouraging class tasks, praising his drawings/writing, ensuring participation in classroom activities ("train" question games). Results after four months: returning to his seat at the first preparatory bell (从最开始不知道什么时候上课，到现在能在第一个预备铃声响后及时回到教室座位上坐好), communicating needs via gesture, controlling classroom noise, actively raising his hand, participating in group discussions, completing writing assignments, asking teachers questions. The author notes "他们就像易碎的陶瓷娃娃" (they are like fragile ceramic dolls) and recommends sustained parental engagement, hospital collaboration, and building support systems and resource networks [20].

**Chinese transition (转衔) case studies.** A Shanghai case study (Huang Xilu, Shanghai Weiyu Junior High School, published 2025-02-17) documented support for "Small Y," a 12-year-old girl with autism and mild intellectual disability transitioning from primary to junior high under the "5-4 school system": (1) multi-dimensional assessment in 5th grade identifying three transition challenges (campus adaptation, friendships, academic gaps); (2) an individualized transition support plan across three dimensions (campus adaptation, social interaction, academic development); (3) implementation including a class teacher with inclusive education experience who conducted summer home visits, physical environment adjustments (visual cues, strategic seating), human environment adjustments (integration partners, "rotating integration partners"), IEP meetings with touring guidance teachers, resource room compensatory courses (e.g., "Peppa Pig picture books" for writing), transition courses ("My New School" theme for campus adaptation and "Making New Friends" for social skills), and home-school collaboration (parents visited campus in summer). After ~9 months, Small Y adapted well with initial anxiety relieved, social skills improved significantly, and Chinese writing ability increased substantially. "转衔"意即从一个阶段过渡到另一个阶段 (transition means moving from one stage to another, involving changes in roles, tasks, and life patterns). Reflections: clarifying needs is the foundation; multi-party collaboration forms a supportive force; specialized support plus psychological support promotes adaptation [35]. A second article (Zhou Xiaoying, Journal of Educational Innovation and Practice, Sept 2025) on transfer from special rehabilitation to regular kindergartens identified three core prerequisite skills: self-care ability (生活自理能力), group adaptation ability (团体适应能力), and social communication ability (社交沟通能力); implemented a three-stage transition model (学时融合/preparation period with 1–2 daily activity segments; 半日融合/half-day integration; 全日融合/full-day integration with embedded support and itinerant guidance), a "6+1" curriculum system (six major courses — art, physical, music, social games, self-care, group activities — plus autonomous play), home-school co-education (home visits, class meetings, WeChat communication, Individualized Family Service Plans), and continuous evaluation: "个别化教育计划、教育安置并不是一成不变，是一个动态过程，需要定期检核与再评估" (IEPs and educational placements are dynamic processes requiring regular review and re-evaluation) [36].

**Chinese intervention-science context.** The Acta Psychologica Sinica paper (2023, Vol. 55, No. 2, pp. 237–256) on pre-service teacher learning of Discrete Trial Teaching (DTT) found: "学习内容以视听双通道方式呈现时,自闭症儿童职前教师的自主学习效果最好" (learning content presented in audio-visual dual-channel format produces the best learning outcomes for pre-service teachers of children with autism); real teaching videos required fewest learning sessions (Exp 1: video M=3.33 < PPT M=4.33 < Word M=5.17, F(2,23)=8.14, p=0.001; Exp 2: video M=4.17 < PPT M=5.17 < Word M=8.17, F(2,23)=19.09, p<0.001; Exp 3: video M=2.50 < PPT M=3.83 < Word M=5.67, F(2,4)=30.33, p<0.001); fidelity improvement: video (41.70%) > PPT (30.00%) > Word (26.27%), F(2,4)=38.25, p<0.001; more autistic children are entering inclusive settings but regular teachers generally lack knowledge of evidence-based interventions, making pre-service training critical [65]. The ECNU journal article on Pivotal Response Training (PRT) notes autism incidence rose from 5–10 per 10,000 to 88:1 (CDC 2012); DTT is the most common behavior intervention model in Chinese special schools but produces mechanical children lacking initiative, poor skill retention/generalization, prompt dependence, and avoidance behaviors; PRT targets "pivotal responses" (motivation, response to multiple cues, self-initiation) with six principles: allow child choice/follow child's lead; instructions clear; intersperse new with mastered skills; turn-taking; reinforce reasonable attempts; direct reinforcement. The US National Autism Center recognized PRT in 2009 and 2011 as one of 11 proven effective methods [67]. A China Youth Daily interview with 黄伟合 (Huang Weihe, internationally certified doctoral-level behavior analyst) emphasizes child-centered intervention ("干预团队要理解自闭症儿童的真正需求，以他们的需求为本"), three principles of functionality, initiative, and flexibility, and notes universities in China have been largely absent from autism intervention research, though Beijing University, Beijing Normal University, Qingdao University, and Tsinghua University have begun offering behavioral analysis courses; intervention before age 3 gives a 90% chance of developing spoken language, at age 3–5 80–90%, after age 6 only ~20%; since 2020 an international health outcomes measurement consortium has worked to establish objective standards for "proven effective" intervention [66]. Chinese autism context facts: only ~20% of autistic children in China are diagnosed, partly because 75–80% of the population lives in rural areas without access to professional diagnosis; average delay of 7.1 months from symptom discovery to diagnosis and 6.5 months from diagnosis to intervention; 88% of families declined disability certification to avoid the record following their children; many miss the optimal early intervention window (before age 3) [18]. 《中国特殊教育》(Chinese Journal of Special Education, publication number CN11-3826/G4, published by the National Institute of Education Sciences) publishes autism research including, in featured recent issues: predictive coding deficits, interpersonal synchronous music activities, neurodiversity perspectives, **friendly classroom environments (友好课堂环境)**, extended reality (XR) technology interventions, transition support from American school-to-adulthood, and music/virtual reality interventions; the site provides an online journal, submission system, and contents organized by research area (autism studies/孤独症研究 among others) [38]. A Chinese book by 孙玉梅 (Sun Yumei, 2015), 《自闭症谱系障碍儿童家庭支持系统》 (Family Support System for ASD Children, ISBN 9787301258842), uses interpretive phenomenology to present common themes of family care for ASD children and proposes practical family support strategies [19].

## 8. Evidence Rating and Strength-of-Evidence Summary

**Well-established EBPs (strong evidence, NCAEP/NPDC-validated)** — highest confidence for classroom use:
- **Visual supports and visual schedules** (among NCAEP's 28 EBPs; National Standards Project: Phase 2 "established"; two systematic reviews — Koyama & Wang 2011: 23 studies; Knight et al. 2014: 31 articles; 2024 Liang et al. review: all 10 studies positive for on-task behavior) [39][40][41][43][4]
- **Antecedent-based intervention** (includes environmental modifications, seating placement, scheduling — one of VCU's Foundational Five) [4]
- **Reinforcement** and **systematic instruction** (Foundational Five; often combined with visual schedules) [4][39][40]
- **Structured/structured teaching (TEACCH)** — leverages visual strengths, organizes environment (widely used in China) [23]
- **Physical activity/exercise and movement breaks** — meta-analytic support for social skills (SMD=−0.54) and motor coordination (81.2% of RCTs beneficial); classroom-based studies show increased on-task behavior [54][55][57]; cognitive engagement is the key mechanism for attention benefits [50]

**Emerging / conditionally supported (use with individualization)**:
- **Ayres Sensory Integration (ASI) delivered by trained OTs** — strong evidence for individualized goals (Acuña 2025), positive effects on cognition and motor per Autism CRC, but inconsistent for core autism characteristics [11][13][15]
- **Flexible seating (therapy balls)** — significant in-seat behavior gains in 86.7% of students with ASD in one RCT-type study; practitioner reports positive; air cushions not supported [46][44][48][47]
- **Fidget tools** — mixed; evidence against fidget spinners generally (impaired attention/memory), but promising single-subject data for students with ADHD specifically (Aspiranti & Hulac) and parental perceptions favorable for autistic children with high sensory-seeking profiles [25][26][27][28]

**Weak or not supported (evidence does not justify routine use)**:
- **Weighted vests** — repeatedly found no effect; "not an evidence-based practice" under What Works Clearinghouse standards (Taylor et al., 2017); "red-light procedure" (Battin et al., 2020); Stephenson & Carter (2009): cannot be recommended [31][32][33][34][12]
- **Sensory diets as a standalone treatment** — one review shows null effects on general outcomes; sparse research (single case study); not recognized in DSM-V; NCAEP found no empirical studies since 2011; low-risk and helpful to some families but not established [12][13][11]
- **General SIT** — Lang et al. (2012): 56% of studies show no benefit; insufficient evidence; avoid large-scale implementation in public schools [21][33]
- **Auditory Integration Therapy** — null effects [13]
- **Air cushions (Disc 'O' Sit)** — no statistically significant effects [46]

**Emerging environmental-design evidence (moderate strength, population-level)**: classroom design accounts for 16% of variation in learning progress (Barrett/HEAD study, 3,766 pupils, 153 classrooms); lighting (natural/combination, LED over fluorescent), noise reduction (acoustic treatment, WHO 35 dB target vs. typical 50–76 dB), visual clutter reduction (curvilinear — mid-level stimulation optimal), and quiet/sensory break spaces are supported by this large-scale evidence plus ASD-specific studies (lighting dissertation showing incandescent lamp treatment effects; the Indian case study on light/color; Mallory & Keehn integrative review) [61][62][63][68][70][8][6][7][59]. Predicted effects on students with ASD specifically, while consistent with sensory-processing research (extreme sensory symptoms in ~95% of children with ASD per the Mallory & Keehn review; 60–90% of children with ASD have sensory problems), rely more heavily on the general classroom-design literature plus smaller ASD-specific studies [8][7].

**Key implementation variables across age levels**: early childhood — sensory tables/bins, quiet cozy corners, simple object/picture schedules, movement as whole-class breaks (10–25 minutes of intensive work before breaks); elementary — visual schedules with prompting and reinforcement, structured seating options, brain breaks (K–5 CASEL-aligned), classroom jobs as movement; secondary — portable/self-managed schedules (tablets, smart watches), self-selected break systems with nonverbal signals, "one person one plan" IEPs with resource-teacher case management (China), and self-advocacy built through environmental auditing with learners [40][51][52][10][37][59][35]. In Chinese mainstream classrooms (随班就读), the recommended package includes: priority seating, visual aids, resource classrooms as quiet/emotional rest spaces, peer buddy systems, shadow teacher support where available, 转衔 (transition) planning courses, and home-school communication logs [37][20][35][36][17].

**List of Queries and Tool Calls Made**

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

## 1. TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children) Model

### 1.1 Model Description and History

- TEACCH stands for "Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children." It is a structured form of visual learning specifically designed for children with autism spectrum disorder. It was developed at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill by Drs. Robert Reichler and Eric Schopler in the 1960s (developed 1966–1972) [2][4].
- TEACCH is described as one of the three most influential autism intervention methods alongside ABA and DIR/Floortime, with its core advantage being that it does not require high-level language skills or intensive one-on-one teaching—instead using environmental design and visual supports to help children with autism complete tasks independently [6].
- The method is based on the "culture of autism" concept—understanding autism as a different way of thinking—and is built on five principles: understanding the culture of autism, collaborative partnership with families (parents as co-therapists), individualization, visual structure and predictability, and a developmental perspective [4].
- TEACCH combines diagnosis, assessment, early education, school education, family education, and vocational training with the goal of promoting independent living for autistic children. It leverages the visual strengths of autistic children by organizing the educational environment and training procedures to improve comprehension, communication, perception, and motor skills [10].
- TEACCH is effective across all autism severity levels and can be tailored to individual needs, complementing other therapies like speech therapy. It applies to individuals of varying ages and skill levels, emphasizing individualized instruction. Implementation involves a multidisciplinary team including psychologists, special education teachers, speech therapists, social workers, and residential care providers. Certification is available through the TEACCH Autism Program in North Carolina, offering two levels: Practitioner and Advanced Consultant [2].
- More than 50 countries use TEACCH methods per a 2024 report from UNC's TEACCH program center [6].
- Two assessment tools are associated with the model: the Psychoeducational Profile (PEP-3) and the TEACCH Transition Assessment Profile (T-TAP, for adolescents and adults). Before receiving an individualized education plan (IEP), children undergo PEP assessment, and programs are designed based on results given the developmental delays and imbalances typical of autism [10].
- TEACCH can be combined synergistically with ABA, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and social skills interventions, with approximately 78% of school-based autism programs using TEACCH alongside other practices [4]. The Chinese source 恩启 notes "TEACCH不是ABA的替代品，而是ABA技能泛化的关键桥梁" (TEACCH is not a substitute for ABA, but a key bridge for generalization of ABA skills), addressing generalization problems often seen in ABA—many children who perform well in ABA teaching settings "cannot do it" once they leave the teaching environment [6].
- A comparison study (Khafaie, 2016) in Iran found TEACCH more effective than Sensory Integration Therapy (SIT); a study by Callahan et al. (2010) found no clear provider preference between ABA and TEACCH models; while some studies suggest ABA may be more effective, TEACCH provides comparable outcomes, especially in natural settings [1].

### 1.2 TEACCH Evidence Base

**Virues-Ortega et al. (2013) meta-analysis (Clinical Psychology Review)** [5]:
- Peer-reviewed meta-analysis published in Clinical Psychology Review (Volume 33, Issue 8, December 2013, pages 940–953, DOI: 10.1016/j.cpr.2013.07.005) by Javier Virues-Ortega, Flávia M. Julio, and Roberto Pastor-Barriuso.
- Used inverse-variance weighted random effects meta-analysis, supplemented with quality assessment, sensitivity analysis, meta-regression, and heterogeneity and publication bias tests.
- Included 13 studies involving 172 individuals with autism exposed to TEACCH.
- **Findings:** TEACCH effects on perceptual, motor, verbal, and cognitive skills were of small magnitude. Effects on adaptive behavioral repertoires (communication, activities of daily living, motor functioning) were in the negligible-to-small range. However, there were moderate to large gains in social behavior and maladaptive behavior.
- Effects were NOT moderated by intervention duration (total weeks), intensity (hours per week), or setting (home-based vs. center-based).
- Conclusion: "limited support for the TEACCH program as a comprehensive intervention for autism," with results considered exploratory due to the limited pool of studies. Cited 178 times.

**Pastor-Cerezuela (2018) review study** [1]:
- Review of 14 studies evaluating TEACCH effectiveness for children with ASD (DOI: 10.23923/PAP.PSICOL2018.2851).
- All 14 reviewed studies reported developmental improvements following TEACCH intervention; 11 of 14 demonstrated statistically significant improvements in child development metrics.
- 5 of 7 studies assessing stress found significant reductions in stress for parents and teachers.
- Interventions varied in duration from 5 sessions to 3 years; sessions ranged from 30 minutes to 7 hours per day; implemented by parents or teachers in home and/or school contexts.
- Methodological limitations identified: shortage of RCTs, small sample sizes, variability complicating generalization. Future research recommended with larger samples including ASD severity and comorbid disorders.
- A meta-analysis cited within this review (Virues-Ortega et al., 2013) found TEACCH had small effects on perceptual, motor, verbal, and cognitive skills.

**Chinese-language meta-analysis (Taiwan) — 郝佳華 & 吳裕益 (2023)** [8]:
- Title: 《結構化教學對自閉症學生認知及行為之影響的後設分析》(A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Structured Teaching on Cognition and Behavior of Students with Autism Spectrum Disorder), published in 《中華民國特殊教育學會年刊》(Journal of the Special Education Association of the Republic of China), 112年度 (2023), pages 269–298.
- Collected 103 studies from two online databases (「全國博碩士論文知識加值系統」National Digital Library of Theses and Dissertations, and 「華藝線上圖書館」Airiti Library) using keywords "結構化教學" (structured teaching), "TEACCH," and "視覺提示策略" (visual cue strategies); 14 and 89 studies respectively.
- After filtering for single-case research design with ASD students as subjects, 8 studies met criteria (7 theses, 1 from Airiti), covering 19 individual cases.
- **Key results:** 15 of the intervention effect sizes (78.95%) reached a large effect size level. Weighted average effect size (Tau-U) was .81 under both fixed-effect and random-effect models, classified as a "medium" effect size. Medium-to-large effects across educational stages and on both cognition/skills and behavior, with greater effects from longer intervention times. Insufficient evidence that the four moderator variables significantly moderate intervention effectiveness.
- Over nearly 20 years, only 8 single-case studies applying this teaching method to autism were found, indicating a lack of research. Intervention topics mostly focused on improving cognitive skills (73.68%); intervention duration was mostly 12 weeks (2–3 hours/week); only 2 studies fully used all five structured teaching elements; most researchers used visual cue strategies or teaching materials.

**Chinese doctoral dissertation (Taiwan) — 倪志琳 (1999)** [17]:
- 《結構教學法對學齡前自閉症兒童學習成效之研究》(The Effects of TEACCH Structure Teaching Strategies to the Learning Outcome of Preschool Children with Autism), doctoral dissertation, National Taiwan Normal University, Special Education Research Institute, advisors 宋維村 (Soong Wei-Tsuen) and 林幸台 (Lin Hsin-Tai), 246 pages, permanent URL: https://hdl.handle.net/11296/3sk99c; cited 60 times.
- Single-subject multiple probe design; four children from the Hong-Ai early intervention program; instruments included Chinese Child Developmental Inventory (CCDI) and PsychoEducational Profile Revised (PEP-R), supplemented by parent/teacher questionnaires and interviews.
- **Results:** (1) All four children showed overall developmental progress on CCDI and PEP-R; rate-of-change indicators exceeded 1.0, showing faster development during intervention than before; children performed better in comprehension-conceptual, situation comprehension, cognitive performance, and imitation than in expressive language and cognitive verbal areas. (2) Except for one child who did not master an imitation goal, all children achieved their individual learning goals and showed maintenance during follow-up; children with lower developmental quotients required longer teaching periods. (3) Parents reported positive effects on parenting attitudes, methods, and emotional adjustment; teachers found structure teaching beneficial. (4) The Hong-Ai early intervention program was validated against Powers' (1992) eight essential components of early intervention for autism (structured behavioral treatment, parent involvement, early initiation, intensive treatment, generalization planning, social/communication skill development, trained and supervised staff, integration with typically developing children).

**Additional evidence claims from lay/clinical sources:**

### 1.3 Core Components of Structured Teaching (TEACCH)

The four fundamental components of structured teaching [3][4][9]:

1. **Physical Structure/Environment Organization (物理环境/环境结构化):** Arranged to minimize distractions with designated areas for activities; clear boundaries, minimized distractions, designated areas (e.g., dividing spaces into study/game/rest areas); creating clear zones in the teaching environment (e.g., reading area, activity area) to help children become familiar with the classroom and provide security [3][4][6][9].

2. **Visual Schedules (视觉时间表/日程表):** Outline daily routines to help children anticipate what comes next; object, picture, written schedules, and first-then boards [3][4].

3. **Work Systems (工作系统):** Step-by-step visual and physical cues guiding children through tasks; task organization, quantity indicators, completion signals. A complete visual work system answers four questions: ①What task to do? ②How much to do? ③How do I know when it's finished? ④What to do next? (做什么任务？做多少？怎么知道做完了？做完之后做什么？) [4][6].

4. **Visual Structure of Materials/Tasks (视觉结构/视觉指令):** Cues, color-coding, and pictorial guides to enhance understanding; visual instructions, organization, clarity, and completed models [3][4].

The Chinese source ALSOLIFE describes four steps of structured teaching: (1) Arrange training spaces according to different training content, with emphasis on visual cues and special placement of toys and items; (2) Establish training schedules/programs emphasizing procedural consistency; (3) Define training content including imitation, gross and fine motor skills, perception, cognition, hand-eye coordination, language comprehension and expression, self-care, social skills, and emotional regulation; (4) Use language, body posture, cues, labels, charts, and text to enhance understanding; apply behavioral reinforcement and behavior modification to reduce abnormal behaviors [10].

The Macau 展智服務協會 (citing 協康會 Heep Hong Society) outlines five core teaching principles: (1) Individualized Education Plan (IEP); (2) Structured Teaching—structured environments and activity arrangements using picture flowcharts and labels for clear guidance and predictability; (3) Visual Prompts—pictures to help autistic children understand and express ideas and aid in planning/organization; (4) Environmental Zoning—clear zones in the teaching environment (e.g., reading area, activity area); (5) Autonomy—encouraging children to actively participate and providing appropriate choice opportunities to build confidence and independence [9].

### 1.4 TEACCH vs. ABA

恩启 compares TEACCH vs. ABA across multiple dimensions: TEACCH adapts the environment to the child while ABA requires the child to adapt to environmental demands; TEACCH uses visual supports and structured independent tasks while ABA uses discrete trial training with language instruction and reinforcement. TEACCH addresses generalization problems often seen in ABA [6].
